Is China behind a wave of AI fake videos targeting Taiwan?
- Published
Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.
A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.
The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.
The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.
Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.
But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.
Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process.
"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.
The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.
More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.
One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.
Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.
Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate.
A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment.
Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan.
The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added.
Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts.
Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said.
"Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."

South Korea lets a North Korean fisherman resettle in South and returns six others
Seoul says that one of seven North Koreans rescued off a fishing boat drifting near a South Korean island earlier this month chose to resettle in the South
SEOUL, South Korea -- Seoul said Friday that one of seven North Koreans rescued off a fishing boat drifting near a South Korean island earlier this month chose to resettle in the South.
South Korea's Unification Ministry said it let the six others return to North Korea aboard their boat across the Koreas’ eastern maritime border Friday morning.
The North Koreans were rescued by South Korea's navy and coast guard in international waters near South Korea's eastern Ulleung Island on Nov. 3.
It's not uncommon for North Korean fishing boats to be found adrift south of the Koreas' eastern and western sea boundaries. South Korea typically returns North Korean fishermen if they want to go home and are not suspected of espionage. But South Korea lets them resettle in the South if they so choose.
North Korea has yet to comment on the fisherman who opted to remain in South Korea. Pyongyang is highly sensitive about defections and often accuses Seoul of enticing its citizens to defect, something the South denies.
The two Koreas remain split along one of the world's most heavily fortified borders since the 1950-53 Korean War ended with an armistice. Citizens from the two countries are not allowed to exchange phone calls, letters and emails with each other.
More than 34,000 North Koreans have fled to South Korea for economic and political reasons since the war's end, mostly in the last three decades. Animosities between the Koreas have deepened in recent years, with North Korea terminating ties with South Korea and focusing on expanding its nuclear program.

Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
- Published
Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.
Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.
She also said Law's motives were financial.
"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.
Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for many of their battles with mental illness.
He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims.
"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."
Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.
The sentencing hearing on Friday followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.
Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.
Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

Indian cricketer Rohit Sharma recently spoke about handling pressure as a captain and the lighter side of his equation with teammates on Family Full House with Rohit Sharma. During the conversation, he revealed that Rishabh Pant is the one who teases him the most in the team.
Family Full House: Rohit Sharma reveals Rishabh Pant pulls his leg the most in the Indian team
The discussion began with contestant Gaurav asking Rohit how he manages to make quick decisions on the field, particularly when the pressure is high. Responding to the question, the cricketer said staying calm helps him assess situations and trust his instincts.
“Field par decision lene mein I think mera sabse bada strength ye raha hai ki jab maamla garam rehta hai tab main koshish karta hu ki apne aap ko thanda rakhu aur calm rakhu, toh jab main vaisa rehta hu toh mujhe decisions lene mein aasani hoti hai. Chahe woh galat ho ya sahi ho, baad mein pata chalta hai, lekin ek baar decision le liya, woh le liya,” Rohit said.
He added that he often relies on his instincts while making decisions during a match.
The conversation then moved to the camaraderie within the team. When Gaurav asked who pulls his leg the most, Rohit initially said that the younger players often tease him before naming Pant.
“Meri taang sab log hi khichte hai yaar. Ab ye jitne bhi naye ladke aaye hai, youngsters saare khichte hai, lekin sabse jyada Rishabh Pant,” he said.
Asked to share an incident, Rohit explained that even small mistakes can become a talking point among teammates. He revealed that the players often share such moments on their team WhatsApp group, allowing everyone to join in the banter.
“Team mein humara ek WhatsApp group hota hai toh uss group mein hum ye saare messages daal dete hai, toh puri team ko pata chal jata hai,” he said.
Rohit added that he does not mind being teased by his teammates, as he sees it as part of their bond. He also acknowledged that he has indulged in similar banter with others.
“Taang khichayi apne log hi karte hai, koi gair aake aapki taang khichayi nahi karega, toh mujhe bura nahi lagta jab humare teammates jitne bhi hai,” he said.
Family Full House with Rohit Sharma airs every Saturday and Sunday at 9:30 pm on Sony Entertainment Television and Sony LIV.

The robots are slowly taking over San Francisco. They're on our roads, our gyms, our coffee shops.
Not all of them are useful, however. At least not yet.
I spent 12 hours seeking out every robot service I could find that's publicly available. Some provided real utility and shocked me at how competitive their costs were compared to their human-driven counterparts. Others clearly needed to work out their kinks.
My ranking is qualitative and listed in order from worst to best. I considered how useful the robots were, how easy they were to use, how much automation is involved, and how much they cost for the consumer.
Here's how I rank the robots.
Tau Robotics' humanoids
Humanoids remain one of the more challenging technical problems for the robotics industry, and my experience with Tau Robotics' humanoid cleaning service underscored that.
For $30 an hour, a human employee from Tau Robotics will bring over two humanoids, which vacuum and mop the floors, clean the toilets, wipe down surfaces, and dust.
Cheap, for sure, but not very effective. They left the house in worse condition than it started, knocking over the trash can and a large mirror. In a few cases, the robots simply shut down.
They're also mostly teleoperated, meaning they're controlled by a remote human employee — all part of the training process, as the robots continue to gather data.
For now, the humanoids need a lot of work.
Ohlso's robot kitchen
Ohlso is a Korean food truck trying to solve the problem of cold-delivered food with a "cook-en-route" concept, in which a robot preps the meal as the truck heads to the delivery destination.
Humans are still involved in the food prep process, such as marinating the meat or vegetables, before the ingredients are loaded onto the truck. From there, the robots cook up the food.
A human also drives the truck and packs up the meals. It's a neat enough idea, but I don't know how well it works in action because the truck was parked the day I tried it.
It's hard to see whether the customer sees any cost savings from having robots instead of a human chef. I got a small serving of braised beef short ribs and a lot of rice for about $17. The meat was cooked through and tasted fine.
Aescape's robot masseuse
A company called Aescape wants to make massage sessions more accessible and less awkward, and I think it succeeds.
You book an appointment online, and then you get a massage by a pair of mechanical arms in the comfort of a private room. A 30-minute session costs $60.
That's a decent cost proposition, considering a private massage by a human can run you well over $100. And for the introverts, that could also be attractive.
The thing is, the robots need to feel good. I thought the arms applied a good amount of pressure to the body and the heated hands were a nice touch. I just wished I could control exactly where on my body the arms hit.
UBTech's robot waiter
Sometimes simple is better.
Hikari Sushi & Bar deploys one robot — UBTech's guest service bot, Cadebot — to help the kitchen deliver larger menu items to tables.
That's it. That's its sole purpose.
The robot wheels over to the table, as it plays a little jingle, delivers the food, and leaves. At least the way Hikari configured it, the robot does not interact with the customer. And honestly, that's fine with me.
Artly's barista bots
The coffee at Artly cafe at Pier 30 wasn't notable, but the barista bots do draw latte art in the shape of a rose or a heart better than most of us ever will.
My cappuccino was $6.79 — a little disappointing, since a similar-quality drink at Starbucks would run me under $5.
Part of the premise of robot labor should be that services are cheaper, right? At least with Artly, there was less pressure to tip.
Matic Robot's vacuum
Matic's robot vacuum is a friendly little home helper. It stands about eight inches tall and is much quieter than a typical manual vacuum.
The company appears to have thought about the user experience with Apple-like precision from the moment you unbox the machine, making it easy to learn how to use.
After the robot does a 3D scan of your home, it's mostly hands-off from there, aside from replacing the vacuum bag or refilling the water tank. It also functions as a mop. The app allows you to schedule cleanups and choose which rooms to vacuum.
It doesn't replace manual cleaning. The Matic isn't always strong enough to pick up every stain, and the robot's shape can pose a barrier in some trickier crevices and corners of the home.
It's also a pricey piece of homeware: $1,500. A top-line vacuum that's much stronger could run you $500.
Waymo's robotaxis
I solely relied on Waymo's driverless ride-hailing service to get to my destinations. And the fact that I was able to rely on it gives Waymo the top spot.
Hailing a Waymo is as simple as hailing any ride-hailing service: You open an app and set a destination. And, to my surprise, most rides were cheaper than Uber. I hailed seven rides and spent $124.69 in total, for an average price of $17.81 per ride.
The autonomous driver isn't perfect. There were moments during my ride when the robotaxi felt stiff or jerked, as if it were tapping the brakes. Overall, I did get to all my destinations safely.

An accused wanted in multiple cases in West Bengal’s Asansol, was on Friday (November 27, 2026) shot in his right leg during an alleged clash leading to an exchange of fire with the police when they went to arrest him on Friday morning. The accused, Pratap Das, is wanted in several cases of robbery, theft, iron smuggling, and cyber fraud across Asansol. Police have been searching for him for the past few days in connection with a cyber fraud case lodged last week at Asansol South Police Station. When the police went to arrest him on Friday (November 27, 2026) from a hideout in the Ismail area, he opened fire at the police team. Later, he was shot in retaliatory fire.
Also read | In latest ‘encounter’, West Bengal police kill a man accused of shooting at a constable two days ago
According to the police, an operation to arrest Pratap was launched on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) when he again opened fire at the police team upon spotting them and managed to flee.
The operation was launched by the Asansol Durgapur Police Commissionerate Special Operations Group (SOG), along with officers from Hirapur police station, following a tip-off that he was hiding in the area and carrying a firearm. The dramatic operation unfolded in the congested neighbourhood, with armed police personnel in plain clothes searching narrow lanes and houses, and climbing boundary walls to trace the accused.
Shots of firing were heard in broad daylight causing panic among residents who witnessed a cat and mouse chase between the accused and police. The accused was seen being dragged from one of the houses out by the police with blood dripping from his right leg and was carried on all fours to a police vehicle.
Local residents in the area said that they had no idea about the accused. “We did not know that he was hiding in our neighbourhood. I went to drop my daughter off at school when I saw police chasing him. It was scary,” said a woman who stays in the area from where Pratap was arrested.
Association for Protection of Democratic Reforms, a civil rights group raised questions about the manner in which police paraded in groups with weapons. “Instead of relying on intelligence inputs, a scientific approach, and proper procedures to apprehend the criminal, the police’s actual objective was to intimidate the general public through a display of firepower,” APDR vice president Ranajit Sur said.
The development comes after a total of five encounters that took place in West Bengal since the new Bharatiya Janata Party government came to power. Five people who have been shot dead by the police during these incidents include three accused in rape cases of minors and two accused of murder.

Decline of deities - the long game the All Blacks cannot afford to lose
- Published
For decades, the All Blacks have defied gravity.
Despite a population, player pool and bank balance smaller than most of their rivals, New Zealand's rugby team have become sporting shorthand for success.
Deservedly so. No other team comes close to them.
England beat the All Blacks this year and last. They play them again on Saturday aiming for a hat-trick.
But, England would need that winning streak to continue until around 2050 just to level up a lop-sided historical head-to-head.
New Zealand have won 36 times to England's 10 in their 121-year rivalry.
For every other nation in Test rugby, the story is the same. New Zealand have the superior record against them all.
A section on the All Blacks' website, titled Rivalries,, external opens by listing South Africa's 40% winning record in their meetings. And the numbers only drop from there.
But New Zealand's grip on the global game appears looser now than ever.
If they lose to England on Saturday, it may not much sway the historical balance between the two teams.
But it would be a sixth defeat in a calendar year, a total matched only once before in the All Blacks past, back in 1949 when a split squad played two Test series in Australia and apartheid South Africa at the same time.
New Zealand's win percentage in 2026 is 58.3%, their third lowest for any year since the start of professionalism.
This campaign, marked by an exhausting schedule and four Tests away to the world champion Springboks, is in keeping with a recent trend.
Since the end of the 2010s - a period in which an all-time great team captured back-to-back world titles - New Zealand have come off the boil.
The 2020s are on course to be their least successful decade since the 1970s.
This current crop of All Blacks are suffering not just by comparison to the previous generation, but when set against every other modern predecessor.
One reason may be a source of strength turning against them.
The All Blacks' culture of promoting within and establishing coaching dynasties was seen as key when they were winning.
A thread ran through the Graham Henry, Steve Hansen and Ian Foster succession in the 2010s glory days. The latter two served under their predecessor and the first two earned their Test stripes with Wales, before taking the top job.
All were schooled as coaches in New Zealand and steeped in the country's rugby traditions.
The in-house production line of leaders ensured continuity and protected a team ethos that has been admired and written about everywhere.
But, in a modern world in which opposition tactics are quickly picked apart and best practice spreads fast, has adherence to tradition held back the team?
New Zealand's rivals have all hired coaching talent from outside.
Rassie Erasmus, South African to the core, may front the Springbok coaching operation, but behind him Irishmen Jerry Flannery and Felix Jones and Tony Brown, a former All Black himself, bring specialist knowledge to different areas.
France, famously patriotic in their hiring, benefited from Englishman Shaun Edwards and South African Vlok Cilliers' work behind the scenes in recent years.
England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales all have or have had head coaches from other countries.
Dave Rennie, who has coached Australia, Glasgow Warriors and Japanese side Kobe Steelers previously, became the first person of Pasifika heritage to lead the All Blacks when he took on the job in March.
He has brought a Scottish contingent to mix up his backroom, with attack coach Mike Blair the most high-profile.
But his regime is still only eight months old. Other issues predate it.

Most pressing is the balance sheet.
New Zealand Rugby is leaking millions. A failure to balance the books means it has built-in annual losses of about NZ$20m (£8.35m), and is projected to lose NZ$66m (£27.6m) between 2027 and 2031., external
The All Black brand is valuable. It has been licensed to sell watches, healthcare and information technology.
The team are still a powerful global draw.
They are among the keenest Test nations to play matches overseas, where they can fill stadiums bigger than Auckland's 50,000-capacity Eden Park and make more money.
A globe-trotting 2026 itinerary has filled coffers, but emptied players.
Still though costs are rising faster than their income.
In turn, that is compromising the All Blacks' ability to keep their centrally contracted stars at home.
As in England, playing for a domestic team is a requirement to play internationally.
Thirty-five-year-old playmaker Beauden Barrett's proposed move to Bristol Bears and out of eligibility at the end of the 2027 Rugby World Cup attracted headlines, but New Zealand are more concerned by other departures.
Back-row star Wallace Sititi, 24, is rumoured to have agreed a move to Stade Francais, while Luke Jacobson, 29, has already announced his own switch to fellow French side Bayonne.
"What bothers us is when All Blacks or highly prospective All Blacks leave in their sort of mid-20s," said New Zealand Rugby chairman and World Cup-winning captain David Kirk this week., external
"When they want to go away for two or three years or something like that in their mid-20s, possibly come back, but possibly not come back. That's a problem for us.
"We're not ever going to win on the money. We just don't have the money to compete with Japan and France, who are the two big payers.
"So we have to compete on the desire to play for the All Blacks and to have a career that's memorable representing New Zealand. And most of the time that's absolutely fine.
"That's why the few people leaving become a bit of a cause célèbre - because not many do."
Richie Mo'unga is one of them.
He was New Zealand's first-choice fly-half at the last World Cup and arguably the best in the position in the world.
He spent three years in Japanese club rugby and international exile afterwards, and has yet to fully find his feet on his return.

New Zealand have the talent to cope. Ruben Love is a coming force at 10. Many of their stars will time stints overseas around World Cups. But it robs them of options and makes cohesion and succession trickier.
Sabbaticals – approved overseas stints which allow players to take up short, lucrative stints at overseas clubs and remain available for the All Blacks – have been a compromise.
Ardie Savea, talismanic All Blacks captain, has been playing in Japan on one this season.
But, overseas clubs hungry for Kiwi talent on a longer-term basis are circling.
There is another angle to the issue that cuts against the All Blacks.
Those who do stay and remain eligible are competing in a weakened Super Rugby tournament.
South African sides left in 2020, throwing their lot in with the United Rugby Championship and the European club scene.
With only Australian sides and the Fijian Drua to compete against, Kiwi provincial sides' fixture lists are a significant step down from international rugby.
It is far from ideal preparation for the Test arena.
Then add in the cross-code lure.
New Zealand Warriors, the Auckland-based NRL side, offer a convenient and potentially lucrative route into the 13-man game for young rugby talent.
After taking a hit during Covid, grassroots rugby league numbers have ticked upwards., external Rugby union's equivalent numbers have been propped up by a rise in women's participation.
For the all-conquering All Blacks, suddenly the problems are stacking up.
Win or lose against England, they and New Zealand Rugby know they are playing a longer game. One they cannot afford to lose.

Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) leader Ashutosh Ranka on Friday warned political parties against changing their stance on the proposed delimitation exercise ahead of a special Parliament session, alleging that the Centre was using women's reservation in an attempt to manipulate electoral boundaries.
In a social media post, Ranka said that the country would closely watch the proceedings of the special Parliament session, which will commence on November 30. He alleged that the proposed delimitation exercise could disproportionately increase parliamentary representation in states that had lagged in population control.
Ranka wrote, "The nation will be closely watching the Parliament proceedings on this Nov 30th. Under the garb of the women reservation bill, which everyone should support, the govt wants to manipulate electoral boundaries, disproportionately increase seats in states which have lagged behind in population control."
He added, "While BJP has had its stand clear on both the issues, what the country should watch out for are those parties and politicians who will be switching sides, for either they would have been paid off, or have lost spine completely. Betrayal of people’s mandate won’t be forgiven this time."
While the CJP activist maintained that the women's reservation issue deserved support across political parties, he alleged that the Centre was using the legislation as a pretext to push the Delimitation Bill, ANI reported.
His remarks come amid an intensifying political debate over the proposed delimitation exercise and the implementation of the women's reservation law ahead of the reconvened Parliament session.
On Thursday, the Lok Sabha Secretariat announced that the second part of the Eighth Session of the 18th Lok Sabha would begin on November 30 (Monday) and was expected to conclude on December 3 (Thursday), subject to the exigencies of government business.
Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Kiren Rijiju said the Centre had requested the Lok Sabha Speaker and the Rajya Sabha Chairman to reconvene the Lower House on November 30 and the Upper House on December 2, respectively, to take up key government business.
The announcement has further fuelled speculation about the possibility of the Delimitation Bill and the Women's Reservation Bill being taken up during the sittings. However, the government has not clarified which Bills will be considered.
Parliament last convened during the Monsoon Session, which ended on August 13, with both Houses being adjourned sine die. The proposed Delimitation Bill seeks to increase the total strength of the Lok Sabha to 850 seats.
While the ruling National Democratic Alliance (NDA), led by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), has maintained that the proposed delimitation exercise is a constitutional necessity to reflect new census data and facilitate the implementation of 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha, the INDIA bloc, led by the Congress, has demanded the immediate implementation of the women's reservation law and opposed linking it to the delimitation exercise.
The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, was first introduced in the Lok Sabha on April 16. It seeks to increase the strength of the Lower House to 850 seats and facilitate the implementation of the Women's Reservation Bill, passed in 2023.
However, the Bill failed to secure the constitutionally required special two-thirds majority of members present and voting in Parliament and was consequently not passed.
(with ANI inputs)

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The Bhopal crime branch police arrested a 26-year-old man with 3.10 grams of mephedrone (MD), an illegal narcotic drug, during a raid in MP Nagar Zone-1, said crime branch police on Friday. According to police, the action was taken following a tip-off that a man carrying MD was waiting for a customer on an open ground behind Shiva Temple, opposite LIC office in MP Nagar Zone-1. The suspect was allegedly waiting for a customer to sell the contraband when police caught him.
Acting on the information, a team surrounded the suspect and recovered a transparent plastic pouch containing 3.10 grams of a white crystal-like substance, identified as MD, from the front-left pocket of his jeans. The suspect was identified as Monis Qureshi (26), a resident of Jahangirabad. He reportedly told investigators that he had procured the drug from Ujjain.
Police have seized his mobile phone and are examining call detail records and WhatsApp conversations to establish his contacts and identify the source of the contraband and potential buyers. A case has been registered against Qureshi at the crime branch police station under sections of Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act. Further investigation is underway to trace other people involved in the alleged drug trafficking network.

For more than a decade, my colleagues and I at the Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology have tracked every experimental medicine that enters human testing anywhere in the world. Last December, I wrote in STAT that China had reached parity with the United States in terms of the absolute number of new drugs introduced into clinical trials each year. Starting in 2018, the rate of U.S. contributions began to stagnate. Meanwhile, in 2013, Chinese organizations had introduced about 30 new experimental drugs. A decade later, the number topped 400. And there is no reason to expect the momentum in either country is changing.
Over the past month, both governments have seemingly been moving to wall themselves off. On Oct. 16, Beijing proposed barring foreign acquisition of its companies’ proprietary cell and gene platforms. Within a week, the U.S. Department of the Treasury proposed restrictions that would bar Americans from taking equity stakes, forming joint ventures, or making limited-partner investments in Chinese biotech companies and their equipment suppliers.
The proposals from Beijing and Washington do not impact licensing. American drugmakers can keep licensing Chinese molecules, and Chinese companies may develop new medicines to sell to the U.S. and European companies.
That open door matters more than either wall. Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several. Restricting investment will not help America win the races it is already losing. The bigger threat to U.S. leadership is not Chinese capital. It is the erosion, at home, of the research enterprise that built America’s lead.
The Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology’s newest analysis, published in September in Drug Discovery Today, emphasizes the importance of these continued engagements. My colleagues and I evaluated the 17,000 new drugs that first entered human trials between 2000 and 2024, separating them into eight different modalities. These ranged from conventional pills to gene therapies. The convergence in the numbers of overall active ingredients that we reported last year turned out to be anything but uniform when looking at the details.
The growth by China was concentrated in a key subset of biologics. By the late 2010s, Chinese sponsors often had introduced more, and more novel, cell therapies annually than American sponsors. By the early 2020s, China had matched or exceeded the U.S. in the introduction of new monoclonal antibodies, a commercially important class of biologic drugs. China took a commanding lead in certain categories of monoclonals, such as multispecific antibodies and drug conjugates.
The U.S. still holds a larger share in two categories: nucleic acid drugs and gene therapy. Dominance in both technologies reflects tools built over decades of Western public and private investment. Examples include lipid nanoparticles that conveyed SARS-CoV2 vaccines, viral vectors, and CRISPR gene editing.
Those differences help explain why the two governments are building different walls. Beijing’s proposal shields cell and gene therapy from outside entities, areas where they have a demonstrated or aspirational determination to lead the world. Platforms must remain domiciled in China while individual products can be marketed abroad. That is a coherent industrial strategy, and it is paying off well. Chinese financial regulators report that foreign deals for Chinese biotech assets reached $120 billion through August 2026, up more than a third from the year before.
Washington’s proposal works differently. The Treasury Department proposal prevents American investors from punting on a piece of Chinese biotech and yet still allows American companies to pay for Chinese molecules. In areas where China now leads, the combined effect would seem at best to be a division of labor. As my co-author and I pointed out in our earlier STAT article, China increasingly invents and owns while American firms are more prone to take licenses, complete late stage development, and pay royalties.
To be fair, biotechnology raises real national security questions, from genomic privacy to research that could be misused for nefarious purposes. Imposed limits on capital flows are a legitimate tool. I am certainly not arguing that U.S. investors should fund Chinese state-linked companies without scrutiny. Nor do our data indicate that all Chinese products are comparable in terms of quality or originality. Higher counts may overstate the number of genuine breakthroughs.
Nonetheless, a decision to cut off scientific and/or economic engagement would seem detrimental to both nations.
Restriction is a defensive move. It does not put a single new medicine into the clinic. It treats “biotech” — which comprises drugs, devices, diagnostics, ag-tech, and many other areas — as one thing. Each of these competitive races is being run at different speeds and with entirely different players, outcomes, and pole positions.
The fundamental problem is the one described in our December 2025 article. American output of new experimental drugs has been flat since 2018. In our earlier study, China’s public sector, including universities and state-linked enterprises, contributed more than twice as many new drugs in 2024 as their American counterparts. All the while, the U.S. universities that built our lead in nucleic acids and gene therapy face shrinking federal research support as has been highlighted by STAT.
A competitor lacking fuel will lose the race even if regulators try to slow the opposition.
Three steps would accomplish more than walls ever can.
First, subject matter experts should take advantage of the public comment period the Treasury Department has opened through Dec. 7.
Those comments should press Treasury on several points. If it does impose restrictions, and it is not obvious that it should, they should be aimed narrowly at transfers of platforms and capabilities rather than at all investment. More clarity is also needed to address “NewCo” deals, in which a Chinese licensor takes a stake in a new U.S. company. Importantly, the regulator should set a date and objective criteria to review whether any new rules are working as intended.
Second, policymakers should prioritize and incentivize investment in areas where America leads or could lead. Nucleic acid and gene therapies depend on academic discovery and specialized manufacturing. Stable funding for proven models such as translational research by the National Institutes of Health, ARPA-H, and domestic manufacturing is the most obvious and reliable way to protect a declining margin. In cell therapy, policymakers should ask candidly why so many early trials now start in China (regulation, investment, technology, or combinations thereof), and how we might alleviate domestic hurdles.
Third, Washington should measure the race in a more nuanced way, such as by drug or disease type. The totals of new experimental drugs, such as those we have previously emphasized, can hide more meaningful long-term outcomes, such as FDA approvals as well as market and public health improvements. Federal agencies could start by tracking first-in-human trials by drug type and sponsor country. As this will take time, it should become a long-term indicator, ignoring annual variations. Policy aimed at the aggregate and/or based solely on short term measures will miss key details.
Walls are what you construct when you think you are under attack or are losing. In the technologies that will define the next generation of medicines, from RNA drugs to gene editing, American institutions still lead. The biggest threat does not come from abroad but from changes in domestic policy, such as cutting biomedical research. Our current lead in these fields was built with reliable investments by the public and private sectors, not barriers.
Michael S. Kinch is a professor of pharmacology at Stony Brook University and the author of six books on pharmaceutical innovation.

UN peacekeepers are preparing to leave southern Lebanon. There’s no plan for what comes next
The U.N. peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon is preparing to end a 50-year mission as tensions between Israel and Hezbollah remain high
NAQOURA, Lebanon -- Among the few buildings still standing in the Lebanese border town of Naqoura are an abandoned hotel occupied by Israeli soldiers, its walls draped with anti-drone netting, and the compound housing the headquarters of the U.N. peacekeeping force.
The roads passing through the once-idyllic seaside town, now largely reduced to rubble, are empty except for the occasional military patrol or convoy of peacekeepers escorting civilians or supplies.
The end of the nearly 50-year mandate of the UNIFIL peacekeeping force is looming in just over a month, and still there is no plan for what comes after it.
The peacekeepers' impending exit, in parallel with an ongoing occupation by Israeli forces and a debate over the disarmament of the Hezbollah militant group, leaves the future of southern Lebanon in limbo.
Lebanon wants the U.N. force to stay. But the U.N. Security Council voted last year to terminate UNIFIL’s mandate at the end of 2026, bowing to demands from the United States and its close ally Israel.
Israel says the mission was a failure, citing Hezbollah’s military buildup over the years. The peacekeepers say they helped preserve calm for 17 years before Hamas’ 2023 attack on southern Israel ignited a regional conflict.
“My mandate is not to disarm Hezbollah,” UNIFIL’s commander, Maj. Gen. Diodato Abagnara, told The Associated Press in an interview. “My mandate is to support the Lebanese Armed Forces, to create the best conditions for the Lebanese Armed Forces to take full control here in the south. It’s not to fight against Hezbollah.”
UNIFIL is set to begin a gradual drawdown of its 7,500 peacekeepers on Jan. 1. Whatever comes after that, he said, “It’s very important to avoid a security vacuum in the south.”
UNIFIL wasn’t able to stop Hezbollah from launching missiles or Israel from carrying out airstrikes in two recent wars. But many residents of southern Lebanon say they still feel safer with its presence.
Mohammed Aoun was late to start harvesting his olive groves this year in the village of Halta, just outside of the Israeli-occupied area. On the first day of harvest earlier this month, as a UNIFIL patrol stopped at the orchard, an Israeli drone was buzzing overhead. The thud of a distant airstrike echoed through the valley.
Aoun said he was hesitant to start picking, but he had already lost out on the previous two years’ harvests. He is apprehensive about the impending departure of UNIFIL forces.
“Of course we feel more secure when we see patrols coming and going; it’s a sort of protection,” he said. “Their presence is important with regards to the security situation. We don’t know what will happen after they leave.”
The U.N. Interim Force in Lebanon was created in 1978 after Israel invaded southern Lebanon to fight Palestinian militants. Israel invaded again in 1982 and didn't withdraw until 2000. During that period, Hezbollah, backed by Iran, emerged as a guerrilla force.
After a monthlong war between Israel and Hezbollah in 2006, UNIFIL was tasked with monitoring violations of U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, which ended the fighting. When a ceasefire ended another Israel-Hezbollah war in 2024, UNIFIL was part of the mechanism overseeing its implementation.
The Lebanese army was to take over security in southern Lebanon after the U.N. force's exit.
But then another war broke out between Israel and Hezbollah in March, linked to the wider Iran war. Israel now occupies large swaths of southern Lebanon, where its soldiers have emptied and demolished dozens of villages.
About 11,000 people remain in a handful of mostly Christian villages in the occupied area, Abagnara said. They depend on UNIFIL to escort the convoys that keep them connected with the rest of the country.
An agreement between Lebanon and Israel for Israeli forces to withdraw in exchange for the disarmament of Hezbollah has floundered, and negotiations between the two countries have stalled.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said in a statement Wednesday that “Israel continues to engage in hostile acts in the south” and his government and France — a Security Council member with close ties to Lebanon — both want an extension of UNIFIL's mandate. Any alternative force should continue to operate under the 1701 framework, with some possible amendments, he said.
U.S. officials have expressed willingness for some sort of international force to remain, but not in its current form. They have suggested that it could be a civilian force or private defense contractor.
Israel wants its military to coordinate directly with the Lebanese army to remove what remains of Hezbollah’s weapons.
Israel’s ambassador to the U.N., Danny Danon, said earlier this month that Hezbollah had "exploited UNIFIL’s presence."
“We do not rely on any international force," he said. "We trust only our own soldiers.”
Lebanon opposes the idea of a civilian contractor and has rejected direct military coordination with Israel.
France is working on a Security Council resolution that would authorize a new international force, a U.N. diplomat said. A Western diplomat said there are also discussions of slowing down UNIFIL's withdrawal and maintaining certain missions to avoid a “power vacuum.”
They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly.
In January, the Lebanese army announced that it had finished removing Hezbollah weapons caches from the border area south of the Litani River.
Hezbollah did not actively oppose the effort but has refused to give up its weapons elsewhere in the country and threatened to fight any attempt to forcibly disarm it.
The Lebanese army has been cautious about any move that might provoke a civil conflict. A Lebanese security official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, said the army’s current policy is to stop weapons shipments from moving around the country — a change from the past, when Hezbollah freely transported arms — but not to raid the militant group’s storage sites.
Hezbollah supporters in the past accused UNIFIL of spying for Israel and sometimes attacked peacekeepers. Now the group says it would accept UNIFIL or another U.N.-mandated force, but not a private security contractor or a force seen as supporting Israel's occupation.
