The Delhi High Court (HC) has refused to grant TikTok an interim injunction in its dispute with a Ludhiana-based businessman over the use and registration of the ‘TIKTOK’ mark, citing the company’s failure to disclose that its application had been blocked in India since June 2020. However, the court has restrained the businessman, Sandeep Singh, from using or relying on a copyright registration for an artistic work featuring the mark until the final disposal of the case. In its November 26 order, Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav said TikTok had not approached the court with clean hands by omitting the blocking order from its petition. The court held that the company had failed to establish the requirements of balance of convenience and irreparable injury necessary for an interim injunction. The court also directed the Copyright and Trade Marks Registries to record that the registration and the related search certificate were subject to the pending proceedings and its order. TikTok, part of the ByteDance group, approached the Delhi High Court under Section 50 of the Copyright Act, 1957, seeking the removal of a copyright registration obtained by Singh for an artistic work titled ‘TIKTOK’. It also sought the revocation of a corresponding search certificate issued by the Trade Marks Registry. According to the petition, TikTok was launched in India in 2017, and its predecessor, ByteDance, had adopted the marks ‘TikTok’, ‘TIK TOK’ and ‘TIKTOK’. These marks, along with the associated goodwill and rights to pursue infringement claims, were assigned to TikTok through a deed of assignment dated July 27, 2023. Singh operates Ralco International in Ludhiana and manufactures and sells industrial and domestic sewing machines, bag closer machines, overlock machines and related products. He applied for registration of the word mark ‘TIKTOK’ in 2019 and subsequently obtained a copyright registration for an artistic work featuring the ‘TIKTOK’ mark in 2024. The work was recorded as having been first published in 2019. Why The Court Denied TikTok Interim Relief A key factor in the court's decision was TikTok's failure to disclose that its application had been blocked in India. The government blocked TikTok in June 2020 under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, citing concerns relating to India's sovereignty and integrity, defence, security of the State and public order. The court noted that TikTok's petition, filed in 2024, did not mention the blocking directions. Instead, the company had claimed continuous use of its trademarks in India. It held that the blocking was a material fact because it affected whether TikTok could use its mark in India, where the balance of convenience lay and whether the company would suffer irreparable injury if interim relief was denied. The court clarified that the blocking directions did not take away TikTok's ownership of its registered trademarks or its right to seek rectification of the Copyright Register. However, the company was not offering its application or other services under the mark in India while the directions remained in force. It consequently found that TikTok had not demonstrated that refusing an injunction would cause irreparable injury. The company was also held to have failed to approach the court with clean hands by withholding a material fact that was within its knowledge. While TikTok's request for an interim injunction was rejected, the court said the questionable copyright registration should not be used to support Singh's claims while the main dispute remains pending. It directed Singh and those acting on his behalf not to use or rely on the copyright registration or the related search certificate in any manner, including on product labels, packaging, invoices, websites, online listings or proceedings before courts and other authorities. Singh has also been restrained from claiming ownership of the artistic work on the basis of the registration or creating third-party rights through an assignment or licence. The court clarified that these directions were issued to maintain the integrity of the Copyright Register and did not amount to granting an injunction in TikTok's favour. It also directed the Copyright and Trade Marks Registries to record that the registration and search certificate were subject to the pending proceedings and the November 26 order. The court made clear that its order does not permit TikTok to resume operations or offer services under its mark in India. The government's blocking directions under Section 69A of the IT Act will continue to operate. Meanwhile, the pending trademark opposition against Singh's Class 7 application will be decided independently by the Registrar of Trade Marks. The court's observations on the merits are prima facie and will not determine the final outcome of the copyright rectification petition.

Man City owners should be forced to sell, say rival club chiefs
- Published
Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell up as punishment for breaking financial rules, senior figures at Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport.
This week, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) David Kogan claimed he has the "stomach" to take action against City, who deny wrongdoing and have appealed.
The IFR has the power to remove directors of a club if they are deemed unsuitable, and even force a sale in the most serious cases.
Now, executives at three top-flight rivals have told the BBC that they believe this is the appropriate punishment for City, who were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018, and failing to co-operate with an investigation.
- Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if Man City sponsors sue 
  - Published19 November
- Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City 
  - Published6 October
The independent commission has yet to decide on a sanction that could range from a fine, to a points deduction, the stripping of past titles, or even expulsion from the league.
But speaking on condition of anonymity, one executive claimed they are among a group of clubs who feel that City's punishment will be irrelevant unless the owners are also forced to sell. They added that anything less will make them question why they are funding the regulator through a levy.
In comments that reveal the level of anger felt by some of City's rivals, another claimed the rule breaches had undermined the league's credibility, and that they would not be able to draw a line under the scandal and move on if the owners were allowed to stay. The club were found guilty of inflating revenues and disguising losses by £900m through "sham" commercial arrangements.
Manchester City's owners are Abu Dhabi United Group - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour.
The executive who spoke anonymously said that clubs had been asked by the Premier League to refrain from publicly revealing their views on sanctions, and let the process run its course, although some are said to have privately made their opinions clear to IFR officials. They acknowledged that some clubs were less opinionated about a punishment.
Other clubs the BBC approached declined to comment, or said they were willing for the independent commission panel and IFR to reach their own conclusions following the publication of the commission's ruling in September.
But the fact that some clubs want the unprecedented sanction of a forced sale will put pressure on Kogan to mete out the harshest penalty possible in what is being seen as a defining test of the watchdog just over a year after it was established.
It also comes amid mounting questions over whether wider UAE trade and investment in UK projects could be impacted by such a move. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club, adding that "they have been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester".
When approached, the IFR declined to comment. But Kogan has consistently said that the IFR will not be influenced by any political pressure.
Earlier this week he told a parliamentary committee that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate City's hierarchy and take action, depending on the outcome of the appeal.
"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," Kogan said.
"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.
"But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so... assuming those circumstances are triggered, if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?"
When asked how any potential legal battles with Manchester City would be paid for, IFR chief executive Richard Monks told MPs that a litigation reserve of £2m was to be built up over the next two years via the levy charged to clubs, which would be paid back if litigation was successful.
"Now clearly - and I'm not talking about a specific case - clearly, there could be a very large legal case of any particular club that would require us to spend more than £2m in terms of litigation costs and barrister costs in particular", Monks added. "So if that happens, we have agreed with government [that it] will effectively lend us the money in terms of cash flow.
"We'd expect to win that litigation, to claim costs and repay government. If we failed in that massive litigation, then ultimately it would be added to the levy and we'd repay government that way."
Last month it was revealed that the IFR would cost clubs in the top five divisions of English men's football £20.3m annually.
Last week, Premier League clubs voted to cover legal expenses for its five board directors if any of City's sponsors sued them. Two UAE-based commercial partners - Etihad and Etisalat - have both said they are considering legal action against the Premier League.
The IFR has the authority to force a sale within section 34 of the Football Governance Act which allows it to investigate whether an owner meets the required suitability standards around honest, integrity and financial soundness. If an owner fails this assessment, the regulator can direct them to take reasonable steps to relinquish ownership within a specified period before issuing an ownership removal order.
City have been approached for comment. The club previously said that the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe", adding that they filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions".

North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
- Published
North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close, in a row over sanctions.
It followed Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp in the eastern city of Wonsan, which is attended by Russian and Chinese children among other nationalities.
The camp has been accused of involvement in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
North Korea's state-run news agency KCNA called the sanctions "a blatant hostile act".
Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.
Confirming the expulsion, KCNA said: "The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours."
The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.
Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.
Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997. It was closed during the pandemic and remained shut for six years.
Switzerland's department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".
It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."
Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.
In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

Hackers reportedly infiltrated the Air Force's cloud systems
The breach was discovered within the last month during system upgrade work, according to Reuters.
Another day, another notable security incident. Hackers are said to have gained access to Cloud One, the Air Force's cloud computing infrastructure. It's not clear who the hackers were and what data they may have obtained, according to Reuters, which first reported the news.
One person familiar with the matter said the hackers exploited a vulnerability to access what's known as the control plane. They compared this to "a universal remote," that could potentially allow someone "to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts." However, it's not clear if the hackers actually did this.
The breach was discovered during system upgrade work within the last month or so, Reuters said. The emergence of the issue has put certain projects on hold, including an effort to shift more mission apps to Cloud One. Some users' admin rights were reportedly revoked and updates to applications that are already running on Cloud One were prohibited, stopping staff from applying various fixes.
The Air Force said it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities." Cyber Command, the military's cyberwarfare division, is said to have been brought in to review the situation.
Cloud One was established in 2017 and it's powered by Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Microsoft Azure. The platform was designed to be a central hub for all of the Air Force's IT needs, including everything from payroll and personnel data to the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System. This tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 Air Force locations worldwide. One of Reuters' sources said "A breach here is a big deal."
Other government agencies have been hit with cyberattacks in recent weeks, including the FBI and USDA. Reported breaches at the CIA and other spy agencies exposed some classified information. Various issues have impacted other agencies this month, such as the National Security Agency's internal communications systems going down and the FAA invoking an hours-long, nationwide ground stop due to a malfunctioning router.

The future of the notwithstanding clause is now up to political leaders
Top court declined to put limits on the override clause. That's not the end of the story
Two weeks after he pieced together the "kitchen accord," Jean Chrétien stood in the House of Commons as justice minister to present a new constitutional resolution, including a Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
In his remarks on that momentous occasion, Chrétien made a specific effort to defend the presence in the Charter of an "override" clause.
"The effect of this provision is, first, that it will be politically very difficult for a government to introduce without very good reason a measure which applies notwithstanding the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in the Constitution," he said on the afternoon of Nov. 20, 1981.
- Supreme Court of Canada rules Quebec's secularism law is constitutionally valid
- Advocate ready to continue fight as Sask. school pronoun policy heads to Supreme Court
- FRONT BURNER Supreme Court to rule on minority rights debate
Chrétien quoted a prominent lawyer — Alan Borovoy, the general counsel for the Canadian Civil Liberties Association — who said the notwithstanding clause would be a "red flag for opposition parties and the press."
"This will make it politically difficult for a government to override the Charter," Chrétien quoted Borovoy as saying. "Political difficulty is a reasonable safeguard for the Charter."
Forty-five years and one week later, amid growing concern that the clause is now being invoked too easily and too casually by governments and legislatures to pass laws that would otherwise be found to violate the rights of Canadians, the Supreme Court of Canada delivered a landmark ruling on the political compromise of 1981.
The court upheld the Quebec legislature's use of the clause in the case of Bill 21 and it did not find that there should be new limits on how the clause can be used. A majority of justices did find that the invocation of the clause does not prevent a court from publicly declaring that the rights of Canadians are being violated — a measure that may, in future, make it somewhat harder for governments to do so.
But the larger task of governing the use of the notwithstanding clause has been left to the players in the political arena. If the notwithstanding clause is to become politically difficult again, it will be up to political actors.
'The courts have a crucial role to play'
The question of whether courts might provide "declaratory relief" — a judicial declaration on whether rights have been unreasonably infringed, but without invalidating the law in question — even after the notwithstanding clause has been invoked had split the governments that filed arguments with the Supreme Court.
The federal government as well as the governments of Manitoba and British Columbia thought it permissible and potentially useful. Ontario, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec were opposed (Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon reiterated his province's opposition to declaratory relief on Friday).
The seven justices of the Supreme Court were also split, but with the majority in favour.
"The five-year expiry period set out in [the notwithstanding clause], which corresponds to the maximum duration of the House of Commons or a legislative assembly under s. 4 of the Charter, is clearly intended to place in the hands of the electorate the choice of whether to renew the override provision," Justice Nicholas Kasirer wrote in Friday's ruling.
"Furthermore, the court's opinion is useful for the public, particularly where a vulnerable minority is affected by an overriding statute."
Justices Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O'Bonsawin concurred that, "courts have a crucial role to play in dialogue between the legislatures and electorate by informing both of the scope of a Charter right and whether and to what extent it is infringed by a statute that invokes the notwithstanding clause."
That courts can offer comment even after the notwithstanding clause has been invoked also goes some way toward answering concerns about recent "pre-emptive" uses of the clause — when governments invoke the clause even before a court has had a chance to pass judgment on the law.
"The court confirmed that Canadians have the right to know when their Charter rights have been unjustifiably infringed when the notwithstanding clause has been invoked," Sean Fraser, the federal justice minister, said in a statement on Friday. "This is an important part of ensuring transparency, accountability and a healthy democracy."
That may be of limited solace to those whose rights are in question. But it points back to the political arena.
The price of liberty?
Even if one disagrees with all previous uses of the clause there might still be a case for what Chrétien called a "safety valve" (one of those who pushed for the clause was Allan Blakeney, the NDP premier of Saskatchewan). And even critics of the clause might need to wrestle with arguments that there could be significant downsides to doing away with it — that, in the absence of a notwithstanding clause, courts might only become more politicized, with political leaders more incentivized to appoint judges who will decide a certain way (as it is in the United States).
A future court may some day decide that a particular use of the notwithstanding clause has gone too far (in Friday's ruling, three justices seemed to allow that there could be some theoretical outer limits). For now, the options for outright overriding the override may be limited to either the difficult (constitutional negotiations to amend the Charter) or the dangerous (reviving the federal Parliament's power to disallow provincial laws).
If the court had ruled on Friday that there were significant legal limits on the use of clause, the result could have been a constitutional crisis.
At the federal level — where the notwithstanding clause has never been invoked — Sen. Peter Harder has proposed a bill that would at least establish new rules and requirements around any use of the clause by Parliament. Under Harder's bill, for instance, the support of two-thirds of MPs would be required to invoke the clause.
It would, in other words, make it somewhat more difficult to invoke the clause.
Eugene Forsey, the late senator and constitutional scholar, once colourfully described the notwithstanding clause as a "dagger pointed at the heart of our fundamental freedoms." One might agree with that sentiment and yet still agree with Roy McMurtry, the attorney general of Ontario in 1981, who said that "political accountability is the best safeguard against any improper use of the 'override clause.'"
If it has become too easy to invoke the notwithstanding clause in recent years, it is still likely not for the court to rewrite the Charter — to change the result of a compromise brokered by political actors. Rather, it suggests that political accountability has been lacking.
"For those who remain concerned about the override clause, let me remind them that it has been said that the price of liberty is eternal vigilance," Chrétien told the House in November 1981.
It is actually unclear who, if anyone, ever actually said that. But the sentiment might still be worthy.
"Pressure groups must remain vigilant," Chrétien said, commending the "vigilance" of women who were then pushing for Section 28 of the Charter, on gender rights, to be excluded from the notwithstanding clause. (On Friday, the Court found Section 28 did not invalidate Bill 21.)
Vigilance may not be the most satisfying answer. But it might be the best or only one available.

Screen-free tweens try their hand at Dungeons & Dragons
Dungeons & Dragons has captivated players for more than 50 years.
In its early days, some parents complained that the role-playing game kept kids holed up inside for hours at a time. NPR even did a 10-minute piece on it in 1979.
More recently, D&D has come back into popular culture through shows including Stranger Things, a 2023 blockbuster movie and an influx of interest during the COVID-19 lockdowns.
Now, what was once a nerdy pastime has become a screen-free parent's dream — a game that relies on imagination, a role of the dice and in-person communication.
"It's a great concoction," Ted Fair says. He's the (grown-up) Dungeon Master for a group of 9- to 12-year-old kids in Washington Heights in New York. "When you're able to sit down with … other people and harmonize like that."
Fair's group is part of Tweens Without Screens, a parent collective that focuses on providing technology-free activities for kids. They host events like knitting clubs and urban hikes. They have multiple D&D groups that meet monthly.
"I feel like part of what's kind of fun about it is we're trying to figure it out as we go along," said Rose Watson, a 12-year-old member of Fair's D&D crew.
In their most recent session, the group explored a cave and discovered a mysterious egg. Possibly a dragon egg? They didn't get a chance to find out! A low roll of the dice meant that instead of successfully stealing the egg, it crashed into pieces on the floor.
"It's like painting a picture in your mind," said Watson. She likes the in-person nature of the game. "A big part of it is getting together with other people and friendship and making jokes."
"And collaboration!" added her 9-year-old brother Leo Watson.

For fellow 9-year-old Amos Slodounik, it's about getting to try on a different personality.
"You can express yourself in different ways. You can be goofy and nobody will care," he said.
And for Benjamin Cho, also 9, the fun is in the imagination. He spent much of the session drawing elaborate tools and creatures for their game (a healing spider donut, for example). "I like D&D because there's a lot of items and things that you can make up."

SpaceX gets FCC approval to deploy 1 million satellites for its AI orbital data center
The FCC expects the initiative, called Starmind, to deploy it first satellite by November 2033.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has approved SpaceX's request to deploy 1 million satellites to build its AI orbital data center. SpaceX filed its application at the beginning of the year, presenting the initiative called Starmind as the better alternative for ground-based data centers. In its filing, the company argued that "orbital data centers are the most efficient way to meet the accelerating demand for AI computing power," since they use "solar power with little operating and maintenance costs."
But can space-based data centers for AI really work? Critics doubt they can. Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and a critic of Elon Musk's space and AI ambitions, told AP that "it's not going to happen. The idea behind sending AI data centers outside our planet is so that they don't consume resources their ground-based counterparts do, like energy and water for cooling.
However, critics of the plan argue that space is a vacuum that traps heat inside objects and doesn't make cooling down hardware easier. In space, heat has to leave the satellites via radiation, and Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to radiating the heat out for all of them. In addition, that many satellites could cause in-orbit collisions and generate a huge amount of space junk.
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr believes that with this approval, though, America is "leading the world into the era of super intelligence." It opens a "bold new frontier," he added. Under the terms the FCC has approved, SpaceX has permission to deploy satellites into orbital layers spanning 50 kilometers, at altitudes between 500 meters and 1,002 kilometers.
The company is required to deploy at lease one authorized satellite and place it into its assigned orbit by November 25, 2033. By the same date in 2035, it must have already deployed 100,000 satellites to their respective orbits. Three years later, on November 25, 2028, it must have already deployed 500,000 of the authorized satellites. All 1 million satellites must have already been placed in their assigned orbits no later than November 25, 2040. Musk previously said that SpaceX will start launching the satellites in 2027, but we'll have to wait and see if the company can stick to that timeline.

(Bloomberg) -- A drone attack on Kuwait killed two Italian civilians and injured two others Thursday, with the Gulf nation blaming Iran for the strike on what its military described as a “vital” facility.
The Italians, technicians working for German defense company Rheinmetall AG, were killed in an explosion involving several drones of Iranian origin, Italy’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
They were carrying out maintenance on detection antennas for the Skyguard air-defense system used by Kuwait’s armed forces, the ministry said. Falling debris also injured a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani, according to Kuwait’s military.
The attack was the second on the country this month.
Iran “firmly and completely” denied carrying out the attack.
“No military or offensive operation of any kind has been carried out by the Islamic Republic’s armed forces in that region,” senior armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi said, according to state-run IRIB.
Renewed tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran have ratcheted up tensions in recent weeks, leaving the region in limbo as President Donald Trump threatens further strikes while mediators seek a deal.
The attacks on Kuwait this month followed a two-month lull in Iranian assaults on the country. Kuwait and neighboring Bahrain have been among Tehran’s targets since its April ceasefire with Washington collapsed. Iran struck an industrial facility in Bahrain on Saturday, injuring two people, one critically.
Unlike previous Iranian attacks on Kuwait, Thursday’s assault appeared to be unsolicited and didn’t follow any reported US attacks on Iranian territory.
“Iran is going on the offensive, gradually abandoning the gray area that has defined the latest phase of the war,” said Bader Al-Saif, assistant professor at Kuwait University and associate fellow at Chatham House. “Analysts fixated on the timing of renewed US-Israeli strikes are remiss in downplaying Tehran’s own agency.”
The risks of shipping energy through the Strait of Hormuz have also risen in recent weeks as Iran launched a wave of attacks on tankers.
A US blockade, meanwhile, is worsening Iran’s economic crisis by preventing it from exporting oil and restricting imports of some essential goods, while inflation has accelerated to around 90%.
Arab states in the Persian Gulf are urging Trump to end the conflict without another round of all-out hostilities after Tehran targeted them with thousands of missiles and drones during the opening weeks of the war.
“With no durable solutions in sight, the region is spiraling deeper into mayhem,” Al-Saif said.

Zelenskyy urges the US to pressure Putin, calling Trump’s 'my friend' remark strange
The Ukrainian president’s comments come amid tensions over delayed Patriot missile deliveries, Starlink disruptions and EU leaders’ failure to agree on a US$49 billion loan to Ukraine.
KYIV, Ukraine: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the US stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington just as a question mark appears over Europe’s future financial commitments to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy said in an interview with the BBC broadcast Friday (Nov 27) that he wants the US to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite US President Donald Trump’s efforts to broker a peace deal.
The Ukrainian president described Trump calling Putin “my friend” at a recent summit in China as “strange” because the Russian leader is “an aggressor and a killer.”
“He can’t be a friend,” Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening it to someone calling Adolf Hitler a friend during World War II.
The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the US and its allies including Israel.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Zelenskyy was “insulting his counterpart,” showing that the Ukrainian leader “is not willing to follow the path of (a) peace settlement.”
Zelenskyy’s comments were broadcast a day after Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and a US envoy trying to mediate an end to the war, complimented Putin on being a “grandmaster” of politics and weeks after Kushner’s partner in peace efforts, Steve Witkoff, described Putin as a “humanitarian.”
Moscow’s invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of troops and thousands of Ukrainian civilians. It also brought heavy sanctions on Russia and diplomatically isolated Putin in the West before Trump resumed relations.
At the same time, Zelenskyy has complained that the Pentagon is not delivering to Ukraine paid-for Patriot missiles that could stop Russia’s ballistic missiles and that SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication, isn’t working properly.
Europe has in the past vowed to stay the course in helping Ukraine fend off Russia’s invasion. But European Union leaders on Thursday failed to reach consensus after fraught talks over a new US$49 billion loan for Ukraine’s economic and military needs next year.
Elections in the EU over the next 12 months could amplify the influence of parties reluctant to send more money to Ukraine and may fray the continent’s support.

Srinagar- The Jammu and Kashmir Services Selection Board (JKSSB) has announced additional safeguards for upcoming examinations following attempts by unscrupulous elements to use unfair means in a recently held Finance Accounts Assistant (FAA) examination.
Under the revised measures, invigilation staff will be selected and deployed through randomisation by the concerned Deputy Commissioners from an identified pool. Examination centres will also be allotted to candidates through randomisation, while the admit-card download window has been shortened from seven days to three days before the examination.
The Board said examination security protocols had been reviewed in consultation with the Police Department. Magistrates will supervise candidate frisking and ensure that only authorised examination-duty staff enter the premises and that no one leaves before the examination concludes.
Centre observers will monitor the movement of invigilation staff and examination material. Unused or unissued question booklets and OMR sheets for absent candidates must be counted, packed and sealed inside examination halls under CCTV surveillance. The Board will also increase the number of jammers at centres in view of recent attempts involving sophisticated electronic gadgets
All deployed staff, including service providers, will be required to deposit mobile phones and other gadgets in designated control rooms, where the items will remain locked until the examination ends. CCTV coverage and live monitoring from JKSSB control rooms in Jammu and Srinagar will continue.
The Board has directed that centre superintendents be permanent government officials, and that Deputy Commissioners constitute flying squads to monitor examination centres and nearby areas. District administrations will impose restrictions around centres under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and deploy police to prevent unnecessary movement.
Candidates will not be allowed to park vehicles near examination centres, and no accomplice will be permitted. Frisking will be strengthened, with metallic items—including water bottles, watches and special goggles—barred. Clothing with large buttons, baggy cuffs or hoodies that could conceal miniature electronic devices will also be prohibited.
JKSSB has advised candidates to focus on their preparation, rely only on information published on its official website and ignore false or fabricated rumours. (KNT)

Thirty-four-year-old Sundar lives in Tappal village in Khair tehsil of Aligarh district, Uttar Pradesh. His name was absent from the state’s draft voter list published on January 6, 2026. However, in the final list published on April 10, his name appears four times, at serial numbers 730, 738, 739 and 757 in booth 19. Each entry carries a different Elector Photo Identity Card (EPIC) number.
The official list of Form 6 applications, used for voter registration, records only two applications from Sundar, dated January 9 and 14. The office of the Uttar Pradesh chief electoral officer (CEO), however, said that he had filed four. The discrepancy aside, the CEO’s office’s response confirms a crucial point: Multiple applications by the same person resulted in the issuance of multiple voter IDs.
The Election Commission launched the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Uttar Pradesh in November 2025, with the removal of duplicate and incorrect entries among its stated objectives. Alt News compared the draft and final electoral rolls across 69 booths in 20 districts, covering 60,558 voters, and cross-checked newly added names against the corresponding Form 6 application lists. The analysis found 230 people whose names appeared at least twice in the final rolls, with some listed three or four times, each against a separate voter ID. Such duplicate entries were found in booths across the political spectrum.
On October 27, 2025, the Election Commission announced the second phase of the SIR across 12 states and Union Territories, including Uttar Pradesh. The exercise, covering approximately 51 crore voters, began on November 4.
The schedule for Uttar Pradesh was subsequently extended four times. The draft electoral roll was published on January 6, 2026. Those whose names were missing from the draft had to submit Form 6 to seek inclusion. Following the fourth extension, the deadline for filing claims and objections was March 6, while the final electoral roll was published on April 10.
At present a special summary revision (SSR) of electoral rolls is going on in the state. The draft roll was published on November 17.
The Methodology
For each of 69 booths in UP, Alt News read the draft list (January 6, 2026) and the final list (April 10, 2026) entry by entry, and matched the count with the totals on each list’s cover page. We treated two entries as the same person only if the name, father’s or husband’s name, age and house number all matched.
We checked every case against the scanned entry. We then looked up Form 6 applications in the Form 9 lists. The latter is a public list of every Form 6 application an election office received, with the applicant’s name, relative and address. The lists we examined cover 13 assembly constituencies. The 69 booths that we chose fall into the three following groups:
One Form, Several Voter IDs
Listed below are 11 voters (chosen randomly from the 230 to explain the nature of the anomalies) whose names did not appear on the January 6 draft list but were all added to the final list. In each of these cases, the entries share the same name, relative, age and house number, but carry different EPIC numbers. We use first names because they are private citizens.
Our findings revealed two patterns: For Ishlok, Najmeen, Himanshu, Pinki, Saurabh and Aakash, every form became a voter ID, and the entries sit next to each other on the list. Saurabh’s are serial numbers 1004 and 1005.
From Sundar to Sunita, the list has more entries than the published Form 6 list has forms. Married couple Vijay Lakshmi and Dharmendra have a cumulative total of five voter IDs. Vijay Lakshmi has three, while her husband has two.
Anushree Verma, whose husband is Akshay Verma, had filled Form 6 twice and received three voter IDs.
Sundar, mentioned at the beginning, had filled the form twice (According to Form 9) and in return got four voter IDs.
The biggest single cluster of duplicate voters is booth 449 in Chachoi, Sikandrabad (Bulandshahr), where the BJP won 94% of the votes in 2022. The final list adds 69 names to this booth.
Of these, 34 entries are for 17 people, each listed twice with a new EPIC. None of the 17 names are on the January 6 draft list. Fifteen of the 17 filed one Form 6 each on the published lists. For two, Hasmuddin and Heema Devi, we found none. Six of the 17 live at house 91. One of them, Vikas, is listed once as female and once as male.
Some duplicates were already there before the revision and were not removed. In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), two brothers appear twice each, at serials 108 and 109 and at 110 and 111 respectively, on both the draft and final lists.
In booth 1044 of Sahibabad, a father and son already on the list at house number 306 were added again with new IDs at house number 840. We found no Form 6 for either.
The published Form 9 lists for Khair village show one applicant, Bhuvnesh, son of Sanjeev Kumar of Simrauthi village, ten times between January 31 and March 6, 2026.
Across the Form 9 lists of the 13 constituencies, 3,369 people were found to have filed Form 6 between two to 10 times.
Missing Addresses, Renamed IDs, Suspicious Deletions
In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), 20 of the 64 new voters have no house number. The field holds a place name, Oramha, for unrelated families.
Across the 37 city booths, 62 new voters were added with house “0” or a blank. In booth 354 of Kairana (Shamli), 48 voters were already listed at “house 3” on the draft list, and eight more were added from at least seven different families.
In Khair constituency, house number 658, under which all four of Sundar’s entries are listed, is associated with 36 voters from approximately 19 families.
A shared or missing house number is not, in itself, evidence of electoral irregularity, as most villages do not have a system of house numbering. The concern, however, is how entries without a verifiable address could be physically checked during field visits.
Moreover, in booth 351 of Sidhauli (Sitapur), three women’s names appeared changed between the draft and final lists, while the EPIC number, husband’s name, house number and age stayed the same. Rekharani became Lakshmi Devi, Gayashri became Meena Devi and Shivrani became Neelam.
We found 15 such cases across 20 rural booths. These changes could be legitimate corrections. However, only the corresponding Form 8 applications, used to request corrections to electoral roll entries, can establish the basis for the changes.
The most striking example of renamed entries is in booth 327 of Gorakhpur Rural. Serial 799 was Bhathwa, male, 53, house 156, on the draft list. On the final list, the same EPIC belongs to Rusha Devi, female, 50, house 56. Rusha Devi, husband Parmeshwar, also appears at serial numbers 924 and 930 of the addition list under two new EPICs. We found no Form 6 for her among the 23,136 applications in the Gorakhpur Rural lists.
In booth 943 of Sahibabad, 298 entries from one part of the 2025 electoral roll were deleted, 280 of them marked as “absent”. The deletions occurred in consecutive chunks of 23, 17, 14 and 10 names (shown in the plot below). Since electoral rolls are arranged by house and lane, such clusters could simply indicate that an entire building or group of homes had been vacated. A door-to-door verification would establish this. Whether such visits were conducted is something the Election Commission can clarify.
It is worth noting how many voters in every 1,000 appear twice or more on the final roll. See the chart below:
Questions for the Poll Panel
The analysis above poses several significant questions for the election commission vis-a-vis the SIR exercise in Uttar Pradesh. Some of them are the following:
- How did one Form 6 become two or three voter IDs – and how many times did this happen across UP?
- Why are repeat applications from the same person, at the same address, not merged before an ID is issued?
- How did officials verify new voters at house ‘0’, blank addresses and catch-all house numbers?
- How to explain the long runs of consecutive ‘Absent’ deletions – were these homes actually visited?
UP CEO’s Response
The Uttar Pradesh CEO initially denied findings by Alt News co-founder Mohammed Zubair, who flagged Sundar’s case of four different EPIC IDs on X. The office responded with the following post:
Mr Fact-checker please fact-check your own facts.
There is no such scheme as “Buy one Get one free” scheme by Election Commission.
As per your post, the voter had submitted only two applications and he got 4 EPIC cards.
This statement is false.
The voter had submitted 4 applications.
If you want to dispute our facts then you post the reference numbers of two applications that you claim he had submitted and we will post the reference number of the remaining two.
The problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long standing one. We do deduplication through ECINET periodically. We are on path to achieving the objective of catching multiple forms submitted by an individual at the submission stage only. We will achieve our objective very soon.
Please do not incite people by making patently false statements about ECI and thereby trying to create disaffection among the citizens towards a Constitutional Body.
You are advised to rectify your mistake by amending or deleting your post after completing your own due diligence now that you have been informed by us about your wrong information.
— CEO Uttar Pradesh (@ceoup) October 17, 2026
The CEO claimed that Sundar had submitted four Form 6 applications, resulting in four separate entries on the final electoral roll. This contradicted the official Form 6 application list, which recorded only two applications from Sundar. However, the CEO’s response also acknowledged that “the problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long-standing one”.
The discrepancy over whether Sundar submitted two or four applications does not alter the central issue: the Commission itself acknowledges that multiple applications by the same voter can result in the generation of multiple EPIC numbers. Its response also indicates that the system does not consistently prevent such duplication at the application stage, necessitating periodic deduplication through ECINET.
On October 19, the CEO directed election officials to expedite the removal of duplicate entries ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections and identify cases in which individual voters had submitted multiple applications during the SIR.
Readers should note that some of the errors documented in this article were rectified by the Election Commission in the intervening period between our initial identification of these anomalies and the publication of this report.

Bleeding, birth defects: Congo residents sue over alleged mining pollution
KOLWEZI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In a small cinderblock home in the scrub beside a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine in Kolwezi, a mother shares a story of devastating loss.
She believes pollution from the neighboring mine is responsible for her family's suffering.
She has lost three children. Two died at birth. A third suffered repeated nosebleeds before dying. One of her two surviving children has stunted growth.
Now she and 26 other residents are taking the company to court in a rare attempt to hold alleged polluters accountable in the Democratic Republic of Congo. They are also suing the government, accusing it of failing to enforce environmental regulations.
Like other plaintiffs, she asked NPR not to identify her, fearing retribution from the company or government. Although the claimants' names are public in court documents, they want to avoid further exposure. Their lawyers also fear the plaintiffs could face intimidation from other locals.
"Our children are the first victims," she said, as the sun set over a nearby mound of mine tailings. "What we're hoping for is to see justice done."
The plaintiffs, whose case began Nov. 3, describe similar problems: contaminated water, nosebleeds, skin rashes, miscarriages and birth defects, which they blame on mining pollution.
The mine, known as COMMUS, is owned by Chinese multinational Zijin and lies in Kolwezi, a city of more than 500,000 people in the heart of Congo's copper belt, a southern region with vast mineral reserves.
Congo is the world's second-largest producer of copper, and also the source of over 70% of the world's cobalt, a metal that is critical to the electric-vehicle revolution because of its use in rechargeable batteries.
Last year, the U.S. signed a sweeping economic partnership with Congo aimed at attracting American investment and challenging the dominance of Chinese companies in the country's mining industry
Despite the global importance of Congo's copper and cobalt mines, however, environmental pollution from the industry has received comparatively little scrutiny.
In Kolwezi, pollution is severe. Neighborhoods near mines are often filled with an acrid smell that residents attribute to the sulfuric acid used to process minerals. A study published in June by environmental research organization Source International — carried out with the advocacy groups RAID and Afrewatch, and scientists from Congo's University of Lubumbashi — also highlighted the scale of the contamination.
Researchers found that levels of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, in Kolwezi were three to six times the World Health Organization's air quality guideline. The highest concentrations were recorded near the COMMUS mine.
These tiny particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure poses health risks generally, but is particularly dangerous for pregnant women and young children.
The researchers also tested dust samples and found residue of copper, cobalt and manganese, which they said pointed to mining waste as the main source. When the study was released, Source International's executive director, Flaviano Bianchini, said that "these are among the most concerning air quality results we have documented in years of monitoring pollution at industrial mining sites around the world."
The study did not examine health impacts directly, and the authors recommended formal epidemiological research. Residents and health workers in Kolwezi nonetheless point to a string of ailments that they blame on a polluted environment.
In a dilapidated health clinic in the shadow of a mountain of waste from the COMMUS mine, nurse Héritier Bukassa said that people routinely break out in itchy hives. "Some sick people scratch themselves with knives to relieve itching," he explained.
Bukassa added that women in the area also suffer from high rates of miscarriage, and that he had referred four babies born with congenital malformations — mostly cleft palates — to hospitals this year alone.
Respiratory illnesses are common too, Bukassa said, especially in otherwise healthy babies who develop breathing problems a few weeks after birth. "No one from the [mining] company has ever come to talk to us about this," the nurse said.
Zijin, the owner of COMMUS, did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Neither did Congo's mining and environment ministries.
The Cobalt Institute, an industry lobby, said that understanding environmental pollution requires "an evidence-based approach that considers all potential sources and contributors." It added that companies perform environmental monitoring and carry out mitigation measures.
RAID, which is supporting the plaintiffs alongside Afrewatch, described the case this month as one of "the most ambitious legal challenges yet brought by Congolese residents over industrial mining pollution."
The suit is an important test case that could lead to communities challenging other mines in the future, it added.
The plaintiffs are seeking $1.3 million in compensation for health problems and medical expenses, as well as $5 million to restore the environment. Their lawyers say they worry their clients might come under pressure or intimidation to withdraw their testimony.
The mother, however, said she had no such fears. "We have a right to a clean environment," she said, "and to health."

Srinagar- Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha on Friday called for a skill-centric, employment-oriented curriculum at Baba Ghulam Shah Badshah University (BGSBU), Rajouri, while stressing the need to align academic reforms with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020.
Chairing the 10th meeting of the university’s Executive Council at Lok Bhavan, the Lieutenant Governor directed the university to develop a long-term framework for self-sustained funding and strengthen industry-academia partnerships.

Sinha underscored the importance of faculty capacity building and called for academic reforms that enhance students’ skills and employment prospects.
He also directed the Executive Council to hold meetings twice a year and ensure the timely conduct of the university’s convocation.
Emphasising the need to maintain institutional discipline and a conducive academic environment, the Lieutenant Governor called for stringent action against elements attempting to disrupt campus harmony.
He further issued directions to strengthen institutional accountability and organise national-level programmes along with student outreach initiatives such as Yuva Connect.

Vice Chancellor Prof. Jawaid Iqbal presented various agenda items before the Executive Council for approval and ratification.
The council also reviewed the Action Taken Report pertaining to its previous meeting held in January 2026.

The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has sought a response from Netflix over its upcoming documentary, Love, Scam aur Dhokha: The Sukesh Chandrashekhar Story, which is scheduled to premiere on December 18, 2026. The communication follows a representation filed on behalf of Chandrashekhar, raising concerns about the documentary's release while criminal proceedings against him are ongoing.
I&B Ministry seeks Netflix’s response over Sukesh Chandrashekhar documentary in seven days ahead of December 18 release
In a communication dated November 27, 2026, the Ministry forwarded the representation submitted by Advocate Anant Malik to Netflix Entertainment Services India and asked the streaming platform to examine the issues raised in it. The Ministry has sought Netflix's comments within seven days of receiving the communication.
The letter, bearing reference number J-11013/19/2025-DM, refers to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, and other applicable Indian laws. It also draws attention to the Code of Ethics governing digital news publishers and OTT platforms, which provides for a three-tier mechanism to address grievances concerning violations of the prescribed framework.
The Ministry further noted that OTT platforms are required not to transmit content prohibited by law and to exercise due caution and discretion. The communication was signed by Kshitij Aggarwal, Deputy Director (Digital Media), and issued with the approval of the competent authority.
Ministry has not ordered a postponement of the documentary
The representation was submitted by Malik on behalf of Chandrashekhar, who is currently in judicial custody at Mandoli Jail in Delhi. It raises objections to the documentary being released before the conclusion of the criminal trials involving him.
As reported earlier, Chandrashekhar's legal team had also issued a notice to Netflix and other parties associated with the documentary, seeking a postponement of its release until prosecution evidence in the pending cases is concluded. The notice raised concerns about the portrayal of allegations that are yet to be tested in court and the potential impact on the right to a fair trial.
Importantly, the Ministry's latest communication does not direct Netflix to stop, postpone or withdraw the documentary. It has asked the platform to respond to the representation within the stipulated period. Netflix's response and the Ministry's subsequent course of action are awaited.
The development comes amid growing scrutiny of how true-crime documentaries portray individuals facing ongoing criminal proceedings, particularly in relation to the presumption of innocence and the right to a fair trial.

Walmart International CEO Chris Nicholas is expected to visit India on Monday (November 30) to meet Flipkart employees, days after the ecommerce major announced Group CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy’s departure. Walmart is also expected to announce details of the leadership transition and a cash payout for executives holding ESOPs during the visit, The Economic Times reported. The payout amount has not been finalised, and it remains unclear how many employees will be eligible. The proposed payment is expected to address liquidity concerns among current and former employees while Flipkart’s IPO plans remain delayed, the report said. Flipkart confirmed Krishnamurthy’s departure on Wednesday, with sources telling Inc42 that Walmart leadership had asked him to step down. His last day will be December 4. Flipkart will announce his successor in the coming weeks, with chief product and technology officer Balaji Thiagarajan and its board overseeing the organisation in the interim. Sources told Inc42 that Walmart’s decision to seek Krishnamurthy’s departure was linked to IPO delays and its push to improve Flipkart’s profitability. In its official statement announcing the departure, Walmart did not disclose a reason for the leadership change. Nicholas thanked Krishnamurthy for his leadership, governance, and contributions, while reiterating Walmart’s confidence in Flipkart’s future. Moneycontrol reported that a contentious meeting with Walmart leadership in Bentonville in the US preceded Krishnamurthy’s exit. Nicholas reportedly criticised his explanations for Flipkart’s continued losses, senior employee exits, and declining morale. However, Walmart executive vice-president of corporate affairs Dan Bartlett disputed Moneycontrol’s account of the meetings. “This story couldn’t be further from the truth,” Bartlett wrote on X yesterday. He said he had attended the meetings and maintained a strong working relationship with Krishnamurthy throughout his tenure. “His meetings in Bentonville were collaborative and constructive. To suggest otherwise would be inaccurate and ill-informed,” he added. Flipkart’s IPO Delay & ESOP Concerns Krishnamurthy’s exit comes amid pressure on Flipkart to improve profitability before pursuing a public listing. Earlier this year, Walmart reportedly asked Flipkart to defer its IPO until at least 2028 and achieve EBITDA breakeven by the end of FY27. Flipkart completed its reverse flip from Singapore to India in March 2026, removing a structural hurdle to a domestic listing. It had been preparing to go public in late 2026 or early 2027 and was exploring a pre-IPO funding round of around $2.5 Bn. Those plans were put on hold in May. The delay has intensified concerns over employees’ ability to monetise their vested ESOPs. In October, former executives, including ex-Myntra CEO Mukesh Bansal, former Flipkart chief business officer Ankit Nagori, and former CFO Sanjay Baweja, wrote to Walmart’s board seeking equal treatment and a full cash-out opportunity. Flipkart announced its second ESOP liquidity event in 12 months in July, allowing eligible current employees to liquidate up to 5% of their outstanding options vested over the preceding three years. Sources earlier told Inc42 that some senior executives had left Flipkart because they could not see a clear opportunity to liquidate their ESOPs. The proposed payout could offer another liquidity window, although its scope and eligibility criteria remain unclear. On the financial front, Flipkart Group’s consolidated operating revenue rose 18.2% YoY to ₹1.45 Lakh Cr in FY26 from ₹1.23 Lakh Cr in the previous year. Its consolidated net loss narrowed 2.1% to ₹8,468 Cr from ₹8,646 Cr. The figures include Myntra and Cleartrip following Flipkart’s redomiciling to India.

A video showing a woman holding a weapon and trying to protect her house and child as a mob attacks and vandalises the house is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it depicts an attack on Hindu homes in Bangladesh. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows a mob attacking Hindu homes in Bangladesh, while a woman tries to protect her house and child.
Fact: The video shows a mob attacking the houses of two men accused of cattle theft in Dakshin Kurshi village, Sunamganj District, Bangladesh, on 25 March 2026. The woman seen holding a child and a sharp weapon while trying to protect her house is the wife of one of the accused. Police confirmed that theft cases had been registered against the accused but condemned the mob attack. Bangladeshi fact-checkers also clarified that the woman is Muslim and that the incident stemmed from allegations of cattle theft, not communal violence. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple Bangladeshi media reports (here, here, and here) from March 2026, which identified the incident as one involving allegations of cattle theft in Dakshin Kurshi village, Dolar Bazar Union, Chhatak Upazila, Sunamganj District, Bangladesh.
According to these reports, villagers were angered by repeated cattle theft. A man named Saifur Rahman was reportedly caught stealing cattle in neighbouring North Kurshi village. During questioning, he allegedly named Ali Hussain, his son-in-law Tarek Mia, and several others as being involved in the thefts. Following this, an agitated mob attacked the houses of Ali Hussain and Tarek Mia in South Kurshi village on 25 March 2026.
The reports stated that more than a hundred people gathered following the allegations and vandalised and looted the houses of the accused. The mob threw bricks and stones, damaged tin walls and household belongings, and attacked women and children. The viral video shows Tarek Mia’s wife, who is also Ali Hussain’s daughter, holding a child and a sharp weapon as she attempts to protect her house from the mob. She tries to fend off the attackers, but they continue to vandalise the house.
Reports further stated that Ali Hussain and Tarek Mia had previously faced theft allegations. Sub-Inspector Abdur Rahman of the Zahidpur Police Investigation Centre reportedly said that police had registered multiple theft cases against the accused and filed a case in connection with the latest incident. However, the officer condemned the mob attack, stating that vandalising someone’s house was unjustified, despite the villagers’ frustration over repeated thefts. The viral video, therefore, depicts an incident arising from allegations of cattle theft in Bangladesh and has no communal angle.
We also found an X post by Bangladeshi fact-checker Shohanur Rahman dated 1 November 2026, stating that the woman is Muslim and the wife of Mohammad Tarek. He clarified that she was trying to protect her father’s house during an attack triggered by allegations of theft.
To sum up, the video of a mob attacking houses in Bangladesh over cattle theft allegations is falsely shared with a communal spin.

Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. In the years since, the Blue Oval has been back to France more than a few times, with varying success. It could never replicate the GT40’s success winning overall, but it celebrated the 40th anniversary with a class win. Now it wants another shot at the really big trophy, and it debuted the car during the Detroit Lions-Chicago Bears football game today: meet the GT41.
“Revealing the Ford GT41 is a significant moment for everyone involved in this program,” said Dan Sayers, manager of Ford Racing’s Hypercar program. “It’s the result of an enormous amount of work across our engineering, design, and development teams and an important milestone on our journey towards 2027. We know the scale of the challenge ahead—the level of competition in Hypercar is incredibly high, and there are no shortcuts to success. Our focus has been on building the right foundations, bringing together the right people and making sure we learn as much as possible from every stage of development.”
Like many other entrants in the World Endurance Championship’s Hypercar class, Ford has chosen the rear-wheel-drive LMDh technical approach rather than building the GT41 entirely from scratch, as Ferrari and Aston Martin do with their cars. LMDh cars start with one of four approved carbon fiber chassis—in this case, Ford is working with Oreca, which has also partnered with Genesis and Acura.

Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.
The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.
Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.
After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.
Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.
"Strobe was a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," said Clinton in a statement after Talbott's death. When Talbott was translating Khrushchev's memoirs while at Oxford, it was Clinton's job to make him breakfast every day, he said, adding, "somehow, I got the better end of the deal."
Both he and Hillary were "deeply saddened" by the passing of "a wonderful friend, and a world-class human being," he said.
Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the U.S. State Department's Foreign Affairs Policy Board.
Talbott also authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled "Our Founders' Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump," which was published in 2020.
He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren.
His first wife, Brook Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

Xabi Alonso called for Chelsea to get back to fundamentals before slipping to new low at Nottingham Forest
Sky Sports analyses the decisions from Xabi Alonso that contributed to Chelsea's 3-2 defeat to Nottingham Forest; Wesley Fofana started despite his controversial interview, while Levi Colwill was dropped; Xabi Alonso called for fundamentals but Chelsea were outrun
Saturday 28 November 2026 00:05, UK
Xabi Alonso called for his Chelsea side to get back to the fundamentals before kick-off - and then watched on as they were outworked and outclassed on their way to a miserable 3-2 defeat at Nottingham Forest.
"Everyone in the club and team, we need to stick together and go through this moment. We have to deal with it and we are responsible," Alonso told Sky Sports after the game, which marked their third successive defeat in the Premier League.
"It is a difficult moment for everyone at the club. For the team and the fans. Disappointed to lose again but we need to keep trying to find solutions.

"We can't stop. We are low in confidence. At this level you need to hold results and not concede so much. That is why we are losing."
The 3-2 defeat was their third successive loss in the Premier League. Alonso now has as many losses in 15 games across all competitions as he did in 34 for Real Madrid (6).
Since March, no side has more defeats in the top-flight than the Blues (14). And their problems are now mounting by the day.
Here, Sky Sports analyses the decisions that contributed to the worrying defeat at the City Ground.
Chelsea failed at the fundamentals
Despite the calls from Alonso to strip the game back to basics and get the fundamentals right, Chelsea felt short from minute one.
At the half-time interval, facing a 1-0 deficit and with zero shots on target, Chelsea had ran 3.8km less than Oliver Glasner's side.
The Forest boss was then quick to point out that they had outrun their opponents by 6km after the game. Yes, Chelsea had more possession, but they were also well behind in high-speed runs.
"I've seen one team jogging after the ball and one team sprinting after the ball and in this day and age, you cannot do that," said Jamie Redknapp.
"Distance covered is not always the barometer, but one thing is for sure, high-speed runs will tell you everything."
Fofana in the firing line - should he have started?
Starting Wesley Fofana in the same week the player had to apologise for his controversial interview, where he said he can "laugh about" the penalty miss that contributed to their Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool and contemplated retirement during injury spells at the club, was a bold move from Alonso. It did not pay off.
The tone was set early on. Fofana's first touches were heavily booed by the travelling Chelsea fans who had made the 130-mile journey in the cold and rain to watch their side slip to yet another dismal defeat.
The centre-back could only watch on as Igor Jesus volleyed in his stunning opener but was at the centre of attention, for all the wrong reasons, for the second.
After misjudging the ball while battling with former teammate Liam Delap, who caused problems all evening, Fofana rushed to atone for his error and fouled the striker in the penalty area.
Morgan Gibbs-White doubled the lead from the spot and ultimately the comeback, led by substitute Emmanuel Emegha, fell short.
He was cautioned for the challenge and eventually taken off for Levi Colwill, who was dropped by Alonso instead of Fofana, and the fans booed him once again.
"It didn't feel like a game for him tonight. He had a bad week with the podcast," said Jamie Redknapp after the game.
"By playing Fofana tonight, you created that. It was inevitable. He is lacking so much confidence; he needs some time.
"He is having a real difficult run of it at the moment."
Caicedo at centre back - why?
After making the decision to drop Colwill, options at the centre of defence were limited with Maxence Lacroix and Reece James both sidelined.
Playing Josh Acheampong at centre-back and giving a rare start to Malo Gusto, an unused substitute on the night, seemed the more obvious choice but Alonso opted to play Moises Caicedo, arguably the best midfielder in the league, in the back four instead.
He was then tasked with dealing with a strike partnership of Delap and Igor Jesus. A difficult task for even the tallest of centre-backs, let alone a makeshift one standing at 5-foot-10.
He gave space to the Brazil striker for the opener and his presence in midfield was missed. He still led the way with 114 passes on the night, but Chelsea needed him in the middle of the park to deal with the likes of James McAtee and Xaver Schlager.
"They have bought players but if they do not sign a centre back, they cannot compete," said Redknapp after the game. He is right.
Emegha's impact was too little, too late
Alonso admitted that Emegha's performance after scoring twice off the bench was the lone positive for his side to take from their trip to the East Midlands. "For sure, he is having a good impact," he said. "He has done well. That is a positive."
He scored his first goal in the 4-1 defeat to Leeds United last time out but lost his place in the starting line-up on Friday.
Danny Welbeck, 36, was given the nod ahead of him and his performance mirrored the struggles Chelsea had as a unit.
Alonso called on the experience of Jordan Henderson and Welbeck to help weather their current struggles but it only whipped up the storm.
Welbeck was a bystander in the first half and had just seven touches before being replaced at the break, Emegha then scored with his first two to help spark hopes of a comeback.
His header for the second, holding off Jair Cunha, was one of the rare moments Chelsea matched the physicality of their opponents. He has to start moving forward without Joao Pedro available.
Alonso said the only way he knows how to address these issues is to attack them on the training ground. He has just five days to do that before they are put to the test against Crystal Palace, live on Sky Sports, who will be desperate for a win.

MGM Healthcare Malar, Adyar, has launched an AI-powered MRI facility, offering specialised imaging services for neurological, cardiac, musculoskeletal, spinal, and other conditions.
The facility was inaugurated by J. Radhakrishnan, Chairperson of the Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission, on Thursday (November 26, 2026).
The system uses deep learning algorithms to correct motion-related artefacts and improve image quality, potentially reducing the need for repeat scans. It also offers specialised fetal and breast MRI, cardiac MRI, whole-body imaging, diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and perfusion imaging.
According to the hospital, the technology can also reduce scan time. A brain MRI that conventionally takes about 35 minutes can now be completed in under 14 minutes. This could benefit patients who find it difficult to remain still for prolonged periods due to pain or discomfort.
Thinesh Ram, senior consultant and head of Imaging and Interventional Radiology, MGM Healthcare Malar, said the system would enable more detailed evaluation of neural pathways and expand the range of diagnostic assessments.
S. Kripanandh, chief operating officer, MGM Healthcare Malar, Adyar, and group chief business officer, said the facility would strengthen the hospital’s diagnostic capabilities and expand access to advanced imaging services in the neighbourhood.

A West Bengal Consumer Commission has directed an airline to pay ₹56,491.78, along with 9% annual interest, to a passenger after cancelling her Delhi-Bengaluru flight without providing an adequate explanation for the decision. The passenger had to arrange another flight at a higher cost and spend two days at a hotel in Gurugram. The commission also ordered the airline to pay ₹10,000 towards litigation expenses, according to a report by Indian Express. The bench, comprising President Shivarama K and members Suma Anil Kumar and Rekha Sayannavar, held that the airline could not avoid responsibility as it had failed to explain the operational difficulties that led to the cancellation. Observing that “the unforeseen operational exigencies have not been explained”, the commission concluded that the airline was guilty of deficiency in service. In its November 19 order, the commission said, “It is not explained as to what kind of unforeseen operational exigencies it has faced. Therefore, mere saying that, because of unforeseen operational exigencies, it has affected the travel and theflight did not take off is not sufficient”. According to the complaint, the passenger booked a Delhi-Bengaluru flight on November 4, 2025, for travel on December 5, paying ₹7,497 for the ticket, Indian Express reported. The complainant asserted that the flight was cancelled without prior notice or alternative arrangements. She also claimed that the crew did not provide any assistance to help her reach her destination by another mode of transport. The cancellation disrupted her doctor's appointment and also resulted in a financial loss of ₹50,000. She also had to stay in Gurugram, Haryana, for two days before undertaking her return journey. The passenger said she stayed at a hotel from December 5 to December 6 and paid ₹15,269 for the accommodation. She later booked another flight for December 7, 2025, and paid ₹48,719 for the replacement ticket. After incurring these losses, she approached the consumer commission seeking compensation. The airline claimed that the flight was cancelled on December 5, 2025, due to operational reasons and that the passengers had been informed immediately. It further alleged that the passenger had refused to travel on the alternative flight offered by the airline and that the full ticket amount had been refunded, the report added. The airline also argued that the circumstances leading to the cancellation were unforeseen and beyond its control. The commission observed that the passenger's flight ticket showed that she had travelled on another flight on December 7, 2025. It also noted that the hotel invoice submitted by her covered accommodation expenses alone. After examining the documents, the bench held that she was entitled to reimbursement of the additional expenses incurred because of the cancellation.
