UN rapporteur Albanese in limbo at airport after being denied entry to Costa Rica
Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories, is stranded at Costa Rica’s main airport awaiting for a court to decide whether she could enter the country after immigration authorities blocked h...
SAN JOSÉ, Costa Rica -- Francesca Albanese, the U.N. special rapporteur on human rights in the Palestinian territories, was stranded in an airport terminal on Friday after being denied entry to Costa Rica.
Albanese posted a photo on X showing a suitcase beside a row of empty seats, with the caption: “This is where I will spend my first night in Costa Rica.”
She is awaiting a court decision on whether she can enter the country or must leave.
Costa Rican immigration authorities blocked her entry on Thursday, saying she was the subject of an international “alert” over alleged ties to terrorism and that her presence posed a national security risk.
Albanese is a high-profile independent investigator scrutinizing human rights abuses in the Palestinian territories. She is among a group of experts appointed by the 47-member U.N. Human Rights Council in Geneva to monitor and report on human rights conditions in individual countries and the observance of specific rights worldwide.
She was sanctioned by the United States in July 2025 over her work and sharp criticism of U.S. and Israeli policies during the war in Gaza. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described her actions as a “campaign of political and economic warfare against the United States and Israel.”
Albanese had traveled to Costa Rica at the invitation of the University of Costa Rica, which was scheduled to award her an honorary doctorate.
After she was denied entry, a habeas corpus petition was filed on her behalf with the Supreme Court’s Constitutional Chamber. The court issued an interim order allowing her to remain in the country and gave immigration authorities 24 hours to explain why they had denied her entry.
While the petition is pending, Albanese remains in a room at the airport. From there, she joined the university’s honorary doctorate ceremony by video call. One of her assistants, who was allowed into the country, accepted the degree on her behalf.
In her speech, Albanese said the decision to deny her entry could be related to the sanctions.
“I am deeply outraged that the Costa Rican government has spread false information linking me to terrorism. Defending human rights is not terrorism, and the government will answer for these insinuations, as it should in a country governed by the rule of law,” Albanese said.
Costa Rica's right-wing government is among a number of governments in the region that have sought to cozy up to the Trump administration, accepting third-country deportees from the U.S. in a move that provoked heavy criticism, and has built a Bukele-style mega-prison as part of its vow to crack down on crime.
Albanese criticized what she described as the Costa Rican government’s complicity in Israeli policies of oppression against Palestinians, citing its signing of a free-trade agreement with Israel that awaits legislative ratification.
Costa Rican President Laura Fernández has not commented on the issue, but her minister of the presidency, former President Rodrigo Chaves, addressed the court’s intervention on social media.
“Yet another usurpation by an increasingly arbitrary judiciary, one that usurps the powers of the other two branches of government and now protects foreigners flagged by international alerts for ties to TERRORIST ACTS!” Chaves wrote about the habeas corpus petition that halted Albanese’s expulsion.
Costa Rica’s ombudsman’s office criticized immigration authorities for “automatically” denying Albanese entry without assessing her case, her official status or her immunity as a U.N. rapporteur.
U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk also said he was “deeply concerned” by Costa Rica’s decision to deny her entry.

UK-based consumer healthcare major Haleon is in early-stage discussions to acquire a controlling stake in nutrition and supplements soonicorn HealthKart in a deal that could value it at $1.2 Bn to $1.4 Bn. Citing sources, Mint reported that discussions have been underway for a few months. Investment bank Avendus is likely advising HealthKart, while a complete sale is also being considered, the report added. HealthKart is simultaneously exploring an IPO in India through a dual-track process. Its choice between a strategic sale and a listing will depend on the terms and valuation offered, the report said. A potential acquisition would expand Haleon’s nutrition portfolio in India. The company, which was spun off from GSK in 2022, sells brands including Eno, Sensodyne, Iodex, and Otrivin in the country. It already operates in the vitamins, minerals, and supplements segment through Centrum. Inc42 has reached out to Haleon and Healthkart for comments on the development. The story will be updated on receiving a response. Founded in 2011 by Sameer Maheshwari and Prashant Tandon, HealthKart owns nutrition brands including MuscleBlaze, HK Vitals, and Gritzo. It also operates an online marketplace and offline stores selling its own products and those of third-party brands. Its portfolio spans protein supplements, dietary supplements, and children’s nutrition. The startup operates more than 200 stores across over 90 Indian cities. HealthKart’s pharmaceutical business, HealthKartPlus, was spun off and rebranded as 1mg in 2015, with Tandon leaving to lead it. Tata Digital subsequently acquired a majority stake in 1mg in 2021. In 2024, HealthKart announced a $153 Mn funding round co-led by ChrysCapital and Motilal Oswal Alternates, with participation from Neo Group and existing investor A91 Partners. The round valued the startup at $500 Mn. Its other investors include Temasek, Sofina, Kae Capital, Peak XV Partners and Sharrp Ventures. Consumer Giants Chase Nutrition The talks come amid a broader push by conglomerates and established consumer companies to acquire digital-first brands, particularly in nutrition, wellness, and healthy foods. In February, Hindustan Unilever acquired the remaining 49% stake in OZiva for ₹824 Cr, making the plant-based nutrition brand a wholly owned subsidiary. Meanwhile, Marico bought an additional 24.1% stake in Plix for ₹1,012 Cr in October, taking its holding in the nutrition and personal care brand to 84.1%. Alongside these acquisitions, nutrition startups continue to attract funding. Last month, Ace Blend raised $9.9 Mn in a Series A2 round led by 3one4 Capital. In June, TruNativ secured $30 Mn from OrbiMed to strengthen its offline distribution, retail, and hotel, restaurant, and catering presence.

Neuralink receives FDA approval for 'pivotal' brain implant trial in ALS patients
The study will evaluate the efficacity and safety of the company’s LINK device.
Elon Musk's Neuralink has received FDA permission to launch the first "pivotal" trial for its implantable LINK brain-computer interface, the company announced. The study represents a more advanced step in the company's efforts to develop a brain implant that allows people with paralysis to control devices using their brain alone. It will be open to a limited number of patients with ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that damages nerve cells controlling voluntary muscle movement.
"We've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US," Neuralink announced on X. "This builds off of our work with 30+ participants with Neuralink to date."
Neuralink hit a milestone last year when the company revealed that its first participant with ALS named Bradford Smith was able to communicate using brain signals alone. "Neuralink has given me freedom, hope, and faster communication. ... It has improved my life so much. I'm so happy to be involved in something big that will help many people," Smith said at the time.
We've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US. This builds off of our work with 30+ participants with Neuralink to date.
Those with ALS may be eligible. To learn more:https://t.co/dWhb5N4GdR pic.twitter.com/Vor7iXXCBA
— Neuralink (@neuralink) November 25, 2026
The FDA authorization was granted on an experimental basis, but it's a key step forward for Neuralink's LINK brain-implant system. The study will evaluate the ability of patients to control digital devices through thought, "with a focus on functional outcomes that improve independence in daily life," Neuralink wrote. It will also assess the system's long-term safety and reliability.
WIth Neuralink's latest system, the company's N1 implant is surgically placed in the skull, then the company uses its R1 robot to insert flexible electrodes into the brain. Neural activity from the brain associated with movement is then interpreted by software, which translates signals into commands for controlling computers or digital devices. The technology is designed to help patients communicate with the outside world, with the eventual goal to let them operate devices without keyboards or other physical controls.
Neuralink said patients with ALS may be eligible for the LINK trial, but it didn't specify other requirements or the number of participants. It now has approval recruit participants, then conduct the study under an approved clinical protocol. If the technology proves to be safe, the trial may allow Neuralink to apply for more advanced trials and eventually release LINK onto the market.

This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026
Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

The wedding of Bihar MLA Anant Singh’s daughter, Shivangi Singh, has been drawing attention online, with coverage now extending beyond India. Shivangi married Rishikesh Kumar, son of CRPF Commandant Ranvijay Kumar, and the event became a talking point, not just for the grandeur of the celebrations but also for the chaos that followed. The wedding took place on Wednesday at Singh’s ancestral home in Nadawan village in Patna. The Mokama MLA, also known as ‘Chhote Sarkar’ across the state, reportedly sent out an open invitation for people to attend the wedding, resulting in a massive turnout. He said, "Koi cinema thodi hai jo ticket lagega (this is not a cinema hall, so nobody needs a ticket)," NDTV reported. With nearly half a million people reportedly present, a figure that has not been verified by Mint, what followed was utter chaos. The family had made arrangements for an estimated four to five lakh guests, with a spread featuring more than 150 dishes. Over 500 halwais (traditional cooks), assisted by hundreds of workers, had been preparing food for several days across four to five massive pandals. A temporary kitchen stretching over 100 feet was set up, with 12 additional tents added when the arrangements fell short. Milk was brought in through tankers, some carrying as much as 10,000 kg. According to reports, 25 lakh rasgullas have been prepared for guests, while another 50 lakh gulab jamuns were made. By evening, a huge crowd had gathered for the feast, as workers distributed plates to attendees. According to NDTV, videos from the wedding surfaced on social media platforms, capturing several aspects of the spectacle, including the chaos. The crowd reportedly overwhelmed the arrangements, after which guests got creative with their eating arrangements. They started using drinking glasses as plates, scooped food straight from giant cooking vessels, and even carried it away in cardboard cartons. Other videos that have taken social media by storm show guests scrambling for sweets. The sweet counter reportedly turned into a battleground, with rasgullas disappearing in the blink of an eye. Describing the situation, one guest in a viral video said, “Getting food here is like winning a war.” The huge turnout also resulted in a massive traffic jam stretching anywhere between five and 10 kilometres, with people arriving in cars, on tractors and on foot. To entertain the guests, Singh did not arrange for a DJ. Instead, a horse race was scheduled. Some spectators found an unusual vantage point atop electricity pylons, where young men climbed the steel structures to watch horses race along a 12-bigha track. Below them, crowds lined the course on all sides, while a new Mahindra Thar stood as the prize for the winner. A total of 52 horses were brought in, with riders from Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, Rajasthan and other states. As the contest progressed, the crowd pushed past the edges and spilled onto the track, prompting the organisers to halt the event and reschedule it. The horse race was not the only attraction. Singh also had a specially built helipad for his VIP guests, who included former BJP MP Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh, who flew in from Uttar Pradesh. Some of the other highlights included the celebrity-like entrance for Singh himself, who rose through the sunroof of an SUV amid a sea of supporters pressed around it. A report noted that he "was arriving for his daughter's wedding, and he did it in a style that would upstage any groom". The groom, Rishikesh Kumar, who holds an MBA degree from Georgia State University in Atlanta, reportedly received a white Land Rover Defender worth ₹3 crore, along with a 100-gram gold chain and an 80-gram gold bracelet. Nathan Lyon and Marnus Labuschagne were dropped from Australia’s squad for the Test series against New Zealand starting on December 9 in Perth.
Off-spinner Corey Rocchiccioli and left-handed batter Jack Clayton have been called up as their replacements in a 13-member squad that will be led by Pat Cummins.
Cricket Australia (CA) chairman of selectors George Bailey said the decision to drop Lyon was taken based on his recent dip in form. After the third Test in South Africa in November, Bailey had revealed Labuschagne would not be considered for selection for the New Zealand Tests after a prolonged period of low scores.
“Nathan has not quite had the impact we would like with the ball in recent matches. We also know he has an extraordinary record and his experience, knowledge and skill can still be valuable to the program we have moving forward,” Bailey said.
“Corey has been a strong performer in domestic cricket for the past few seasons and has traits that are well suited to Australian conditions,” Bailey added.
Lyon, who has taken 577 wickets in 145 Test matches for Australia, took just six wickets in two matches at a lowly average of 43.66 in the recently concluded South Africa series.
His opposite number Simon Harmer, on the other hand, managed 14 wickets in three matches at an average of 29.35.
Beau Webster and Cooper Connolly are other notable exclusions, while one player, likely an opening partner for Travis Head, will be selected after the sixth round of the Sheffield Field.
Australia squad for New Zealand Tests
Pat Cummins (capt), Scott Boland, Alex Carey, Jack Clayton, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Michael Neser, Matthew Renshaw, Corey Rocchiccioli, Steve Smith, Mitchell Starc.
*One player to be added following round six of the Sheffield Shield

Morgan Gibbs-White scored twice as Nottingham Forest beat Chelsea at the City Ground for the first time since 1997.
Igor Jesus' brilliant volley opened the scoring after just five minutes, before Gibbs-White struck twice in the second half as Chelsea were consigned to a fourth defeat in five matches.
Forest ran out 3-2 winners despite Emmanuel Emegha twice pulling goals back.
Here's how I rated the players and how you rated the players.

WhatsApp is exploring ways to let users buy and install a data eSIM for international travel without leaving the app, the company said in a blog post on November 26. The feature will roll out “in select countries soon”.
To offer this additional telecom service, Meta has partnered with:
- Reliance Jio (India)
- Verizon (US)
- Smart Axiata (Cambodia)
- Smart Communications (UK)
- Other eSIM providers and telecom operators
The company did not specify which countries would be included in the initial rollout, how much the plans would cost, or when they would become available. WhatsApp’s head, Kunal Shah, said the company was “starting our early explorations” into eSIMs in a post on X.
How it may work:
“… when you land, you can keep using WhatsApp on your same phone number as you normally would without having to find the closest airport kiosk to buy a local SIM card, hunt for a cafe with Wi-Fi or rack up roaming charges.” – WhatsApp
What the rules say about selling a foreign eSIM in India
Foreign SIM cards are regulated by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) under its revised terms and conditions issued in January 2022. These terms govern the issuance and renewal of no-objection certificates (NOCs) for the sale and rental of international roaming SIM cards and global calling cards issued by foreign telecom operators.
The DoT’s terms require sellers to verify buyers using copies of their passports, valid visas, and proof of identity and address, or through a digital Know Your Customer (KYC) process prescribed by the department. If a traveller does not require a visa for the destination, the seller must collect a valid travel ticket and an undertaking specifying the countries the buyer intends to visit.
The other conditions include:
- The SIM can only be used outside India. The policy does not permit these foreign SIM cards to be used within the country.
- Every eSIM sale must be reported to the government. The eSIM operator must submit monthly reports to security agencies containing complete details of the SIM cards sold or rented, their validity periods, and the purchasers’ addresses.
- The NOC is valid for three years. The DoT can suspend it before its expiry in the interest of national security or in cases of improper conduct.
- The NOC holder must operate a grievance redressal mechanism on par with those offered by Indian companies.
As of December 2024, 29 entities held NOCs, according to the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India’s (TRAI) July 2025 consultation paper on foreign SIMs in export-bound machines.
In January 2024, the DoT directed Google to remove Airalo and Holafly from the Play Store. Apple subsequently removed the apps from its App Store, as MediaNama reported. However, at the time of writing, both Airalo and Holafly were available on the Google Play Store, while only Airalo was available on the Apple App Store.
TRAI recommendations on international SIMs and eSIMs
In February 2025, TRAI recommended introducing an authorisation framework for the sale and rental of international roaming SIM cards and global calling cards issued by foreign telecom operators. It proposed a validity period of ten years for the authorisation. The DoT accepted the recommendation in principle.
Separately, in December 2025, TRAI recommended a dedicated International Machine-to-Machine (M2M) SIM Service Authorisation under Section 3(1)(a) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023. The framework would cover foreign SIM cards and eSIMs embedded in machines manufactured for export. TRAI proposed a processing fee of Rs 5,000, with no entry fee or minimum net-worth requirement.
What could happen when DOT’s SIM binding goes live
On November 28, 2025, the DoT directed eight messaging platforms, including WhatsApp, to keep every account linked to its registered SIM card. The direction also requires platforms to stop providing services to users if their registered SIM is removed, replaced or deactivated.
The direction was issued under the Telecommunications (Telecom Cyber Security) Rules, 2024, which introduced the category of a telecommunication identifier user entity (TIUE) for services that use mobile numbers to identify users.
The initial 90-day compliance period ended on February 26, 2026, but none of the platforms had implemented the requirement by then. The DoT subsequently extended the deadline to December 31, 2026. The requirement is scheduled to become operational from January 1, 2027. Meta confirmed in April 2026 that it was testing SIM binding among regular Indian users.
A messaging app has three ways to comply with SIM binding, according to Parag Kar, an independent telecom consultant, who outlined these methods at a MediaNama roundtable in November 2026:
- The messaging app can ask the device’s operating system (OS), such as Android or iOS, whether the registered SIM card is present in the device.
- The app can query the telecom operator through CAMARA, the GSMA’s interface for network services, to check whether the SIM is active.
- The app can send a standard SMS-based one-time password (OTP) to the user’s mobile number or use silent SIM/device binding over the telecom network to verify the number directly on the device, similar to the methods used by banking and Unified Payments Interface (UPI) apps.
The first method can establish whether a SIM card is present in the device, but not whether it is active. The second and third methods can verify the SIM’s status and activity.
In November 2026, an industry source told MediaNama that the DoT had issued a clarification stating that messaging apps would have to check for the presence of a SIM card every 24 hours.
However, an Indian telecom operator may not be able to identify the Indian SIM as active on its network if a user travels abroad and relies on a data eSIM provided by an operator such as Verizon or Smart Axiata without an active international roaming plan on their Indian SIM. In such a situation, a CAMARA-based lookup may not be able to verify the Indian SIM’s activity. The same limitation could affect SMS-based OTP verification.
If messaging platforms implement SIM binding through either of these methods, users may have to keep their Indian SIM active on an international roaming plan while using a foreign data eSIM abroad.

In July, Montana became the first state to license clinics to offer patients who are not terminally ill drugs and devices that the Food and Drug Administration has not approved. Supporters call state Senate bill 535 a first-in-the-nation expansion of the “right to try.” Critics say it lets patients, including medical tourists from other states, pay out of pocket for unproven therapies. They are both right, in different ways. While the expansion of access to experimental treatments may provide patients with hope, the risks that patients may pay high costs for ineffective and even unsafe treatments remain high.
The goal is to expand access to experimental therapies, with stem cell, anti-aging therapies, and biologics being likely use cases. But the law leaves major questions unanswered: How much will patients pay? Who will bear the cost if complications arise later? And, because these therapies are being used outside a rigorous research setting, how will anyone know whether they actually work?
For patients, a primary concern is likely to be cost. SB535 makes patients financially responsible for the experimental treatment — with the price set by the company supplying the drug or device. The required patient agreement must describe “all the anticipated costs” of the treatment itself. But patients will likely face additional costs, including travel to Montana for those out of state, and follow-up care.
Patients are also, in theory, responsible to pay out of pocket for medical care related to any complications — they are not supposed to go through their insurance companies. But how will insurers determine if a medical problem stems from an experimental treatment? That’s left ambiguous by the law. Long-term medical effects will be particularly hard to trace, especially if a product hasn’t yet had robust safety testing and documentation of its long-term side effects. Thus, care for complications may fall on patients, or it may be paid by insurers who had no say in the use of an experimental treatment.
And how are people to judge whether a treatment is worth its price? For approved therapies, there’s trial data on survival rates, plus continued post-market study. These data help clarify the expected benefits for specific patients. SB535 does not require companies to conduct comparable analyses, nor are companies bound to set prices with any value framework in mind.
Proponents of SB535 argue that skipping costly trials will lower development costs and, eventually, prices. However, if companies wish to generate evidence for conventional FDA approval, they will need to go beyond the requirements in SB535. If they fail to collect detailed patient characteristics such as history of disease and patient demographics, it will be hard to determine how the drug might work in a larger patient population. Supporters say the data will resemble real-world evidence, but the validity of real-world evidence still depends on clear study methods and consistent data collection and reporting.
It’s also possible that SB535 could undermine the rigorous testing needed for FDA approval. That’s because SB535 does not require the same patient protections, data collection requirements, or oversight that the FDA requires. Some companies may forgo the clinical trial FDA pathway entirely, while others may find that direct access disincentivizes patients from enrolling in trials.
None of this means patients with few options for treatment should be dismissed or ignored. But they can make an informed decision about how much to pay for treatment only if the true costs and risks are visible. Montana currently has no systematic way to assess how patients interpret costs, what they actually incur and pay, or how those costs relate to short- and long-term outcomes.
If other states want to expand access to experimental treatment, there are other models they could look to, such as CMS’s Coverage with Evidence Development. It requires systematic collection and reporting of data on clinical effectiveness and short- and long-term harms.
States could also require companies to collect data on outcomes for 15 years, just like the FDA does for cell and gene therapies. These types of data can enable transparency and may help patients make informed decisions about potential treatments in consultation with their care team.
Montana can still move in that direction by requiring standardized cost disclosure before consent, a registry with defined long-term follow-up, and independent evaluation of financial and clinical outcomes.
Without those steps, we will not know whether state right to try laws can be a cost-effective way to generate evidence and access to emerging therapeutics. Patients who try may be left physically and financially vulnerable, with little knowledge gained from their risk.
Skye A. Miner is a behavioral and social scientist at RAND, a nonprofit, nonpartisan research institution. She specializes in the ethics of emerging technologies. Hannah O. James is an associate policy researcher at RAND who researches the value of U.S. health care spending and state-level health policies.

Srinagar- The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), Srinagar Bench, has declined to defer the Jammu and Kashmir Police Sub-Inspector examination scheduled for November 29, allowing the Jammu and Kashmir Services Selection Board (JKSSB) to conduct the test as per schedule.
The Board on Friday informed candidates and the general public that the OMR-based written examination for the post of Sub-Inspector in the Home Department will be held on Sunday, November 29, 2026.
The matter came up before the tribunal in Original Application (O.A.) No. 1326/2026, titled Bilal Ahmad Khoja and Others versus Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir and Others.
The applicants had approached the CAT seeking interim directions to defer the upcoming SI examination and stay further recruitment proceedings for the Finance Accounts Assistant (FAA) posts, for which the examination was held on November 15, 2026.
They had raised concerns over the fairness, transparency and sanctity of the examination process.
In response, the JKSSB placed before the tribunal the existing government protocols, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and additional preventive measures recently notified by its Controller of Examinations to ensure fairness and transparency in the upcoming SI examination.
Taking note of the safeguards presented by the Board, the tribunal declined to grant interim relief to stay the FAA recruitment process and also refused to defer the November 29 SI examination.
The JKSSB reiterated its commitment to conducting free, fair and transparent examinations and advised candidates to focus on their preparations.
It also urged aspirants to rely exclusively on information published on the Board’s official website and refrain from paying heed to false, misleading or fabricated rumours.

- Players can use private chat in Roblox to message others without worrying about the privacy.
- Click or tap a player's username in the chat to start a private conversation.
- Players can also use the /w or /whisper command to send a private message to a specific player.
Chatting with friends on a public server can get weird, especially when you realize other players in the lobby can read and react to it. Luckily, Roblox has a private chat feature that lets you keep things private. In this guide, we will tell you how to use private chat in Roblox.
What Is Private Chat in Roblox?
Private chat is a feature that lets you send private messages to other players in Roblox while playing an experience. This is useful when you want to talk to a friend without everyone else reading your messages. Follow these steps to start a private conversation inside a Roblox experience:
- Join a Roblox game.
- Open the chat box by pressing the [/] key on PC or tapping the chat icon on mobile.
- Wait for other players or someone to send a message in the chat.
- Click or tap on their username.
- Type your message and press Enter or Send.
This lets you send a message privately without worrying about privacy. Keep in mind that you need to verify your age on Roblox to text.
How to Whisper in Roblox
You can also use a command to send private messages in Roblox without selecting a username.
- Open the in-game chat.
- Type /w and select /whisper
- Press space and enter the player’s username.
- Add another space and type your message.
- Press Enter or tap Send.
For example, type ‘/whisper Player123 Hello!’ to whisper to that player.
Note: The private chat does not stay in Roblox chat history.
That is how you create private chat in Roblox. Do you think Roblox should make this feature simpler? Let us know in the comments.
Can other players see private messages in Roblox?
Once you start a private chat, only you and the other person you are talking to can see the chat.
What happens to the chat if I leave the experience?
Private chats are temporary and will be deleted once you leave or join another experience.

How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia
Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.
"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."
Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.
"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."
The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.
Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.
That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.
The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.
A sacred day for all
Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."
Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well
"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."
When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.
"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.
Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.
"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."
The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.
"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."
Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."
(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")
"I'm thanking God"
This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.
Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."
Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.
"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

From Mahanadi Coalfields’ IPO drawing strong institutional demand despite a muted retail response and Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO to faster US economic growth amid persistent inflation, a slowdown in vehicle sales in the festival season and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi’s record-breaking double century in men’s List A cricket, here is this week’s news in numbers.
Selective appetite
Mahanadi Coalfields’ ₹8,981-crore IPO closed with an overall subscription of 1.52 times, driven overwhelmingly by qualified institutional buyers (QIBs), whose reserved portion was subscribed nearly five times. Retail investors subscribed to just 0.46 times their allotted portion, while non-institutional and existing shareholder categories remained undersubscribed.
The company’s shares are scheduled to list on 27 November. The IPO comprises a 10% stake sale by parent Coal India through an offer for sale (OFS), meaning the proceeds will go to Coal India rather than Mahanadi Coalfields. India’s largest coal producer, Mahanadi accounted for around 21% of domestic output in FY26, producing 218.31 million tonnes. However, its production fell 3.1% from the previous year, while revenue and net profit also declined marginally. It remained Coal India’s largest subsidiary by production.
Plot twist
Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, 11 days after his resignation amid reports of his alleged relationship with a Chinese spy. The announcement sent the chipmaker's shares soaring 31.5%, marking its third-largest single-day gain since its 1999 listing. Most of Nvidia's biggest daily gains came during the dot-com era of the early 2000s, with only three of its 10 biggest rallies recorded in the 2010s and 2020s.
The stock had fallen 24.5% between Huang's resignation on 12 November and 20 November. The decline coincided with a broader sell-off in AI-linked stocks, even as Indian equities rallied amid renewed foreign investor inflows. The controversy first emerged on 29 October, when reports linked Huang to a Singapore-based businesswoman suspected by US intelligence officials of having ties to Chinese intelligence.
Economic pulse
The US economy grew at an annualised rate of 4.3% in the third quarter of 2026, its fastest pace in three years, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. This was higher than the advance estimate of 3.4% and the growth of 2.2% in the previous quarter. The stronger-than-expected growth comes as the US continues to grapple with persistent inflation, complicating the Federal Reserve's efforts to bring price increases under control.
The Fed's preferred gauge, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, rose 3.8% year-on-year in October, up from 3.7% in September. Core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy, increased to 3.3%, its highest in three years. Both measures rose 0.3% from the previous month. The combination of strong growth and persistent inflation leaves the Federal Reserve with less room to cut interest rates. Markets are pricing in another 25-basis-point rate increase at its 8-9 December meeting. The final decision will depend on incoming economic data and policymakers' assessment of inflation.
Numbers Talk
56.3: HSBC Flash India Composite PMI in October, marginally up from 56.2. Manufacturing activity rose to a nine-month high of 56.0 from 54.7, while services activity eased to 55.3.
15%: Decline expected in India’s sugar production to 26.5 million tonnes in the 2026-27 season due to smaller cane area and uneven rainfall, the Indian Sugar and Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) said on Wednesday.
₹15,000 crore: The value of India's development assistance project for Nepal announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday during talks with Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah.
96%: The share of employees in India who use artificial intelligence (AI) daily or two to three times a week, the highest among nine Asia-Pacific markets surveyed by Boston Consulting Group (BCG).
18.8%:The year-on-year growth in unincorporated non-agricultural establishments to 9.47 crore in July–September 2026, according to the quarterly bulletin of the ASUSE.
Lower gear
Vehicle retail sales growth slowed sharply during the 2026 festive season, with registrations rising just 2.2% year-on-year, compared with 21.3% in 2025 and 11.8% in 2024, according to the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA). Growth moderated across all major vehicle categories. Two-wheeler sales rose 3.7%, down from 21.6% a year earlier, while commercial vehicle growth more than halved to 7.1% from 15.1%.
Passenger vehicle registrations fell 7.2%, reversing a 25.4% increase in the previous festive season. The slowdown follows an exceptional 2025, when GST rate cuts lowered vehicle prices and helped release pent-up demand, creating a high base for comparison. Higher inflation may also have weighed on spending, with retail inflation rising to 6.1% in October and food inflation reaching 8.9%. Geopolitical tensions have added to uncertainty over energy prices and the economic outlook.
Cricket sensation
Fifteen-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi rewrote the men’s List A cricket record books on 24 November, scoring 204 off just 53 balls for India A against the UAE in the Rising Stars Asia Cup in Doha. He reached his double century in 52 balls, becoming the fastest batter to the milestone in List A cricket.
The previous record, held by New Zealand's Chad Bowes, stood at 103 balls—almost twice as long. Sooryavanshi also struck the fastest List A century, off 28 balls, and the fastest 150, off 40 balls. His innings included 28 sixes, the most in a men's List A innings. Shubman Gill also features among the fastest List A double-centurions, having reached 200 in 117 balls against the West Indies in September. List A cricket covers recognised senior one-day matches, including ODIs and domestic 50-over games.

The Indian contingent returned from the ITTF World Youth Championships 2026 with one medal after the Under-19 Boys Team won bronze in Istanbul, Turkey.

Earlier this month, drones and ground robots searched simulated disaster zones in a competition testing whether machines could help military medics quickly find casualties and identify which needed lifesaving care first.
It was all part of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency's "Triage Challenge," an event meant to test companies and universities on whether their tech could be a viable solution for medics on future battlefields filled with enemy drones and AI.
DARPA is the Pentagon's research arm tasked with finding potential answers to tough military problems, like how missiles can strike their targets when GPS disappears and how to stop adversaries from wrecking havoc on economic markets.
At the Disaster City facility in College Station, Texas, a facility built to replicate disasters to test emergency response teams, medics and robots faced scenarios like responding to tornado destruction and a nighttime attack on a military outpost.
Ground robots and drones had 15 minutes to find actors and mannequins representing wounded troops and civilians. In another test, they were given the casualties' locations and had five minutes to assess how urgently they needed help.
The machines also had to identify injuries, check whether casualties responded, and decide who needed to be evacuated first — all without touching patients.
Jeremy Pamplin, the event's program manager and a retired Army physician, told Business Insider in September that rapid triage focused on severe bleeding and breathing problems, identifying someone a medic needed to reach immediately.
"Teams have to get out there, recognize these problems really fast and say, 'yep, that's somebody you got to go see right now," he said. Robots and drones could help medics find "needles in the haystack," he said of simulated patients, "to try to save the most lives they possibly can."
Military officials have previously warned that the US military is unlikely to control the air in future conflicts, potentially leading to major casualty evacuation challenges the US military has not experienced in decades. That prospect has prompted medical units to begin training to treat frontline casualties for days, or even weeks, before they might receive advanced care.
Drones scouted ahead of medics and ground robots, sending casualty information to the medics' phones. A separate element of the event tested whether algorithms could predict what treatment patients would need hours later.
In a major war, medics may have to focus scarce resources on casualties they can save, an ethical dilemma most medical providers in the US military have little experience confronting.
Pamplin hopes technology can help medics make such decisions with better information. Robots could locate and assess casualties while predictive algorithms help medics anticipate what treatment each patient needs and how long they can wait.
That type of mechanical help might aid medics not just by saving more lives, he said, but also by "relieving the burden of doubt from our young medics and war fighters as they're trying to manage those situations."

Formula 1's one-race wonders
- Published
You've been handed the chance of a lifetime.
A chance to sit in the cockpit, on the grid, at motorsport's top table: Formula 1. The very pinnacle of everything you've strived for in your whole life.
What would you do?
"I sang the Grand Prix theme tune while I was sat on the grid. I thought I was watching it on telly," says Tiff Needell - one of 166 lucky or unlucky drivers, depending on your standing in motorsport, who graced an F1 race only once.
There are many reasons why a driver may only get one chance to race elite sport's fastest and most sophisticated machines, and, although F1's super subs were more of a feature in the 1960s and 1970s, the helmet-for-hire phenomenon is alive and driving in ultra-professional, modern F1.
Just ask Japan's Ryo Hirakawa, who only last month achieved his "dream", external when he got behind the wheel of a Haas at the Mexican Grand Prix following Esteban Ocon's controversial departure from the team.
"I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy," Hirakawa said after scoring a point - admittedly, following a few demotions for others. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."
Within a week there was nothing the Toyota factory driver could do as Haas' 2027 driver Rafael Camara was drafted in for the American team early, for the rest of 2026.
Hirakawa is a reserve driver for Haas as a result of the team's association with Toyota - the Japanese being in the right place at the right time.
The percentage of F1 test and reserve drivers who make it to the grid is typically low, and those who do tend to be drafted in for one shot at very unlikely glory.
The days of the aristocrat who fancies a pootle around the track are gone, and years of preparation are required even to be standing in the pit garage.
Injuries, sponsorship fails and outright cheating are just some of the reasons why it does not work out for some hopefuls.
Needell, known better for his time behind the wheel on Top Gear and other auto TV shows, got his big break at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. But his journey to the paddock was initiated a few years earlier - in the media.
"I won a car in a magazine competition," he says. "I was the kid on the terraces, on the fences - and made it on to the grid. We had no money at all in our family, so I was a working civil engineer five days a week and a mechanic in my garage five nights a week. At the weekend I was the van driver, the mechanic and the racing driver.
"I bumbled my way up to the top of the national scene and then got offered a professional drive in Formula 3. And after two years of that I moved up into the [long since defunct] Formula 1 British championship.
"I was out at the Nurburgring trying to get an F1 drive when I got the call. I was hanging around the paddock trying to chat up an F2 team, trying to say I had a sponsor, which of course I didn't.
"Ensign called me and said: 'This weekend would you like to drive?' I rushed home from the Nurburgring in my orange Ford Capri, had half a day's test at Donington and on to qualifying for the Belgian GP at Zolder.
"I got my chance because Clay Regazzoni crashed and hurt his back at Long Beach.
"A lot of that in the olden days was due to injuries - chances would come up when someone had crashed and got injured. It was dangerous back then."
Needell was in, but this was old-school F1 where you had to pre-qualify to show you were fast enough to qualify for the Grand Prix itself.
"There was something like 30 drivers trying to pre-qualify, and somehow I made it to the back of the grid - 23rd in the Ensign. It was so much cheaper then - aluminium chassis and a Cosworth DFV engine and away you go."
While the back of the grid beckoned, a 29-year-old Needell was in very good company in the form of double world champion Emerson Fittipaldi, who was having a bad weekend in his Skol Fittipaldi car.
"I found myself on the back row of the grid, sitting by one of my big heroes. It was all a bit of a dream," says Needell.
In contrast to today's VIP treatment, Needell's parents and his girlfriend (now wife) drove to Belgium in the family car and watched from the crowd as he lined up on the grid.
"When the mechanics started the engine and left me sitting there - me and Emerson - I actually started humming the theme tune [to Fleetwood Mac's The Chain]," Needell says.
"For 12 laps I battled with Emerson for the honour of being last place at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. Then the engine broke."
A failed attempt to qualify for Monaco a week later put the brakes on his F1 dream and eventually resulted in Needell pursuing a career as a Le Mans racer and TV presenter.
Often the reason F1 careers could be so fleeting would be of a driver's own making.
Hans Heyer did not qualify for his one and only race - the 1977 German Grand Prix at Hockenheim - but he thought he would contest it anyway, starting from the pit lane for the ATS team in a car that was never supposed to be there.
The German may have achieved his dream at his home race, but it came with disqualification after he had already retired with gearbox failure on lap nine.
And what of Marco Apicella? It has taken 73 years, since Alberto Ascari triumphed, for Italy to celebrate one of its own F1 world champions in Kimi Antonelli as he secured the 2026 title in Mexico last month.
For a country and a Ferrari team so important to the sport, that is a long time to wait - and Apicella was a good example of why it may have taken a while.
Rushed in at the last minute after only two hours of testing to replace a disgruntled, if experienced, Thierry Boutsen in the underwhelming 1993 Jordan, Apicella lasted approximately 800 metres of his home race after a multi-car collision during the first lap of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.
That was the end of Apicella's F1 career and he would end up embarking on five unsuccessful attempts to win Le Mans.
1 of 5
So what's the best any of the one-hit wonders have done in their first and only grand prix?
There have been a smattering of points finishes over the years, and Dorino Serafini's shared second place on the podium with legend Ascari at Monza in the final race of F1's maiden season is difficult to top for an F1 one-shot.
But Germany's Markus Winkelhock is surely up there as one of sport's super-sub icons of the modern era.
A last-minute replacement in the newly acquired, yet painfully slow, Spyker team's car at the 2007 European Grand Prix at the Nurburgring, the touring car driver took up the F1 super sub's favoured qualifying position on the grid: last place.
F1 ran in Winkelhock's family - father Manfred contested 56 grands prix in the eighties before his death from a crash during a sportscar race in 1985.
But Markus went one better than his uncle Jo, who never contested an F1 race despite trying to qualify seven times.
But, by his own admission, Winkelhock was a long way from ready. "I had one day testing in Silverstone and one day in Paul Ricard," Winkelhock told Motorsport magazine., external
"The first couple of laps it felt like a PlayStation - so unreal, everything was so fast. You're accelerating till you reach the braking point.
"But after all the [practice] sessions I could feel my neck already.
"I told my mechanics to put some beddings on the side of the headrest, in case the neck is completely done, to lean on with the helmet."
Then came some early rain from the Eifel mountains and an inspired decision from the pitwall of a team with very little to lose.
Winkelhock was on exactly the right tyres, at exactly the right time, as the rain came down, and Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button slid helplessly into the gravel trap along with several others.
Winkelhock's orange Spyker simply danced through the rivers of rainwater flowing across the tarmac, sitting 33 seconds ahead of the field - a country mile for F1.
He said: "I didn't know it was for the lead. I was just driving. At the point they told me, 'You're P1'. I really didn't understand anything that was going on because this race was really crazy."
But when the rain stopped, so did Winklehock - first swallowed up by the faster cars on a drying track, and then by a hydraulic issue on lap 15, having led for six laps.
Make no mistake, a lost F1 career is very often a driver's glittering career in the making in sportscars at Le Mans, or on the ovals of American Indycar.
But even back in the day when other sporting codes, such as rallying's frighteningly fast Group B, were at the height of their popularity, F1 was the pinnacle for most.
"Being a grand prix driver was where you wanted to go," concludes Needell. "But I always had my eye sideways for any other drives.
"Single-seaters are the best cars to drive and they are made and designed to race. And the ultimate is the grand prix car. Everything else is second best.
"I was so proud I got there on no sponsorship and no money. I suppose I was a bit annoyed I couldn't stay for longer.
"But as I always say, 'unluckier than a few, but luckier than millions'."

People with higher levels of mindfulness are more likely to have healthier social media habits and better mental health outcomes, according to a review of 43 studies involving more than 28,000 participants.
Mindfulness involves observing one’s thoughts and feelings without judgement.
Researchers led by University College London analysed the studies and found that people who reported being more mindful in their daily lives were more likely to report healthier patterns of social media use.
The findings, published in the journal PLOS One, also showed that higher levels of mindfulness were associated with lower levels of depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness and fear of missing out (FoMO).
Previous studies have shown that cultivating mindfulness through practices such as meditation or mindfulness-based therapy can help reduce symptoms of stress, anxiety and depression.
The review contributes to the debate over whether social media use poses a risk to mental health or aggravates existing mental health problems, the researchers said.
Lead author Dr Marc S Tibber from University College London’s Division of Psychology and Language Sciences said the findings supported a shift away from simplistic questions about whether social media was inherently good or bad.
“Our findings support a move away from reductive questions about whether social media is inherently good or bad, towards an exploration of how complex interactions between individuals, technologies, and the broader social contexts in which they are embedded shape both the potential benefits and harms of social media for mental health,” Tibber said.
The review suggested that mindfulness may play a protective role, he said, adding that it could be a potential target for interventions aimed at promoting healthier digital engagement, although further research was needed.
The studies included participants aged 10 to 92, with university students accounting for the largest group at 46.5 %.
The analysis found that mindfulness, including mindful use of social media, appeared to weaken the association between online experiences and poorer mental health outcomes.
In one of the studies, participants were asked to complete mindfulness exercises, monitor their smartphone use and track their moods. The study found significant improvements in stress, anxiety, FoMO and problematic social media use.
Tibber said the findings were consistent with his observations as a clinician, suggesting that mindfulness could help people develop a healthier relationship with social media.
“By supporting people to notice their thoughts, feelings, and impulses without immediately acting on them, mindfulness may make it easier to step back from habitual reactions, direct attention more deliberately, and engage with social media in a more intentional way,” he said.
“This matters in an online environment where platforms are designed to attract and retain our attention,” Tibber added.

Prosecutors ask for 25 years for man who sold products used by 93 to kill themselves
Prosecutors sought a 25-year prison sentence for a Canadian man who sold products online knowing buyers were likely to use them to kill themselves
NEWMARKET, Ontario -- Ontario prosecutors on Friday sought a 25-year prison sentence for a Canadian man who pleaded guilty to aiding 14 suicides after selling products online knowing buyers were likely to use them to kill themselves.
Kenneth Law, 61, apologized to victims’ families from the prisoner’s box, saying that his actions were “categorically wrong” and promising never to repeat them.
Prosecutors argued that Law was motivated by money. His lawyers sought a 12-year sentence, describing him as a misguided believer in the right to die rather than a “mercenary predator.” A sentencing decision is expected in February.
Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of counseling or aiding suicide involving people in Ontario. The judge is also considering the deaths of 79 people in the United Kingdom.
At a hearing in September, families of people who died after buying lethal products from Law described their lives shattered by grief. Police said Law sold sodium nitrite, a substance commonly used to cure meats that can be deadly if ingested.

Prosecutor Katie Doherty said 93 people, including 12 teenagers, died after using Law’s products.
“These were vulnerable people ... What they needed was help, but what they found was Mr. Law and his products for death,” she said. Doherty rejected suggestions that Law acted altruistically, saying he sold to anyone who paid upfront.
The former chef shipped products to more than 40 countries over nearly 2 1/2 years, knowing customers were likely to use them to kill themselves, according to an agreed statement of facts.
Defense lawyer Matthew Gourlay argued that Law did not cause customers’ struggles or their decisions to kill themselves. “In short, Mr. Law did not kill anyone,” he said.
Aiding suicide carries a maximum sentence of 14 years in Canada. Prosecutors requested 12 1/2 years on each count, with two terms served back to back and the others at the same time.
Credit for time in custody would reduce the proposed term to about 19 years and eight months. The defense sought additional credit for harsh detention conditions.
Prosecutors acknowledged Law’s guilty plea spared families a trial and that he had no prior criminal record. Law has been detained since May 2023. Prosecutors are expected to withdraw 14 first-degree murder charges after sentencing.
Authorities in the United States, Italy, Australia and New Zealand also have investigated the case. A prosecutor had said that it involves some 431 packages of lethal substances that were sent to the U.S.

COPENHAGEN, Denmark—If we lived in the world that Volvo’s product planners expected back when the current XC90 debuted in 2015, both it and the smaller but related XC60 (which arrived in 2017) might have been the last of their kind as everything went electric. As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in the critically important US market. At the same time, Europe and China are electrifying, which seems like an argument against spending resources on developing all-new replacements for models that might not have an eight-year lifespan in most markets.
So instead, Volvo has given the XC60 and XC90 another lifecycle refresh. The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. And that’s no bad thing—both were, and remain, handsome shapes that are popular with Volvo’s customer base.
Instead, the Swedish automaker’s attention has been on bringing the technology up to date for model year 2028 standards. Which means a much bigger battery for the PHEVs, with sufficient capacity for a couple of days of daily driving for most of us before needing to be recharged. There’s also new, modern infotainment and interiors that are now even nicer to spend time in than before.

We first saw the revamped 2028 XC60 (and learned about its technical details and those of the XC90) in September, but with the cars going into production now and due to reach the first US customers in the first quarter of next year, we got the opportunity to spend some seat time with the updated cars.
Charge!
Both the midsize XC60 and three-row XC90 use the same PHEV powertrain. Under the hood, there’s a 2.0 L four-cylinder direct-injection gasoline engine that generates 247 hp (184 kW) and 226 lb-ft (306 Nm) together with a 70 hp (50 kW), 122 ft-lb (165 Nm) electric motor, both of which drive the front wheels. At the rear axle there’s a second electric motor, with an output of 174 hp (130 kW) and 228 lb-ft (309 Nm). Combined output for the hybrid system is 455 hp (339 kW) and 560 lb-ft (759 Nm).
There’s also a much bigger battery, with a net capacity of 37.9 kWh (41.2 kWh gross). If you set the car’s mode to Pure, which relies solely on the rear electric motor for propulsion, that translates to an EPA range estimate of 78 miles (126 km) for the XC60 and 73 miles (116 km) for the larger, draggier XC90. Which is significant—when the average driver drives fewer than 30 miles a day, it means these PHEVs carry enough electrons for a couple of days of tailpipe-emissions-free driving before it needs to be plugged in again or the engine to fire up.
There are new matrix LED headlights but still with the Thor’s Hammer DRL.

When it is time to plug it back in, expect it to take about four hours with a level 2 charger of at least 16 A, or 27 hours if you’re limited to 120 V. In Hybrid mode, where you get the benefit of both electric motors and the gas engine, Volvo expects a combined efficiency of 67 mpge in the XC60, and 61 mpge for the XC90.
Even if the gas engine is running and you’re in Hybrid or Power mode (which keeps the engine on all the time), you can drive these Volvos as if they were EVs with one-pedal driving: just move the transmission from D to B. The Volvos are always using their electric motors to slow the car before the friction brakes intervene, and in B you get the same amount of lift-off regen regardless of mode. For city traffic, it’s very effective. (In Pure, although only the rear motor deploys energy, both front and rear motors regen brake.)
In power mode, with all 455 hp unleashed, you can chirp the wheels on a wet day, but these model year 2028 cars are about one large male human heavier than the outgoing model year, both of which were already pretty heavy. So don’t expect performance-car performance. The XC60 is the sweeter to drive on a winding road, but both are entirely at home cruising on a highway or creeping along in a city, which is where cars like these spend the vast majority of their time. There’s more road intrusion into the cabin of the XC60—the larger Volvo rides on air suspension that does a much better job of filtering that out.
The XC90 is a more cosseting experience.
Credit:
Volvo
The XC90 is a more cosseting experience.
Credit:
Volvo
A first-drive event like this isn’t the best place to get a good read on real-world efficiency. We usually have to share cars with other journalists, and there’s limited time to drive on roads that may not be representative—too sinuous, or not enough traffic, for example. We need to try all the different drive modes and see how cars respond to different inputs. And it’s rare you’ll spend the entire day with one car, finishing at the same point you started.
That said, I can’t give you a definite read on range and efficiency for these two plug-ins. But my unscientific estimate is that my drive partner and I, in an XC60, drove about 60 km in a mix of city driving and higher speeds on the way to Malmo in Sweden, which is on the other side of a gigantic bridge, and we used about half the battery pack to do so. (Volvo asked us to put the PHEVs in Hold or Charge mode at 50 percent to leave some state of charge for whoever drove the cars after lunch.)
Thus, there was little charge left in the XC90 when it was my turn to drive the final stint back into Copenhagen. Since I wasn’t worried about combined efficiency, I ran the car in Charge mode for about 20 min, regenerating the battery from an indicated 10 km to an indicated 21 km, then switched to Pure once we reached the city, with about 16 km to go.
