Massage time
Volvo already had a reputation for great automotive interiors, and with this refresh, it has pushed things forward a little. There’s a new wood finish, new textiles, and new backlighting. The resemblance between the two interiors from the front seat is now quite strong, particularly since the test cars Volvo brought to Denmark wore identical color schemes inside.
Our final 1.6 km to the hotel took more than 30 minutes to negotiate thanks to a reception for very important people that apparently took place next to the hotel. Most of this jam was on one street, with our destination in sight, but the frustration was in part ameliorated by Volvo’s secret weapon: its seat massage function.
Lots of other OEMs offer massaging front seats, which inflate and deflate the internal air bladder to massage your shoulders, back, and sometimes butt. But none massage you with quite the firmness of a Volvo seat. And they have the power to distract you from terrible in-car situations, as I discovered when stuck in a V90 Cross Country with Nigel the Cat, whose way of remonstrating with me about his trip to the feline ophthalmologist was to scream at high volume until he ran out of breath, at which point he’d pant for a few minutes, then start again. The seat in that car is the only reason we both made it home safely. And so, in Copenhagen, I set the seat to pulse and did some box breathing.

As well as new interior materials, you’ll also notice a new infotainment screen in both cars. Gone are the old 9-inch displays, replaced by a new 11.2-inch touchscreen that stands a little proud of the dash rather than recessed into it. Just this one upgrade alone really lifts both interiors; the old, small screen was showing its age. Most Ars readers will recoil at the news that Gemini has replaced the previous Google Assistant, but at least the voice-recognition capabilities are improved. Gemini will still struggle with some commands—I asked it to tell me my current efficiency, which it failed at, but it’s rather good at looking stuff up on the Internet while I drive.
There are also some updated advanced driver-assistance systems, like a warning if cyclists approach your opening door, and an updated 360-degree parking view. But there’s no point-to-point assist like Mercedes is introducing, or a hands-free “level 2+” system like Super Cruise; Volvo’s experience with the EX90 may have left it a little gun-shy.
With a battery big enough for daily driving and a more modern interior experience, there’s a lot to like about both the 2029 XC60 and XC90. However, we still don’t know how much they’ll cost when they go on sale in Q1 next year. With twice the battery capacity, it’s reasonable to expect a slight price rise, but without knowing how much, it’s hard to say whether it’s a good deal or not.
Jonathan is the Automotive Editor at Ars Technica. He has a BSc and PhD in Pharmacology. In 2014 he decided to indulge his lifelong passion for the car by leaving the National Human Genome Research Institute and launching Ars Technica's automotive coverage. He lives in Washington, DC.

An 18-second-long video has been circulating on social media, which shows Sandeep Khirwar, Special Director General (SDG) of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), making a remark regarding the transportation of the bodies of two Special Police Officers (SPOs) in a dumper truck.
In the viral clip, Khirwar can be heard saying, “All military trucks and vehicles in the area were occupied. So we had no choice but to transport the bodies of our two martyred SPO personnel in a dumper truck. But the real issue is not whether they were transported in a dumper or a garbage truck. Their families received the bodies of their loved ones. What more could they possibly want?”
X user @cutegirlindia21 shared this video and wrote, “Kashmir Police Chief has stated that the bodies of 2 martyred Kishtwar Police officers had to be transported in a garbage truck. The bodies were placed alongside garbage after the Indian Army refused to provide an ambulance to the Kashmir Police.”
🛑 Heartbreaking 💔 😢
Kashmir Police Chief has stated that the bodies of 2 martyred @KishtwarPolice officers had to be transported in a #garbage truck. The bodies were placed alongside garbage after the #IndianArmy refused to provide an ambulance to the Kashmir Police. https://t.co/Jm9i7bScN0
— A N U S H I ❤️T I W A R I🇮🇳 (@cutegirlindia21) November 16, 2026
According to an NDTV report published on November 14, the bodies of SPOs Bobby Chand and Rashpal Kumar — who lost their lives in a recent terror attack in the Kishtwar district of Jammu and Kashmir — were transported to their native village Kiyar in a dumper truck without coffins. This incident sparked significant outrage among locals, with many questioning the manner in which the bodies were transported.
Against this backdrop, the purported video of SDG Sandeep Khirwar began to circulate. Several other users on X, including @RedDeFactoIND, @NetaNamax, and @unknownnewss, also shared the video with similar claims.
The video is also circulating on Facebook with similar assertions.
Fact Check
To determine the authenticity of the viral clip, Alt News used relevant keywords to search for information regarding statements made by Khirwar. We did not find any credible news reports or official statements that substantiate the claims made in the viral clip.
We observed that the viral video bears an ANI logo. Performing a ‘reverse image search’ using keyframes from the clip, we found the original video, which was posted by ANI on its official X account on November 16, 2026. In the video, Sandeep Khirwar, SDG of the CRPF’s Jammu & Kashmir Zone, is seen speaking to the media in Srinagar regarding the deaths of two SPOs in Kishtwar.
#WATCH | Srinagar, J&K: On the mortal remains of two missing SPOs recovered in Kishtwar, SDG, CRPF J&K Zone, Sandeep Khirwar says, “Every loss of life to any jawan in the security forces is a huge loss to all of us… We stand with their families, and we will make sure that they get justice.”
— ANI (@ANI) November 16, 2026
While the visuals of the video matches, the audio is different. In the original footage, Khirwar states: “All I can say is that, every loss of life to any Jawan, of any security forces are huge loss to all of us and we owe our utmost respect to all the fallen. And we stand with their family. We will make sure that they get justice, the families get justice.” He does not make any mention of the bodies being transported in a dumper truck, nor did he claim that the families were ‘grateful’ upon the recovery of the bodies.
Further, we found that the Khirwar’s voice and manner of speaking in the viral clip does not match the way he is heard speaking in the ANI footage, indicating that the original audio has been digitally altered or manipulated. We ran the viral clip through AI-detection Hive Moderation, which revealed that it is 98.9% likely to contain AI-generated speech.
On November 17, the official X handle of the CRPF’s Srinagar Sector addressed the viral claim. They stated that the video had been digitally tampered with and that false statements had been attributed to Sandeep Khirwar, clarifying that no such statements were made by him.
This claim is false and misleading. The video was digitally manipulated, with fabricated remarks attributed to CRPF Special DG Sh. Sandeep Khirwar, who is not the Kashmir Police Chief. The original footage contained no such statement. This is an attempt to spread misinformation and create an anti-India narrative.
— Srinagar Sector CRPF 🇮🇳 (@crpf_srinagar) November 17, 2026
Thus, the viral clip has been digitally manipulated using AI, falsely attributing statements about the transportation of SPOs’ bodies in a dumper truck to Sandeep Khirwar. The original footage by ANI does not carry any such comment.
Sajahan Ali is an intern at Alt News.

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.
Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
Following a Yellow Level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

Quick Answer
To schedule a message on WhatsApp, open a chat, compose your message, press and hold the send button, select a date and time, and confirm. You can schedule texts, images, and videos in individual and group chats from 10 minutes to 14 days in advance, even if your phone will be offline or switched off.
Ever been in a situation where you wanted to text someone on WhatsApp on a particular day, but forgot when the day arrived? Well, you can rejoice, as the Meta-owned chat app is finally introducing the ability to schedule messages on WhatsApp.
Message scheduling is one of the most requested features, WhatsApp says. And quite rightly so, since apps like Google Messages, Signal, and Telegram have had it for a while. Nevertheless, it’s good to see it finally catching up with the competition. Here’s everything you need to know about scheduling messages on WhatsApp.
How Do Scheduled Messages Work on WhatsApp?
Scheduled messages, like standard WhatsApp messages, support text, images, and videos. You can schedule a message anywhere from 10 minutes to 14 days ahead of time, in both individual (one-to-one) and group chats.
Once scheduled, WhatsApp automatically sends the message at the set time, even if your phone is offline or switched off. The recipient sees it as a standard message; there are no indicators to tell that the message was scheduled.
How to Schedule Messages on WhatsApp
WhatsApp hasn’t introduced a separate button to schedule messages for later, nor has it nestled it under multiple menus. Instead, it has built the functionality directly into the send button, which you currently use to send messages. If you’ve used scheduled messages on apps like Signal, Telegram, and Google Messages, you’ll feel right at home with scheduling WhatsApp messages.
Once message scheduling is available, you can schedule a WhatsApp message like this:
- Open WhatsApp and go to the individual or group chat for which you want to schedule your message.
- Type your message or attach photos or videos, like you normally do.
- Now, instead of tapping the send button, press and hold it until you see the date and time picker pop-up on the screen.
- Set the date and time when you want the message to go out.
- Confirm by tapping the green send button (with your scheduled date and time) at the bottom.
That’s it! Your message will now be sent on the specified date and time.
WhatsApp says all your scheduled messages appear in one place, and you can delete the ones you no longer want to send if you change your mind. (We’ll update this guide with instructions on how to do that once we get our hands on the feature.)
Scheduled messages are also protected by end-to-end encryption, just like regular WhatsApp messages, meaning no one outside the chat, including WhatsApp itself, can read them.
Who Can Benefit From Scheduling Messages on WhatsApp?
Being able to send a message at a future point is quite useful, and different people will find it useful in different ways. An obvious use case is wishing someone on their birthday or anniversary, especially if you don’t share the same time zone. But other than that, scheduling can make life easier in many other ways. Say someone asked you to remind them about something at a specific time tomorrow. Instead of setting a reminder for yourself to send that message, you can schedule the message in WhatsApp today and forget about it.
Similarly, if you coordinate with a team on WhatsApp and have an update to share late in the evening but don’t want to disturb everyone right away, you can schedule the message for the next morning instead. You could also schedule nudges for deadlines or upcoming meetings. Another handy use case for scheduling is reminding yourself. If you use WhatsApp for notes and reminders, you can now combine that with the scheduling feature to remind yourself about something later.
Limitations of Scheduling Messages on WhatsApp
- No WhatsApp Business support: The feature is currently limited to regular WhatsApp accounts.
- Group membership restrictions: People who join a group after you schedule a message won’t receive it.
- Limited editing options: WhatsApp’s documentation currently describes deleting scheduled messages, but doesn’t confirm editing or rescheduling them.
When Is Message Scheduling Coming to WhatsApp?
Message scheduling is said to roll out globally in the coming weeks on both Android and iOS. The rollout started on November 25, 2026. Make sure you’re running the latest version of WhatsApp on your phone. If you still don’t see the option to schedule messages, you’ll need to wait until WhatsApp enables the feature for your account. WhatsApp hasn’t mentioned whether scheduled messages will be available on the web version, too.

Editor’s note, : This story was originally published on November 22, 2023, and reflects events that took place that year. We’re republishing it in its original form for this year’s Thanksgiving week.
How America broke the turkey
An investigation reveals how the company behind the White House turkey pardon — and the rest of the industry — really treats its birds.
Late into the night on November 2, 2023, a few animal rights activists opened an unlocked barn door and stepped foot into a sea of turkeys living in gruesome conditions. It was one of several barns at a sprawling factory farming operation in Owatonna, Minnesota, that raises turkeys for Jennie-O, the country’s second-largest turkey producer and this year’s supplier to the annual White House turkey pardon ceremony.
Inside this story
- An undercover investigation into one of America’s biggest turkey companies revealed sick birds in inhumane conditions.
- Part of the problem is the farms themselves, where turkeys are overcrowded and suffer from high rates of disease.
- But the biggest problem is the bird’s biology. To boost profits, turkey companies have bred turkeys to grow twice as fast, and nearly twice as big, as they were in the 1960s.
- The rapid growth causes a range of health issues, and many turkeys are so top-heavy they can hardly walk.
“We documented a lot of really horrific health issues,” activist Kecia Doolittle, one of the investigators, told Vox. “It was about as bad as you can imagine.”
They found numerous turkeys who were dead and rotting, Doolittle said, and many who had trouble walking. There were also live birds pecking at dead birds, and dozens of birds with visible wounds — each a sign of cannibalism, a persistent problem in turkey farming.
Doolittle also alleges there were a number of turkeys who were immobilized and unable to access food and water. In a letter to Steele County’s attorney and local law enforcement, Bonnie Klapper — a former assistant US attorney advising Doolittle — said the conditions are a violation of Minnesota’s animal cruelty law, which stipulates that “No person shall deprive any animal over which the person has charge or control of necessary food, water, or shelter.” (Minnesota is one of the few states that don’t exempt agricultural practices from their animal cruelty statute.)
“It smelled terrible,” Doolittle said. The air made her throat burn, likely due to high ammonia levels from the turkeys’ waste, which gives the birds eye and respiratory issues.
The activists found a sign on the property that read, “Jennie-O Turkey Store cares about turkeys — you should, too!”
“Jennie-O Turkey Store takes the welfare of the animals under our care seriously and has robust animal care standards throughout our supply chain,” a spokesperson from Hormel Foods, Jennie-O’s parent company, told Vox via email. “We conduct routine audits at our facilities to ensure that our standards are being met with animal-handling practices and policies set forth by the National Turkey Federation and the American Veterinary Medical Association.”
Doolittle rescued two of the birds — whom she later named Gabriel and Gilbert — and took them to veterinarians in Wisconsin, who urged her to euthanize Gilbert. “They both had really severe infections, they both had parasites,” Doolittle said, but Gilbert was in especially bad shape, with a wound under his wing, an infection on his face, and pecking wounds on part of his genitalia.
But Doolittle wanted to give him a chance to recover. Both birds were treated and given a combination of antibiotic, pain relief, and antiparasitic drugs; Gabriel is on the mend, while Gilbert’s condition remains touch and go.
Sherstin Rosenberg, a veterinarian in California and executive director of a sanctuary for rescued poultry birds, wrote in a veterinary opinion that Gabriel and Gilbert’s condition “suggests serious animal welfare problems” in Jennie-O’s facility.
The findings, while disturbing, are common across the turkey industry. Numerous animal welfare groups have found similar conditions at operations run by Jennie-O’s competitors — even the ones that brand themselves as more humane. That’s because turkey farming is incredibly uniform, with companies using generally the same practices and the same breed — the Broad Breasted White turkey — that’s been bred without regard for their suffering.
How the poultry industry broke the turkey
Like everything else in the US — cars, homes, cruise ships — the turkey has become supersized.
The poultry industry has made turkeys so big primarily through selective breeding. The Broad Breasted White turkey, which accounts for 99 out of every 100 grocery store turkeys, has been bred to emphasize — you guessed it — the breast, one of the more valuable parts of the bird. These birds grow twice as fast and become nearly twice as big as they did in the 1960s. Being so top-heavy, combined with other health issues caused by rapid growth and the unsanitary factory farming environment, can make it difficult for them to walk.
Another problem arises from their giant breasts: The males get so big that they can’t mount the hens, so they must be bred artificially.
Author Jim Mason detailed this practice in his book The Ethics of What We Eat, co-authored with philosopher Peter Singer. Mason took a job with the turkey giant Butterball to research the book, where, he wrote, he had to hold male turkeys while another worker stimulated them to extract their semen into a syringe using a vacuum pump. Once the syringe was full, it was taken to the henhouse, where Mason would pin hens chest-down while another worker inserted the contents of the syringe into the hen using an air compressor.
Workers at the farm had to do this to one hen every 12 seconds for 10 hours a day. It was “the hardest, fastest, dirtiest, most disgusting, worst-paid work” he had ever done, Mason wrote.
In stressful, crowded environments, turkeys can be aggressive and peck one another, and even commit cannibalism. Instead of giving turkeys more space and better conditions, producers mutilate them to minimize the damage. They cut off a quarter to a third of their beaks, part of their toes, and their snoods — those fleshy protuberances that hang over their beaks — all without pain relief.
Turkeys are excluded from federal laws meant to reduce animal suffering during transport to the slaughterhouse and during slaughter itself, so you can imagine — or see for yourself — how terribly they’re treated in their final hours. According to the nonprofit Animal Welfare Institute, the Jennie-O slaughter plant near the farm Doolittle investigated was cited nine times in 2018 by the US Department of Agriculture for turkeys who’d been mutilated by malfunctioning equipment.
Strangely, despite the horrific reality of turkey farming, we still use the animal as a symbol of giving thanks. Nowhere does the song and dance of celebrating turkeys while we torture them feel more disconcerting than at the White House’s annual turkey pardon.
The mixed message of the White House turkey pardon
Every Thanksgiving, the US president “pardons” a turkey or two in what is essentially a PR stunt for the turkey industry, as the birds are selected by the chair of the National Turkey Federation, an industry trade association. This year, that was Steve Lykken, president of Jennie-O.
The two turkeys selected for this year’s pardon — named Liberty and Bell — could have ended up among the 46 million or so birds on Thanksgiving tables this year. Instead, they were transported from Minnesota, the country’s top turkey-producing state, to Washington, DC, in a stretch black Cadillac Escalade. “They’re on their way in a pretty lavish coach,” Lykken told Minnesota Public Radio.
The annual story makes for feel-good if hammy coverage by the nation’s largest news organizations, but it papers over the darkness of American factory farming — including not just the animal cruelty but also the dangerous working conditions at slaughterhouses, environmental pollution, and unfair treatment of turkey contract farmers.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment about the Jennie-O investigation video.
This year, industry is especially looking forward to the pardon amid the devastating bird flu. The disease, which has been resurging this fall, has resulted in the killing of 11.5 million potentially infected turkeys since early 2022. Increasingly, producers are killing the birds in the most brutal fashion imaginable, deploying a method called “ventilation shutdown plus” that uses industrial heaters to kill them via heatstroke over the course of hours.
“To have something that’s fun, that can draw positive attention to our industry, is very welcomed” in light of the outbreak, Ashley Kohls, executive director of the Minnesota Turkey Growers Association, told Minnesota Public Radio about this year’s pardon.
This week, Liberty and Bell will be moved to the University of Minnesota to live out the rest of their lives. If the turkeys knew what went on there, they might not want to go: The university helped build the state’s turkey industry and still conducts research on turkeys to ensure the industry’s success. The university’s interim president formerly served as the president of Jennie-O and the CEO of Hormel, its parent company.
Meanwhile, Doolittle’s pardoned turkeys, Gabriel and Gilbert, assuming both survive, will spend the rest of their lives at an animal sanctuary, showing humans what these birds can be like when allowed to live on their own terms. “They’re just the most curious, loving, intelligent guys,” Doolittle said.

Theatrical cinema in India continues to hold its ground despite the growing number of entertainment options available to audiences, according to Ashish Saksena, COO – Cinemas at BookMyShow. Speaking at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, Saksena said the big-screen experience remains relevant because of the collective experience it offers viewers.
IFFI 2026: BookMyShow COO Ashish Saksena says theatrical cinema is ‘not fading away’, believes it will coexist with OTT
Saksena shared his views during a panel discussion titled ‘One Film, Multiple Paydays: Extracting a Film’s Full Value’, where he discussed the changing cinema landscape and the opportunities available to the industry. Reflecting on the theatrical business in 2026, he said audiences continue to seek out films that offer a compelling experience on the big screen.
“Audiences today have more entertainment choices than ever before. Yet, the desire to experience a compelling story on the big screen, surrounded by an audience, remains deeply relevant. Theatres offer something that goes beyond watching a film. They create a shared cultural experience that cannot quite be replicated elsewhere,” he said.
Saksena added, “The theatrical business in India is not fading away. If anything, it is finding newer reasons to thrive.”
He also spoke about BookMyShow's role in the cinema ecosystem, including how audience insights and market intelligence can help filmmakers and producers understand a film's reach and reception. According to Saksena, the platform's involvement extends beyond ticketing and theatrical discovery.
He pointed to BookMyShow Stream, the company's transactional video-on-demand (TVOD) service, as another avenue for films to reach audiences after their theatrical release. He also mentioned the Red Lorry Film Festival (RLFF), which provides independent and distinctive cinema with curated screening opportunities.
Looking ahead, Saksena said technological developments and improvements in theatrical presentation could give audiences more reasons to visit cinemas. He cited premium formats, enhanced viewing technologies and immersive sound as areas that could contribute to the experience.
Addressing the relationship between theatrical releases and streaming platforms, he said both models can continue to operate alongside each other. “OTT and theatrical cinema can, and will, coexist. While one offers convenience and choice, the other will continue to draw audiences with its scale, spectacle and collective emotion,” he said.

Srinagar- Syed Faisal Qadri, a senior advocate practising in the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, was on Friday appointed as the Advocate General of the Union Territory.
Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha appointed Qadri to the post, which had remained vacant for over two years since former Advocate General D C Raina resigned in October 2024.
Qadri has represented the government and its departments in several important constitutional, service and legal matters.
According to a notification issued by Achal Sethi, Commissioner-Secretary, Department of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Qadri’s appointment has been made under Section 79(1) of the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.
As per the terms and conditions of the appointment, Qadri will receive a monthly remuneration of Rs 1 lakh, besides rent-free furnished accommodation in Jammu or Srinagar. If he opts to stay in his own residence, he will be entitled to a compensatory allowance of Rs 12,000 per month.
He will also be entitled to use a car for official purposes for free, a monthly sumptuary allowance of Rs 3,000, medical reimbursement, and travel allowances on par with a sitting high court judge.
The notification also specifies his professional fees for appearances before the high court, Supreme Court and other courts and tribunals, with separate rates for effective and non-effective hearings.
The Home Department will provide him security as per requirement, the notification said.

A Bengaluru consumer commission has directed a real estate company and its two directors to refund ₹2 lakh to a 41-year-old man who cancelled a residential plot booking after the builder allegedly failed to provide essential property documents. The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (Bengaluru Urban), in an order dated October 7, directed Virtue Infra Builders Pvt Ltd and its directors, R M Harikrishna and Aravinda Kumar, to return the booking amount with 9% annual interest from July 19, 2024, until payment, Times Of India reported. The commission also awarded ₹25,000 towards compensation and litigation expenses. This includes ₹10,000 for deficiency in service, ₹10,000 for pain and suffering and ₹5,000 towards litigation costs. The opposite parties have been given 45 days to comply with the order. According to the complaint filed by Muni Rao, he approached the company to purchase a residential plot in its Virtue Star City project at Mathkur village in Bengaluru North. Based on the company's representations about the property's title, approvals and availability for immediate registration, he agreed to purchase plot No. 66, measuring 1,410 sq ft, TOI reported. On July 19, 2024, Rao paid ₹2 lakh as an advance booking amount. The payment comprised ₹1.5 lakh through cheque and ₹50,000 through an online transaction. However, the company allegedly failed to provide the complete legal documents required to verify the property's title and the legality of the transaction. These included mother deeds and title documents, a land conversion order, an approved layout plan, RERA approval and e-Khata documents. Unable to verify the property's legal status, Rao decided to cancel the booking and sought a refund. However, despite repeated requests, phone calls and emails, the company allegedly failed to return the money, according to the complaint. On August 21, 2024, the company acknowledged its liability to refund the booking amount through an email. It assured Rao that the money would be credited by November 20, 2024, and apologised for the delay. However, the refund was not processed even after the promised deadline, prompting Rao to approach the consumer commission. The commission noted that the builder and its directors failed to appear despite receiving notice and did not file their written version. Consequently, the matter was heard ex parte. After examining Rao's affidavit and supporting documents, the commission observed that the company had failed to furnish the necessary property documents despite receiving the advance payment. It also noted that the company had acknowledged its liability to refund the money but failed to honour its assurance. Holding the company and its two directors jointly and severally liable, the commission observed that the complainant had neither received possession of the plot nor been refunded the deposited amount. It concluded that their conduct amounted to deficiency in service and unfair trade practice. The commission directed the opposite parties to refund the ₹2 lakh booking amount with 9% annual interest from July 19, 2024, along with the total compensation and litigation costs of ₹25,000. First time in 1952, a 1976 freeze: Tracing the journey of delimitation in India
The first delimitation exercise was carried out in 1952. Since then, four delimitation commissions have been constituted in 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002.
The Union Cabinet on Friday cleared the Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, which seeks to pave the way for delimitation in the country to implement women's reservation in Parliament and state legislative assemblies. The proposed amendment comes three years after the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023, was enacted, providing for one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies.
Under the delimitation process, constituency boundaries are redrawn and seats are allocated among states and Union territories based on their population. The exercise is key to implementing women's reservation, as the 2023 law's rollout is linked to a delimitation exercise following a Census.
ALSO READ: Govt’s delimitation plan: 50% seat hike for every state, Lok Sabha strength ceiling rises to 850
Deep Dive
Article 81 of the Constitution provides for the principle of “one person, one vote, one value” by seeking to ensure, as far as practicable, an equal ratio between a state's population and the number of Lok Sabha seats allotted to it. Article 81(2)(a) states: “There shall be allotted to each State a number of seats in the House of the People in such manner that the ratio between that number and the population of the state is, so far as practicable, the same for all States.”
The only exception to this provision is for states with a population not exceeding six million. They are exempt from the requirement of maintaining the same population-to-seat ratio as other states, allowing them to retain adequate representation in the Lower House despite their smaller populations.
ALSO READ: How Centre's delimitation plan could change India's electoral map: A look at state-wise numbers
Article 82 of the Constitution provides for the readjustment of the allocation of seats and the division of states into territorial constituencies after every Census. Article 81(3), meanwhile, defines the population to be considered for the purpose of seat allocation and delimitation. It states: “In this article, the expression ‘population’ means the population as ascertained at the last preceding census of which the relevant figures have been published.”
Delimitation exercises in India over the years
The first delimitation exercise was carried out in 1952, based on the 1951 Census. Since then, four delimitation commissions have been constituted in 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002. The 29-year gap between the last two commissions was the result of the Constitution (42nd Amendment) Act, 1976, which froze the allocation of Lok Sabha seats among states, based on the 1971 Census, until the publication of figures from the first Census conducted after 2000.
According to an earlier Hindustan Times report citing former chief election commissioner SY Quraishi, the freeze was intended to ensure that states which had performed well in family planning programmes did not lose their proportional political representation in the Lok Sabha.
In 2002, under the Atal Bihari Vajpayee-led government, the delimitation exercise was taken up again. However, the decision was to allow constituency boundaries within states and Union territories to be redrawn based on population, without changing the number of Lok Sabha seats allocated to each state or UT. This was intended to ensure that states which had made progress in population control did not lose their share of parliamentary representation to states with higher population growth.
The Delimitation Commission, headed by retired Supreme Court judge Justice Kuldip Singh, was constituted in 2002. Its exercise was completed in 2008, with delimitation orders coming into effect in most states and Union territories in February that year. The erstwhile state of Jammu and Kashmir was excluded from the exercise. The process was also deferred in four northeastern states of Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland and Manipur through presidential orders issued on February 8, 2008, citing concerns over security and public order.
The Constitution (84th Amendment) Act, 2001, extended the freeze on the allocation of Lok Sabha seats among states until the publication of figures from the first Census conducted after 2026. It, however, allowed the redrawing of constituency boundaries based on the 1991 Census. The Constitution (87th Amendment) Act, 2003, subsequently provided for the use of the 2001 Census for this purpose, without altering the total number of seats allotted to individual states.
The existing constitutional freeze is linked to the publication of the relevant figures from the first Census conducted after 2026. It is not triggered merely by the completion of the Census exercise.
Southern states have argued that a fresh population-based allocation of Lok Sabha seats could reduce their relative share of parliamentary representation, as states such as Uttar Pradesh and Bihar have recorded higher population growth than several southern states. However, the latest proposal seeks to retain the existing proportional share of states while increasing their Lok Sabha seats by 50 per cent.

In late November, social media users claimed conservative podcaster Katie Miller — the wife of White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller — posted on social media that car seat mandates would "kill the birth rate."
For instance, one Facebook user claimed in a video (archived), "Katie Miller, the wife of Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, wants you to know that the fastest way to kill birth rates is mandating more car seats."
The video featured a purported screenshot of Miller's X post. Similar claims spread on other social media platforms, including Instagram, Facebook and X. Snopes readers also searched our website to find out whether Miller actually made the statement.
In short, the post was genuine. Miller published it on her X account on Nov. 25. As such, we rated the claim as correctly attributed.
While a 2024 study suggested that car seat mandates could discourage some families from having a third child, it did not establish that they were the "fastest way" to reduce birth rates.
We reached out to Miller, the study's authors and several experts on birth rates and fertility for comment and will update this article if we receive responses.
What Miller wrote on X
On Nov. 25, Miller made a post (archived) on her X account that began, "The fastest way to kill the birth rate is mandating more car seats."
In the post, Miller argued that car seats made motherhood more complicated, citing the width of vehicles, car seat anchors and difficulties traveling with the seats. She also said car seats were a factor limiting the number of children she and her husband had.
The post read in full:
The fastest way to kill the birth rate is mandating more car seats.
Car seats make motherhood significantly more complicated and difficult, from vehicle width and anchors to traveling with them.
I'm not alone in saying that a limiting factor on the number of children we have is car seats.
Miller was responding to an X post about new car seat requirements in California:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the legislation, known as Assembly Bill 435, in October 2025. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, children ages 8 through 15 will have to use a child restraint system unless they meet five criteria for wearing a seat belt safely. These include how children sit in the vehicle and how the seat belt fits across their bodies. The law does not require all children under 16 to use booster seats.
Do car seat mandates affect birth rates?
There is some research suggesting that car seat requirements can influence families' decisions to have more children.
A 2024 study titled "Car Seats as Contraception," published in the Journal of Law and Economics, examined the relationship between car seat laws and birth rates in the U.S. (An earlier version of the paper was made available online in 2020.)
The researchers, Jordan Nickerson and David Solomon, found that women with two children who were both legally required to use car seats were 0.73 percentage points less likely to have a third child in a given year. The effect was limited to households with access to a car and a male household member present. The researchers suggested that the difficulty of fitting three car seats in the back of many vehicles could explain this finding. They estimated that car seat mandates resulted in approximately 8,000 fewer births in the U.S. in 2017 and prevented 57 children from dying in car crashes that year.
The study suggested that car seat mandates could discourage some families from having a third child. However, it did not establish how significant the effect of car seat mandates was compared with other factors affecting birth rates in the U.S. It also did not state that introducing more car seat mandates was the "fastest way to kill the birth rate," as Miller claimed. Moreover, the study was published before California passed the new legislation and did not assess the potential effect the new requirements could have on birth rates in that context.
Meanwhile, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, car seats reduce children's risk of injury in crashes by 71% to 82%, compared with seat belts alone. Booster seats reduce the risk of serious injury by 45% among children ages 4 through 8.
For further reading, we previously investigated whether Vice President JD Vance made a similar statement about car seats.

Doctors keep missing the ‘perfect storm’ for eating disorders
Anorexia, binge eating, and other disorders can emerge before and after childbirth, but the women who struggle with them often slip through the cracks of the U.S. health care system.
Research is limited, but we do know a few things: About 4.3% of pregnant women and more than 9% of new mothers experience eating disorders. Women with a history of eating disorders appear more likely to experience postpartum depression and anxiety and to report problems feeding their newborns. And obstetricians typically receive very little training about these conditions or how to use the few screening tools we have validated for eating disorders in pregnancy.

Medicare’s 2027 physician pay changes spell trouble for specialists
In the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ recent update to how Medicare pays physicians, the agency cut the payment rate for certain services provided on the same day by 20% when the services are provided by the same physician or practice.
A bit wonky, I know, but it’s part of the agency’s broader shift away from specialist care and the fee-for-service model, and one of many reimbursement challenges that specialists are contending with.
What does this mean? Opponents say the policy change will force patients to return for separate appointments and increase out-of-pocket costs and wait times. People with Parkinson’s disease, for example, could struggle to get outpatient Botox injections that are critical for relieving pain. Read more.

- A claim has circulated for years that the Apollo 11 astronauts couldn't get an insurance policy to cover the first manned mission to the moon and instead signed autographs on postmarked envelopes, called insurance covers, for their family to sell to support themselves should something go wrong.
- The rumor has circulated online for years across social media and Reddit.
- The insurance covers were authentic, but claims that the astronauts "couldn't get" insurance appeared to be misleading. A newspaper article from around the time of the moon landing in 1969 reported that the astronauts received insurance coverage on par with other government employees of the time.
- Snopes reached out to NASA as well as the families of the Apollo 11 astronauts to verify the details. We will update this article if we hear back.
A claim has circulated for years that the Apollo 11 astronauts couldn't get an insurance policy to cover the NASA space flight mission that culminated in the first humans walking on the moon and instead signed autographs for their family to sell to support themselves, should something go wrong.
People sharing the claim on social media and Reddit purported that the astronauts signed customized postal envelopes, called insurance covers, that were then postmarked on landmark dates — such as July 20, 1969, the day the Lunar Lander touched down on the moon's surface. 
(Reddit)
The claim appeared to be mostly true based on credible reporting from 1969 as well as reporting from NPR in 2012 following the death of Neil Armstrong, in addition to the existence of the insurance covers in question for sale on sites like eBay, their presence in NASA collectible archives and the Smithsonian National Postal Museum. Three varieties were produced for Apollo 11, as well as later Apollo missions 12-16.
However, evidence also indicated the astronauts received insurance coverage on par with what other government employees of the time received, so claims that the astronauts "couldn't get" insurance were misleading.
Snopes bases its ratings on evidence we've been able to independently verify firsthand, so we've left this claim unrated. We reached out to NASA and the families of astronauts Buzz Aldrin and Neil Armstrong and will update this article if we hear back.
A newspaper clip from The Associated Press, titled "Astronauts Get Usual Insurance," was published in Santa Ana, California's The Register on July 27, 1969 — days after the astronauts returned to Earth on July 24.
AP reported that "The Apollo 11 astronauts were not covered by any special government life insurance contract when they flew to the moon and back," attributing the information to a NASA spokesperson at the time.
However, the article quoted NASA as verifying that the astronauts were offered the same policies available to other government employees and service members at the time.
It was reportedly the first policy to cover a travel accident during space exploration, and it also covered "disease endemic to the lunar surface or its environs."
The full article read:
The Apollo 11 astronauts were not covered by any special government life insurance contract when they flew to the moon and back, a NASA spokesman says.
"They have the same government or military policies that are available to other government employees or servicemen," he said.
The value of such policies is determined on a sliding scale related to base pay, and differs among all the astronauts.
Under terms of a contract with Life magazine, the astronauts received individual $50,000 policies.
And a Houston firm, Harland Insurance Services, says the Apollo 11 crew was the first to be covered by travel accident insurance during space exploration.
The company said each of the three astronauts is covered for $50,000 in special policies that extend through the quarantine period. The policies provide insurance not only against accidents but against "disease endemic to the lunar surface or its environs."
An oil executive and a bank president paid the premiums, the company reported.
(The Register — July 27, 1969)
Following the death of Armstrong in 2012, NPR talked with a space historian about the insurance covers. Their report stated:
About a month before Apollo 11 was set to launch, the three astronauts entered quarantine. And, during free moments in the following weeks, each of the astronauts signed hundreds of covers.
They gave them to a friend. And on important days — the day of the launch, the day the astronauts landed on the moon — their friend got them to the post office and got them postmarked, and then distributed them to the astronauts' families.
It was life insurance in the form of autographs.
A certificate of authenticity included in an eBay listing (archived) of one of the insurance covers in question, dated July 20, 1969, said "these covers played an integral role in the flight, giving the crew confidence they had left behind a tangible asset that could be sold, if needed, to raise money for their families."
The certificate of authenticity was allegedly from the Buzz Aldrin Family Space Collection, whom we reached out to for verification. We will update this piece if we receive a response.
In 1972, the astronauts of Apollo 15 were reprimanded for the unauthorized "smuggling" of insurance covers to the moon and back, apparently with the intention of selling them for personal gain.
A report in the July 12, 1972, edition of The New York Times said the Apollo 15 astronauts brought 400 covers to the moon, and then "100 of these were sold by a German stamp dealer for a sum reported to be more than $150,000."
The story reported the astronauts arranged the deal through an acquaintance who in return would set up a trust fund for the astronauts' children.
The Times reported that "this part of the arrangement was never fulfilled," and cited a NASA spokesperson as clarifying that the astronauts decided "the deal was improper and refused the establishment of the trust fund" and that "they had also refused an alternate suggestion that they accept valuable stamps in exchange and therefore had made no money at all on the venture."
According to a 2011 follow-up piece by the Houston Press, the astronauts were not fired but reassigned, and none ever flew in space again.

Indian consumers are more discerning than ever, particularly when setting up their dream homes. After spending months obsessing over every little detail of their humble abode, from furniture and wall colours to lighting and décor, the last thing they want is an appliance that sticks out like a sore thumb. Imagine walking into a beautifully designed home. The walls are painted in soothing colours, the furniture has been carefully chosen, the lighting is just right, and every little detail reflects the homeowner's personal taste. Everything looks picture-perfect, except for a bulky, old-fashioned table fan and that clunky room heater sitting awkwardly in a corner. Indian consumers often face this eyesore and must choose between aesthetics and performance, with few options that bring the best of both worlds together. Gazal Kalra and Shalabh Gupta experienced this gap firsthand when they struggled to find aesthetically pleasing home appliances without compromising functionality. Inspired by their experience, they launched NUUK, a design-led home appliances brand, in 2023 to bring aesthetics and functionality together in everyday appliances. Today, NUUK boasts a portfolio of 20 products and variants across five categories — cooling, floor care, food preparation, heating, and garment and fabric care. Since its launch, NUUK has sold more than 6 Lakh units across categories via its website, ecommerce marketplaces, quick commerce platforms and other sales channels. The brand has also won Red Dot Design Awards, an international honour for design excellence, thrice and earned recognition at Kyoorius Design Awards, a national award that celebrates creative and design excellence. In FY26, the company reported net revenue of approximately ₹70 Cr, with revenue in April and May 2026 growing 2x YoY. To support its next phase of growth, NUUK has raised over $10 Mn from Vertex Ventures SE Asia & India SEA and Good Capital. Everyday Appliances, Reimagined The architects behind NUUK’s concept and its subsequent growth, Kalra and Gupta, bring complementary expertise, making them a natural fit for the venture. While Kalra brings expertise in human-centred design from her time at Stanford Design School and experience building and scaling businesses as cofounder of Rivigo, Gupta brings a strong understanding of strategy, consumer behaviour, and digital-first brand building from his stints at McKinsey, Twitter (now X), and Noise. For the NUUK founders, building a design-led home appliances brand meant improving how everyday appliances look, work and fit into consumers' daily lives. “Every design decision must serve a purpose. It should make the product more intuitive, convenient and effective without compromising performance,” Kalra said, citing the example of NUUK’s flagship air circulator, HĀLO, which addresses two common problems with conventional fans — noise and limited airflow direction. The product also includes a mood lighting feature, adding another design element to a product usually treated as purely functional. The same approach extends to the kitchen. While developing BRĪSK, NUUK’s toxin-free ceramic air fryer, the founders said that they identified concerns around cooking surfaces used in conventional air fryers. “We spent over 24 months researching and testing alternative materials before developing the air fryer with a Swiss-engineered ILAG CeramicTech surface that is free from lead, cadmium, PFOA, PFAS and PTFE,” Kalra assured. BRĪSK, Kalra added, also features a 360-degree Rapid Air Circulation system to cook food evenly and up to 30% faster, plus an ILAG ceramic surface for a non-stick effect, durability, and easy cleaning. For its floor care segment, the founders turned their attention to addressing all the challenges of cleaning Indian homes. The result is REN PRO, a cordless vacuum cleaner with 34 kPa suction and a FlexiStick bending rod. The product's adaptive suction technology automatically adjusts power based on detected dust levels, helping optimise battery life. “We want every feature to solve a problem and not add complexity,” she said. To stay ahead of the innovation curve, the founders started paying attention to the post-sales journey of their products. Gupta shared the case study of KRÜSH, a blender that customers used for smoothies and shakes rather than chutneys or dry masalas. “As customers began raising concerns about discolouration, dampness and lingering odours, we introduced a separate stainless steel jar with KRÜSH PRO, making it suitable for a wider range of kitchen tasks,” he said. NUUK’s LĪT fan went through a similar evolution. Customers wanted a taller model with stronger oscillation, prompting NUUK to introduce LĪT PRO with a ProLift stem and a more powerful sweep. Reflecting on these changes, Gupta said, “In both cases, the new version answers something people told us rather than something we guessed. That's how we approach every product: listen for the friction, then design it away.” Building The Manufacturing Backbone As NUUK expands across categories, it faces the challenge of scaling production while maintaining consistent quality across very different appliances. Addressing this requires close control over product specifications, engineering and quality standards. NUUK follows a partnership-led manufacturing model. While the company owns product conception, engineering and design, its manufacturing partners operate the production lines. Its in-house new product development team handles everything from consumer insights and industrial design to product architecture, feature definition and technical specifications. To execute this model, NUUK works with a network of Indian and global appliance manufacturers, including Zetwerk and Epack Durable. Its manufacturing partners operate facilities across Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Haryana. Localising the component base is another part of this strategy. NUUK works with both Indian and global suppliers, selecting components based on quality and performance. According to Gupta, locally sourced components account for 30% to 100% of a product’s material value, depending on the product. NUUK is gradually increasing the use of Indian components across its portfolio. Maintaining quality across this network also requires checks at multiple stages. The brand’s components are inspected upon receipt against specifications defined by its team, while finished products undergo in-process inspections. Every production lot also goes through a pre-dispatch inspection against agreed acceptance standards before it is released. The company is now working towards making 100% of its products in India from 2027. This would build on its existing manufacturing partnerships and localisation efforts, as it looks to develop production capabilities that meet global standards. NUUK’s Next Phase Of Growth NUUK's next phase of growth will depend on how effectively it can build on its existing categories while expanding into new areas. The company currently operates across five categories, with fans accounting for around 51% of its revenue, followed by vacuum cleaners at 18%, and food preparation appliances and room heaters at approximately 12% each. Deepening its presence across these categories while introducing products for more specialised consumer needs will be central to this effort. NUUK is also strengthening its brand and consumer outreach, having brought in filmmaker and actor Karan Johar as its brand ambassador. NUUK has continued to expand its portfolio with products such as SĒRV MAX, a multi-cook electric kettle, and is also exploring further opportunities in its heating range. One of its new category bets is indoor air quality. NUUK has recently launched STĀCK, an air purifier that features four-stage HEPA-14 filtration and sensors that track PM2.5, PM10, temperature and humidity. Beyond product expansion, NUUK plans to strengthen its presence across online and offline channels while continuing to invest in product innovation and manufacturing capabilities. To accelerate its offline expansion, it has expanded its presence across five cities through Vijay Sales and Broadway. Over the next 12 months, it plans to expand to more than 200 stores across large-format and multi-brand retail outlets. Its ambition over the next three to five years is to build one of India’s leading home appliance brands, with products designed around the needs of Indian households. As NUUK scales its categories and manufacturing capabilities, the larger test will be to prove that good design can do more than turn heads. So, can NUUK make its design-led business model work at scale?

As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.
To rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build new data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy—like Scandinavia. But logistical challenges, a scarcity of key components, and a swell of anti-data center protests are getting in the way.
An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German company Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a new breed of chip—photonic processors—meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.
Whereas regular GPUs transmit and process data by shuffling electrons around, photonic processors use waves of light. Because light doesn’t generate heat as it travels and allows more data to be processed simultaneously, photonic processors supposedly consume less energy and require minimal cooling—one of the largest sources of cost for data centers.
The aim isn’t to replace GPUs with photonic processors, but to run them side-by-side. Whilst GPUs excel at grinding through masses of additions and multiplications—linear math—photonic processors are best suited to complex, nonlinear calculations.
Few photonic processors are running inside data centers today. But Q.ANT recently rolled out its chips to facilities operated by cloud company IONOS as part of a pilot program. It says that more than 30 teams of engineers are now developing AI models optimized for photonic computing.
Earlier this month, WIRED spoke with Michael Förtsch, founder and CEO of Q.ANT. We discussed the energy bottlenecks constraining AI development, how photonic processors differ from regular chips, and the challenges Q.ANT faces in trying to popularize a new class of hardware.
This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
WIRED: Michael, could you start by outlining the problem Q.ANT is aiming to solve? Why does the world need photonic processors to run AI models?
Michael Förtsch: The overall problem is the cost generated by the huge amount of energy consumption.
If you compute the way we think light should be used—not as a direct replacement for a GPU, but as a coprocessor—you basically have a new processor that takes care of the heavy math.
The cost driver today is the access to the memory. The less data you need in order to complete a job, the more efficient and better your system. We execute complicated math in a single step, where [regular chips] need thousands of steps. This saves a bunch of data—or memory access points.
How would you explain to the layperson how photonic computing works? How can light be used to perform mathematical computations?
Light is a wave. What is a wave? A sine function. [The sine function is a mathematical rule that, when plotted to a graph, produces a smooth repeating wave. —Editor] If I want to model something that’s round in shape with only linear functions, I need an infinite amount of data points and lines in order to describe something very simple: a circle. If I have the sine function at hand, because light is a wave, I need two points and I have already described the circle in all its beauty.
Light is very, very gifted to operate on complicated equations.
What distinguishes the type of problem best left to regular chips from problems that should be delegated to photonic processors?
The Nvidia H200 GPU is a masterpiece of technology. It’s art. It’s truly hard to attack it in its homeground. But light has strengths where the GPU is weak—and vice versa.
Linear math? Please route it to the GPU. Non-linear and complex stuff? Please route it to us.
We believe we will be much stronger in everything related to pictures and videos: image recognition, segmentation, and generation. Then, everything that’s related to robotics and physical AI.
What is the estimated gain in energy efficiency tied to using photonic processors alongside GPUs for AI tasks?
I’m not saying photonic computing will come for free. But I see that photonic computing, in combination with [CPUs and GPUs], can bring you a lot more artificial intelligence at a fraction of the energy.
Under simulation, we are ending up at around four or five times energy reduction. But in real hardware we are not yet demonstrating it.
Can any task run on photonic hardware by default, or do they need to be configured in a certain way?
There’s no need to learn a different language than C++ or Python. And you can already execute [preexisting] code on our machines.
But if you take something that has been optimized for a GPU only, you should not expect that automatically things will run faster. You have to do some adaptations.
It’s a chicken and egg problem, right? Until developers are building models to run on this type of processor, it’s going to be difficult to sell them to cloud providers. Equally, until photonic processors are available for people to use, it’s going to be tough to convince developers to design for them.
You’re right.
Whether it’s photonic or any other processor technology, it will need time to get the credibility and trust that’s needed for a company like Google to build data center infrastructure around it.
That’s the reason we chose to go into data centers with proof of concept systems, to validate that photonic computing is robust enough to withstand that environment.
We want to invite the world to compute on our systems. We are building a new chicken, so you can start producing eggs. Let’s find out together whether they’re tasty or not.
What else should I understand about why photonic processors are not already widely in use?
If hypothetically we received an order of 100,000 [photonic processors], we at Q.ANT are ready, but I’m not sure about the suppliers.
Hardware is not software. On the assembly side, it will need [time] before we have the same robust supply chain as the semiconductor world.
Do you expect to suffer from the same problem as other hardware challengers in securing capacity with the big chip manufacturers?
[To produce Q.ANT chips] you only need 90 nanometer node technology, from the 2000s. A lot of foundries already use this capability to produce chips that are super cheap. With this technology, you can use the same line to produce high-performance chips with a much higher street price, without massive upfront investment in your assets.
That resonates well with the industry.
Are Q.ANT processors built to function alongside a particular brand of GPUs—say, Nvidia or AMD—or are they totally agnostic?
There’s no need to go single-sided with a particular GPU. We want to have the freedom to cooperate with any of them.
Either way, we are not competitive to GPUs, we complete their function set.
Can you imagine a future in which AI models run entirely on photonic processors, or will they always be a sidekick?
If we see an opportunity in five years to attack the GPU as well, we would not be shy about taking it. But at the same time, I do not know what workloads in five years are going to be like.
It depends on the architecture of future AI models, you mean?
Absolutely.
Could the chance to perform certain calculations more cheaply with photonic processors change the way that AI engineers design future models?
The core message is that we need to do something to fight the energy cost in the AI stack.
That’s where we see the future of AI: very data-optimized models that allow for tasks of the same quality, but at a fraction of the energy—and therefore a fraction of the operating cost.

Climate focused PE firm GEF Capital Partners announced the first close of its fourth India-focused climate fund at $615 Mn, exceeding its initial target. The fundraise is approximately 40% larger than the firm's previous $440 Mn fund, making it GEF Capital Partners' largest fundraise to date. Fund IV will primarily target mid-market, growth-stage cleantech businesses operating India and South Asia. The first close attracted a diverse pool of global institutional investors, including pension funds, sovereign investors, foundations and family offices. The fund's limited partners are primarily based across Europe, Japan, the UK, Singapore and the US. "India's energy transition is increasingly becoming a driver of industrial growth and global competitiveness. We see significant opportunities in businesses that improve resource efficiency, accelerate electrification and strengthen sustainable supply chains," said Raj Pai, cofounder and managing partner, GEF Capital Partners. GEF Capital Partners' existing India portfolio includes companies such as ReNew Power, Indian Energy Exchange, Premier Energies, Sterlite Electric, Sahyadri Farms, Arya.ag, TI Clean, Yulu Bikes and Hero Motors. In August, the PE firm led Yulu’s $93 Mn Series C funding round, which followed its leading participation in agritech startup Arya.ag’s $80.58 Mn Series D round in April. India's energy transition and sustainable industrial growth’s funding landscape has witnessed a sharp uptick in recent months, with cleantech startups raising $433 Mn across 23 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 267% YoY compared to $118 Mn across 16 deals in the year-ago quarter. A bulk of this growth has been driven by electric mobility investments, which accounted for over 70% of the total inflow during the quarter. The concentration in a handful of large electric mobility rounds, with investors increasingly emphasising unit economics, capital efficiency and the ability to scale.

Indore (Madhya Pradesh): Three people were injured after a speeding car rammed into an e-rickshaw and a motorcycle on the ring road near Piplayahana Square Bridge under Tilak Nagar police station limits on Friday morning. The collision was so severe that the e-rickshaw was completely mangled, with its rear portion breaking off and landing several feet away. The car driver abandoned the vehicle and fled the spot.
According to police, the accident took place around 6.30 am on the Ring Road, shortly after the e-rickshaw driver descended from Bengali Bridge and approached Shani Temple. The e-rickshaw was heading towards Choithram Mandi to buy vegetables. Alfesh Khan (22), a vegetable vendor was driving the vehicle while his brother Mojib Rahman was sitting inside it.
A speeding car (MP09ZY9959), allegedly being driven rashly, hit the e-rickshaw from behind, throwing both brothers onto the road. The car continued ahead and struck a motorcycle (MP09DM5846) carrying Ghanshyam Karole (45) and Raja Sanwle (26), causing both riders to fall.
Alfesh, Ghanshyam and Raja sustained injuries, while Mojib suffered minor injuries. Passersby took the injured to MY Hospital.
Police seized the car and registered a case under sections 125(a) and 281 of the BNS. Further investigation is underway.

Why the Army detonated toxic explosives in Iowa
It was probably the least bad option.
On Wednesday, the Pentagon blew up about five tons of lead azide, an unstable explosive stored at an ammunition plant in Iowa, in order to dispose of it, sending a toxic plume of lead dust into the sky the day before Thanksgiving.
The detonation was briefly halted by a lower court before a federal circuit court cleared the way on Monday, and went forward despite serious public health concerns.
There was a real need for haste, according to the Army: The lead azide was sufficiently unstable that it was at risk of detonating on its own in an uncontrolled explosion, and falling temperatures in Iowa reportedly made such an explosion more likely. An uncontrolled explosion would have be more dangerous and unpredictable, and could have caused worse lead pollution.
At the same time, though, Iowa residents are angry and alarmed by a lack of clear information, poor communication by the Army, and the potential health hazards.
The potential for things to go sideways had President Donald Trump nervous enough that he tried to pass the decision to Rob Sand — not the current Iowa governor, but the incoming Democratic governor-elect — and let any consequences fall on his head.
The lead plume produced by the blast — which will take place inside reinforced concrete bunkers, along with other steps to mitigate the risk — could still spread as far as 100 miles from the site, according to the Washington Post.
The American Lung Association has urged anyone near the blast to remain inside for one to two days afterward, among other guidance, and on Tuesday, the Health and Human Services Department recommended that children and pregnant women evacuate from the path of the plume, which could stretch into neighboring Missouri.
The lead risk all around us
Emergency munitions detonations in the US are pretty rare — there are, thankfully, better ways to dispose of toxic materials these days (and questions about why the Army didn’t pursue them in this case).
But despite a great deal of progress in the US — including banning things like new lead paint and pipes and leaded gasoline in the 20th century — lead remains a serious public health threat.
Part of that is because of how dangerous it really is: Lead is not just a neurotoxin, but one with no safe levels of human exposure; even a little bit can be harmful, especially to children.
But as my colleague Dylan Scott reported in 2024, it also keeps popping up nearly everywhere we look, including in our food supply.
According to Dylan’s reporting, there are three big reasons for lead’s seeming inescapability: Active disregard, negligence, and the fact that it’s just really hard to get rid of. Lead was widely used in the US decades ago, before those bans on lead paint and leaded gasoline, and some of that lead is still around, in the soil, in old houses, and in other materials dating back to that time.
It’s also not a problem that the US can easily address alone, since lots of lead exposure is the result of goods being imported into the US.
“If we really want to solve this,” Drew McCartor, the director of a global public health nonprofit, told Dylan at the time, “it requires a whole-of-government commitment to work outside of our borders.”
One link for later
➨ Follow “Maslow’s hierarchy of hosting.” Thanksgiving is almost upon us, and if you’re feeling a little angsty about your holiday obligations, consider this guidance from the event planner Megan Fitzgerald: Your hosting needs, at a minimum, start with a clean space, a bathroom stocked with adequate toilet paper, and enough cups and water to go around. (Plus, of course, the food.) Basically, everything else is extra.
Before you go…
- Did you know…that, with very few exceptions, US grocery stores sell only one breed of turkey? It’s called the Broad Breasted White turkey, and it’s been bred to grow twice as fast (and become nearly twice as big) as its forebears did in the 1960s.
- Today’s trivia: What’s the name for the astronomical phenomenon that occurs when Earth’s natural satellite is at its perigee? (Here’s a hint: It’s happening tonight. You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword. Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.)
- Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday, we asked you which 19th-century author and activist is known as “the mother of Black feminism.” That would be Anna Julia Cooper, who was one of the first African American women to receive a PhD. She lived to 105, well into the 20th century.
