Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.
"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in those species."
Daoust went on to get a Ph.D. in chemistry, searching nature for novel pharmaceuticals. Her work ultimately led her back to mushrooms, a group of organisms to which humans are more closely related than plants. And yet, many of our modern medicines and therapeutics come from plants.
"Mushrooms share a lot more in terms of their biochemistry with us than plants do," says Daoust, which means "you have more chances of finding something that's going to have bioactivity in a human than you would with other source organisms."
Daoust is now vice president of science and innovation at Monterey Nutra, a company that specializes in the genetics and cultivation of mushrooms and sells fungal extracts and powders. Her team focuses not on the poisonous varieties, nor the psychedelic ones that contain psilocybin. Rather, they are interested in the functional or medicinal mushrooms that Daoust likens to tiny cauldrons of potentially useful molecules.
"We love to look for soft things that can't run away very fast," says Daoust, "because they typically produce really interesting chemistry to defend themselves or to communicate with others in their environment to survive."
The claim
Daoust says that certain types of fungi may have specific uses.
For instance, lion's mane — a soft chandelier of a fungus — may aid cognition. Reishi and turkey tail, which are mushrooms that grow as hard brown scales on decomposing trees, could bolster immune health.
And on social media, influencers and advertisers promise that medicinal mushrooms, taken as supplements, can slow aging and improve energy levels, focus and immune health.
The evidence
Robust clinical trials proving such connections — and their safety — are largely lacking, according to Abby Langer, a registered dietitian based in Toronto. "In my opinion, I don't think that there's much evidence for functional mushrooms as of now," she says.
Langer says mushrooms accumulate and concentrate the materials in the ground they're grown in, both good and bad — so one has to be cautious.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
She grants that in certain communities (in parts of Asia, for instance), mushrooms have been incorporated into their healing practices for generations. However, "just because something has been used for a long time doesn't mean that it's safe, that it's effective, that the dosing has been established," Langer says. "There are a lot of unknowns."
Still, she acknowledges that empirical support for the potential positive impacts of mushrooms is growing. "The clinical research on specific functional mushroom products is young," she says, "but it's accumulating fast and already includes some impressive results."
Mushrooms are a good source of vitamin D2 and antioxidants. Their cell walls contain beta-glucan, which has been linked to gut health, including a lower risk of Crohn's Disease, and immune response. Research into the effects of mushrooms on cognition have been mixed.
In addition, there's work out of Japan looking at how PSK, a purified extract from turkey tail, improved immune response in cancer patients. A meta-analysis considered 8,009 patients in eight randomized controlled trials who had undergone surgical removal of a gastric tumor and in almost all cases chemotherapy. Those who were also given PSK showed a 12% reduction in risk of death.
"This is not something that we brush off," says Santhosshi Narayanan, an integrative oncologist based at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who recognizes the potential of PSK.
Even so, she admits that this "does not mean that PSK or any mushrooms alone cures cancer. It just shows to us that we need to pay attention to these natural products." Narayanan says there's still a lot to figure out with this particular extract, especially for populations outside Japan with different genetics or treatment regimes who might experience unwanted side effects.
"We need to do more research and understand how we can use it," she says. "Like which people, which type of patients benefit from which type of mushroom — because that itself is a whole science."
Narayanan and her colleagues also surveyed 2,349 studies examining the relationship between medicinal mushrooms and cancer, but only 39 were robust enough to be included in their 2023 analysis. Of that subset, "31 studies showed beneficial effects of the mushrooms, resulting in improved quality of life, reduced [side effect] profiles of different chemotherapeutic drugs, improved anti-inflammatory and anti-metastatic effects, and improved [disease-free survival] as well as [overall survival] in a few trials," according to the report.
Six studies didn't reveal any advantage and two highlighted worse outcomes. Overall, the analysis was unable to make clear conclusions about "the complex biological effects of mushrooms on the immune system in cancer."
The bottom line
In Narayanan's estimation, there's not yet enough evidence to support routine clinical use in cancer treatment.
And Langer recommends considering a few nutrition basics before introducing a supplement for gut health or cognition. "Take a closer look at what you're eating, how you're eating, when you're eating," she advises, "and see if there's any tweaks that you need to make."
Maybe it's possible to eat more fiber or protein, reduce consumption of alcohol or sugar-sweetened beverages, skip fewer meals, or eat out less often, she says.
"There's so many things that people can potentially improve on," Langer says, "before adding something else that's promised to be this panacea for everything that ails you."

Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory.
Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid’s 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.
But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.
“We knew right away that the impact was successful, that DART made a really, really large mess,” said Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist at the International Space Science Institute in Bern, Switzerland. “However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess. We were still missing pieces of the puzzle.”
Following up
The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft recently arrived in the vicinity of Didymos and Dimorphos after a two-year journey from a launch pad in Florida. On Wednesday, ESA released Hera’s first views of the scar left by DART on Dimorphos. The images show the car-sized impactor carved out a crater the size of a stadium, nearly as big as Dimorphos itself, a rugged chunk of extraterrestrial rock measuring about 500 feet (151 meters) across.
Mission planners selected Didymos and Dimorphos for the deflection experiment because they are similar to many near-Earth asteroids, but there’s no risk of them striking our home planet. Scientists weren’t sure what Hera would find when it got to the double asteroid, currently orbiting the Sun about 120 million miles (193.5 million kilometers) from Earth.
“I would say we had two kinds of predictions: either we made a crater, or we reshaped the asteroid,” said Patrick Michel, Hera’s principal investigator from Côte d’Azur Observatory in Nice, France. “In fact, we did both because the crater is so large that the shape has changed. Therefore, we are in a sort of a transition between just cratering and global transformation, and we are still not sure how this can happen.”
Hera found Didymos, the larger of the two asteroids, spinning on its axis just as DART observed on final approach in 2022. Dimorphos is no longer so stable.
“As Hera returned more images, it became clear that the DART impact has left Dimorphos tumbling wildly in its orbit,” says Michael Kueppers, ESA’s Hera mission scientist.
The Hera spacecraft will fly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos over the next six months to obtain more detailed observations. Hera will release two small sub-satellites to attempt landings on Dimorphos and collect data on the asteroid’s composition, internal structure, and mass.
Scientists will use this information to reconstruct the dynamics of DART’s impact four years ago and better understand how a future deflection mission might move an asteroid off a trajectory that actually threatens Earth. Near-Earth asteroids come in many shapes and sizes, with different densities and makeups, so knowledge of Dimorphos’s physical properties will anchor predictive computer models teaching scientists how best to deflect all types of asteroids.
“Once we understand, we have a breakthrough, which really solves planetary defense,” Michel said in an interview with Ars.
What a mess
In its initial reconnaissance this month, Hera spotted hundreds of boulders surrounding the double asteroid. This was not entirely unexpected. A picture taken by the Hubble Space Telescope shortly after DART’s impact showed a cloud of material streaming behind Didymos and Dimorphos, but scientists were astonished by the extent of the debris swarm in Hera’s first images.
“As we approached Didymos and Dimorphos, we quickly realized the asteroids were not alone,” said Naomi Murdoch, planetary scientist at the Institut Supérieur de l’Aéronautique et de l’Espace in Toulouse, France. “In fact, they had a lot of company.”
An image released by ESA on Wednesday combines 11 long exposure frames from Hera’s hyperspectral camera. Image processors on the ground digitally removed the relatively bright Didymos and Dimorphos to reveal a panoply of dimmer streaks and dots, each of which is a rock fragment ranging in size from a football to a washing machine, Murdoch said.
“Hera came to visit two asteroids, and we found hundreds of companions,” Murdoch said.
One obvious explanation for the boulders is they were thrown off Dimorphos when DART slammed into it. But scientists cautioned they need more information before they can say that with surety. Hera is the first space mission to undertake a sustained study of an asteroid with its own moon. The debris around the two asteroids might be relics from the creation of Dimorphos some time in the ancient past.

PlayStation’s Black Friday 2026 sale is live through November 30, 2026, featuring discounts on PS Plus memberships, games, controllers, and more. However, if you’re already subscribed to PS Plus, you might have noticed that most membership discounts are reserved for new and returning subscribers. Fortunately, there are still a few ways existing subscribers can save on their memberships.
PlayStation Plus Black Friday 2026 Deals and Discounts
Running from November 16 to November 30, 2026, PlayStation Store Black Friday deals offer up to 33% off 12-month PS Plus plans. Your eligibility depends on your current tier and when your plan expires. Here’s an overview of the deal:
| PS Plus Tier | 12-Month Discount | Eligible Subscribers | 
|---|---|---|
| Essential | 20% off | New & returning subscribers (no active plan) | 
| Extra | 25% off | New & returning subscribers (no active plan) | 
| Premium / Deluxe | 33% off | New & returning subscribers, plus existing Essential/Extra members upgrading | 
How to Get PS Plus Black Friday Discounts as an Existing Subscriber
If you currently have an active PS Plus membership, here are the three best ways to save during the Black Friday 2026 sale:
1. Upgrade Your Current PS Plus Tier
As confirmed by Sony in its official PlayStation Blog post, existing Essential and Extra subscribers can claim a Black Friday discount when upgrading to PS Plus Premium or Deluxe. Keep in mind that the discount only applies to the remaining time left on your current billing cycle – not a full extra year.
2. Disable Auto-Renew and Let Your Plan Expire (Before Nov 30)
If your PS Plus subscription expires before the Black Friday sale, which ends on November 30, 2026, your best option may be to turn off auto-renewal so your account reverts to a “returning subscriber” status.
To disable PS Plus auto-renew on your PS5, follow these steps:
- Go to Settings -> Users and Accounts -> Account -> Payment and Subscriptions -> Subscriptions -> PlayStation Plus.
- Select Cancel Subscription.
Canceling only stops automatic renewal; you won’t lose access until your expiration date. Because PlayStation tracks subscriptions down to the exact minute you purchased them, even players whose plans expire on November 30 can wait for the membership to lapse and immediately grab a discounted 12-month plan.
3. Check for the “Cancel Subscription” Retention Offer
If your membership expires after November 30, turning off auto-renew is still worth trying. Multiple subscribers on Reddit have reported receiving personalized renewal offers ranging from 15% to 25% off. Although these offers vary from account to account, they’re worth checking before renewing your subscription at full price.
How to Claim the PS Plus Black Friday Deal as a New or Returning Subscriber
If you’re new to PlayStation Plus or no longer have an active membership, claiming the Black Friday discount is much more straightforward.
Simply sign in to your PlayStation account, visit the PlayStation Plus membership page, and select your preferred 12-month subscription tier to view the available discounts, which are automatically applied.
Also, check out the list of monthly PlayStation Plus free games you’re in for a treat after you’re subscribed successfully.
Can You Stack PS Plus Black Friday Deals?
No – existing subscribers generally cannot stack an extra discounted year onto an active PlayStation Plus. Because canceling only turns off auto-renew rather than ending the plan early, longtime members whose renewals fall after November 30 are effectively locked out of the main 12-month promotion, a restriction that has sparked widespread frustration across the PlayStation community.
Even if you miss out on the PS Plus membership discounts, there are plenty of other PlayStation 5 Black Friday 2026 deals worth checking out, including discounts on PS5 controllers, gaming headsets, and games. Make sure to grab your favorite deals before the sale ends on November 30.

Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.
As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We’ve got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist “here’s my laptop and monitor” setups to “I really like collecting things.” Without any further ado, let’s dig in:
Jeremy Hsu
As an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.
I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).
Accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.
My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.
I have a simple standing desk, but it’s not the easiest to change positions, so I wouldn’t recommend it for anyone who wants to adjust frequently. Whenever I’m sitting, I sometimes switch between a simple wooden chair from Ikea and a more ergonomic chair.
Aside from an assortment of coasters and a tea container turned pen holder, my desk also holds a painted dinosaur sculpture (courtesy of my young son) and two versions of the Spot It! Matching game (also for my son’s entertainment).
Last but not least, I have a pair of Powerblock dumbbells tucked under my work desk. I wouldn’t say they feature heavily in my work day, but they’re easily accessible if I have 15-20 minutes to spare.
Nick Indge
Greetings from my basement hobbit hole! My desk sits across from a workbench area that was already here when we got the house. I have labeled drawers full of PC parts, tools, and cables accumulated over decades. The drawer organization was quite the upgrade over my previous solution of “chuck everything in unlabeled storage tubs.”
My current PC setup is an AceMagic W1 mini PC running Fedora, and a Blackview Intel N150 I keep on Windows for audio recording (PipeWire is fussy). The two are connected to my inputs and monitors via a KVM so I can switch back and forth at the press of a button.
The monitors are mismatched thrift finds. One is an HP, the other Sansui. The TV is a similar story—an old Samsung LCD that set me back $10 at the thrift store. I use it as a third monitor for watching PC streams. An Onn Android box is also connected, though it rarely earns its keep.
Below the TV sits a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, a repurposed B2B video-conference gadget modded to run LineageOS. It handles smart-home controls and tracks my solar production during the day. There’s also a Flashforge 5M printer in the corner, and the pegboard wall holds tools, Mega Man figures, and about 10 years’ worth of convention badges.
The back closet is the scary part: old consoles, spare drives, boards, and parts for every project I’ll get to “eventually.” The chair is a Dowinx gaming chair I grabbed on a Slickdeals whim—it’s fine, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.
The rug-patterned Dude mousepad really ties the desk together, man.
Ryan Whitwam
I’m something of an outlier at Ars, in that I use Windows most days. I’m no great lover of Windows 11, but I still use it thanks to years of computing inertia. My machine is custom, built in early 2024 with a Raptor Lake Core i7 (that thankfully did not fall victim to the overvolting bug) and an RTX 4070 Ti. It has long been my preference to build my own PC for gaming and work to ensure easier repairs and upgrades. Although with the prices of components being what they are, I hope all these parts last a very long time.
The primary monitor on the bottom is an Alienware ultrawide OLED. I got it for gaming, but it’s also a nice productivity display that gives me lots of room to keep windows visible. Above that, I have an Asus ProArt LCD calibrated in sRGB for photography work. I’ll get to the keyboard, but I do want to point out my preferred mouse, a Logitech MX Vertical. I have carpal tunnel issues, and this thing has been a lifesaver.
I believe organizing my desk before taking the photo would be a form of lying, so rest assured this is what it looks like on an average day. I have a few organizers to keep phones and various accessories from getting scattered around my Uplift sit-stand desk (seen here in sitting mode), which I quite like. The chair is a Herman Miller Aeron, which I don’t like as much. It’s fine and has plenty of adjustments, but the mesh is very hard. You should only buy one on sale, and if you do, get a cushion.
Above the desk are some Star Trek cross-stitches, courtesy of my talented wife. The dangling ’90s-era computer components are a mobile I put together many years ago, featuring a neat Intel i486 DEC socket board and some SDRAM.
Aurich Lawson
I’m not a particularly neat person. My natural state is to have two or three projects half-exploded all over every surface: piles of 3D-printed prototypes, spools of wire, a soldering iron, laser-cut acrylic for a pinball project, the packaging from something I recently opened and need to sort through. Those aren’t random examples; that’s the contents of my workbench behind me on the opposite wall of my office as I type this. It’s a bit of a mess.
To combat that tendency, I make a concerted effort to keep the desk where I spend so many hours of the day calm and a place where I can focus. It doesn’t always last! But I’m always at least striving for it, and what I find helps is having a very intentional design where everything has a place.
My desk surface is made from rubberwood butcher block, on Flexispot motorized legs. I recently picked up another rubberwood slab to build the cantilevered shelf. The supports neatly tuck away my M1 Max Mac Studio, which is still a great little workhorse with 64 gigs of RAM, and my Arturia audio interface, which I use to record line-in sources like synthesizers.
On the left is a task lamp and a pen holder with six discrete holes. This fits in with the intentional design part: I have to pick the six things I want handy, and I can’t just pack it with more and more stuff. Currently that’s my Apple Pencil, a Pentel mechanical pencil, an Olfa mini snap-off blade knife, and a selection of three Pigma Micron pens in different line widths.
The right side holds an Aiyima 10th anniversary hi-fi stack: A20 amp, D20 DAC, and T20 pre-amplifier. The speakers are SVS Ultra Evolution Nanos. They’re sitting on the latest version of some 3D-printed stands I’ve been designing. I print them with hollow legs and then fill them with concrete for mass and stability.
Since I know Ryan is going to flex on everyone with his keyboard collection, I have to try my best to keep up with my daily driver. It’s a Percent Canoe v2 case, running Holy Panda switches modified with 63 gram SPRiT springs for a slightly lighter touch, and GMK Bento keycaps. This was a pandemic build project, and it has served me well since.
I used to run multiple monitors, but I’ve found that I don’t focus as well with them and prefer a singular spot to pay attention to. I’m using an Apple Studio Display because I’m very picky about pixel density. I opted to order it without the stand so I can run it on an ergo arm.
When I built the shelf for my desk, I fabricated a mounting bracket for the arm out of schedule 40 steel pipe and a 3D-printed sleeve that sits in a pocket CNC’d out. Since it sits flush on the underside, I don’t have to use a clamp that would extend down into the space where I keep my Mac and audio interface.

My office setup is probably a lot simpler—basic?—than most of my Ars colleagues. I use an adjustable wood-top desk that allows me to stand or sit while I work. I do almost all of my writing and editing on a MacBook Air, and I have a spare available in case I need it. Sometimes I travel with both MacBooks so I can use one for writing and the other for monitoring a rocket launch, press conference, or other event. I also work a lot from my porch, where I can enjoy the fresh air and quiet mornings on our ranch in rural Texas.
An iMac and a second monitor stand behind the laptops. I generally use them to watch conferences, rocket launch livestreams, weather radar, or live news. It just depends on what’s happening any given day. One of the things I love about the space beat is there’s something happening nearly every day, and it’s possible to cover much of it from home. There are often multiple things happening the same day, so the dual-screen setup becomes especially handy then. For example, I can use one monitor to watch what SpaceX is doing at Starbase, Texas, and another to watch a rocket launch in Florida. I use a ring light behind my desk for TV interviews or podcast appearances.
Absent from my desk is my large collection of space swag stowed away in storage boxes. Perhaps I will bring it out to add to my workspace for a future Ars Staff Source. For now, I use a mouse pad from the European Space Agency that I’ve had for at least 15 years. The mouse pad features ESA’s astronomy missions that were in development or operations at the time. All of the missions have now launched, and some have long been decommissioned. It’s a good reminder of how long it takes to design, develop, build, and launch science missions. Anyone who says this stuff is easy is being dishonest.

CSR not just legal obligation but investment in India’s future: Karnataka Guv
Bengaluru, Karnataka Governor Sudha Yadav on Friday said CSR should not be viewed merely as a legal obligation, but as an investment in society's future and in building a developed India.
She said industries must cultivate a spirit of giving back to society the wealth they earn from it.
The governor was speaking at the BCIC CSR Conclave-2026, organised by the Bengaluru Chamber of Industry and Commerce here as part of its Golden Jubilee celebrations, officials said.
She said the vision of 'Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas' could be realised only through the active participation of society and the corporate sector, alongside government efforts.
Collective efforts involving all sections of society would be the driving force behind building a new India, she added.
Quoting renowned industrialist J R D Tata, Yadav said the fundamental principle of Corporate social responsibility should be to give back to society many times over what businesses receive from it, according to a statement issued by Lok Bhavan.
She stressed the importance of integrating social responsibility with business objectives and ensuring that corporate initiatives contribute to sustainable social development.
"Profit is the fuel that keeps the engine running, but purpose is the compass that gives it direction," she said.
Noting that India had made significant strides in CSR, she flagged several challenges, such as the uneven distribution of CSR funds, limited participation by Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises , and inadequate assessment of the long-term impact of projects.
She called on industry bodies and business organisations to work together to address these concerns.
The governor said industries were undertaking commendable CSR initiatives in areas such as women's empowerment and health, education, school infrastructure and tree plantation. However, she emphasised that launching projects was not enough; they had to be sustained and responsibly managed until the intended outcomes were achieved.
Referring to school infrastructure projects in rural areas and tree plantation drives, she said many saplings failed to survive due to inadequate maintenance.
She also pointed out that several regions continued to lack basic infrastructure and adequate development opportunities.
Yadav said greater attention should be paid to improving the living standards, education and social progress of tribal communities.
She urged industries and business organisations to look beyond their immediate areas of operation and contribute to the development of backward and remote regions of the state.
Instead of undertaking isolated projects independently, industries could join hands to identify priority areas and implement comprehensive development programmes, she said.
Yadav suggested that industries adopt specific regions, assess their needs, set clear development goals and implement projects in a phased manner.
Regularly assessing a project's baseline, the progress made and the number of beneficiaries reached would help ensure that CSR initiatives delivered measurable results. Such an outcome-oriented approach was essential to fulfil the true purpose of CSR, she said.
The governor called on the corporate sector to recognise its social responsibility and make meaningful contributions through CSR initiatives towards the vision of a developed India.
"At a time when India is achieving new development milestones, it is the collective responsibility of all stakeholders to build a nation that offers future generations better opportunities, equality and sustainable development," she added.

In the process, we also found behind-the-scene photos related to the movie shared on Instagram by Anushka Pimputkar, the woman in the viral clip. In one of the photos, she is seen with Avinash Narkar, the actor who is standing next to her in the viral video.
To sum up, the viral video does not show a real incident of a woman trying to record a fake molestation clip on a bus. It is a scene from the trailer of the Marathi film, ‘Janak’. Social media claims presenting the footage as real are false.

Viewers of the second season of The Hunting Wives, currently streaming on Netflix, will find a poignant message at the end of the season finale: “In Loving Memory of Salli Newman.”
Newman was the senior vice president of television production at Lionsgate, producer of The Hunting Wives. She died of a heart attack on December 8, 2025, in her Burbank home at the age of 67, according to her family.
Hunting Wives showrunner Rebecca Cutter told Entertainment Weekly that Newman died during the filming of Season 2. “So we dedicated the final episode to her,” Cutter said. “And, yeah, that was really sad. She was such a hard worker. She so loved the show, and it was just really devastating.”
Newman was also included in the 2026 Primetime Emmy Awards In Memoriam broadcast on September 24.
Watch on Deadline
Newman moved to Los Angeles after graduating from Montana State University and launched her show business career at 19, training as an actor and stuntwoman while working as a secretary/assistant at Consolidated Film Industries.
“Salli soaked up all the knowledge she could from industry veterans,” her family notes, “and worked hard to learn her craft. She created Firebrand Productions in 1990 and spent the next 30 years as an independent producer, working on both made-for-tv movies and feature films, plus several series for both networks and streaming services.”
Among her many producing, co-producing or executive producing credits were D2: The Mighty Ducks (1994), When a Man Loves a Woman (1994), Naomi & Wynonna: Love Can Build A Bridge (1995), Bunheads (2013) and 31 episodes of Greenleaf (2018-2020).
In 2020, Newman was hired as a Senior VP of Television Production at LionsGate Films in Santa Monica, where she worked until her death in December 2025.
Newman is survived by four sisters, two brothers, stepmother Joan Newman, five step-siblings and numerous nieces and nephews.
The second season of The Hunting Wives, starring Malin Akerman, Dermot Mulroney and Brittany Snow, is available to stream on Netflix.

Thirteen dead as mine disaster highlights illegal hunt for gold
- Published
It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.
Rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and at least 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.
Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.
Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.
Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims.
"We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely."
Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.
Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high – spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.
This included state-owned mining company Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have said the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.
On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately announced that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.
But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures.
"[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he said, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector.
"It's still very massive and very big because this has been going on for a very long time."
Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.
Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, said that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments".
"As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.
In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects.
Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.
But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common – whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.
Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.
Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.
There are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.
Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, said the total casualty figure "is still unclear".
"Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it."
The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic issue behind it.
"This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," said Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman.
"We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched.
"Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going."
As rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.
More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.
As she waits for news of her father, Rani says: "I hope he's found soon."

Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
- Published
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.
Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.
The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.
Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.
"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.
If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.
The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".
Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.
A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.
A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.
Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.
She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".
Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.

The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.
All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. Feijóo said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while Sánchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.
While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.
The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.
Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.
Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.
Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.
Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.
Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".
He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign. As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

The message from the Trump administration to one of the world’s leading semiconductor companies was clear: Give the US government a chunk of your company. Right now. Or else.
Do not make the “mistake of thinking that this is a negotiation,” Commerce Department lawyer David Shapiro told the chief financial officer of the Intel Corporation in August 2025, according to internal notes from a company call contained in a federal lawsuit. “The President is expecting to announce a deal on these terms on Friday.”
Shapiro acknowledged that “the Board could choose not to accept the offer,” according to a summary of his remarks prepared for Intel’s directors. But the Trump administration official “noted that rejection will have consequences that [Shapiro] cannot predict.”
Days later, the board gave the administration what it wanted. “It is my Great Honor to report that the United States of America now fully owns and controls 10% of INTEL,” Donald Trump posted to his social platform. “The United States paid nothing for these Shares, and the Shares are now valued at approximately $11 Billion Dollars. This is a great Deal for America.”
President Trump was similarly jubilant on Monday, announcing that he had “convinced” Nvidia’s board of directors to rehire chief executive Jensen Huang. The proclamation was a shock. But it wasn’t entirely without precedent.
Fifteen months earlier, the Trump administration had interfered with the leadership decisions at another major chipmaker, court documents allege. Then, as now, allegations swirled that the company’s CEO was too close to China. Then, as now, the Trump administration dealt itself into the company’s financial future.
It’s part of a broader shift within the government in general and the Commerce Department in particular, a former member of that department tells WIRED. Out are old metrics “like creating jobs or the US being more competitive or owning more of the market share,” this ex-Trump administration official says. When dealing with private companies, a single overriding concern is: “Are you going to give back to the government in cash?”
Documents unredacted as part of a shareholder’s lawsuit against Intel’s board show how far the administration has been willing to go to get what it wants. The lawsuit’s allegations were previously reported by WP Intelligence.
“The Board, operating under the shadow of the President’s threats,” the lawsuit alleges, “caved to the government’s extortion.” A second case, asking for internal records, was filed in April by the same shareholder, Richard Paisner, against Nvidia.
“It’s just straight-up coercion,” says Scott Lincicome, a vice president at the libertarian Cato Institute. “The company starts making decisions not based on what’s best for the company in the short or long term, what’s best for shareholders, but what’s best for politics and what the government is demanding.”
“That’s not what you want from any company,” he adds. “When you’re talking about the world’s most innovative companies and these kinds of bleeding-edge technologies that have not only huge economic implications but national security ones, then that’s a huge problem.”
Representatives for Intel declined to comment for this story. The White House, Commerce Department, and Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment.
The parallels between Nvidia’s government-assisted autogolpe and Intel’s alleged forced sale aren’t exact. In the Intel case, Trump all but accused the company’s boss of being compromised by Beijing; in the Nvidia situation, the president reportedly dismissed concerns from his own intelligence agencies about the executive’s connections to China. But both instances show a growing fusion of private enterprise and public office.
During the Biden administration, Intel won awards for up to $11 billion in government grants and contracts, much of it under the CHIPS Act, which was meant to help build semiconductor manufacturing and assembly plants in America and bolster domestic research.
At the time, there was some grumbling inside the Commerce Department, which administered the CHIPS and Science Act grants, about funding what was seen as a “failing incumbent” in the semiconductor space, says the former official. (Intel had, in recent years, fallen on hard times.) But by March 2025, Intel had received about $2.2 billion of the grants. That’s when President Trump told Congress that the CHIPS Act was “a horrible, horrible thing.” The rest of Intel’s money was put on hold, tied to hitting certain milestones, while the administration said it was renegotiating the deals.
The same month Lip-Bu Tan was hired as Intel’s new CEO. Soon after, his ties to China made him a Trump target, when Reuters reported that Tan had invested in “hundreds of Chinese tech firms,” some with connections to Beijing’s military. Tan’s former firm, Cadence Design Systems, pleaded guilty to violating US sanctions by selling semiconductor designs to a restricted Chinese military university, and agreed to pay more than $140 million in fines. Tan was never personally charged, but the violations happened while he was the CEO.
Two weeks later, the president was watching Maria Bartiromo’s show on the Fox Business Network. It mentioned a letter a senator had sent Intel about the China ties. Trump posted, “The CEO of INTEL is highly CONFLICTED and must resign, immediately. There is no other solution to this problem.”
Tan went to the Oval Office on August 11 to see if there was, in fact, another solution. He got 40 minutes with the president, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Tan claimed his experience in China was a strength, not a detriment. According to the book Regime Change, Tan argued that there was no way he could’ve known about every one of the deals his many companies made; Trump, who had his own sprawling business empire, surely knew what that was like. Tan promised to give up his holdings in China, according to a letter Tan shared with Intel’s board, and put any proceeds into a blind trust.
“The primary goal was to eliminate any worries about Lip-Bu himself, his Cadence background, and his investments with China,” according to a source with knowledge of the matter. But there were major financial concerns for Intel, too. “We had declining revenues and needed money.”
Neither Tan’s letter, excerpted in the complaint, nor Trump’s social media posts praising the CEO after the meeting mentioned anything about giving the government a chunk of the company. Yet Trump later insisted that a deal had been cooked up right then and there. “He came in, he saw me, we talked for a while. I liked him a lot, I thought he was very good,” the president told The Wall Street Journal. “I said, ‘You know what? I think the United States should be given 10% of Intel.’ And he said, ‘I would consider that.’”
“I should’ve asked for more. It was so easy,” Trump later recalled.
According to the court filing’s review of Intel’s internal documents, Shapiro—a former partner at the New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz—made a verbal offer on August 18. Ultimately, in exchange for the cut of Intel, the Trump administration would free up the $8.9 billion US government grants that it had already won. They wanted about a tenth of the company’s stock for free, in exchange for Washington keeping the commitment it had already made.
Then came the call in which Shapiro insisted there was no room for negotiation. “The board needs to consider,” he said, according to Intel’s summary of his remarks included in the court documents, the “benefits of having a friend in this administration and what the administration can do to help Intel (including with customers).”
Intel’s board met, and decided they hated the deal. “The economic terms that had been proposed [by] the Administration were not, in their current form, attractive to the company,” minutes of the meeting, reprinted in the lawsuit, noted.
But they went ahead with it anyway. Paisner’s lawyers say in the court documents the board took the offer thrust forward by the administration. Intel’s attorneys disagree, arguing in their motion to dismiss that there was some back-and-forth deal-making, and it made the agreement more favorable to the company. The grants became “immediately available” while “strategically aligning the interests of Intel’s stockholders and the US Government.”
On August 25, Lutnick released a video with Tan, sitting side-by-side on cushioned chairs. “I really look forward to have the US government be my shareholder,” Tan turned to Lutnick and said. “And we can work together and make Intel great again.”
Inside the company, the video was “a surprise to everyone,” according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter. Some employees joked that it was reminiscent of a “hostage video.”
Not long after that, Nvidia—led by Tan’s friend Jensen Huang—made a $5 billion investment in Intel. “I love seeing their stock price go up, making the USA RICHER, AND RICHER,” Trump posted. “Who would not want to make deals like that?”
Deals, plural. On the day Tan was hauled to the Oval Office, Trump announced that his administration had been negotiating separately with Huang. The Nvidia leader was beyond eager to sell more of his semiconductors to China. “And I said, if I’m going to do that, I want you to pay us as a country something,’” Trump said. They settled on 15 percent of all sales of the H20 model chip. Months after that, they cut a second deal: a 25 percent bounty on sales of Nvidia’s even-more advanced H200 chips.
In their lawsuit against Nvidia, Paisner’s attorneys argue the surcharges amount to “unlawful taxes,” and that the board’s “decisions to enter into such agreements are the product of mismanagement and breaches of fiduciary duty.”
In court, NVIDIA’s lawyers insisted that the company “did not enter into any illegal ‘agreement’ with the government but instead engaged with the government and stated that it would comply with federal regulations.” Moreover, the attorneys say Paisner is trying to make a political point, rather than a legal one. “When asked about his purpose in bringing this action,” they write, “Paisner was candid: ‘It’s to make a public point of how NVIDIA conducts itself.’”
The attorneys wrote this in May, months before Nvidia’s and Huang’s recent drama. Last week, board chair Harvey Jones said on the company’s quarterly earnings call that it did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” citing his “disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms.” (Not to mention mounting evidence that the company’s most sophisticated chips were making their way to China, in violation of US law.) But, according to The New York Times, after days of pressure from top administration officials, the company and the government essentially struck a deal Sunday night to reinstate Huang.
“Don’t think for a second that politics ever play a role in this company, not even a little bit,” Huang said during his first company-wide meeting after rejoining the company, WIRED reported. “We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”

With Hyderabad recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of over 300 on Deepavali and many other days recording poor air quality earlier this year, doctors and public health experts have called for a coordinated effort by hospitals to track the health effects of pollution and build a city-level database that can help shape public policy.
The issue came into focus during a panel discussion on ‘Impact of Mobility on Air Quality and Public Health’ at Cyberabad Moves, where doctors said that the effects of polluted air went beyond respiratory illnesses and were also linked to cardiovascular problems and strokes. They stressed that the health consequences of daily exposure to pollution, particularly during commutes, needed to be documented through local medical data.
Pawan Mukulutla of WRI India, who moderated the discussion, pointed out that congestion was only the most visible consequence of the way people travelled. The less visible costs included exposure to polluted air, unsafe roads and the lack of pedestrian infrastructure. He cited Hyderabad’s AQI crossing 300 on Deepavali and said particulate matter levels, including PM2.5 and PM10, had been several times above prescribed thresholds.
Pool health data
Dr. Sudheer Vinnamala, Regional Medical Director of KIMS, said hospitals could work together to create a Hyderabad-level health database by sharing anonymised information on respiratory illnesses, strokes and cardiovascular conditions with public health authorities.
“What you can’t measure, you can’t manage,” he said, arguing that such a database could help identify vulnerable groups and establish a clearer picture of the relationship between air quality and health outcomes.
He said doctors could also use daily AQI information to alert patients with asthma and other respiratory conditions when pollution levels deteriorated, allowing them to take precautions and avoid unnecessary exposure. Hospitals could play a role in reducing pollution and traffic by encouraging carpooling, staggering appointments and arranging last-mile transport links from Metro stations.
Dr Vishwanath Gella, a pulmonologist at AIG Hospitals, said pollution affected people with and without pre-existing health conditions. He said doctors were seeing patients with asthma, respiratory infections and other lung-related complaints, with an increase in cases during periods of poor air quality, particularly around Deepavali and in winter.
Children face daily exposure
Dr Shailaja Tetali of the Public Health Foundation of India said research into school travel patterns showed that around 80 per cent of children lived within two to three kilometres of their schools. A majority travelled by public transport, walked or cycled.
While walking and cycling offered physical activity, children using these modes were also exposed to roadside pollution and faced road safety risks. She said improving infrastructure around schools could address several of these concerns, as interventions within a three-kilometre radius could cover a large proportion of children’s daily journeys.
She called for authorities to act on existing evidence instead of repeatedly commissioning studies, suggesting that interventions could first be tested in smaller areas and then replicated across the city.
Poor road design
Orthopaedic surgeon Dr Gurava Reddy of KIMS-Sunshine Hospitals said poorly designed roads and junctions contributed to crashes, pointing to inadequate visibility, obstructed sightlines and sudden turning movements as factors that made roads dangerous.
He said several improvements could be made through better road engineering without requiring large investments, provided authorities were willing to address design flaws.
The panel also discussed the responsibility of hospitals and other large establishments, which generate considerable traffic through patients, visitors and employees. Participants said medical institutions could reduce unnecessary trips through better appointment scheduling, shared transport and last-mile connectivity.

Reducing sugar exposure during the first 1,000 days of life is associated with a substantially lower cancer risk decades later, and a slower biological ageing process, the results of a U.K.-based study have shown.
The article, ‘Early-life sugar restriction causally reduces adult cancer incidence and slows biological aging’ published in PNAS, analysed 64,761 adults in the U.K. Biobank, coinciding with a policy-level sugar rationing period in the U.K. People whose first 1,000 days occurred during sugar rationing had 36% to 69% lower incidence of liver/intrahepatic bile duct, rectal, prostate, breast, and lung cancers later in life. There were markers that indicated that these people had 2.2 fewer years of biological aging, and they were left with persistent healthier eating habits, even 50 years later.

What happens now for Bayern Munich and Musiala?
- Published
Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players - have collided over recent weeks.
During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.
This neurological condition causes a brief, sudden lapse in awareness and responsiveness. Musiala had two of these lapses during pre-season games, but episodes already happened during the previous year.
At first, the shock among fans and observers was huge. Bayern kept Musiala's condition a secret for some time, and only a few insiders knew about it. In the days after Musiala's lapse during a friendly against Heidenheim, speculations arose over whether the player's medical issue had been known before he signed a highly lucrative contract extension in February 2025.
But it has been confirmed by sources close to the team - and Bayern themselves - that the condition had not been detected before April 2025. One source described Musiala, at the time of signing his new contract, as being "in great health".
In April 2025, days after suffering a muscle tear, Musiala caused a high-speed car crash which cost him his driver's licence. Munich's public prosecutor's office responded to a recent enquiry saying there is no evidence that the accident was caused by a lapse, nor that it was the cause of Musiala's condition.
Nevertheless, checks a couple of days after the crash revealed he was suffering from absence seizures. Musiala's camp consulted numerous experts and hired doctors to treat the player, with the knowledge of Jochen Hahne, Bayern's team doctor. How close the consultations between the external doctors and Bayern's medical staff are remains a point of discussion, among many other things in this complex matter.
Soon after, Musiala's football-related injuries became an issue. He broke his fibula and injured his ankle during the Fifa Club World Cup after colliding with then PSG goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. He needed months to recover and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, likely related to the leg injury.
After the 2026 World Cup he had a metal plate removed from his left foot, which affected his pre-season preparation. Musiala just recently recovered from a weeks-long absence due to a hamstring tear.
On top of that, new incidents related to his neurological condition have come to light. Days before his recent return to training Musiala had another lapse, just like he did on the morning of a Champions League game against Real Madrid in April.
All of this is the tragic story of a highly talented footballer who might never return to his previous level and must deal with a medical condition for the rest of his life.
Absence seizures require daily medication. There are other high-level athletes, such as England rugby union player Tommy Freeman, who have had to deal with the same condition.
Rummenigge goes on the offensive
A controversy erupted last Friday, as Bayern faced Cologne in what was supposed to be an ordinary league game. Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, once chairman of the board and now a member of Bayern's supervisory board, asked a TV crew to come to his section in the stands.
The unscheduled post-game interview unfolded in a way that no-one at Bayern, not even other members of the club's hierarchy, expected.
"He has a health issue, which is known, and it is known that he has a contract which includes hefty sums of money," Rummenigge said. "You need to talk to the family, to the player and most importantly to the agency, because these sums are - with all due respect - not justifiable any longer."
A day later, chairman of the board Jan-Christian Dreesen and club president Herbert Hainer tried to defuse the situation at the yearly membership assembly, but were also attacked by club member Jonathan Hoffmann.
Hoffmann, a neurologist, said it wouldn't help to go after Musiala publicly, for which he received applause from many of the present members.
One might wonder why an experienced deal-maker like Rummenigge would willingly put down one of his players who could still be valuable to the club, even if it's just for a sale.
He might have been agitated by the way the home game against Cologne went. Harry Kane suffered a ligament tear in his ankle early in the game and star winger Michael Olise had to leave the stadium on crutches.
But, even more importantly, it has become clear that Rummenigge was unhappy with how contract negotiations with Musiala's camp - between October 2024 and February 2025 - unfolded.
Bayern and particularly Max Eberl, the club's director of sport, were running out of time, as Musiala's contract would have ended with the conclusion of the 2025-26 season. If they hadn't reached an agreement before April or May 2025, Bayern would have felt obliged to sell Musiala during the summer transfer window.
Bayern under pressure during contract negotiations
Musiala played an impressive Euro 2024 for Germany and was one of Bayern's best players during the period of negotiations. Among others, Real Madrid were interested, but only for a free transfer in 2026.
Keep in mind, Musiala has quite a unique profile as a No 10 that can also come from the wing and break down low-block defences with his dribbles and passing.
Under pressure and confronted by a shrewd negotiator in Christian Schmid, Musiala's agent and a trained lawyer, Bayern agreed to a salary package that could earn Musiala, in a best-case scenario, £21m a year, with £15m as a base salary. Bayern also agreed to grant a signing fee of close to £25m, paid over the stretch of the contract. Musiala even got his wish granted of receiving his own box at Allianz Arena.
Some reports indicated that the fact Musiala's deal includes sick pay for six months, in the case of injury or illness, could be interpreted as circumstantial evidence that the player's representatives may have known about his condition beforehand. A standard Bundesliga contract only offers sick pay for six weeks before insurance would shoulder the payments.
But even six months is a short period in comparison. Premier League players receive their full basic wage for the first 18 months. And, when Bayern negotiate with top players, they ultimately compete against Europe's elite.
Rummenigge, and to a lesser extent his long-time boardroom compatriot Uli Hoeness, made Eberl responsible for the unfavourable terms - arguing that Schmid essentially played Eberl.
Eberl has been the target of criticism from the two former powerbrokers for quite some time. At a recent supervisory board meeting, Hoeness is said to have attacked Eberl for his inactivity over the Musiala issue in the past six months.
That being said, Bayern bought into the Musiala hype for a couple of years, hoping that they would have a superstar of their own who could be marketed across the globe.
The relationship between the club and agent Schmid has been strained to say the least, with Rummenigge particularly disliking him. Some sources believe this was one of the root causes for Rummenigge's recent attack on live TV.
When a 16-year-old Kennet Eichhorn came on the market during the summer, as he wanted to leave second-division side Hertha Berlin, Bayern were interested but ultimately dropped out of the race for the highly touted midfielder. Eichhorn is represented by Schmid and ended up joining Bayer Leverkusen.
Kompany is backing Musiala
Hoeness met with Schmid during the summer to discuss how to proceed with Musiala, but the player's agent did not indicate that they would agree to a wage reduction. Hoeness called the matter a "dilemma" for Bayern during a TV show earlier this month, but did not go as far as Rummenigge.
As long as Musiala is not medically forced to retire, he will receive the wage that was agreed upon in February 2025. Even if Bayern would intend to part ways with the player, they would need to do everything in their power to get the player as close to his previous form as possible.
The release clause of £125m, which could be triggered next year, seems unrealistic. Any comments by Bayern bosses against Musiala, or further leaks to the media, may indeed lower his market value down to zero - unless the player can simply shake things off and perform again.
Eberl and head coach Vincent Kompany have come out to back Musiala. Joshua Kimmich, one of Bayern's veteran players, also criticised the treatment of Musiala after a 2-1 loss to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday. "Of course, the club is above all and bigger than the player, but not bigger than the human. This is an absolute no-go and also not Bayern-like," Kimmich said.
Even football players' union Fifpro condemned Rummenigge's comments. On Wednesday, Bayern put out a statement saying that a meeting between the club and Musiala's representatives took place on Tuesday, in which it was agreed that the player's health should be paramount.
Whether the damage can be repaired is up in the air. As Bayern have a number of attacking players sidelined, they need a healthy and mentally prepared Musiala in the coming weeks and months.

Bisleri faces fresh FSSAI prosecution after bacteria found in Bengal sample
The sample was collected from Bisleri's manufacturing plant in Telipara village in Jalpaiguri district. Both the primary laboratory and the referral food laboratory confirmed the presence of coliform bacteria in the sample.
Fresh trouble brews for Bisleri after the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) sanctioned prosecution against the company over a water sample from its West Bengal unit. The sample was found to contain coliform bacteria, and the findings were confirmed by two laboratories.
The sample was collected from Bisleri's manufacturing plant in Telipara village in Jalpaiguri district. As per a report by news agency PTI, both the primary laboratory and the referral food laboratory confirmed the presence of coliform bacteria in the sample.
This form of bacteria can enter water systems through sewage leaks or damaged pipes, among other pathways.
The sample belonged to batch number PB 201. Following the findings, the sale of the batch was prohibited on August 12, 2026. FSSAI has now sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, in connection with the case.
EARLIER ACTION OVER GOA UNIT SAMPLE
The latest action comes days after FSSAI sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri in a separate case involving a packaged drinking water sample collected from its manufacturing facility in Goa.
According to FSSAI, the regulatory sample, categorised as "Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)", failed to meet the prescribed bromate limits and was declared unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
Following an appeal by the company, the sample was sent to a referral food laboratory for further examination. The laboratory also declared it unsafe after detecting polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). FSSAI subsequently sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International over violations related to unsafe packaged drinking water.
Bisleri, however, maintained that its packaged drinking water was safe for consumption and said the issue concerned a single batch manufactured at its Goa facility in September 2025.
The company said FSSAI collected six samples from the Goa facility on September 30, 2025. While initial testing found that five samples met all applicable standards, the sixth recorded a bromate level of 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre.
Bisleri said it appealed against the findings, following which the sample was sent to a referral laboratory. The company maintained that the referral laboratory found bromate levels within the prescribed limit but separately flagged the presence of PAHs.
The company also said it had not received any notice from FSSAI and had subsequently got the same sample tested at an FSSAI-approved laboratory, which also found bromate levels within permissible limits. Bisleri said it submitted the independent test results to FSSAI's Western Regional Office on February 2, 2026, but received no further communication and understood the matter to have been closed.
The company said it conducts more than 90 quality tests across its 10-step manufacturing process and would continue to cooperate with the regulator.
FSSAI WIDENS CRACKDOWN ON PACKAGED WATER BRANDS
Meanwhile, FSSAI has widened its scrutiny of the packaged drinking water market, bringing brands across the sector under its scanner. The regulator has collected random samples from different packaged water brands as part of an expanded inspection drive, with reports of the tests expected soon.
Samples of several packaged water brands, including Bisleri, had also been collected earlier. The latest exercise puts the wider bottled water market under scrutiny as FSSAI steps up checks on the quality of packaged drinking water.
Apart from testing water quality, the regulator is also examining brands using names and labels that closely resemble those of established packaged drinking water companies. FSSAI is expected to take action against companies found using misleading or lookalike names and labelling.

The old Hollywood cliché is that "all press is good press." Ariana Grande seems on a mission to prove the opposite.
A quick scan of Grande's recent headlines outlines a rocky year for the 33-year-old singer and actor. In June, news broke that Grande and her boyfriend Ethan Slater had split, three years after the "Wicked" costars first drew attention and plenty of criticism for their romance (including from Slater's ex-wife, Lily Jay).
Around the same time, Grande kicked off her much-anticipated arena tour to support her 2024 album "Eternal Sunshine," which, in a strange choice, overlapped with the rollout of her latest album, "Petal." Released in July, the new album performed well on the charts, but reviews were mixed, with some critics describing the music as "pussyfooted" and "frustratingly vague."
Throughout the summer, Grande's performances and music video premieres were overtaken by rampant speculation about her health, culminating in a spiky public statement from her team in August: "She looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny," it read in part.
Less than three months after leaving the stage, however, Grande is back in the press, appearing on red carpets and late-night TV shows to promote her new movie, "Focker-In-Law." Although People reported in September that Grande would remain "committed" to her promo obligations for the movie despite her planned break from the public eye, the rapid turnaround makes for an untidy narrative.
"She's always in the news for the wrong reasons," Larry Kopp, a longtime PR professional and founder of The TASC Group, told Business Insider. "All press is not good press when you're talking about someone like Ariana Grande."
In the upper echelon of celebrity where Grande resides, publicity is all but guaranteed; the challenge is in diligently curating it. Each public appearance will attract attention to how she looks, who she's with, and where she's going, while each misstep will be magnified. If the story can't always be all positive, it should at least be coherent.
This is where Grande and her team have floundered in recent years. For such a beloved and multi-talented celebrity, Grande has displayed remarkably weak ownership of her image, PR pros agreed. Representatives for Grande did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.
"Where Taylor Swift and Beyoncé are so intentional in every single step that they take, Ariana Grande feels scattered," said Mike Fahey, the founder and CEO of the PR agency Fahey Communications.
"One day she's Glinda, the next day she's putting out a new album," Fahey continued, referring to Grande's role in the recent "Wicked" films, for which she was Oscar-nominated and then Oscar-snubbed in consecutive years. "Personally, even as a pop culture consumer, I have been very confused by the cadence."
Although Grande is both a gifted singer and a comedic actor, Fahey said her versatility is obscured by a slapdash combination of aesthetics, personas, and public missives: "There doesn't seem to be any overarching strategy."
Grande has a knack for needlessly making the news
As the first "Wicked" film proved, Grande's comedic chops are some of her most valuable skills, celebrated by fans and critics alike. And many critics are praising Grande's scene-stealing turn in "Focker-In-Law," in which she plays a discerning former FBI hostage negotiator and foil to Ben Stiller's bumbling, well-meaning everyman. With savvier navigation of the PR machine, Grande's return to the limelight could have been tallied cleanly as a triumph, a highlight on her résumé.
Instead, the statement released by Grande's team in August laid the groundwork for a visible flip-flop — a dangerous game to play when all comments and actions are thoroughly documented and analyzed online.
"In 2026, in the social media era, contradictions are hypocrisy," Fahey said.
Announcing that Grande would be "taking a step back from visibility" was ill-advised and ill-timed, Kopp and Fahey said. It added fuel to the speculative fire surrounding her well-being, when a simpler solution was obvious: let the embers simmer down naturally. After playing 41 sold-out shows, most fans would have expected Grande to take a break anyway, and she could have done so without a formal announcement.
"Good publicists understand that less is more," Kopp said. "When a PR team comments, they're creating a story. They're putting scaffolding on the story. They're building it up."
Kayley Cornelius, a celebrity PR specialist at Press Box PR, agreed that Grande's statement left too much open to interpretation.
"Her team may have felt that gave her room to finish the work she wanted to do and then take a break," Cornelius said via email. "But if you're a fan reading that statement, you could quite reasonably take it to mean you won't be seeing her for a while. That makes the next time she does appear a story in itself."
This isn't the first time Grande has seemed to contradict herself in public. In 2024, Grande announced plans to scale back her pop-star career to focus on musical theater; the "Eternal Sunshine" deluxe edition arrived less than five months later, followed closely by the Eternal Sunshine Tour and then another brand-new pop album. Grande also dropped out of the West End revival of "Sunday in the Park with George," scheduled to open in London next summer.
On Tuesday, in the midst of "Focker-In-Law" release week, Grande announced a tour documentary, "The Eternal Sunshine Diaries," and a new concert film.
"She has no throughline," Kopp said. "A good business manager, a good publicist, a good lawyer, good people around her should be giving her good advice, and it doesn't seem like they're giving it to her. Or they're giving it to her, and she's not listening."
A real break could help refresh Grande's image
Grande has been famous since she was a tween on Nickelodeon, but ever since 2018, when she dominated headlines with her whirlwind engagement to Pete Davidson and her smash-hit breakup anthem "Thank U, Next," Grande has been an obsessive fixture of tabloid coverage and social media snark.
"One of the recurring themes in Ariana's media coverage has been how often the conversation around her personal life carries over into her work," Cornelius said. "Even when she's had major career moments, particularly with 'Wicked,' the headlines haven't always been about her performances."
It's a vicious cycle that repeats every time Grande steps out with a new hairstyle, a new boyfriend, or yet another new song about the haters. "Is it really my fault you all gave me your hearts of your own accord? I don't really think so," Grande sings in her latest No. 1 hit, "Hate That I Made You Love Me."
She may be right, and the harsh, competitive fame game is the true culprit here. Contradictory statements and overlapping projects are nickels and dimes in the grand scheme of public interest. At the same time, Grande is a multimillion-dollar brand, and if she wants to keep it that way, she isn't exempt from playing along.
"Her movies are blockbuster smashes," Fahey said. "You can't say it's the public's fault when the public has built you into the celebrity that you are today."
"I would tell her to take an actual break, actually get better, heal whatever it is that's haunting her right now," Fahey continued. The cycle is plenty fed, and an earnest reprieve from scrutiny could give her team the time and space to reset her reputation — and Grande the time she may need to refine her vision as an artist, then return with a project imbued with passion and meaning, something that will stand the test of time.
"No more personal life in the news, no more chicanery, no more drama. Just stay out of the news as best you can for a while," Kopp said. "The great thing about someone like Ariana is that her art, her music, is still there. It doesn't go away."
