The quest for beauty and the enduring appeal for fair and blemishfree skin goes back to ages and across cultures. However, in recent years, this has been landing people in hospitals with serious health issues, as it happened in the case of the 17-year-old girl from Areekode in Malappuram district in Keralam.
Persuaded by many social influencers who raved about a face cream which gave them fair, blemishfree skin, she had also been using the same for over a year. The product with the brand name F-TUNES - claimed to contain turmeric and other “natural ingredients” and cited Dubai as the place of manufacture. She was hospitalised after she developed severe symptoms like fainting spells, swelling on legs and fall in blood pressure and was diagnosed with Membranous nephropathy, a condition wherein the immune system gets dysregulated, triggering nephrotic syndrome (heavy loss of protein through urine). Doctors traced her condition to the heavy mercury content in the face cream she was using. Lab analysis of a sample of the skin lightning cream obtained from the patient revealed that the product contained 12,500 ppm of mercury, way over the legal limit of 1 ppm
After prolonged treatment, the girl is now recovering. The police and drug regulatory authorities have begun a crackdown on the dubious cosmetic products in the market . The Health Minister has also threatened action against social influencers who are peddling dubious cosmetics online
Mercury is a highly toxic heavy metal and it can inhibit tyrosinase, a key enzyme produced by skin cells to produce melanin, the natural pigment that gives colour to skin and hair. The mercury in the face cream stops the production of new melanin and thins out the skin, giving it a lightening effect. The higher the content of mercury, the more spectacular the lightening effect, which consumers perceive as the product’s effectiveness.

Prem Kishore occasionally turns to Artificial Intelligence (AI) for help when it comes to raising his six-year-old son. “It’s the big feelings that can be difficult to talk about, because we don’t always have the right words. I usually seek advice from my friends or psychologists, but if they’re not available, I turn to AI,” says the creative professional, 43, who splits his time between Bengaluru and Dubai.
Kishore recalls how he visited an AI video generator to create an avatar of a doctor, who chatted with his son about healthy boundaries and consent.
As AI becomes more enmeshed in our day-to-day lives, families are turning to it for advice, research and assistance in managing the mental load of modern-day parenting. A 2026 consumer trends report by GIPSI, the research arm of agency Tonic Worldwide, combined search and social media data with a survey of 50,000 people, and found that 52% of Indian Gen Z parents now use AI instead of their usual search engines, and 48% use it as an adviser. In India, Google Gemini recently launched a series of commercials featuring Shah Rukh Khan in which he directs two fathers at very different stages of their parenting journeys towards the chatbot for advice. Apps such as Fambot and AVA seek to help families with administrative tasks by syncing to their calendars, email and online shopping orders.
Eighteen years ago, when I first became a parent, Dr. Spock’s Baby and Child Care was the de facto gift to all new parents along with a Johnson & Johnson baby care set. I kept the book for a number of years after I had my second child and referred to it frequently. But today, new parents can seek advice from podcasts, influencers, online communities and yes, AI chatbots. There is a lot of advice out there, available in seconds. But how much of it is actually helping parents?
Author-editor Sanjana Kapur, 40, who’sraising a nine-year-old in Bengaluru, admits that parenting feels a little nerve-racking today. “There’s so much information out there, that you’re constantly worrying if you’re making the right decision, or how even your smallest reaction will affect your child. The world has become such a complicated place, and parents are nervous even when kids are at school now,” she admits.

ఈ ఘటన నేపథ్యంలో, పోలీసులు కొంతమంది వ్యక్తులను ఊరేగిస్తున్నట్లు చూపించే వీడియో ఒకటి సోషల్ మీడియాలో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) వైరల్ అవుతోంది. ముంబైలో యువ జంటపై దాడి చేసిన వారిని పోలీసులు ఇలా ఊరేగిస్తున్నారని ఈ వీడియోను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన వాదనలో నిజమెంత ఉందో ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ముంబైలోని కుర్లా వెస్ట్‌లో యువ జంటపై దాడి చేసిన నిందితులను ముంబై పోలీసులు రోడ్డు పై ఊరేగిస్తున్నట్లు ఈ వీడియో చూపిస్తోంది.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోలో గుజరాత్‌లోని సూరత్‌లో 18 ఏళ్ల సంతోష్ మోరే హత్య కేసులో అరెస్టైన నిందితులను చూపిస్తున్నారు. ఈ హత్య కేసుకు సంబంధించి సూరత్ పోలీసులు నిందితులను ఊరేగించారు. ముంబైలో యువ జంటపై దాడి చేసిన వారిని కాదు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన వాదన తప్పు.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేమ్‌లతో రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, 2026 నవంబర్ 14న Gujarat Live అనే ఇన్‌స్టాగ్రామ్ ఖాతాలో అప్‌లోడ్ చేసిన వీడియో లభించింది. ఈ వీడియో ముంబైలోని కుర్లా ఘటనకు ముందే అప్‌లోడ్ చేయబడింది. ఆ వీడియోలో ఉన్న వివరణలో, సూరత్‌కు చెందిన యువకుడు సంతోష్ మోరే హత్య కేసులో అరెస్టైన నిందితులను చూపిస్తున్నట్లు పేర్కొన్నారు.
దీనిపై కీవర్డ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలతో కూడిన పలు మీడియా రిపోర్టులు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) లభించాయి. ఈ రిపోర్టుల ప్రకారం, 8 నవంబర్ 2026న సూరత్‌లోని రసూలాబాద్ ప్రాంతంలో 18 ఏళ్ల సంతోష్ మోరేను కత్తితో పొడిచి హత్య చేసినట్లు ఆరోపణలు ఉన్నాయి. ప్రేమ వ్యవహారానికి సంబంధించిన వివాదం, గత కక్షల కారణంగా ఈ హత్య జరిగినట్లు సమాచారం. ఈ కేసులో జావేద్ అలియాస్ నవాబ్ షేక్, హన్సరాజ్ కుష్వాహా, షకీబ్ మానియార్, షాహిద్ షేక్, పీయూష్ సాహూలను నిందితులుగా గుర్తించారు.
2026 నవంబర్ 12న సూరత్ పోలీసులు తమ X ఖాతాలో అప్‌లోడ్ చేసిన వీడియోలో కూడా ఇలాంటి దృశ్యాలే కనిపించాయి. ఈ వీడియోలో అదే నిందితులను పోలీసులు ఊరేగించడం చూడవచ్చు. ఈ వీడియోకు జత చేసిన వివరణలో, ఖటోదరా పోలీస్ స్టేషన్ పరిధిలోని ఆజాద్ నగర్‌లో ఒక యువకుడి హత్య కేసులో నిందితులను ఖటోదరా పోలీసులు అరెస్టు చేసి, చట్టం గురించి వారికి గుణపాఠం చెప్పారని పేర్కొన్నారు.
చివరిగా, హత్య కేసులో నిందితులను సూరత్ పోలీసులు ఊరేగిస్తున్న వీడియోను, ముంబైలో యువ జంటపై దాడి చేసిన ఘటనకు సంబంధించినదిగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Suresh Mittal is 87. According to Uttar Pradesh’s latest draft electoral roll, his father, Vansh Mittal, is 23. Both are registered at house number 869 in booth 111 of the Dholana constituency in Hapur. The same roll lists Vansh as the son of Ajay, a 56-year-old in the same house.
Suresh is not an exception. Alt News found 1,10,875 voters in the Special Summary Revision (SSR) draft roll whose father or mother, registered in the same booth and the same house, is recorded as the same age as them or younger. The draft was published on November 17.
A Year of Revisions: First SIR, Now SSR
The draft comes at the end of a long year for UP’s voter list. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the rolls began on October 27, 2025 and ended with the final roll on April 10, 2026. In those 166 days the state’s electorate shrank from 15.44 crore to 13.39 crore.
As per the process of SIR, every voter was supposed to be issued an enumeration form, which was supposed to be collected by booth-level officers (BLOs). The Election Commission’s software then allegedly went through the data looking for what it called logical discrepancies. One of these was a parent less than 15 years older than the voter. About 2.22 crore voters in UP were sent notices for such discrepancies, and the Commission says hearings were completed on all of them.
On October 15, six months after the SIR’s final roll, the Election Commission ordered a Special Summary Revision (SSR) in 17 states and Union territories, including UP. The SSR draft roll, which merges the SIR roll with all supplementary lists, has 13.58 crore electors. Claims and objections can be filed till December 16, and the final roll is due on January 4, 2027.
What We Found and How
The SSR draft rolls are machine readable. We took every voter whose entry names a father or a mother, and looked in the same booth for a voter with that name living in the same house. If that ‘parent’ turned out to be the same age as the voter, or younger, we flagged the entry.
We found 1,10,875 such cases spread across all 75 districts and 403 constituencies.
In 35,523 of these cases, parent and child are the same age. In the other 75,352, the parent is younger, and in 6,860 of them by 20 years or more.
Some of the cases are shown below for representation:
What did SIR Actually Achieve?
The SIR was designed to weed out exactly this kind of error. It had enumeration forms, BLO visits, software flags and hearings. A parent who is younger than their own child is perhaps the most basic inconsistency a voter list can have. This raises a larger question: if a process this elaborate left the most basic errors untouched, what did the SIR actually achieve?
Moreover, spotting these anomalous entries is no rocket science. Each one is a contradiction between two lines of the same booth’s roll, often on the same page: An 87-year-old whose father is 23, a 123-year-old woman whose mother is 45, two women who are each other’s mother. A simple check on the roll itself would have thrown them up. Either no such check was run, or nobody acted on what it found.
As of now, all 1,10,875 are in the draft, and the window for corrections closes on December 16.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
- Published
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.
"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.
Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.
Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.
On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.
The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.
The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.
Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.

Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.
"My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said.
"Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?"
The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of New York City during the holidays.
There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.
Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.
"The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.
He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".
"We have a lot to be thankful for this Thanksgiving."
Some groups were not able to maneuver as easily. The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band is one of those missing out, due to a schedule conflict on Saturday.
“‘This can’t be happening’,” Rina Browder, mother of a snare drummer in the band, told local news, describing the band’s reactions.
"They were devastated. They've worked so hard for this. So many practices."
Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.
Speaking to the BBC on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.
The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.
"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua said.
But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".
The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.
Badua was hopeful his group would have the same experience he had when he first performed at the parade in 2003, as student drum major.
"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."
Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it needed to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.
"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Professor Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.
By Friday, 3,500 donors had stepped up to help the 410 students and their travel party. "This is truly phenomenal," said Houser.
While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain brought by the storm to eastern areas of the US.
Hundreds of thousands of homes were without power in the storm's aftermath Friday, and coastal areas had flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.

What changes in the new delimitation bill: Women's reservation, delimitation commission and 50% seat increase
The Centre will constitute a Delimitation Commission after the commencement of the proposed legislation, instead of constituting it from time to time.
The Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, seeks to bring forward the implementation of 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies by linking it to a delimitation exercise that will increase the number of seats allocated to every state and Union territory by 50%.
The bill, cleared by the Union Cabinet on Friday, November 27, provides for a uniform increase in seats over and above the existing strength, while protecting each state's current share of representation until 2051. It will be introduced in Parliament during the special sitting beginning November 30.
The proposed legislation replaces the earlier Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, which was defeated in the Lok Sabha in April, after Opposition parties raised concerns about the possible impact of delimitation on the representation of states, particularly those in southern India.
What changes in the new delimitation bill
- The long title of the new bill has been revised to make clear that it seeks to give effect to reservation of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and state Legislative Assemblies, along with the readjustment of seat allocation and the division of states and Union territories into territorial constituencies.
- Centre will constitute the Delimitation Commission as soon as may be after the commencement of the proposed legislation, instead of constituting it from time to time.
- The definition of “population” has been omitted from the bill. Instead, “latest census figures” has been defined as the latest census figures published on the date of commencement of the proposed legislation.
- The duties of the Delimitation Commission have been recast. The allocation of seats in the Lok Sabha and the total number of seats in state Legislative Assemblies will be readjusted in accordance with the proposed legislation. The division of states and Union territories into territorial constituencies will be based on the latest census figures.
- Seats reserved for women will be allotted by rotation in such manner as the Delimitation Commission may determine.
- The new bill provides for a 50% increase in the number of seats to give immediate effect to women's reservation under Article 334A of the Constitution.

Apple continues to expand its retail footprint in India. The iPhone maker is all set to launch its seventh official store in the country in Hyderabad on December 10. As per its website, the new store will open at Lake Shore Mall in Hyderabad’s Kukatpally. The new outlet will offer the complete lineup of Apple products and services, including the latest iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, MacBook Pro, Apple Watches, AirPods and HomePods. According to Deccan Herald, the company has also revealed the barricade for the Kukatpally store, which features a pearl-inspired Apple logo set against iridescent tones. It takes inspiration from the city’s historical title as the City of Pearls. The new outlet will join the company’s six other flagship stores in the country. The Cupertino-based big tech giant already operates retail outlets in Mumbai’s BKC and Borivali, Saket and Noida in Delhi NCR, Hebbal in Bengaluru and Koregaon Park in Pune. Notably, Apple already has a healthy presence in the city. Hyderabad is home to the company’s retail customer team and the R&D division for maps. The move comes as Apple continues to deepen its presence in India by launching retail outlets, leasing spaces for corporate offices and scaling local manufacturing. In January this year, the iPhone maker leased an additional 57,000 sq ft of office space at WaveRock IT Park in Hyderabad for five years at a monthly rent of ₹71.6 Lakh. With this, the total footprint of its campus in the city now stands at nearly 6.34 Lakh sq ft. A week ago, Apple also reportedly opened its second office in Bengaluru. Located at Embassy Zenith in the startup hub’s Vasanth Nagar, the 14-story building stands directly opposite the 150-year-old Bangalore Golf Club. Not just this, the company is also aggressively doubling down on manufacturing in India. The country has become one of its largest production bases outside China, with iPhone exports crossing ₹2 Lakh Cr in FY26. At the same time, it is also expanding its services ecosystem in India. The OEM has launched new offerings such as Apple Pay and Fitness+ in the past few months, which are expected to create new revenue streams for the iPhone maker going forward. All these bets appear to be paying off. Buoyed by strong demand across iPhones, Macs, iPads and other products, Apple India’s net profit zoomed 66% YoY to ₹5,311 Cr in FY26 as operating revenue grew 31.4% YoY to ₹1.04 Lakh Cr. The original equipment manufacturer (OEM) also reported record India revenues in Q4 FY26, with its iPhone vertical setting a revenue record and Mac and services revenue reaching new highs. However, near-term momentum faces pressure due to chip and memory shortages. The company recently said that it expects supply chain constraints to impact iPhones, Macs and iPads globally, potentially influencing product availability in India. In another headwind, the iPhone maker Apple also suffered a major outage earlier this month, which brought many of its services to a standstill for thousands of users globally.

NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International after a packaged drinking water sample collected from its plant in West Bengal tested positive for coliform bacteria. This is the second time the food regulator has initiated prosecution against the bottled water major this week, following a similar action over a sample from its Goa plant.West Bengal sample was collected from Bisleri's plant in Telipara village in Jalpaiguri district, news agency PTI reported citing sources. Both the primary and referral laboratories confirmed the presence of coliform bacteria, which can enter water systems through sewage leaks, damaged pipes and other sources.Following the findings, the FSSAI prohibited the sale of a specific batch of the product, numbered PB 201, on August 12. The regulator has now granted sanction for prosecution over violations of food safety rules.Responses from the FSSAI and Bisleri International could not be ascertained immediately.
Second case after Goa plant sample fails test
The latest action comes days after the FSSAI announced prosecution proceedings against Bisleri over a sample collected from one of its plants in Goa.
In that case, the regulator said the "sample was found non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006."Bisleri subsequently appealed against the findings, following which the sample was sent to a referral food laboratory. The second laboratory also classified it as "unsafe" after detecting polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), according to the FSSAI.The findings confirmed violations related to unsafe food practices, prompting the regulator to initiate prosecution under the Food Safety Act, 2006.On Monday, Bisleri International maintained that its products were safe for consumption. The company also said it would cooperate with the FSSAI to address the concerns raised.
FSSAI steps up packaged water surveillance
The action against Bisleri comes amid an expanded nationwide crackdown on packaged drinking water quality.
FSSAI CEO Rajit Punhani said earlier this week that the regulator was collecting packaged drinking water samples across the country. Laboratory testing is expected to be completed within one to two months.He said the enforcement drive was aimed at ensuring compliance and not creating panic.Punhani also said the regulator had undertaken enforcement activities covering several food and beverage products over the past year. It would soon extend inspections to packaging materials used for food products.The central regulator has also written to state food commissioners and regional directors, asking them to step up surveillance, inspections and sampling of packaged drinking water and mineral water. It has directed them to take action against companies found violating food safety norms.This year, the FSSAI has intensified enforcement against food business operators and e-commerce companies. It has also taken action against manufacturers of energy drinks and alcoholic beverages.

X is adding its first-ever parental controls
Any responsible adult should probably check on their teen's X usage.
Elon Musk's X has finally introduced parental controls for kids aged 13 to 17, allowing parents and guardians to manage their teen's experience on the platform. Teens' accounts will now default to protected mode, with sensitive media restricted and targeted advertising blocked. The new settings will also give families "additional tools on top of those defaults," the platform announced.
Those extra tools let adults in charge of teens see how much time their kids have spent on X and set a daily limit, require approval for new followers, and limit For You recommendations to accounts the teen already follows. They can also filter specific words, turn off sensitive media content, allow parents to control who can send direct messages, and see which accounts their teen has chatted with one-on-one (without seeing the messages themselves).
To use the new parental controls, follow the guide in X's help center. "Linking starts with the parent or guardian and finishes with the teen. Both users have to agree," the platform states.
X emphasized that the new controls let parents manage content without prying into their kids' lives. "Parents and guardians cannot read private messages, see searches or viewing history, post as their teen, or access the account," the company wrote. Parents will be able to control up to five teens' accounts.
There are reasons that parents should probably keep teens far away from X. In the last five years, it's been rife with issues including hate speech, AI-generated CSAM, misinformation, deepfake images, a lack of moderation, unauthorized AI training, propaganda, algorithms that amplify partisan content, AI bots, human trolls, and the omnipresence of awesome role model Elon Musk.
Even X admits that it's not aimed at kids or teens. "While X is not designed for or promoted to children, and users must be at least 13 or older where required by law, we take extra care with the young people who are here," the company wrote. While claiming that "child safety is a top priority at X," the platform likely introduced the new rules to comply with current or future regulations in multiple states and countries.

A third bill will seek to facilitate an increase in the number of seats in the UTs of Delhi, J&K and Puducherry which have assemblies.
NEW DELHI: Amid growing support for the delimitation bills with support of DMK, the Sharad Pawar-led NCP faction and YSRCP, the Union Cabinet cleared the legislation to increase Lok Sabha’s maximum strength from 550 to 850 by proposing a uniform increase of 50% in constituencies in every state, while freezing any fresh delimitation to revise the numbers till 2051.Government circulated the Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill for delimitation and operationalisation of women’s quota from 2029, and another bill for setting up a Delimitation Commission to MPs on Friday as numbers appeared to be falling in place for Parliament’s nod to the government’s centrepiece legislation, only months after a united opposition had voted down the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill with similar objectives.A third bill will seek to facilitate an increase in the number of seats in the UTs of Delhi, J&K and Puducherry which have assemblies.“The objective of the present bill (Constitution amendment) is to give immediate effect to one-third reservation for women, including women belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, in Lok Sabha and legislative assemblies of states and Union Territories, through a delimitation exercise.
Such delimitation shall provide for an increase of 50% in the number of seats in Lok Sabha and assemblies of states and Union Territories over and above the number of seats existing immediately before such delimitation,” the Constitution amendment bill said.The new bill is different from its previous version in making an explicit constitutional provision to assuage the concerns of parties like DMK and NCP (SP) of any diminishment of the existing share of states in LS, opening the path for them to junk their past opposition and join the BJP-led NDA in backing the Constitution amendment bill that needs support of two-thirds MPs for passage.For the simultaneous pursuit of the two objectives, the bills have been predicated on the numbers of two Census exercises. For determining the respective share of states in LS, the 1971 Census -- the one which was used for determining the current share of states in LS, is being retained. However, for redrawing the boundaries of LS constituencies in states, the 2011 Census numbers will be used: something which frees the government of the need to wait for the findings of the enumeration currently underway.In the proposed maximum strength of 850 in Lok Sabha, 815 will be for states and 35 for UTs with assemblies -- Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir. The real overall strength of Lok Sabha is likely to be around 816. LS currently has a strength of 543 against the maximum possible strength of 550.The government is set to table the bills, key for implementation of women’s quota, in Lok Sabha on Nov 30. The bills are more granular in their legal casing as well as political outreach, while keeping the same broad agenda of rolling out one-third reservation for women in LS and state assemblies from 2029, when the next national election is due.Signalling his likely change of stand, DMK chief M K Stalin said the share of Tamil Nadu, which has 39 LS seats, should not fall below its current 7.18%, and the existing proportion of parliamentary representation among states, as determined on the basis of the 1971 Census and frozen earlier, must remain unchanged for another 25 years. The government had offered to meet the condition in April itself and the new bill addresses both of Stalin’s points.NCP(SP) was more categorical, with its senior functionary Jitendra Awhad quoting party boss Sharad Pawar to say that the party, an INDIA bloc constituent, had decided to support delimitation.DMK’s 22 MPs in LS, NCP (SP)’s eight and four of YSR Congress, which is also expected to support, takes NDA’s strength in the House to 355. With 360 needed for the bills’ passage in the House, which has three vacancies, NDA appears all but certain to cross the threshold amid indications from the governing alliance that some more MPs may either abstain or even back it.Attention is also focused on whether the speaker will give his ruling on the legality of the split in TMC which has resulted in 20 MPs belonging to Mamata Banerjee’s party aligning themselves with NDA. A favourable ruling will free them from any legal encumbrance in taking an independent course.
The Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, which will amend eight Articles of the Constitution, also proposes to raise the ceiling on the size of a state assembly from 500 to 650. It is being explicitly done for Uttar Pradesh as its assembly, the largest in the country, currently has 403 members.Passage of the bill will also provide the government an effective plank to showcase its pro-women credentials in the run-up to a crucial round of state elections, and government is likely to build political capital out of it by getting endorsement from assemblies of states where BJP and its allies are in office.With a new delimitation bill being tabled, government will withdraw the earlier legislation which is still pending in Lok Sabha.

Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
- Published
Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.
Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.
South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.
A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".
Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.
"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.
"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."
Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.
Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.
In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat
- Published
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.
It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.
The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.
A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.
Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.
Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. The party's leader Qiulae Wong has previously said she will negotiate first with the party that secures the largest number of seats.
Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.
But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.
Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.
Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.
In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.
"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.
A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.
Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden, moving to Australia.

Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028
- Published
Guinea-Bissau's military rulers have postponed elections scheduled for next week by two years, delaying the return to civilian rule.
Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the presidential and parliamentary elections, originally due on 6 December, would now take place on 26 November 2028.
The announcement came exactly a year after the military seized power, promising to return the country to civilian rule within 12 months.
In a statement, the presidency said an assessment of electoral preparations had found that there were insufficient "technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the polls as planned.
It said the delay would provide more time to ensure the elections were credible, transparent and inclusive, with all candidates given equal opportunities.
The presidency also reiterated its commitment to holding the country's first-ever local government elections but gave no date for the vote.
Gen N'Tam was sworn in as transitional president a day after the military overthrew President Umaro Sissoco Embaló in November 2025.
The coup took place three days after general elections and a day before provisional results were due to be announced.
Both Embaló and his main challenger, Fernando Dias, had claimed victory.
Embaló, who has since been living in exile in Morocco, was barred from returning to Guinea-Bissau last month, despite expressing an interest in contesting the elections.
Guinea-Bissau has experienced several coups and attempted coups since gaining independence from Portugal in 1974.

Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.
Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.
The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi’s blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.
Some major features are still missing, though. As noted, there are no native apps yet. Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.
Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service. It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi plan, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan. It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.
If you want to get Kagi Mail without the $25 per month subscription, you can subscribe for $9 per month or $99 per year, and there’s a 60-day trial right now.
Opinion: An alternative more of us should maybe consider
That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product. To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.

In a powerful explosion that launched gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound.
The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people. Residents within a 5-mile area of the facility were advised to evacuate, while people farther out were told to shelter in place, close windows and doors tightly, turn off fans, and set indoor air systems to recirculate.
Local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously. A KWQZ journalist, at a reportedly safe distance from the blast, said on the live broadcast that he could see and then feel the shockwave roll through the crop field in which he was standing. He put a mask on for the rest of the broadcast.
Lead is a neurotoxin that does not break down in the environment and poses significant health risks, particularly to young children and pregnant people.
In the hours leading to the detonation, the Army released maps showing modeled drift and distribution of the plume. They indicated that airborne lead would travel around 100 miles to the southwest of the facility, while dust deposition would cover around 200 square miles in that direction. Researchers and government workers have already collected air and soil samples from the area, which will act as baseline readings for lead levels in the aftermath and fallout of the detonation.

Bengaluru-based stock market research and advisory platform StockGro has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Dubai-headquartered banking group Emirates NBD to explore digital investment solutions for customers in the UAE and India. Signed at the Dubai FinTech Summit on November 19, the MoU envisages combining Emirates NBD’s banking and wealth expertise with StockGro’s investment research, expert advisory, and AI-powered analysis, the startup said in a statement. The collaboration builds on StockGro’s existing UAE presence and will help it bring its research tools to a wider investor base through the bank’s distribution network and customer relationships. The MoU was signed by Neeraj Makin, group head of strategy, analytics, and venture capital at Emirates NBD, and Ajay Lakhotia, founder, MD, and CEO of StockGro. Hitesh Asarpota, CEO of Emirates NBD Capital, and Mohammed Al Bastaki, group head of private banking and wealth management, were also present. A Growing Investor Base The collaboration comes amid rising investor participation in Dubai’s capital markets. According to the Dubai Financial Market (DFM), the exchange added 55,460 new investors in the first nine months of 2026, taking its total investor base to above 1.3 Mn. Lakhotia said rising incomes, strong consumer spending, and rapid digital adoption are strengthening the UAE’s capital markets and drawing more local investors into them. "What they need now is research and expert-backed advice they can trust. With Emirates NBD, we can bring the tools loved by over 37 million Indian investors to the UAE, and help every investor move from confusion to conviction,” Lakhotia added. For Emirates NBD, Makin described empowering emerging investors across the UAE-India corridor as “a vital economic opportunity as well as a strategic priority”. "StockGro's intuitive, community-driven platform lowers the barrier to entry, transforming how individuals engage with capital markets," he said. Combining Research And Reach In India, StockGro contributes research and trade calls from more than 150 SEBI-registered research analysts, alongside its market analytics and research tools. These include Stoxo, its AI-powered research tool, which helps users analyse market data, review portfolio performance, and conduct fundamental, technical, and sentiment analysis. The company says it has more than 37 Mn active users. It launched its UAE app in July 2025 as an education and awareness platform, with access to market data through a partnership with DFM. The app covers stocks listed on DFM and the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange (ADX). Under the MoU, the companies will explore how Emirates NBD’s customer relationships and distribution network could extend the reach of StockGro’s research and AI-powered tools.

- The claim that several popular candy products contain dangerous levels of arsenic — a semimetallic element that is a highly toxic carcinogen in its inorganic form — lacks sufficient evidence.
- The rumor stems from a January 2026 study the Florida Department of Health's "Healthy Florida First" initiative conducted, which purportedly found that out of 46 popular candies, 28 contain dangerous levels of arsenic.
- Snopes spoke with two arsenic experts, both of whom said the Florida study lacks critical information. One expert noted that the testing method Florida used is typically adopted when testing soil and water but not food, and cannot differentiate between very toxic arsenic (III), less toxic arsenic (V) and relatively nontoxic organic arsenicals.
- While a spokesperson for Healthy Florida First initially replied to our inquiries, they stopped responding when we posed more complex questions regarding their methodology and testing conditions.
- The lack of information regarding testing methodology and conditions does not mean the study's results are categorically false, but until further information about the test and its results is made accessible to the public, we cannot rate this claim.
In January 2026, Florida first lady Casey DeSantis announced that the Florida Department of Health conducted a study purportedly finding that several popular candy products contain dangerous levels of arsenic. The department lists Nerds, Laffy Taffy, Hershey's and Sour Patch Kids products, among others, as examples.
Arsenic is a naturally-occurring, semimetallic element that can be found in soil, water, air, etc. In its organic, less dangerous form, arsenic is combined with carbon and commonly occurs in seafood. Inorganic arsenic, however, is carcinogenic and "has been recognized as a human poison since ancient times," according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
As Halloween approached in 2026, Florida's "Healthy Florida First" findings resurfaced on social media.
For example, one X user wrote, in part, "Florida's Department of Health tested 46 popular candies and found 28 were laced with this POTENT CARCINOGEN."
As DeSantis said, Florida did conduct a study (archived) purportedly detecting arsenic in 28 out of 46 candy products, approximately 60% (the products tested belong to 10 brands). However, the findings lack critical information about testing conditions and methodology. While Healthy Florida First initially replied to our inquiries, a spokesperson for the initiative stopped responding when we posed more complex questions raised by an arsenic expert whom Snopes spoke to.
Below, we look into Florida's findings and break down expert opinions, as well as available primary evidence, regarding dangerous arsenic levels in candy.
What did Florida's study claim?
The study by Healthy Florida First, an initiative DeSantis leads, identified 28 candy products purportedly containing dangerous levels of arsenic. It lists "approximate 'safe' consumption amounts per year, based on developmental age, where arsenic was detected."
While all products tested from Mondelêz International (the maker of Sour Patch Kids and other products) and Tootsie Roll Industries purportedly tested positive for dangerous levels of arsenic, other companies, such as Mars, Ferrara Candy Company, The Hershey Company and Smart Sweets had mixed results. Products tested from Yum Earth, UNREAL and Annie's are categorized as "risk not identified."
The study then lists recommended consumption limits for children and adults per year for each product.
Snopes contacted the Florida Department of Health and DeSantis' office seeking comment regarding online criticism that its method of testing, the "EPA Method 6010D," tests for inorganic arsenic in things like soil, rather than food. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency says its analytical test method "6010D" measures trace elements and metals, usually in soil and water.
Isabella White, a spokesperson for the health department, said via email that the contracted study was conducted at a "certified laboratory that specializes in food, environmental, pharmaceutical, cosmetic, and forensic testing, as well as advanced analytical sciences." Her statement continued:
Samples were obtained from commonly used retail outlets, including both brick-and-mortar stores and online retailers, to reflect real-world consumer purchasing patterns. Samples were analyzed using EPA Method 6010D for the multi-elemental determination of metals in solid and liquid samples. The laboratory followed its established quality assurance plan to validate and verify all results.
The Department approached this evaluation conservatively to ensure the protection of children, identified as the most sensitive and susceptible population. Candy products were screened for arsenic and lead using consumption-based risk assessment models and minimal risk levels established by the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR) to estimate potential health risks associated with consumption.
The ATSDR, a subsidiary of U.S. Health and Human Services, stipulates a minimal risk limit of 0.0003 mg of arsenic per kilogram per day for one year or more (regarding oral exposure to inorganic arsenic).
Experts push back, say study lacks critical information
According to arsenic expert Barry Rosen, an emeritus professor of cellular and molecular medicine at Florida International University, the Florida study's use of ICP-OES (Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectroscopy, or EPA Method 6010D), is not the optimum method for solids. Like the online criticism of the study, he also noted that the method is typically used for soil and water but not food, and cannot differentiate between very toxic arsenic (III), less toxic arsenic (V) and relatively nontoxic organic arsenicals, writing via email, "This is a major drawback to that method."
Rosen outlined several aspects of Florida's study that lack sufficient information. For example, given that sugar and metals, such as aluminum, can interfere with arsenic test results, he questioned how the researchers digested the candy, how they removed solids, and whether sugar was present in the extracts.
"Their methodology may not be sufficient to allow them to draw their conclusions, but I'd really need more information before deciding," Rosen said.
We shared several of Rosen's follow-up questions regarding the study's methodology with Healthy Florida First, at which point we ceased receiving responses.
"Based on the publicly available information, I would treat Florida's findings as preliminary and would not use them to set annual limits on how many pieces of candy people can eat," wrote Yong Cai, another arsenic expert and professor at Florida International University's department of chemistry and biochemistry. He did acknowledge it is "plausible that some candies contain measurable arsenic."
For an independent comparison, Cai pointed to a 2018-2020 study by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration that found up to 3.3 parts per billion (PPB) of total arsenic in three samples of plain milk chocolate bars. Cai noted, "Those samples represent a small category and do not independently verify Florida's results for the specific products it tested."
Although Healthy Florida First does provide some contextual information for its findings, it does not make critical information available to the public, such as the assumed child body weight used for calculations and how its calculations accounted for exposure from other foods and drinking water. Healthy Florida First did not respond to multiple requests for further comment.

According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.
Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft’s target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. “Needless to say, we aren’t here yet,” Henderson wrote.
The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company’s post-incident report, dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.

Prepaid payment instruments (PPIs) recorded 1.06 billion purchases totaling Rs 21,964.01 crore in October 2026, according to the Reserve Bank of India’s entity-wise PPI statistics. These figures reflect purchases of goods and services only, and exclude fund transfers and cash withdrawals. They do not represent the total volume of all PPI transactions.
Key observations
Increase over September: Purchase volume increased 23.4% to 1.06B from 861.83M in September, and value rose 15.4% to Rs 21,964.01 crore from Rs 19,038.63 crore. Compared to October 2025, volume grew 28.7% from 826.28M and value rose 32.4% from Rs 16,594.59 crore, according to the RBI series.
Average transactions per day: In October, wallets and PPI cards averaged 34.30 million daily purchases, an increase from 28.73 million in September. The daily purchase value rose to Rs 708.52 crore from Rs 634.62 crore.
Decline in average purchase value: Although purchase volume and overall value increased, the average purchase value fell by about 6.5%, from Rs 220.91 in September to Rs 206.56 in October.
Cards vs wallets
Wallets accounted for 73.1% of combined wallet and PPI-card purchases in October, according to RBI data:
- Wallets processed 777.38M purchases, up 22.5% from 634.52M in September. Their purchase value rose 11.7% to Rs 16,175.01 crore from Rs 14,482.53 crore.
- PPI cards processed 285.95M purchases, up 25.8% from 227.31M in September. Their purchase value rose 27.1% to Rs 5,788.99 crore from Rs 4,556.10 crore.
Fund transfers and cash withdrawals
In addition to recording purchases of goods and services, RBI also records fund transfers via PPIs and cash withdrawals using PPI cards. In October:
- Wallets recorded 115.57M fund transfers worth Rs 9,101.46 crore.
- PPI cards recorded approximately 513,711 fund transfers worth Rs 136.27 crore.
- PPI cards recorded 1.77M ATM cash withdrawals worth Rs 915.19 crore.
- Cash withdrawals at PoS terminals accounted for 3,571 transactions worth Rs 0.45 crore.
Fund transfers accounted for approximately 28.8% of the total value of PPI transactions, including purchases and cash withdrawals.
Wallet issuers
IDFC FIRST Bank had the highest wallet purchase value of any issuer: Rs 3,374.99 crore from 171.88 million purchases, about 20.9% of the wallet total. ICICI Bank recorded Rs 1,564.97 crore from 65.63 million purchases, and HDFC Bank Rs 1,063.03 crore from 30.79 million.
Selected non-bank wallet issuers
RBI provides entity-wise statistics for 39 banks and 48 non-bank issuers. In October, the following five non-bank wallet issuers reported the highest wallet purchase values among non-bank entities:
- One Mobikwik Systems Limited: Rs 3,356.22 crore, up 13.9% from Rs 2,946.65 crore in September. Its Rs 409.57 crore rise was the largest absolute increase among the five.
- Tri O Tech Solutions Private Ltd.: Rs 1,735.64 crore, up 9.7% from Rs 1,581.71 crore.

CRTC orders Bell, Rogers, Telus to stop charging prohibited wireless fees by Dec. 27
Bell faces a fine of up to $10M for selling locked mobile devices
Canada's telecommunications regulator says Bell, Rogers and Telus have charged consumers fees that are prohibited under the Telecommunications Act, and has ordered them to stop by Dec. 27.
At the same time, the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) has threatened Bell with a fine of up to $10 million for violating the government's wireless rules by selling customers cellphones locked to its network.
The CRTC's decision targets charges for providing and setting up cellphones when signing up for a service plan. The regulator ruled on Friday that a cellphone handling charge from Bell, a cellphone setup charge from Rogers and a SIM and eSIM provisioning fee from Telus are prohibited.
The CRTC also ruled that fees charged by Rogers and Telus to replace broken or lost SIM cards are not prohibited, nor are the shipping fees charged by Rogers.
SIM cards are microchips needed to connect a customer's device to a mobile network.
In June, the regulator banned fees to activate, change or cancel internet and cellphone services. Following that ban, major carriers introduced SIM card and other hardware-related charges that the CRTC flagged as potential disguised activation fees.
"We identified a number of fees charged by certain of the largest telephone companies that appeared to be prohibited. We notified them that the fees may be out of compliance," Sheehan Carter, the CRTC's acting vice-president of consumer analytics and strategy, told reporters at a virtual briefing on Friday.
"Since these companies chose to continue those fees, and they argued that they were not prohibited, we immediately took action to decide the issue."
In a statement to CBC News on Friday, Rogers said it disagrees with the CRTC's position on device set-up charges.
"These charges help recover real costs, and we're pleased the CRTC's decision on the shipping charge and SIM replacement fee clearly reflect this," a Rogers spokesperson told CBC News in an email.
Spokespeople for Bell and Telus say their respective companies are reviewing the regulator's decisions.
According to a CRTC report released in February, Bell, Telus and Rogers collectively controlled nearly 90 per cent of Canada's mobile wireless sales and roughly 86 per cent of wireless subscribers, as of 2024.
Matt Hatfield, executive director of the non-profit advocacy group OpenMedia, says Friday's ruling blocks some anti-consumer practices adopted by Canada's three largest telecom providers. However, he worries they will simply tweak their fees again to get around the rules.
"This is just one round of whack-a-mole in a game customers always lose. Canada's telecom companies keep finding new ways to lock in and surcharge their customers," he told CBC News in an emailed statement.
"As it stands, these practices were a net win for the companies. They profited while they lasted, and they'll now start on new ways of abusing customers that the CRTC will take time to identify and address."
Bell faces up to $10M fine
The CRTC also said Friday it found that Bell sold customers cellphones that were locked to its network — limiting their ability to take advantage of better offers from rivals.
"The CRTC rules require that cellphones must be unlocked, so that Canadians have the freedom to choose their provider," Carter said.
He said the CRTC is considering fining Bell up to $10 million, in the "upper range" of what's allowed under the Telecommunications Act. Earlier this month, BCE, Bell's parent company, booked $6.18 billion in operating revenue for the three months ending Sept. 30.
The CRTC banned phone locking in 2017, along with the unlocking fees carriers had been charging, in a bid to make it easier for consumers to switch providers.
In August, the CRTC temporarily suspended this requirement, allowing carriers to lock devices for up to two business days, after which they unlock automatically. It required that consumers be able to request immediate unlocking at no charge. This followed applications from Bell and Telus, which argued that selling unlocked phones increased theft and fraud.
In July, Telus filed an application for a temporary exemption from the regulator's phone-unlocking rules. The company proposed to start locking devices for 60 days.
On Friday, the CRTC formally denied this request.
Carter said the regulator had seen no evidence that Telus had actually sold locked devices, only that it intended to do so. As a result, he said no fines were appropriate at this time.
In June, the CRTC warned Telus in a letter that its $15 charge for SIM cards may be considered an activation fee, which is prohibited under the Telecommunications Act.
"Every SIM card and eSIM comes with real costs associated with providing it to customers, and we believe those costs should be reflected in the price of the product, rather than requiring carriers to provide it free of charge," a Telus spokesperson stated in an email.
Keldon Bester, executive director of the Canadian Anti-Monopoly Project, sees charges for SIM cards as an activation fee in disguise.
"You really cannot access telecom services without access to a SIM card," he said. "To break that out as a separate charge, I think, runs in the face of the CRTC's aim, which is to say that the process of moving carriers should be as seamless as possible."

Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.
Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.
The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.
The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?
Surviving blackouts
Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.
Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.
I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.
To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.
Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.
Raving through the war
I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.
We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.
Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.
What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.
Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.
Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.
It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.
There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.
How does it all end?
The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.
So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.
But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.
Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.
And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."
Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.
Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.
At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.
The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.
