Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing in F1 crash?
- Published
Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?
If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.
A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.
Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?
Someone, somewhere, knows something.
The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.
Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.
"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.
"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."
His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.
They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.
"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.
"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."
Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.
The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.
Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.
What happened next, though, was not part of the script.
While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.
The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.
Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.
Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.
Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.
In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.
Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.
It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.
"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.
He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.
"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.
"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."
By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.
But there were plenty of theories.
Theory: it was not a real diamond
Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.
"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.
"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.
"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."
Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.
"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.
"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.
"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."
Theory: someone pocketed it
"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.
"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].
"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.
"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."
There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.
Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up.
"What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find.
"Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car.
"There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones.
"Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."
Theory: Klien crashed on purpose
Sidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.
And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose.
"For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.
Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to.
"Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell.
"He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond.
"No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."
While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond.
His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers.
"When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there.
"It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."
In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue.
"No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell.
"I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."
Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."
Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1.
"You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.
Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.

12 strategies to cut your risk of dementia. Take this quiz to start
Follow the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast on the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.
It's one of the biggest fears about getting older: losing your memory. A growing body of evidence shows we can do a lot to lower the risk of dementia, starting with changes to our day-to-day habits.
For decades, dementia was seen as something determined by genes or bad luck: a disease that strikes late in life with little anyone can do about it. That thinking has radically changed.
In 2024, the Lancet Commission, an international panel of experts, identified 14 modifiable risk factors for dementia and estimated that about 45% of dementia cases could be prevented or delayed. And lifestyle changes, when sustained over time, can be a powerful form of prevention. Last year, a large clinical trial from the Alzheimer's Association, called U.S. POINTER, found that older adults at risk of cognitive decline who combined physical activity, healthy eating, cognitive exercises and social activity could protect brain health, thinking and memory.
A score for your brain
So where do you start? One good place is a free, five-minute online tool called the Brain Care Score. You can take it with friends and family members as you gather for the holidays.
It was developed by Jonathan Rosand, a neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, and his colleagues. It's now supported through the Global Brain Care Coalition.
"The Brain Care Score tells you how to reduce your risk of brain diseases in the future, especially dementia, stroke and depression," Rosand says. "And it tells you what you can do to live a longer, more flourishing life."
The score covers 12 factors in three areas. The higher your score, the lower your risk. Those factors are:
- Physical health: blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and body weight
- Lifestyle: diet, exercise, sleep, smoking and alcohol
- Social and emotional health: stress management, relationships and a sense of purpose
According to the coalition, the tool, "wasn't built to label risk. It was built to give people options and to show them that small changes made today can matter years from now."
Why blood pressure matters for your brain
High blood pressure might seem like a heart issue, but it's one of the biggest risk factors for dementia, and many people don't know their numbers.
"The higher your blood pressure, the more stress on your blood vessels," Rosand explains. "The more stress on your blood vessels, the more they break down over time," and the more they break down, the more likely they are to block or rupture. He says high blood pressure can increase the risk of stroke and dementia.
That's why the first step in calculating your score is to know your numbers: blood pressure, blood sugar (measured as A1c), cholesterol and body weight. You can ask your healthcare provider, check your patient portal or use a blood pressure cuff at a pharmacy. If you've been prescribed medication for high blood pressure, he says, taking the medicine is one of the most important things you can do.
Small gains add up
What if you take the quiz and don't love your number? The whole point of knowing your score is to use it as an assessment, a place to begin and a way to strategize about what changes you can make to your daily lifestyle habits. There's no need to overhaul your life.
In an analysis of real-world data from thousands of adults, each one-point improvement in the Brain Care Score was linked to up to a 4% lower risk of dementia, stroke or late-life depression. And even people who change their habits late in life can benefit.
The key is to pick one change that feels doable, such as:
- Adding 30 minutes of sleep to your daily routine if you're not well rested
- Putting an extra serving of greens on your plate
- Adding in a 20-minute walk each day and resistance bands for strength training
- Calling a friend to get together or joining a group activity
- Getting your blood pressure checked
Researchers say one healthy change often leads to others. Better sleep, for example, can make it easier to exercise and eat well, so the benefits can multiply across the score.
Purpose and connection count too
One part of the score that surprises people is the value placed on relationships and purpose. A 2025 study found that people with a higher sense of purpose were about 28% less likely to develop cognitive impairment.
That means joining the class or the volunteer gig you've been putting off can be considered a form of brain care.
You can retake the quiz over time to track your progress, and you can share it with family and friends. Healthy habits can be contagious.

‘Can’t comment without reviewing it’: Supriya Sule on possible support for delimitation bill
She said theirs is a disciplined party and they will issue a whip when they receive the Parliament’s special sitting agenda
Nationalist Congress Party – Sharadchandra Pawar (NCP–SP) leader Supriya Sule on Friday refused to comment on the delimitation bill, saying she had not seen it and questioning how she could comment without reviewing it. She said theirs is a disciplined party and that when they receive the agenda of Parliament’s special sitting, Amol Kolhe, their leader, will issue a whip.
“I do not know that. I do not know anything,” she said when asked about Union home minister Amit Shah’s statement that Congress leader Rahul Gandhi cannot stop the passage of the delimitation bill. Sule refused to comment on the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK)’s softened stance on delimitation, which indicated they would support it if it were fair. “You will have to ask the DMK,” she said.
“If you have to take an exam, you must do your homework. You will have to study history, geography, physics. I do not know how I will speak until I get the exam paper [agenda]. I have not even received the syllabus. I can only speak after I get the syllabus.”
Deep Dive
The comments came amid speculation that the NCP-SP, a key constituent of the opposition bloc, could support the government on a Constitution amendment and the delimitation bills to roll out women’s quota that did not get the required support earlier this year.
The Union government on Thursday said a special sitting of Parliament will be held from November 30, fuelling speculation that it was looking to reintroduce the bills.
NCP-SP has eight members in the Lok Sabha and one in the Rajya Sabha. It voted against the bills when they were first moved in April.
Sule on Thursday said any support for the bill is conditional on three things: “First, the women’s reservation must be implemented. Second, there should be a 50% increase in Lok Sabha seats across all states, and third, opposition parties should have adequate representation in the delimitation commission that will redraw the boundaries.”
She said delimitation should be viewed in the context of increasing population. “The population in parliamentary constituencies is increasing, and it is becoming difficult for MPs like me to manage it.”
Sule said that their party will review the provisions. “If they align with the three issues we have raised, we can support the bill,” said Sule.
She added that her party will vote for the bill if it is in the country’s interest. “There have been instances where the ruling and opposition parties have come together on issues in the country’s interest... The same could happen with the delimitation bill if its provisions are in the country’s interest. Who knows?”

Ente Photos is a privacy-focused Google Photos alternative offering 10GB of free storage, end-to-end encryption, open-source code, selective album backups, cross-platform access, easy photo imports, collaborative sharing, and on-device AI features like face recognition and Magic Search.
When we think about a dedicated photo app, we instantly remember Google Photos or the default gallery on our phone. We do not have many trustworthy options. That’s when I came across Ente. Ente is a dedicated photo app available as a standalone app to install on Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, and Linux operating systems.
Is Ente the real challenger to the Google Photos app? Can we replace the gallery on our phones with Ente? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Features That Make Ente a Worthy Photo App
Ente has some exciting features that really make it stand out from the few others available. Here’s what makes it worthy.
Generous Free (Forever) Storage Plan
Ente offers a 10GB free storage plan for your photos and videos. Ente claims the plan is free forever. 10GB of free cloud storage dedicated to photos and video backup seems a good deal. That too without any ads.
Google offers 15GB of free storage space for each Google account. There is no dedicated storage space for the Google Photos app. As Google’s free storage is tied to all Google products as a whole, Ente’s 10GB looks big.
If you exhaust the generous free space on Ente, you can upgrade to a paid plan that offers storage starting from 50GB to 2TB for a monthly or annual subscription.
End-to-End Encrypted Backups
The photos and videos you back up on Ente are end-to-end encrypted by default. Ente claims they never use our data to train their models or spy on us.
The photos we back up via Google Photos are not end-to-end encrypted. Google may use our data to train their AI models, serve us customized ads, etc. You can prevent Google from using your data to show you personalized ads, but they can read your data. That’s where Ente succeeds.
The backup is end-to-end encrypted with keys before it leaves our device. The encryption keys are derived from our password using advanced key derivation functions. That means only the password you set can decrypt the data.
As the source code of Ente is publicly audited, the trust factor improves. When I tried to sign up on Ente, it provided me with a recovery key or the master key that I can use in case I lose my password.
The encryption process involves only us, the users, and they can never access the data. Even in the unfortunate event of a data breach, our data can remain safe as it is end-to-end encrypted.
Fully Open-Source Platform
Ente’s entire codebase for photos and its other apps is available for public audit on GitHub with more than 29k stars. The stars do not necessarily mean the project is good, but they give some form of trust.
The internet rewards the sensation. If someone had found a mismatch between Ente’s tall claims and the code, they surely would have flagged it and made an issue out of it.
Backup of User-Selected Albums
When you give permissions for Google Photos on our device, it backs up all the available albums, photos, and videos. We cannot select or ignore certain albums.
Ente, on the other hand, gives users the option to select which albums to back up. The albums that we choose not to back up are ignored by Ente as well. I loved this feature personally, as a lot of unnecessary data gets uploaded and wastes storage space. We can also customize the albums for backup anytime.
Easy Accessibility on All Platforms
Ente Photo has an app for every major operating system. We can install its app on Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. If we do not want to install the app, we can use it on the web through Ente.com.
Import Data From Google and Apple
Just download the Google Takeout that only has Google Photos data, import it into the Ente desktop app, and you are all set. It’s that simple to import data from Google Photos.
If you are an Apple user, just install the Ente app on your mobile device. Ente will read the data directly from your iCloud library and import it.
If you have iCloud shared albums, select the photos you want to import into the Ente app, and then save them to your device library for Ente to read them automatically.
Better Sharing and Collaboration Features
Ente Photo app provides us with three ways to share albums with others. You can share with a person on Ente, create a public link and share it with non-Ente users, or create a collaborative link to let non-Ente users add photos without an Ente account.
This does not put pressure on non-users to create an Ente account before collaborating with Ente albums, unlike the Google Photos app.
On-Device Machine Learning Features
There are a few machine learning-based features, like Magic Search, where you can search for photos with descriptions of how you remember them, Face Recognition, Memory Lane, Map and Location, and Jump to Date. These are all the latest advances in AI features.
To protect and maintain your privacy, all the machine learning happens on your device itself and is never sent to Ente’s servers. The machine learning feature is not enabled by default. You have to enable it manually and choose to disable it whenever you need to do so.
Is Ente Photos safe to use?
Yes, the Ente Photos app is safe to use to back up your photos and videos. It provides end-to-end encryption based on your password, and only your password can decrypt the data. Once you forget your password and also lose the recovery key they provided, you may never get to access the backup. The entire codebase of the Ente Photos app is available for public audit on GitHub.
How do I transfer photos from Google Photos to Ente?
You can transfer photos from Google Photos to the Ente Photos app in two ways. You can either download Google Photos data from Google Takeout, or download the entire library from the Google Photos app and drop it into the Ente Photos desktop app. It will read the data and import it to back it up safely.

Hamas said Israel tried to kill an adult son of the Palestinian movement's chief, Khalil al-Hayya, in an overnight strike on Friday (November 27, 2026), with a Gaza security source telling AFP he survived.
Editorial | Damning report: On Justice Muralidhar’s report on Israeli atrocities
The strike follows a series of killings by the Israeli military in recent days that have targeted Hamas officials, despite a ceasefire in the war-shattered Palestinian territory.
Separately, Gaza's civil defence agency said Israeli forces killed seven people across the territory on Friday (November 27).
"Izz al-Din al-Hayya, the youngest surviving son of Hamas political bureau chief Khalil al-Hayya, along with his family and the family of his late brother Azzam, survived an Israeli assassination attempt early on Friday targeting a residential apartment in the Rimal neighbourhood, west of Gaza City," a security source in Gaza told AFP.
When asked by AFP, the Israeli military said it was looking into the incident.
Bassem Naim, a member of the Palestinian Islamist movement's political bureau, told AFP that "Israel's attempt to target the youngest son of Hamas political bureau chief Khalil al-Hayya... constitutes 'state terrorism,'" while Hamas issued a statement calling the targeting "cowardly".
Four of Mr. al-Hayya's sons have already been killed in Israeli attacks, including one in May and another in an Israeli strike targeting Hamas leaders in Doha in September 2025.
Two others were killed before the war on Gaza.
Israeli strikes continue
Gaza's civil defence agency, a rescue force which operates under Hamas authority, said an Israeli drone strike west of Rafah city in southern Gaza killed three people on Friday (November 27), with nearby Nasser Hospital confirming it received three bodies following the strike.
The Israeli military told AFP it had struck "three terrorists in the area".
Another drone strike west of Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza killed one person, the civil defence and Al-Shifa Hospital said.
The Israeli military said it was checking the incident.
The civil defence agency said two more people were killed in an Israeli drone strike near Gaza City's Al-Shifa Hospital, with the medical facility confirming it received two bodies.
The Israeli military told AFP it struck "a terrorist in the area," adding that there was "no harm to the hospital or any medical practice" in the vicinity.
Israeli gunfire in the Rafah area killed another person, the civil defence said. The Israeli military said it was checking that incident.
Israel and Hamas regularly accuse each other of violating the ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025, after two years of devastating war.
More than 1,650 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the truce, according to an AFP tally based on data from the Gaza health ministry, which also operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
In the same period, the Israeli military says seven of its soldiers have been killed, as well as one civilian contractor.

After backlash from sellers frustrated by Etsy’s new AI policies, which appeared to allow the company to train AI on user artwork, Etsy has now clarified its stance.
In a note published on Monday, CEO Kruti Patel Goyal discussed recent tweaks to the company’s terms of service and admitted that her team “should’ve given you more context on what the updates meant for your creative content.”
“Our recent terms update was meant to reflect the evolving technologies we’re using to build better tools and experiences for sellers and the Etsy community,” Goyal wrote this week. “It was not meant to enable us to train AI models for the purpose of creating copycats of your items. We do not and will not do that.”
Aaron Meshon, a longtime professional illustrator and Etsy seller, told Ars that even though the company had dialed back its AI language somewhat, the changes were mere “sugar coating.”
He said he still plans on shutting down his 15-year-old Etsy store on December 1.
“I would say I’m losing 20 percent of my yearly income,” he said. “It’s a few mortgage payments.”
He noted that Etsy’s announcement also seems to be rather tone-deaf, given that many retailers make a substantial portion of their annual revenue in the run-up to the end-of-year holiday season.

Mumbai Indians has named Rohit Sharma as its captain for the 2027 Indian Premier League season, marking the veteran opener’s return to the leadership role after a two-year stint under Hardik Pandya.
The decision comes after Mumbai Indians traded Pandya to Punjab Kings in a player swap involving India pacer Arshdeep Singh ahead of the IPL 2027 season. With the captaincy vacant, the five-time champion has opted for experience, handing the responsibility back to the man who led it to all five of its IPL titles.
Rohit, who captained Mumbai from 2013 to 2023, guided the franchise to championships in 2013, 2015, 2017, 2019 and 2020. He was replaced by Pandya ahead of the 2024 season, a decision that sparked considerable debate among the franchise’s supporters.
“Mumbai Indians has been a huge part of my life, and leading this team has always been something I have always taken great pride in. The conversations with Nita Bhabhi and Akash about the season ahead have been exciting, and I have a lot of belief in what we can achieve,” Rohit said.
“I am ready for the 20th season, to the challenges ahead, and to giving our Paltan plenty of moments to celebrate. The focus will be on playing our brand of cricket, competing together and enjoying the game,” he added.
Mumbai endured a difficult transition under Pandya, finishing outside the playoff places in 2024 before reaching the playoffs in 2025 and facing another challenging campaign in 2026.

The Supreme Court has directed HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Sammaan Capital and PNB Housing Finance to grant unconditional sanction for the prosecution of their officials within a week in alleged subvention scheme frauds involving real estate developers and financial institutions, PTI reported.
A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana warned that the heads of these institutions would have to appear personally before the court if they failed to comply with the order.
"We direct all the banks or financial institutions referred to above to issue unconditional sanction for prosecution within one week, failing which the CMD and Chairman shall remain present in court to show cause as to why appropriate action be not taken against them," the bench said.
The order came while the apex court was hearing a batch of petitions concerning subvention schemes, under which homebuyers were allegedly subjected to loan recovery proceedings after developers failed to meet their financial commitments.
Under a subvention scheme, a bank or financial institution sanctions a home loan and disburses the amount directly into the builder's account. In return, the developer agrees to pay the equated monthly instalments (EMIs) on behalf of the buyer until possession of the flat is handed over.
The arrangement is generally governed by a tripartite agreement between the homebuyer, the developer and the lender.
The scheme is intended to reduce the immediate financial burden on homebuyers, who do not have to begin paying EMIs while waiting for their homes to be delivered.
However, problems arise when developers fail to honour their commitment to pay the EMIs. In such cases, banks can demand repayment from homebuyers, leaving them liable for loans even when they have not received possession of their properties.
The petitions before the Supreme Court concern allegations that banks and developers were involved in arrangements that left homebuyers facing loan recovery proceedings despite builders failing to meet their obligations under the tripartite agreements.
The court is examining cases involving alleged collusion between financial institutions and developers to dupe homebuyers, particularly in the National Capital Region (NCR).
During Thursday's hearing, Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), told the court that the agency was facing difficulties in obtaining prosecution sanctions under Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. This included cases where HDFC Bank had granted conditional sanctions.
Bhati also informed the bench that the CBI had filed its sixth supplementary status report. Investigations had been completed in 25 of the 55 registered cases, with 22 chargesheets filed and closure reports submitted in three cases.
The bench said granting prosecution sanction was the responsibility of the banking authorities and directed the CBI to complete the remaining investigations within two weeks.
The court also said it would prescribe timelines for completing the trials and would not permit delaying tactics.
In July last year, the Supreme Court had allowed the CBI to register 22 cases over what it described as an "unholy nexus" between banks and developers to dupe homebuyers in the NCR.

Mamdani is providing funding for an existing program that helps formerly incarcerated people resettle with their families and provides mental health support, among other resources. The program pays families up to $500 a month for a year to house and support the reentry of their family members released from incarceration.
The program is for people who are already being released from Rikers or from prison and is not a way of ending incarceration early. While the eligibility criteria is still in its proposal stages, any domestic violence cases or cases with active protective orders are ineligible. This program, which has existed since 2021, places formerly incarcerated people with their families, not other New York residents. An independent study found in 2023 there was a high success rate and growing demand for the program.
On Nov. 20, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the city's plan to close its jail on Rikers Island. The plan includes building four outer-borough-based facilities to house incarcerated people and more therapeutic bed services. Critics of Mamdani's plan claimed part of the effort would pay New Yorkers a monthly stipend to house formerly incarcerated people from Rikers Island.
The same day, former New York police officer John Chell made the claim to Fox News host Sean Hannity:
CHELL: Let me tell you something that's crazy. … One of the proposals is have civilians get paid by the city to house criminals. Let me say that again. Civilians to get hired … would you like a robber in your basement?
HANNITY: John, I mean, you can make money doing this. I mean, you know, adopt a prisoner. I think every liberal should.
CHELL: It's great. So, you're going to adopt a prisoner, but when you come home from a hard day's work and your Samsung TV is gone, who are you going to blame?
A Facebook post claimed that under this initiative families would get paid $500 per month to house "killers and rapists":
The above claims are missing key information. The Mamdani administration plans to give more funds to and to expand the existing Kinship Reentry Program, which unites formerly incarcerated people with family and loved ones. The program is reportedly under demand and has a high success rate, with little available evidence that it has placed New Yorkers in unsafe situations with "killers and rapists." It does not simply place strangers among New York residents. As such, we rate this claim as mostly false.
We should note that Rikers is a jail and not a prison. A jail is used largely to house pretrial defendants — those who have not yet been convicted of a crime. As such, most people housed in Rikers — 86% according to Vera Institute, a progressive research and advocacy group — have not yet been convicted of a crime.
Snopes reached out to the Mamdani administration and the Osborne Association, which runs the reentry program, to learn more about who qualifies to participate. New York's City Hall told us over email that the program is intended for people already returning home from incarceration at Rikers and is not a mechanism to secure release from custody. The city also said the program is intended to promote housing stability, support successful reentry and prevent formerly incarcerated people from entering the costly homeless shelter system.
What is the Kinship Reentry Program?
Through this program, incarcerated people are housed with their family members or loved ones — not complete strangers, as people making the claim asserted.
Founded in 2021 by the Osborne Association, a nonprofit group focused on services for incarcerated people and their families, the Kinship Reentry Program supports formerly incarcerated people's housing and reintegration with family members and loved ones. The program gives cash and additional services to families helping their loved ones resettle into society following incarceration.
According to a 2023 assessment by researchers at the University of Chicago, the program offered $500 monthly payments for one year to eligible families that "are trusted to deploy the funds at their own discretion, with a few restrictions: tobacco, alcohol, lottery tickets, and illegal substances, and the requirement to provide receipts."
In addition to direct financial assistance, participating families receive financial management assistance, clinical and therapeutic services and peer support.
Families also have a case manager checking in twice a month, tenant advocacy support with their landlords, referrals for other services, and financial literacy training.
How does the program work within Mamdani's 'Close Rikers' plan?
According to Mamdani's "Close Rikers Strategic Plan", the administration would invest more money into the Kinship Reentry Program and expand the number of families who could participate in it.
The city told Snopes over email that the expansion does not increase the $500 monthly payment to participating households. Additional funding supported an expansion in the number of families served, program management and various clinical services.
The plan document states:
Invest $3.55M in FY27 and $7.1M annually thereafter to expand the Kinship Reentry Housing Program from supporting 50 to 300 families. This program provides a stable home for people returning to community from Rikers or prison, including 100 people with diagnoses of serious mental illness, substance use disorder or other complex behavior health needs. It provides direct financial assistance, financial management services, clinical therapeutic support, peer navigation and other wraparound resources.
According to the "Close Rikers Strategic Plan," the reentry program has served more than 250 families. Three in four families completed the full 12-month program; 90% reported better family relationships and 94% reported better financial stability. Only two of over 250 families had their loved ones return to incarceration during the program period.
Is the program safe for New Yorkers?
As noted above, the program supports people with mental illnesses and substance use disorder. We reached out to the Mamdani administration and Osborne Association to learn more about which formerly incarcerated people qualified for the program and what additional support family members receive.
The city told us over email that the administration was working with the program to finalize eligibility requirements. The program was specifically for people leaving Rikers within six months who faced housing instability and barriers to family reunification.
While the city's proposed eligibility criteria did not include exclusions based on criminal charges, any domestic violence cases or cases with active protection orders would be ineligible. Families participating in the program would have to demonstrate financial need and voluntarily agree to house their returning family member without coercion. Families must also establish the person is legally permitted to reside in the home.
Per City Hall, the participants must enroll in supportive services programs with their families and commit to a 12-month program with monthly check-ins and quarterly home visits. Participants would undergo pre-screenings, include assessing their medical needs, income, public benefits and outstanding arrears.
The majority of the participants according to the University of Chicago's 2023 study were women, and most families were people of color. The assessment found that participants in the program were enthusiastic about the support provided and demand for the program exceeded availability, leading to a waitlist.
The claims by critics that such a program would bring "killers and rapists" into New York City neighborhoods, has little to no evidence given the success rate of the program. We also asked the Osborne Association for comment on the above criticisms and will update this post accordingly.
For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous claims about Mamdani, including a rumor that he was "furious" about a Times Square billboard featuring Jesus Christ.

India invited Pakistan to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum held in New Delhi from 20 to 22 November 2026. Pakistan confirmed its participation, with Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik attending. The invitation was extended to SCO member countries as part of the forum, which focused on civilisational and cultural ties. The invitation sparked political criticism in India, with opposition leaders questioning the government’s stance on Pakistan amid tensions over terrorism (here, here, and here).
Amid this, a video purportedly showing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national president Nitin Nabin is circulating on social media (here, here, and here), claiming he said India invited Pakistan to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit under pressure from China.
In the video, Nabin allegedly says that China is pressuring India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit in exchange for an agreement to reclaim 200 sq km of Indian territory occupied by China. He also allegedly remarked that although the Tejas aircraft lack engines, their airframes have been built, adding that the US would supply the engines whenever it chooses to do so. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows BJP national president Nitin Nabin saying that China pressured India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. The original footage shows BJP national president Nitin Nabin speaking about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls at a rally in Chandigarh. The Hiya AI voice detection tool also indicated that the viral audio was likely a deepfake, suggesting that fabricated audio was added to make it appear as though he said that China pressured India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit in exchange for reclaiming 200 sq km of Indian territory. The BJP has also filed a police complaint over the manipulated video. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether BJP national president Nitin Nabin made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible news reports or official statements corroborating the viral claim.
We noticed the viral video carries an ANI watermark. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 22 November 2026, featuring the extended version of the same footage of BJP national president Nitin Nabin, wearing the same attire and speaking against an identical background. In the original video, Nitin Nabin is speaking about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls at a rally in Chandigarh, defending the removal of deceased voters’ names and duplicate entries.
We also found the full speech on the BJP’s official YouTube channel, where it was livestreamed on 22 November 2026. The original footage contains no remarks about China pressuring India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit.
We analysed the viral video using the Hiya AI voice detection tool, which indicated that the audio was likely a deepfake. This suggests that fabricated audio was added to the original footage to make it appear as though BJP national president Nitin Nabin said that China pressured India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit.
The Delhi BJP filed a police complaint on 23 November 2026 against unknown persons over the manipulated video of Nitin Nabin, seeking an FIR and action against those responsible. The complaint was subsequently transferred to the Delhi Police’s Special Cell IFSO unit for investigation (here, here, and here).
To sum up, this video of BJP President Nitin Nabin allegedly saying that China pressured India to invite Pakistan to the SCO summit is a deepfake.

Asia made a big AI bet on Nvidia. What happens now?
- Published
Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world.
Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology.
Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a near-trillion dollar surge in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence.
The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University.
From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes.
Nvidia is everywhere
In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist.
That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one.
For one, Nvidia was able to grow rapidly by outsourcing chip production instead of having to spend heavily to build its own manufacturing plants.
It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC.
That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ.
"The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports".
Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island.
To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors.
On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain.
It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics.
"Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says.
In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to market research group CBRE, external. The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025.
In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States.
But in a timely example of the importance of AI to this region, Singapore this week further raised its growth forecast for this year as the technology boosts its economy.
The world's biggest tech firms - Google, Microsoft, Oracle - also plan to boost their spending on infrastructure in the region by roughly 60% this year, CBRE added.
The demand for neoclouds, which are specialised data centres which power AI, has also risen rapidly, it said.
For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC.
Huang's return carries risks
In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation.
In Taiwan, where he was born and the home of "Jensanity", investors jokingly described his return as a "one man saves the village" story.
Social media and groups on messaging platform Line saw posts like "Old Huang is back," while some investors said "Daddy is back to save my life" and "the humanitarian corridor is open."
However, some said the episode should also prompt a closer look at how effective Taiwan has been in building a "non-China" semiconductor supply chain, and how risks from the industry's heavy reliance on Nvidia should be managed better.
Asia's technology industry has been under increasing pressure from the US in recent years. The administrations of both Joe Biden and Donald Trump have tightened rules on the export of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China.
Those efforts seem to have been renewed. Just last week, Washington announced new rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The latest move not only restricts the export of high-end chips to China, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train AI models.
This will hit South East Asian countries, which have invested billions in data centre infrastructure to cater to Chinese firms. Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region, according to the Financial Times, although it is unclear if this is only a temporary move while it figures out how to comply with the new export rules.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment.
Then there is the growing bipartisan backlash against President Trump and Nvidia after he said he "made the deal" to "convince" the company‘s board to reinstate Huang.
Huang is also due to testify before Congress next week. And as Democrats prepare to take control of the US House and Senate in the New Year, Huang is likely to face further risks.
"Jensen's return may resolve the immediate leadership crisis, but it does not resolve the legal and political overhangs," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist from Saxo Bank.
Investor concerns about the trillions of dollars being poured into AI and the pivotal role Nvidia plays in the industry were already sending tremors through global stock markets.
Some fear that while the company and its charismatic leader have been crucial in driving AI's growth that concentration of influence also poses a threat.
Especially now when it appears that Huang's future - which is still uncertain - could impact economies that are heavily exposed to the AI industry.
"I would say the President and White House would love to brush this over and say its fine but I believe Democrats in Congress will definitely be probing", Ray Wang, founder of San Francisco-based Constellation Research said.
"The story is not over yet... Jensen coming back is probably the biggest, baddest return ever. The question is what will happen next?"

After more than a decade of federal service, prosecutor Zach Dembo quit his job at the Department of Justice in 2025, protesting the politicization of the federal workforce. In January, he's returning to federal employment — as a congressman.
During President Donald Trump's second term, the Department of Government Efficiency began mass layoffs of federal workers and slashed contracts that didn't align with Trump's agenda. Believing politics interfered with his long-standing nonpartisan role, Dembo resigned.
"It's very clear there was a political agenda rather than truly trying to make things more efficient," Dembo said, adding that DOGE went in "with a chainsaw rather than a scalpel" and kneecapped federal agencies' ability to serve the American people. He launched his campaign in July of last year, and on November 3, he flipped Kentucky's sixth district.
Dembo wasn't the only federal worker who responded to DOGE by entering politics: Sam Forstag, then a smokejumper for the US Forest Service in Montana, was away at a union steward training when he got the infamous "Fork in the Road" email offering federal workers the chance to resign.
"There's something deeply insulting about being eight years into wildland fire, putting your life on the line for public safety and public service, and getting an email from quite literally the richest man in the world calling our work low productivity," Forstag said, referring to de facto DOGE head Elon Musk.
Forstag ran for and ultimately flipped Montana's first congressional district.
He and Dembo are among several former civil servants who say DOGE's cuts and upheaval had an unintended consequence: pushing them into electoral politics. And while voters may support improving government efficiency, DOGE's approach of slashing the federal workforce didn't resonate with them — a Quinnipiac poll from June 2025 found that 57% said that Elon Musk and DOGE's work was either not so good or poor.
In a statement, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said, "President Trump was given a clear mandate to eliminate waste, fraud and abuse from the federal government," and had made significant progress in making the federal government more efficient.
Forstag said his coworkers were "probably some of the most efficient workers" in the federal government, and the slew of DOGE cuts and job losses didn't address government inefficiencies that affected his constituents, such as spending hours on hold with Medicaid or waiting in long lines at the post office.
"It was heartbreaking hearing some of these people's stories and having to find ways to try to help them get through," Forstag said. "And it's really the thing that spurred me to run."
DOGE's cuts prompted thousands to either leave or be separated from the federal workforce: From January 2025 to October 2026, federal employment fell from around 3.01 million to 2.7 million. The cuts were especially pronounced in some of the country's most prominent battleground states, including Georgia and Texas. In Kentucky, where Dembo was victorious, separations increased 91% from 2024 to 2025.

Two screenings of Pakistani TV show cancelled in India after backlash
- Published
Until Wednesday, the weekend plans of some television enthusiasts in the Indian city of Bengaluru involved dressing up, having an elaborate dinner and finding out what happens next in the lives of a wildly popular fictional Pakistani couple.
Then geopolitics intervened.
Two private screenings of Dar-e-Nijaat (Door to Salvation), a Pakistani television drama that has become something of a sensation on Indian social media, were called off after an online backlash and police scrutiny.
The serial, which airs on Pakistan's ARY Digital, is available to Indian viewers through some YouTube channels, though the broadcaster's official channel is blocked in India.
The controversy comes amid a renewed appetite for Pakistani entertainment in India, even though cultural engagement remains a sensitive issue following a brief but intense military confrontation between the two nuclear-armed neighbours in May last year.
A similar gathering in Delhi, featuring quizzes and even a virtual interaction with the show's director, had already divided opinion online last week.
In Bengaluru, one screening, scheduled for Saturday at a restaurant, offered a Persian and Arabic dinner alongside two episodes of the serial for a small ticket charge. The other - scheduled at a private theatre and meant only for family members - asked guests to dress in their "best Pakistani ensemble".
As promotional posters circulated online, several social media users questioned the appropriateness of such gatherings and called for police intervention. Both events have since been called off.
The backlash has coincided with calls to block the release of another Pakistani drama in India.
The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi demanding that Netflix's upcoming Pakistani series, Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo (Gather whatever is left), be barred from release in India.
Featuring Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan, Sanam Saeed and other stars with many Indian fans, the series is Pakistan's first Netflix original. Its global premiere is scheduled for 4 December.
In its letter to Modi on Tuesday, the AICWA argued that releasing the series in India would disregard the sentiments of families affected by terrorism. India has long accused Pakistan of supporting cross-border terrorism, an allegation Islamabad denies.
The association has also sought permanent legislation prohibiting Pakistani entertainment content in India. Netflix is yet to clarify whether the series will be available to Indian subscribers.
The developments have revived an old debate in India over whether cultural ties with Pakistan should be kept separate from political differences.
India and Pakistan share a rich cultural heritage, but relations between them have often been fraught since they were carved out of British India as independent nations in 1947.
And cultural exchanges have often been among the first casualties of political tensions. Pakistani ghazal singers with devoted audiences in India have periodically found themselves unable to perform there. Indian films, immensely popular in Pakistan, have disappeared from its cinemas. Artistic collaborations have flourished during periods of relative calm, only to unravel when tensions flare again.
The early 2010s were a particularly fertile period. Pakistani singers Atif Aslam and Rahat Fateh Ali Khan were among the most recognisable voices in Hindi cinema. The launch of the television channel Zindagi in 2014 brought Pakistani serials into Indian living rooms, introducing viewers to stories whose language and emotional worlds were familiar, but whose treatment of everyday life often felt refreshingly different.
By 2016, Fawad Khan was appearing in some of Bollywood's most prominent productions. But attacks on Indian security forces in Uri that year and in Pulwama in 2019, both of which India blamed on Pakistan-based militant groups, narrowed the space for cultural collaboration. Pakistan - which has constantly denied any involvement - also imposed restrictions on Indian entertainment.
Even as formal exchanges dwindled, Pakistani dramas found new audiences in India on YouTube, while music continued to travel across the border through streaming platforms.
But the events of last year disrupted even this relatively informal relationship.
On 22 April 2025, militants killed 26 people, most of them tourists, in Pahalgam in Indian-administered Kashmir. India blamed Pakistan-linked militants; Islamabad denied involvement. In May, India launched military strikes on what it described as terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered Kashmir. Four days of fighting followed before a ceasefire was announced.
Amid widespread anger in India, the government asked streaming platforms to discontinue Pakistani-origin content, while social media accounts of several Pakistani celebrities were blocked.
Fawad Khan's much-anticipated return to Hindi cinema with Abir Gulaal was thwarted when the film was denied permission for release in India. Criticism of India's military action by Pakistani artistes fuelled further anger.
For much of the past year, Indian audiences have encountered Pakistan on screen largely through the prism of national security. In December, millions flocked to watch Dhurandhar, Aditya Dhar's espionage thriller, whose success inspired a fascination with the gangsters, spies and political intrigues of Karachi.
But in recent months, a more familiar kind of fascination with Pakistan has begun to resurface.
Pakistani songs like Alfaaz have become hugely popular on Indian social media, while Dar-e-Nijaat, a story about marriage, heartbreak and domestic life, has found an enthusiastic audience.
Written by the celebrated Urdu novelist Umera Ahmed, the serial revolves around the marriage of Zaryab (Durefishan Saleem), a young woman recovering from a romantic betrayal, and Abu Bakar (Sheheryar Munawar), a deeply religious man.
Though the drama explores questions of faith and redemption, it is Abu Bakar's tenderness towards his wife that has earned him perhaps the highest accolade in the contemporary vocabulary of courtship: a "green flag".
It was this enthusiasm for the drama that prompted the organiser of one of the screenings in Bengaluru to plan an event at a private theatre in her apartment complex.
What she had envisaged as a small family gathering, she said, had been interpreted quite differently once the invitation found its way onto X.
"My family was saying why should we cancel?" she said. But ultimately, she decided to call it off.

Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor
As dawn broke one recent morning over camp, we got one of our first full views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro, normally hidden behind clouds.
Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts. The beating sun bakes you during the day, walking so close to the equator, but the nights quickly dip below freezing. Snow remains constantly in sight from humid rainforest and alpine landscapes, freshly charred from a wildfire three weeks before. And always beckoning is the peak, within sight, but seemingly never nearer; the high altitude means hikers need to walk slowly or else risk exhaustion and altitude sickness.
A group of friends and fellow hikers and I spent days camping at altitude to acclimatize before a final summit push during our second-to-last evening on the mountain. We trudged through heavy snow under the stars, cresting a massive volcanic crater rim, and leaned against drifts of what had become a full blizzard to reach the top in the early morning hours. I stood on the peak I'd seen only from a distance for the last week but saw only whiteness: all snow and ice, the absence of life and color heightened by my low oxygen levels.
Days later, having descended and decompressed and readying myself to fly back home, I looked back at the mountain one last time. For a few minutes, in the dusk light, the clouds parted and she revealed herself before disappearing again into the darkening evening, still as elusive as ever.

(Bloomberg) -- A powerful Thanksgiving storm is sweeping up the US East Coast toward New York, as adverse weather knocks out power to more than half a million homes and businesses across the nation while snarling holiday travel.
The strengthening storm has already led to the postponement of events including Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade, which has been rescheduled for Saturday, marking the first time the annual holiday procession has been delayed. The governors of New York and New Jersey both declared a state of emergency, warning of damaging winds, heavy rainfall and severe coastal flooding through Friday.
The conditions complicate journeys for those heading to family gatherings, though the days leading up to Thanksgiving tend to see greater travel than the holiday itself. AccuWeather meteorologist Alyssa Glenny said wind gusts have already reached 72 miles per hour at Stingray Point, Virginia, with coastal areas of New Jersey and Long Island bracing for gusts up to 80 mph as the storm pushes northward.
“We’re looking at the afternoon going into the evening for peak rainfall in New York,” Glenny said via telephone. “Once we get to midday, early afternoon, the wind is going to pick up and then the next 12 hours is the window for peak winds.”
The National Weather Service has issued coastal flood warnings for various New York and New Jersey counties, encompassing all five boroughs of New York City. In a statement, Mayor Zohran Mamdani urged the city’s residents to use caution if traveling.
There were also about 400 reported flight cancellations across the US, with Baltimore/Washington International Airport and New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport among the most impacted, according to FlightAware data. While elevated, the disruption is far below the levels recorded earlier this month after the US Federal Aviation Administration imposed a nationwide ground stop due to an equipment outage.
Meanwhile, there are over 668,000 US power outages as of about 1 p.m. Eastern Time, according to PowerOutage.com. That includes about 5% of customers in Maryland, Virginia and Missouri, with the latter enduring heavy snowfall from a winter storm.
“With the power outages, we always are concerned with downed trees that could impact travel,” AccuWeather’s Glenny said. “Along the coastal areas — like those locations in Southern New Jersey, Ocean City, Maryland where they’re having the coastal flooding — there are definitely some travel impacts with flooded roadways in that corridor.”
The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed due to the high winds making it too dangerous to send the balloons above the streets of Manhattan. The city adopted new wind rules after the 1997 Thanksgiving parade, when gusts hurled a gigantic Cat in the Hat balloon into a lamppost, injuring spectators.
“The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration,” Macy’s said in a statement.
The balloons have been grounded because of weather just once in the parade’s history, in 1971, while in 2019 they were required to fly at lower heights because of high winds. This year’s rescheduled event is due to start at 8:30 a.m. in New York on Saturday.
“Tomorrow we’re going to start to see the impacts winding down and then we’re kind of just dealing with cleanup,” said Glenny. “By Saturday, for places like New York City, we expect a dry day. By the afternoon we could even have some breaks of sun.”

Kenneth Law apologizes in court to families of victims
Crown seeks 25-year sentence for Kenneth Law, who admitted to selling poison
WARNING: This article contains details of suicide.
An Ontario man who sold products online to people who used them to take their own lives apologized in court today to the families of his victims.
Kenneth Law, 61, said his actions were "categorically wrong" and vowed never to repeat them. He made the comments from the prisoner’s box after lawyers for the Crown and defence laid out what they believe would be an appropriate sentence for him.
On Friday, prosecutors argued money was the motivation for Law, who sold potentially deadly substances and equipment online to people knowing they would likely use the products to take their own lives. They sought a 25-year sentence for Law in what they called an unprecedented case.
Law's lawyers, meanwhile, argued the 61-year-old was not a "mercenary predator" but rather a misguided man committed to his belief in the right to die and whose actions did not warrant a "de facto life sentence."
Law's reasons for selling his wares over nearly two and a half years were a focal point as the Crown and the defence laid out what they believe would be an appropriate sentence for Law, who pleaded guilty earlier this year to 14 counts of aiding suicide in the deaths of 14 people in Ontario.
The former chef has been linked to dozens of deaths worldwide, including 79 in the United Kingdom that are being considered as part of the sentencing process.
Scores of grieving family members and friends told the court about the lasting impact of Law's crimes over two days in September as his sentencing hearing got underway. Some delivered the message in person, others did so by video and others in written statements read by prosecutors.
Both sides noted the unique nature of the case and the resulting absence of meaningful jurisprudence as they made their arguments in a Newmarket, Ont., court.
"No case such as this has come before this court, and hopefully it never will again," said Crown attorney Katie Doherty. "Part of ensuring that that happens is to denounce and deter the offender's conduct with a sentence that is fit and proportionate in all the circumstances."
The scale of Law's operations should be counted as an aggravating factor, as should the fact that his actions "actually caused death," she argued.
Ninety-three people died because they used the products purchased from Law, including 12 teenagers, she said.
"These were vulnerable people ... What they needed was help, but what they found was Mr. Law and his products for death," Doherty said.
Law's intentions not altruistic: prosecutor
Law's actions run contrary to his claim of an altruistic purpose, the prosecutor argued. The only factor that determined whom he sold to was whether they paid upfront, she said.
"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr. Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Law's guilty plea, which spared grieving families a lengthy trial, and his lack of a prior criminal record count as mitigating factors, she said.
The maximum sentence for aiding suicide is 14 years and Crown attorney Katie Doherty argued today that Law should face 12 1/2 years for each count, with two to be served back to back and the rest at the same time.
After subtracting credit for the time Law has spent in custody since his arrest in May 2023, he would be left with 19 years and 7 1/2 months to serve.
'Mr. Law did not kill anyone': defence
Defence lawyer Matthew Gourlay argued that while Law sold the victims the tools they used to end their lives, he was not "the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all of these victims to seek out his products in the first place," nor did he play a role in their decision to use the products in the way they did.
"In short, Mr. Law did not kill anyone," he said.
Law's actions and sentence should also be considered in the context of the ongoing, unresolved debate in Canadian society over assisted dying, Gourlay argued.
"To be very clear, the context in no way justifies Mr. Law's choice to act outside of lawful bounds," he said.
"But in my submission, you do need to look at that social context in order to evaluate what a proportionate sentence for Mr. Law might look like, and you have to do that especially because of the relative dearth of meaningful sentencing jurisprudence in this area."
An appropriate sentence under the circumstances would be 12 years — nine for the cases involving sodium nitrite and three for those involving other equipment, to be served one after the other — minus credit for the time he's already served, the defence lawyer argued.
Law should also receive enhanced credit for his time in detention due to the particularly harsh conditions he faced, which included lockdowns, triple bunking and "a life-threatening case" of flesh-eating disease he contracted at the Maplehurst Correctional Complex, he argued.
Law shipped products to over 40 countries
Law's plea deal in May came soon after he was set to stand trial on the aiding suicide charges and another 14 counts of first-degree murder related to the same victims.
Prosecutors are expected to withdraw the murder charges after Law is sentenced.
