PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.
Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.
Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.
Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.
The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.
The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
A French cinema icon faces a #MeToo reckoning
With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.
He became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."
But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.
On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.
"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said in a written statement.
Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters").
The court also ordered his name to be listed in France's national sex offender database.
"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said.
Accusations against Depardieu sparked a national debate
The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.
Even French President Emmanuel Macron weighed in, drawing criticism from women's rights activists when he said the actor "makes France proud." Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."
The controversy exposed divisions in a country where some prominent cultural figures had pushed back against the #MeToo movement.
In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to make advances toward women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.
Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors. His career spanned hundreds of films, from "The Last Metro" and "Jean de Florette" to the popular "Asterix" franchise.
His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

World chess champion Gukesh Dommaraju insisted he was approaching his first title defense with the mindset of a challenger on Sunday as he and Javokhir Sindarov faced the media ahead of their historic showdown in Geneva, the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title.
The two 20-year-old grandmasters appeared side by side at the United Nations’ European headquarters in Geneva, where they struck a respectful tone before their best-of-14-games encounter begins on Tuesday at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, the affluent suburb overlooking Lake Geneva.
Pressed on whether defending a world championship was more difficult than winning it the first time, Gukesh politely rejected the premise.
“I don’t think I’m here to defend anything,” the Indian said. “I’m here to win it all over again. That’s the mindset I’m in.”
Sindarov, the fast-rising Uzbek challenger roughly six months older than Gukesh who enters the match as the oddsmakers’ favorite despite being a relative newcomer to the game’s highest level, was similarly reluctant to dole out predictions. Asked to assess his chances of becoming world champion, he put them at a diplomatic 50%.
“It’s a hard match and 14 games,” Sindarov said. “Everything can happen.”
The contest brings together two players whose careers have traced sharply divergent trajectories since Gukesh became the 18th and youngest ever undisputed champion in December 2024.
The Chennai native, who was only 18 when he defeated China’s Ding Liren to shatter the age record previously held by Garry Kasparov, has struggled badly for form since reaching the summit. After climbing to a career-high No 3 in the world that month, he has plummeted to No 26 following an extended string of underwhelming performances, making him the lowest-ranked reigning world champion since Elo ratings were introduced in 1971.
Sindarov, meanwhile, has surged from No 25 a year ago to a career-best No 4 after a breakthrough 12-month stretch that included winning the Fide World Cup in Goa last November and an unbeaten masterclass at this year’s Candidates Tournament in Cyprus, where he finished with six wins and eight draws against a stacked field including Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura and Anish Giri to earn a shot at Gukesh’s title.
The 22-place gap between them is the widest of any world championship matchup since the title was reunified in 2006. Sindarov also holds a 2½-½ advantage in their three previous classical meetings, with two wins and one draw.
Yet both men played down the significance of past results on Sunday.
“Whatever has happened till now, I think just gets erased when we sit at the table for Game 1,” Gukesh said. “It’s a completely different match, completely different opponent and different place.”
He acknowledged Sindarov’s sustained run of success, describing the Tashkent-born challenger as one of the world’s strongest players and predicting a formidable assignment.
“Sindarov has just been in very consistent and very good form,” Gukesh said. “It’s for sure going to be a real test.”
Sindarov was equally complimentary about the champion, pointing to his extraordinary performances in winning the title as evidence that his recent difficulties should not be overinterpreted.
“Gukesh’s performance in 2024 is something fantastic,” Sindarov said, adding that he had experienced the Indian’s strength firsthand in January when they played to a 78-move draw at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee. “Sometimes you have some bad periods.”
The two players also revealed contrasting approaches to preparing for the championship. While Gukesh deliberately pared back his tournament schedule this year, Sindarov continued regularly entering competitions against elite opposition, reasoning that he needed more experience at the highest level.
Sindarov added that he had accepted an invitation to the four-month Grand Chess Tour circuit before winning the Candidates and saw little reason to withdraw afterward.
“Even after I won Candidates, I wanted to have more experience because I didn’t play that many strong tournaments in my career,” he said. “I’m happy with my decision.”
Gukesh said the strategy had not surprised him or his team, who expected the challenger to take advantage of his momentum and accumulate experience against the world’s strongest players. The trade-off was that Sindarov’s busy slate also gave Gukesh and his team a wealth of recent games to study for clues about the challenger’s approach.
The preparations have also given Sindarov an appreciation for the peculiar demands of a world title match. He once found it difficult to believe that players could spend three or four months preparing to face a single opponent. Now, having devoted much of the past six months to the task himself, he wonders whether even that is enough.
“I was thinking six months is enough time,” he said. “But maybe even this six months ... is also maybe not enough to prepare for such a hard tournament.”
The Indian, by contrast, can draw on his experience in the pressure-cooker environment of the world championship stage, where the psychological and physical demands of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Gukesh said he had been surfing, running and spending time outdoors, while Sindarov has taken up padel, playing regularly during his training camp.
“If I would be, like, 30, 40, maybe it will be tough,” Sindarov said. “But because I’m young, I think it’ll be not very hard, like, physically.”
Gukesh will again work with Polish grandmaster Grzegorz Gajewski, who helped guide his successful 2024 campaign, as well as South African mental conditioning coach Paddy Upton, who was part of the backroom staff for India’s cricket team when they won the 2011 World Cup and the Indian men’s hockey team when they claimed bronze at the Paris Olympics in 2024. Sindarov revealed he is working with Ukrainian coach Roman Vidonyak, although neither player has publicly disclosed the full composition of his team of seconds, the trusted advisers responsible for preparing openings and analyzing the opponent.
The match will be staged at the Fondation Martin Bodmer, a museum and research library housing rare manuscripts and books, including a Gutenberg Bible, a Shakespeare First Folio and a first edition of Isaac Newton’s Principia. Both players inspected the playing hall on Saturday ahead of Monday’s technical meeting.
Unlike most recent world championship tilts, the players will not compete inside a purpose-built soundproof enclosure. Fide has abandoned the familiar transparent cube in order to preserve the atmosphere of the historic venue, relying instead on enhanced security measures and strict limits on the number of spectators and media admitted to the playing hall.
Sindarov admitted that he had expected to play inside the traditional fishbowl, but was impressed by the stage. “The playing hall is really very beautiful,” he said. Gukesh, meanwhile, said he had checked the chairs, lighting and even the floor to ensure he would be comfortable during games that could last four or five hours – and occasionally even longer. As for the rare books surrounding the board, the champion admitted he had barely looked at them. “I don’t think I’ll be reading in between the games,” he joked.
The glass enclosure, designed to shield players from distractions, was first used during Garry Kasparov’s 1995 title defense against Viswanathan Anand at New York’s World Trade Center and has featured in numerous subsequent championships, including Gukesh’s victory over Ding in Singapore two years ago. Sindarov admitted the setting would take some getting used to, having never played a tournament in which there was nobody else competing nearby.
The match carries a $2.5m (£1.9m) prize fund, with $200,000 awarded for each decisive game and the remainder divided equally between the players. Sindarov will open with the white pieces on Tuesday after the drawing of lots at Sunday’s opening ceremony, with the players alternating colors throughout the match. The first to reach seven and a half points will be crowned champion, with rapid and blitz tiebreaks scheduled if the contest finishes level after 14 games. Three of the past five world title matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023.
The winner will join or continue a centuries-spanning lineage stretching back to Wilhelm Steinitz, who became the first official world champion in 1886. Gukesh is seeking to retain the crown he won as a teenager, while Sindarov is attempting to become the first player from Uzbekistan to capture the title.
For now, neither is allowing himself to dwell too much on what victory might mean.
Sindarov, who will turn 21 on 8 December, the scheduled date of Game 12, said he had made no pledges or wagers about how he might celebrate winning the championship.
“I really want to focus on my next 20 days and try to play my best chess,” he said. “Then we’ll see.”
Gukesh, who celebrated his 2024 triumph by fulfilling a promise to go bungee jumping, was more cryptic when asked whether he had another stunt up his sleeve.
“I have a couple of things in mind,” he said, smiling. “I think you’ll get to know in time, maybe.”

The Hindu, in association with Kauvery Hospital, conducted a webinar on Friday titled ‘The Role of Robotics in Knee Replacement’. Orthopaedic specialists discussed the use of robotic-assisted technology in total knee replacement (TKR), its benefits, post-operative recovery, costs and the role of surgeons in performing the procedure.
The experts were Mukunth K., senior consultant, orthopaedic surgeon, joint replacement and sports injuries, Kauvery Hospital, Alwarpet; P.R. Ramasamy, head of the department of orthopaedics and pelviacetabular and joint replacement surgeon, Kauvery Hospital, Tiruchi; and Manivannan, consultant, orthopaedics, arthroscopy and joint replacement surgeon, Kauvery Hospital, Salem.
Dr. Mukunth explained how robotic-assisted technology helps surgeons plan knee replacement procedures through bone mapping, precise measurements and real-time guidance. He said the technology helped surgeons make accurate bone cuts and position implants closer to the intended alignment. He compared the robot’s role to GPS navigation, emphasising that the surgeon remained in control of the procedure.
He said manual measurements during conventional surgery could vary by 2–3 mm, even in experienced hands. Greater precision in bone cuts and implant alignment could help reduce soft-tissue trauma and blood loss during surgery and improve post-operative outcomes.
Dr. Ramasamy explained the steps involved in robotic-assisted knee replacement. He said the procedure involved less damage to the surrounding bone, which could make a future revision surgery easier. He also clarified that robotic technology was not used for revision surgery in patients who had undergone conventional knee replacement 15–20 years earlier. The aim of robotic-assisted TKR was not limited to pain relief but also included helping patients return to their routine activities sooner, he said.
Dr. Manivannan discussed post-operative recovery and mobility. He said accurate implant positioning could help patients regain mobility and muscle strength sooner, with recovery potentially being two to three weeks faster than with conventional surgery. Hospital stays could also be shorter, and patients could become fully functional within six to eight weeks.
Responding to questions on cost, the panel said robotic-assisted knee replacement costs between ₹3.5 lakh and ₹5.5 lakh, depending on the hospital, city and patient’s health condition and that the procedure is covered under health insurance.
The webinar was moderated by Soma Basu, journalist.
Webinar can be viewed at https://newsth.live/THKARY

Navy takes delivery of latest stealth frigate Vindhyagiri under ₹45,000-crore project
The Indian Navy has taken delivery of Vindhyagiri, the final stealth frigate built by GRSE under the ₹45,000-crore Project-17A programme.
Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers Ltd (GRSE) on Friday delivered Vindhyagiri, the third and final guided-missile frigate of the P17A series built by the Kolkata-based public sector shipyard, to the Indian Navy, GRSE said.
“The delivery marks the successful completion of GRSE’s P17A frigate building programme and represents another significant step towards strengthening India’s maritime capabilities,” it said. The Navy is expected to commission the warship into service within two months.
The seven-ship Project-17A programme is worth around ₹45,000 crore. The Nilgiri, Udaygiri, Taragiri and Mahendragiri were built by Mumbai-based Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Ltd (MDL), while Himgiri and Dunagiri were constructed by Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers (GRSE).
All six frigates have been commissioned, strengthening the Navy’s operational capabilities and combat readiness in the Indian Ocean Region, a strategic maritime expanse where challenges include China’s carefully calculated bid to expand its influence and efforts to defend the rules-based international order.
The P17A (or Nilgiri-class) platforms reflect India’s advanced warship-building capabilities, featuring 75% indigenous content and being equipped with cutting-edge weapons, sensors and systems designed to dominate the maritime battlespace. The P17A, a successor to the Shivalik-class stealth frigates (P17), marks a significant leap forward in warship design and capability.
The P17A frigates can undertake a wide range of maritime operations, including fleet air defence, anti-surface warfare, anti-submarine warfare, maritime interdiction, surveillance and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief (HADR).
The frigates are equipped with modern weapons and sensors, including the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile, the Barak-8 surface-to-air missile system, MF-STAR surveillance radar and anti-submarine warfare capabilities. The warships have a displacement of 6,670 tonnes, are 149 metres long, can reach a top speed of 28 knots and carry 225 personnel.
The Navy is working towards becoming fully self-reliant by 2047, when India celebrates the centenary of its Independence. Around 60 warships are under construction at various Indian shipyards.

While Islam is the fastest-growing religion in the world, it is not the fastest-growing religion in the U.S. — Hinduism and the nonreligious population are both growing faster, according to the World Religion Database. In addition, the statistic of "fastest-growing religion" is rather dubious, because it's much easier for a smaller population to grow at a high rate than a larger one (10 to 15 and 10,000 to 15,000 both represent a 50% growth rate, as an example).
Back in 2004, Snopes published an article called "Allah or Jesus?" that fact-checked the authenticity of a copypasta detailing a conversation an unnamed narrator had with an imam about the beliefs of the Muslim faith, specifically on the topic of jihad and the idea that Muslims are commanded to kill all nonbelievers. We found that the post originated as an opinion piece published by Rick Mathes, a prison minister in Missouri, though a spokesperson for the Missouri Department of Corrections claimed the events in the story never happened.
More than 20 years later, the copypasta is still making rounds online, and like a game of telephone, small bits and pieces of information change from post to post. As early as 2005, a new sentence began to appear at the top of the story: "The Muslim religion is the fastest growing religion per capita in the United States, especially in the minority races."
This article is not an attempt to relitigate the legitimacy of the copypasta's claims about Muslim beliefs. It is an attempt to review the claim that Islam is the fastest-growing religion in the United States, at the request of our readers. In recent years, the Pew Research Center, one of the best authorities on religious demographics, has published multiple reports claiming that Islam is the fastest-growing religion worldwide. According to a 2026 Associated Press story, Pew predicts the world will have more Muslims than Christians by 2035.
However, the demographics of the United States are vastly different than the demographics of the world as a whole. Snopes inspected the available demographic evidence for the U.S. and determined the claim is false, and that Hinduism and the nonreligious population are both growing faster than Islam. 
How demographers track religion
Statistics about religion in the U.S. are hard to come by. The Census Bureau, a reliable source on demographic information for most other topics, has never directly asked Americans about their religious beliefs in deference to the separation of church and state. In 1976, Congress even passed a law forbidding such a question from ever being included on the census.
As a result, the most-reliable statistics on the country's religious makeup come from pollsters and academics. For our analysis, Snopes examined data from from three different places: Pew's Religious Landscape Study, the Public Religion Research Institute's American Values Atlas and Boston University's World Religion Database.
Both the Religious Landscape Study and the American Values Atlas produced their estimates using surveys. Tens of thousands of randomly selected participants from across the country were asked about their religious affiliation, among many other questions, in an attempt to create a representative sample of the nation.
Meanwhile, Dr. Gina Zurlo, a senior researcher and lecturer at Harvard Divinity School who is also the editor of the World Religion Database, told Snopes via email that the WRD's estimates relied on both surveys and migration data, making statistical assumptions about people's religions based on their reported ethnic identity.
How religions grow
Three factors influence how the population of a religion changes at a national level:
- Birth and death rate
- Conversion in and conversion out
- Immigration and emigration
Children are generally raised with the same religious practices as their parents, though they may choose to disaffiliate from that religion later. According to both Zurlo and Pew, birth and death rates are far and away the largest factor in tracking religious affiliation, and serve as the primary explanation for Pew's prediction that there will be more Muslims than Christians worldwide by 2035.
Simply put, Muslims have more children than Christians on average (3.1 children per woman for Muslims compared with 2.5 for Christians). This is a result of large-scale demographic changes across the globe. Decades of statistics show that more-developed countries have lower birth rates, and many developed nations have large Christian majorities and small Muslim populations. While the number of Christians is still projected to grow over the coming decades because of Christian populations in areas with high fertility rates such as Sub-Saharan Africa, that population growth is offset by the low fertility rates in places such as Europe.
The other two factors are much less important at a worldwide scale, but they do play a role at the national level.
While the religious conversion factor does include conversion between two different religions, the most common kind of religious conversion in the U.S. is, far and away, disaffiliation. Pew also predicts that by 2070, the U.S. will not be majority Christian. However, that's not because the non-Christian religious population will skyrocket — it's because more and more Americans will identify as agnostic, atheist or "nothing in particular." Younger generations across Europe and America are consistently less religious than older ones.
Finally, the third factor reveals that this entire exercise is also a claim about immigration. The original text specifically suggests the Muslim population is growing faster in "the minority races" than it is among the majority white population (most immigrants to the U.S. are non-white, though the census classifies Middle Eastern and North African people as white).
"In twenty years there will be enough Muslim voters in the U.S. to elect the President," the copypasta concludes, suggesting the country needs to seriously consider whether Islam is compatible with American life. (The statistics we show further down reveal that the claim about voters is hard to rate, but generally false — the political influence of any given population grows as the population grows, and the U.S. Muslim population is around 2% or less of the entire population — not large enough to generate that level of political influence.) The rhetoric reminded us of the many false claims we've checked suggesting that Muslims in the U.S. are planning or enacting Shariah, or Islamic law, in the U.S., using the entire religion as a straw man in the process.
The copypasta's clear anti-Muslim stance makes its position clear — the author seems to want no Muslims in the U.S. for any reason — but it never explains why the Muslim population is seemingly growing. If large numbers of people were converting to Islam, the post surely would have mentioned it. Birth rates, meanwhile, would not increase the size of the Muslim population at the rate suggested by the claim. Therefore, the growth must be mainly from immigrants, another common target for straw man attacks.
Zurlo said immigration is indeed the main contributing factor for the growth of the Muslim population in the U.S. (though it's certainly not at the level suggested in the copypasta). According to Pew's 2023-24 data, about 60% of Muslims in the U.S. are immigrants themselves, and another 20% have at least one parent born outside the country, compared with 44% and 15% of U.S. Muslims in 2007, respectively.
The perils of working with small populations
All in all, the population of Muslims in the United States remains relatively small. The surveys conducted by Pew and PRRI estimate that between 1% and 2% of the total adult population of the U.S. identifies as Muslim. The World Religion Database, which attempts to factor children into its estimates, found the same: between 1% and 2%. In total, that places the Muslim population of the U.S. as somewhere between 3 million and 6 million people.
However, this small population size comes with a large caveat when combined with the claim's statistic of choice — "fastest growing religion per capita."
As previously stated, much of the data on religion comes largely from surveys. When responsibly combined with other statistical modeling techniques, surveys are powerful tools that can produce highly accurate estimates across a large population. However, they also introduce a level of uncertainty and statistical variance to the data.
If the population you're trying to study is large, this level of uncertainty and variance doesn't particularly affect your ability to draw conclusions. But if the population is quite small, problems emerge. Take the following, exaggerated example:
Say a pollster conducts a survey of 1,000 Americans each year, asking each person what their favorite fruit is. In Year 1, 890 of those surveyed say apples and five say bananas. In Year 2, 900 say apples and 10 say bananas.
Now, calculate the growth rates of these groups. The population of people who prefer apples grew at a rate just over 1%. The population of people who prefer bananas, meanwhile, grew at a skyrocketing rate of 100%.
The problem lies in the magnitude of the numbers. It is much easier to go from two to three than it is to go from 10,000 to 15,000, but both represent a growth rate of 50%.
As a result, the statistic of "fastest-growing religion" is innately biased toward Islam and other religions that make up a small proportion of the U.S. population — Hinduism and Buddhism, for instance.
Interpreting the data
After a survey is conducted, firms such as Pew and PRRI must adjust their estimates based on any external factors and possible biases they couldn't control in order to ensure their conclusions are accurate. However, their publicly available data included only raw figures from the survey, before the adjustment, so we could not fairly analyze and present them. As such, Snopes produced our main chart using the World Religion Database's figures.
Because the percentage of Christians is so large when compared with everything else, we produced two charts: one including only religions practiced by at least 1% of the U.S. population and a second that included smaller minorities practiced by at least 0.1% of the population.
The steepness of the lines shows that Islam is not the fastest-growing religion in the U.S. Over two different time periods — from 2000 to 2025 and 2020 to 2025 — Hinduism, Jainism, Zoroastrianism, Chinese folk religions and all nonreligious designations grew faster, Snopes found.
In 2000, the World Religion Database estimated there were around 3.42 million Muslims in the U.S., representing about 1.2% of the country's population. The figure grew to an estimated 4.85 million Muslims (1.4% of the population) in 2020, then to an estimated 5.16 million, or 1.5% of the total population, in 2025. In other words, the U.S. Muslim population grew about 51% between 2000 and 2025, and 6.6% between 2020 and 2025.
The Hindu population, meanwhile, grew from 1.18 million (0.4%) to 2.63 million (0.8%) to 3.15 million (0.9%) over the same time span, a 167% growth rate since 2000 and a 19% growth rate in the past five years.
The nonreligious population grew at roughly the same rate as the Hindu population, from an estimated 33.71 million people (12%) in 2000 to 73.26 million people (21.6%) in 2020 to 86.89 million (25%) in 2025. Between 2000 and 2025, that's a 157% growth rate, and between 2020 and 2025, it's 19% growth.
We also produced two more charts specifically plotting the growth rates of the religions between 2000 and 2025 and between 2020 and 2025. The higher the bar, the larger the growth rate, and if the bar points down, the religious population shrank. Christianity was the only religion that grew over the 25-year period but shrank in the five-year period. 
The trends generally agreed across sources. Pew's statistics showed that while 78% of U.S. adults identified as Christian in 2007, just 62% did in 2024. Most of that loss was offset by the growth of the country's nonreligious population (16% unaffiliated in 2007, 29% in 2024), with all non-Christian religions combined growing from 5% to 7%, mostly from Muslims and Hindus, who made up less than 1% of U.S. adults in 2007 but 1% of U.S. adults in 2024.
PRRI's survey also found the share of Christians is decreasing and the share of nonreligious people is increasing, from around 71% Christian and 21% nonreligious in 2013 to 66% Christian and 28% nonreligious in 2025. The population of all non-Christian religions, meanwhile, remained relatively stable from year to year, around 7% total, including the 1% that identifies as Muslim and 1% that identifies as Hindu.

Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A
- Published
Max Verstappen triumphed in a thrilling Las Vegas Grand Prix ahead of the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.
There were 34 lead changes across the 50 laps of racing as Dutchman Verstappen held off attacks from Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, plus his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar.
Ferrari had to deal with another intra-team battle on track as Charles Leclerc received a 10-second time penalty after colliding with Lewis Hamilton.
Here, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
After Las Vegas, have Ferrari now reached a crossroads? With Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc's on-track antics, is their partnership sustainable? Should Ferrari consider a change of direction, potentially bringing Oliver Bearman into the equation? - Michael
The battle between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at Ferrari is one that keeps on giving - but not in a way Ferrari would want.
The collision in Las Vegas for which Leclerc was penalised was just the latest flashpoint for the team in a season that has been full of them.
The drivers argued over race strategy in relation to each other in Zandvoort and Singapore.
Hamilton made an aggressive dive down the inside at the first chicane on the first lap at Monza, only for Leclerc to shove him on to the gravel.
Hamilton ignored calls to pit in both Singapore (because he didn't want to just circulate behind Leclerc) and Brazil (because, he said, he had not been given enough information about the weather).
There was the first-lap incident at Turn Four in Mexico in which their fighting led to both going off track and letting in Max Verstappen to win a race Ferrari should have finished one-two.
And now Las Vegas, where first Hamilton earned a 10-second penalty for gaining a position on Lando Norris on track in an incident that also involved Leclerc, then Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for tipping Hamilton into a spin later in the race.
Leclerc was on the receiving end of team principal Frederic Vasseur's ire in Las Vegas - the Frenchman calling the situation "unacceptable". But inside Ferrari they felt both drivers had a degree of culpability for the Mexico situation.
Somehow Vasseur needs to get a handle on this.
Ferrari want to allow them to race. And it's hard to imagine two drivers of such standing would accept anything else.
The problem is that doing so, amid their battle for supremacy within the team, is harming the team's results.
The concern for Ferrari is this is happening when there is relatively little at stake. It's easy to imagine how combustible it could become if Ferrari have a car capable of challenging for the title next year.
Both want to be the driver to deliver that next championship, for very different reasons.
Hamilton would get his eighth, which he feels he was unfairly denied in Abu Dhabi in 2021. And Leclerc would win his first, and complete the journey of being the first Ferrari academy driver to win the world championship for the team.
At the moment, this is not an existential question, but it's easy to see how it could become one, and Ferrari left with a decision of it being one or the other if they can't find a way to race without compromising the team.
But that's not just on Vasseur.
Both drivers have buy into that and, as Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have largely done at McLaren, accept there will be days when they have to sacrifice themselves for the greater good of Ferrari while ensuring they are ahead of the other more often than not on speed and fair racing.
It's then up to the team to decide when there comes a point to impose team orders if either or both are in a title fight with another driver.
It remains to be seen whether either of them can fully buy into that in circumstances when they individually end up losing out.
Why does George Russell often feel the need to try mind games and make comments, such as those about Max Verstappen? It often backfires on him and are usually made when he's got nothing to race for. Shouldn't he focus on himself? - Nick
This, as Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff pointed out after the race in Las Vegas, is a rivalry that goes back years.
"They've known each other so long," was Wolff's verdict. "Since karting. I think it's probably been a bit of cat and mouse. Provocations on either side. Another good factor of entertainment."
Verstappen also had a bit of a set-to with Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson in Mexico practice, which was not dissimilar in some ways.
There, stewards ruled that both had driven in an "unacceptable manner" and both drivers admitted their moves had been unnecessary and clumsy.
There's no question Russell believed what he was saying about Verstappen's driving in final practice at Las Vegas. According to the stewards, he was in the right, as Verstappen was given a warning for his changing direction in the braking zone.
Are these mind games? Or just Russell saying what he thinks? He feels he has a valid point to make.
Making it in public does not seem to affect Verstappen in any way. Does it change anything? Verstappen is a remorseless, ruthless competitor on track whether he is provoked or not.
Yes, he admitted satisfaction when he saw Russell make his late-race error in Las Vegas. But did he race any differently because of the Briton's comments? That's unlikely. Verstappen was just doing what he felt was right to win the race.
Ultimately, it's Russell's career, and it's up to him how he conducts himself, what he chooses to say in public and what he does not.
Track design, cold temperatures, energy deployment strategies or just the unwillingness of one team-mate to hold station behind another. What was the dominant factor in Las Vegas that led to such a hectic race? - Tim
The extraordinary Las Vegas race, with long trains of cars unable to break free of each other, was a combination of technical factors. Nothing to do with the willingness or otherwise of team-mates to hold station.
It was a combination of the track characteristics, particularly the long straights, the energy deployment demands of the engines, which are energy starved, and the cold temperatures and track surface and the effect they had on tyre behaviour.
As Max Verstappen said: "It was just the tow (in) combination with the deployment. Of course, when you are within a second, you have the overtake mode as well, and around here that is powerful. So, you could not pull away."
The tow provided a significant lap time gain of well over 0.5secs a lap. That's why a car in front could not pull away from a car behind even if it was slightly quicker.
The overtake mode provides an extra 0.5MJ of electrical energy per lap for a car following another by under a second. So that's another factor preventing someone pulling away.
Then the batteries were running out before the end of the straights, so a car running in front in free air was suffering from that, too.
On top of that, Las Vegas is a smooth track which is light on tyres. So degradation was almost non-existent. That kept tyre temperatures under control and allowed people to push hard throughout.
If the tyres had shown their usual behaviour of surface overheating leading to sliding, there would have been less action as drivers would have found it much harder to follow each other closely. As is usually the case in F1.
Drivers have been pushing for years for tyres to behave in this way, but so far Pirelli has been unable or unwilling to provide them. It only happens occasionally in specific circumstances.
The flip side of the argument is that so-called zero-deg races are sometimes boring as much as they are sometimes great, because drivers pushing to the limit can means less overtaking. Not in this case, though

With a move to engines with a smaller electrical component in 2030, are F1 cars becoming less relevant to modern road cars? The argument was always that F1 is the test bed for future road car technology. - Paul
The current F1 engines, with a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, were decided upon five or so years ago when the road-car market was slightly different to now.
The push for electrification is still there, and will continue. But consumer take-up of electric cars, especially in the performance market, has not been what manufacturers expected. Hence a slight shift in focus.
That said, it's not as if the current F1 engines are especially road relevant. With a few exceptions, road cars tend to be either full electric, plug-in hybrid, where the electrical element is much less than 50-50, or full internal combustion.
So there is an argument the new engines, with sustainable fuel and a hybrid element that is about 12-13% of total output normally or 25% when on overtake mode, are more relevant to road cars, not less, at least in their fundamental architecture.
The sustainable fuel is key here.
If this can get to a point where it is available to the mass market - and F1 is simplifying the demands on its make-up for the next ruleset in an attempt to help make the fuel more cost-effective for exactly that reason - it could be a game-changer for emissions in the road-car market.
That's because there will inevitably be a lot of legacy internal combustion vehicles on the road globally for many years, even after the new-car market becomes fully electric.
So if emissions from these can be reduced by 80%, as is the ballpark figure for the carbon-impact reduction of sustainable fuels versus fossil fuels, that's a major step.
Don't forget, too, the 2030 rules were the product of talks between the manufacturers and the FIA.
It was the manufacturers who pushed back against FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem's initial desire for a naturally aspirated engine with no hybrid element.
And they did that exactly because it made them more road relevant.

Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism — the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. To submit a question, fill out this anonymous form. Here’s this week’s question from a reader, condensed and edited for clarity:
You’ve lived in a red state all your life. Is it wrong to pick up and move to a blue state now?
Try asking yourself: Where can you fight the longest?
I’m considering moving my family from a red state to a blue state. I’ve lived in a red state my whole life, and as a lesbian with a wonderful trans wife, it is hard. Moving to a blue state could give my wife and I better nondiscrimination protections, better worker protections, and better access to health care.
However, I feel like moving would be abandoning the good fight in my home state. I am well aware of how the red state exodus and the red state brain drain are already affecting our community. It’s hard to weigh what may be best for my wife against what’s best for our fellow red state residents.
Dear Should I Stay or Should I Go,
I feel your question deep in my bones. Not long ago, I made the decision to move with my partner from the US to Canada, where I’m originally from. We’re also a queer couple. And we grappled with many of the same questions you’re wrestling with now.
Is it selfish to leave? If you leave, would you be putting your own family’s well-being above the well-being of your wider community? Does that mean you’re reneging on your values?
A few key philosophical ideas really helped me navigate these questions, so I’ll walk you through them. Whether you agree or disagree, they should clarify the terms in a way that makes it easier for you to decide one way or another.
Let’s start with your concern about how to weigh what’s best for your wife against what’s best for your wider community.
One strain of thought in modern philosophy — promoted by utilitarians like Peter Singer — says that we should aim to maximize the overall good, and that means doing good impartially rather than prioritizing certain people just because they happen to be our nearest and dearest. This perspective has become so influential in the past century that it’s probably shaping your thinking here, even if you’re not explicitly aware of it.
Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column?
Fill out this anonymous form! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here!
But I want you to know that other philosophers have pushed back. Bernard Williams, a staunch critic of utilitarianism, argued that it can actually be totally normal and morally appropriate to show partiality toward our loved ones.
In a famous passage, Williams said that if a man sees two people drowning, and one is his wife and the other is a stranger, and he pauses to consider whether rescuing his wife would maximize the overall good more than rescuing the stranger, he has had “one thought too many.”
Williams argued that moral agency does not sit in a contextless vacuum — it is always some specific person’s agency, and as specific people we have specific commitments. When you got together with your wife, you made a commitment to ensuring her well-being, over and above your general wish for all people everywhere to be well. Utilitarianism says you have to consider everyone’s well-being equally, with no special treatment for your own family members — but to Williams, that’s just an absurd demand. It alienates you from a core part of yourself, destroying your integrity as a moral agent.
According to this view, putting your wife’s safety first isn’t some moral lapse that should embarrass you. Honoring special obligations to our nearest and dearest is actually part of what makes a life ethical.
Besides, even though living an ethical life does sometimes involve being willing to sacrifice some of our own well-being, it’s important to recognize that everybody exists at a different vulnerability level. We shouldn’t expect someone who’s trans to take on risk to the same degree as someone who is not particularly marginalized or endangered.
Given the assault on trans rights in recent years, I’d be really skeptical of anyone who tries to argue that you and your wife have a moral obligation to stay put and “fight the good fight” if she’d be happier and safer elsewhere. Mind you, I also want to caution you to consider all the factors that go into making a happy life before you come to any decision about moving. If your wife has a robust and loving community of friends in your current red state, but knows nobody in the blue state you’re thinking of moving to, she may end up unhappier there on balance. (Plus, as the recent midterms showed, red states don’t necessarily stay red, and even blue states can pass anti-trans rights ballot measures.)
I also think a bigger reframe is in order here. You say, “I feel like moving would be abandoning the good fight in my home state.” But would it really? I’d argue that the key consideration is: Where can you keep fighting the longest? The hardest? The most effectively?
The work of contemporary philosopher Lisa Tessman is instructive here. In her book Burdened Virtues, she argues that situations of oppression can demand certain traits of people — like sustained anger at injustice, fierce loyalty to one’s group, constant vigilance and sensitivity to others’ suffering — that can damage the people who embody them even though they are real virtues. These traits can undermine the well-being of the bearers over time, keeping them from flourishing. What’s more, they can potentially even warp their bearers’ moral character — for example, when anger grows into an all-consuming state.
You said that you’ve lived in a red state your whole life and found it hard. So I think it’s worth asking yourself: Are the traits you’ve had to develop under those circumstances — however virtuous they may be — actually eroding your ability to keep showing up, both for yourself and for your wider community, in the way you’d like? If you feel that, say, constant vigilance is starting to take its toll, moving might give you a mental reset that allows you to be more — not less — active in enacting your values.
Plus, a quick look at the historical record can defuse the idea that leaving a place means “abandoning the good fight.” Consider what happened in the Great Migration, the exodus of Black Americans from the Jim Crow South. Did those migrants “abandon the good fight”? Absolutely not. Once in the North and West, they built up political power and institutions that ended up feeding into and supporting the civil rights movement.
The point is not that the two situations are exact parallels — they aren’t. The point is that when people leave a place, they can choose to use the affordances of their new home in a way that helps their old home. So, although worries about a red state exodus and red state brain drain are totally understandable, I don’t think they decide the question of whether a move would be net-negative or net-positive for your wider community.
What will decide that is what you choose to do with your newfound resources — including, plausibly, an increased sense of safety, security, and mental health — if you do relocate.
Life gets busy really fast, especially after a big move. (I should know — months after moving, I still haven’t gotten around to putting up any art on my walls!) So, if you leave your home state, my strong recommendation to you is this: Make a plan, in advance, for how you will keep fighting the good fight once you reach your new destination. Will you organize remotely? Can you connect right now with the relevant leaders at red state groups you want to support? Which organizations will you donate to, how much will you give, and when?
To boost accountability and prevent mission drift, be as concrete and specific as possible, discuss your plans aloud with your wife, and write them down.
And once you’ve done all this? My dear, let go of your guilt and live.
Bonus: What I’m reading
- I loved this Aeon essay about “love with nowhere to go.” It notes that, although we have established social scripts for grief that arises in the wake of a death, we don’t have practices for recognizing and working through grief that’s not death-related. That’s a problem because “when we are unable to honor other profound losses, we become strangers to ourselves.”
- Noema published an absolutely wonderful piece by Atoosa Kasirzadeh on how AI is changing math — and how it should! In fact, the AI revolution can have the great effect of reorienting the field to things that really matter according to humans. In my opinion, this is a model for how many other fields should adapt, so it’s really worth reading even if you’re not “a math person.”
- Most Westerners don’t have a good window into how people in China think about AI. So I was excited to see Persona publishing Jen Zhu on why the West’s habit of thinking about AI as an arms race misses the mark from a Chinese perspective. “When you watch a competitor sprint, you assume the finish line is the same as yours,” she writes. “But China is not running America’s race. It is continuing a 3,000-year-old project of ordering society as a single organism, harmonized rather than unleashed.”

US preparing to unveil plan for new tariffs on global trading partners
- Published
The US is preparing to announce plans for new tariffs on several countries as early as Wednesday, the BBC understands.
The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and Japan among at least 14 jurisdictions affected.
The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.
Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.
The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.
While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.
Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.
The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, which remain locked in a trade dispute.
Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.
In the run up to the Shenzhen summit, the US accused China of not fully living up to the terms of what it agreed in October 2025.
Washington said Beijing was falling short on its commitments, "particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals".
However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.
The Trump administration's tariff policy has been criticised for putting up prices for American consumers and damaging the global economy.

Five-try Ireland beat Australia in autumn finale

Ireland secured a fifth-place finish in the inaugural Nations Championship thanks to a 38-14 victory over Australia in London.
While last week's 20-17 win over South Africa was the undoubted highlight of their campaign, victory on Friday night ensured Ireland won all four games they played in November.
After Italy narrowly beat Fiji in the first game of the day, Ireland started slowly in a sparsely populated Allianz Stadium with the Wallabies taking a deserved lead through Jeremy Williams' try.
Andy Farrell's side took control of the contest through 24 unanswered points either side of half-time with Robbie Henshaw, Nick Timoney and Robert Baloucoune crossing for scores, while Sam Prendergast converted all three and added a penalty.
Kalani Thomas briefly stalled Ireland's momentum, but replacement back row James McNabney marked his second cap with a pair of tries in the final seven minutes to give the number two side in the world a comfortable, if not always convincing, victory.
After what was their final Test match of 2026, Ireland finish the year with a record of 10 wins and two losses from 12 internationals.
After making only two forced changes from the side who beat the Springboks six days ago - the banned Dan Sheehan and ill Mack Hansen the ones to miss out - head coach Farrell had called on his squad to back up their performance against the reigning world champions.
The early stages, however, had none of the tempo or accuracy from last week in the Aviva Stadium. Sloppy knock-ons, coupled with a pair of scrum penalties, saw Ireland struggle to gain a foothold in the contest.
For all Australia's territory and possession, the Wallabies took until the 23rd minute to press home their advantage on the scoreboard.
Previously undone by a couple of kicking errors, Les Kiss' side looked most dangerous when keeping the ball tight and it was lock Williams who burrowed over for the game's opening score.
Australia's deserved lead, however, lasted just three minutes. A midfield penalty allowed Prendergast to kick for the corner and give Ireland their first visit to the opposition 22.
After a sharp attack down the short side was thwarted before the line, Ireland came back inside and Stuart McCloskey spun out of a tackle well to put his centre partner Henshaw over for the try.
Three minutes before the break, again aided by an Australia penalty, Ireland doubled their lead.
Tadhg Beirne did well to gather a line-out with one hand and, with Ireland's centres joining the maul, number eight Timoney broke off the base for the simple score.
Prendergast converted both scores and added a penalty with the last kick of the half to put Ireland in a commanding 10-point lead at the break despite their shaky start.
If Ireland started slowly in the first half, they flew from the traps after the restart.
Jacob Stockdale had already almost executed a fine chip-and-chase reminiscent of his best days in the green jersey before his Ulster team-mate Baloucoune scored Ireland's third in the 43rd minute.
Baloucoune, 29, gathered Prendergast's measured cross-field kick over the head of James Ramm to score his fifth try of the autumn.
Australia threw everything at getting back into the game but a penalty for coming in at the side, which halted a 19-phase attack under the posts, summed up a frustrating evening with ball in hand for next year's World Cup hosts.
Scrum-half Thomas did score his first international try to reduce Ireland's lead to 24-14 with 25 minutes to go, but a comeback never felt likely from an Australia side who used Kurtley Beale from the bench for the utility back's first cap in five years.
While the game lost further shape in the final quarter with the arrival of a glut of replacements, Ulster's McNabney caught the eye in a short cameo.
Having had his debut against Fiji cut short by a head injury two weeks ago, the back row was the beneficiary of a fearsome Irish scrum shortly before his first try and then finished things off with another close-range score in the final minute.

New Delhi, Nov 27: The Central Government has authorised state governments and Union Territory administrations to exercise powers under Sections 7 and 8 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967, in relation to the Islamic Research Foundation (IRF), which has been declared an unlawful association.
According to a notification issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs on November 26, the direction has been issued under Section 42 of the UAPA.
The IRF was declared an unlawful association by the Central Government through a notification dated November 13, 2026, issued under Sections 3(1) and 3(3) of the Act.
The latest notification directs that the powers exercisable by the Centre under Sections 7 and 8 of the Act shall also be exercised by state governments and Union Territory administrations in relation to the association.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann stumbling while climbing the stairs to board an aeroplane in an intoxicated state. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann stumbling while boarding an aeroplane in an intoxicated state.
Fact: The video is manipulated and does not show Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann stumbling while boarding an aeroplane in an intoxicated state. It appears to have been created by manipulating original footage of former US President Joe Biden stumbling while boarding Air Force One in March 2021. The video also contains visual anomalies, and DeepFake-o-meter analysis indicated that it was AI-generated/manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a similar video uploaded on the Guardian News YouTube channel on 19 March 2021. The video shows former US President Joe Biden stumbling while climbing the stairs to board Air Force One.
The incident took place when Biden was boarding Air Force One to travel to Atlanta, Georgia, where he was scheduled to meet Asian American community leaders. In the original footage, Biden trips on the aircraft stairs, recovers, and continues unaided. He then turns around and salutes at the top of the staircase.
A comparison of the viral video with the original footage reveals striking similarities. The sequence of movements, including the stumbling and falling, appears remarkably similar. Several elements of the aircraft and its staircase also match.
These similarities indicate that the original footage of Joe Biden stumbling while boarding Air Force One has been edited to make it appear as though Bhagwant Mann is involved in the incident.
We then examined the viral video closely and noticed several visual anomalies. In the initial frames, one of the air hostesses appears to have a visibly distorted hand and foot. Additionally, the feet of the person resembling Bhagwant Mann appear to merge with the carpet on the aircraft staircase.
We further analysed the viral video using DeepFake-o-meter, which indicated that the video is AI-generated/manipulated.
To sum up, this viral video allegedly showing Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann stumbling while boarding an aeroplane in an intoxicated state is AI-manipulated.

'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
‘Medicare for all’ is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That's certainly true of the coming fight over "Medicare for All."
The midterm elections resulted in victories for several candidates who made universal, government-funded health coverage, or some variation thereof, a central pillar of their campaigns, including new Democratic U.S. senators-elect from Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and Texas. They — and many of their soon-to-be colleagues — say they will push the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to finally solve the healthcare affordability problem, which so many voters complained about on the campaign trail.
But while virtually every elected official supports making healthcare available and affordable for all Americans, the details of getting there cleaved the Democratic Party the last several times healthcare topped the national agenda. The Clinton health reform effort in 1993-94 fractured over differences within the Democratic majority, as those who wanted a dramatic overhaul like Medicare for All argued with those who saw incremental changes — such as a public option — as more politically feasible. The Affordable Care Act, which despite incendiary politics made incremental reforms, barely squeaked into law in 2010 after similar disputes..
And, so far, it appears history is about to write another stanza of this epic poem.
"It's cosplay"
So why is something so popular in the abstract so hard to accomplish?
For one thing, most Americans have no real idea what the phrase "Medicare for All" actually means. "It's cosplay," said Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan who has written about health policy for years. "When you say 'Medicare for All,' people think 'Healthcare — good. We should have more of it.'"
Mollyann Brodie — who oversees KFF's public opinion and survey research program as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the health information nonprofit — points out that in the long history of Medicare for All, support rises and falls dramatically depending on how the policy is described to voters.
"I can move it up to three-quarters [percent approval] if I talk about it being a guaranteed right to healthcare or eliminating insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket costs," she said of survey respondents' support, on a recent episode of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast. "I can plummet that support down to the 20s if I talk about it requiring people to pay more in taxes or threatening the current Medicare program."
Medicare faces headwinds
A second problem Democrats face is that the Medicare program itself, which covers adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities, is on less-than-firm financial footing. As of this year, the trust fund that underpins the hospital insurance part of the program is projected to become insolvent in 2033.
Costs are rising for Medicare beneficiaries as well. The program requires significant out-of-pocket spending on premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance. At the same time, traditional Medicare fails to cover much-needed services such as dental, vision, hearing, and, most expensively, long-term care. Beefing up Medicare benefits would be expensive and likely require large tax increases, according to most outside estimates.
The new Democratic majorities in Congress will have to decide whether their priority is to reverse the spending cuts made by the Trump administration — both to the Medicaid program for low-income and disabled people and to Affordable Care Act health plans — or to expand coverage and lower costs, turning back time to before President Donald Trump's second term began.
"Expectations are super high among voters right now, and they are demanding action on healthcare costs," Brodie said.
There are already indications that Democratic leaders are listening to the Medicare-for-All wing of their party. A day before being officially nominated as the next speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York voiced support for expanding government-funded coverage, including by lowering the age of Medicare eligibility and covering all children.
Of course, even if Democrats can pass legislation to restore what was cut by the GOP, there is every expectation that Trump — who has referred to Medicare for All in the past as "a socialist takeover of our healthcare system" — would veto those efforts. And the new majorities, while large, are not veto-proof.
Finally, Democrats must face a reality that both parties often forget: The larger your majority, the more ideologically diverse it will be. While the next Congress will include more progressives pursuing Medicare for All, it will also have plenty more moderate members from swing districts currently represented by Republicans. It's the reverse of the splits that plagued the GOP in the current Congress, with conservatives from safe red districts pitted against moderates from purplish ones.
A deeper dissatisfaction?
There is one big difference in the coming Democrat-on-Democrat debates compared with those in 1993 and 2009. One thing that has hamstrung Democrats trying to fix the health system is resistance from a plurality, if not a majority, of Americans who are relatively satisfied with their current health coverage. During the Clinton-era health reform debate, those people were represented in the famous "Harry and Louise" ads sponsored by the health insurance industry, featuring a couple at their kitchen table worrying that proposed changes would leave them worse off financially.
KFF's September tracking poll found instead that not only was the professed support for Medicare for All at its highest since the organization started regularly asking about it, but also a majority of respondents said they would support the policy even if it meant eliminating the private insurance industry. That's a first, and a significant change at that. It suggests the public is so fed up with the status quo that they'd rather risk something completely new than stick with what they have.
Of course, that sentiment could change fast when industry opposition revs up its counter-campaign. Still, the survey results suggest the next health reform debate could start with a public ready for something bigger. Now it's up to the people who could make it happen to get on the same page.
HealthBent, a regular feature of KFF Health News, offers insight into and analysis of policies and politics from KFF Health News chief Washington correspondent Julie Rovner, who has covered health care for more than 40 years.
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

Spain's former central bank head chosen as next European Central Bank president
Eurozone leaders have chosen a new president of the European Central Bank
BRUSSELS -- European leaders have chosen the former head of Spain’s central bank, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank as the key EU institution confronts inflation driven by the war in Iran and worries about high government debt and borrowing costs in Europe.
Leaders from the 21 European member countries that use the euro also filled two other top posts at the ECB, which decides borrowing costs for the 359 million people in the eurozone.
European Council President António Costa said on X that the body agreed on the three appointments at a summit in Brussels.
De Cos’ nomination still must pass review by the European Parliament and the ECB’s governing council, but those steps are formalities.
The appointment puts an experienced central banker with a reputation for backing lower interest rates and monetary stimulus in charge at a time when several European governments are struggling with heavy debt loads and rising borrowing costs. De Cos, 55, served on the ECB rate-setting council from 2018 to 2024 through his post as head of the Spanish central bank.
A review of his speeches by Commerzbank analysts “suggests that de Cos is among the monetary policy doves,” or policymakers who lean toward lower rates to support growth.
De Cos won out over another main contender for the post, former Netherlands central bank head Klaas Knot, who was regarded as a hawk, or someone who favors higher rates to ward off inflation.
In 2020, De Cos joined the council majority under Lagarde in backing 1.85 trillion euros ($2 trillion) in pandemic stimulus to keep rates low and support the economy during widespread closures and travel restrictions. De Cos praised the massive pandemic stimulus in a speech that year, saying it “has been clearly successful in curbing financial market deterioration in all euro area countries” as well as lowering borrowing costs for eurozone governments and corporations.
Commerzbank analyst Marco Wagner said that “especially against the backdrop of rising government debt in numerous countries ... many governments are likely to prefer a dovish ECB president.” France in particular is struggling with high debt and burdensome interest costs. However, with inflation at 4%, above the bank’s target of 2%, the bank could still raise rates at its Dec. 17 meeting presided over by Lagarde.
In some circumstances the ECB can intervene to lower borrowing costs for governments hit by market turmoil it views as unjustified, but analysts say the central bank is unlikely to bail out French politicians who can’t agree on how to reduce their deficit.
De Cos is currently general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, an international organization of central banks in Basel, Switzerland.
Lagarde, 70, said Oct. 30 that she would resign on Feb. 7, nine months before the end of her eight-year term. She has said she decided to resign early to be able to speak more freely about matters not related to monetary policy, but her resignation also enables EU leaders to choose a successor while pro-EU French President Emmanuel Macron is still in office and guards against the possibility that right-wing presidential candidate Marine Le Pen might win the election and influence the choice.
The eurozone leaders also filled two upcoming vacancies on the bank’s six-member executive board, which runs the bank’s day-to-day operations. They chose German economist Markus Brunnermeier, a professor at Princeton University, to replace Philip Lane, whose term ends in May. Lane held the influential post of chief economist, proposing rate moves for the full governing council to consider and decide upon.
They also chose Laurence Boone, head of corporate and investment banking in France for Spanish bank Santander, for a seat being vacated by Germany’s Isabel Schnabel, who is resigning in January.
The ECB sets interest benchmarks for the 21 countries that use the euro, influencing borrowing rates throughout the economy: everything from overnight loans between banks to credit cards, home mortgages and government bonds.
Lower rates can spur a slumping economy, while higher ones restrain inflation when it’s above the bank’s target of 2% annually.
The bank’s ability to act swiftly — in contrast to the often drawn-out negotiations among the 27 European Union national governments — has given it a leading role in combating Europe-wide crises such as the pandemic and the peak period of the eurozone’s debt crisis in 2010-12.
The president leads meetings of the bank’s rate-setting council at its headquarters in Frankfurt.
Lagarde is regarded as having steered a pragmatic middle course based on building consensus among the national bank heads who sit on the rate-setting council. She resisted being pigeonholed as a hawk or a dove, saying she was an “owl,” the bird associated with wisdom in Greek and Roman mythology.
She congratulated De Cos on Thursday, praising his “intellect, warmth and good humour” in a note posted online.
“If he is confirmed, I know these qualities will serve him well as ECB President,” she said.
___
McHugh reported from Frankfurt, Germany.
