An RTI response from Northern Railway has revealed that there is no official data to substantiate media reports claiming that over 5,000 passengers missed their trains at New Delhi railway station due to traffic restrictions imposed during an Opposition protest rally in the national Capital on October 8.
The reports emerged following the Opposition protest on October 8 against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Mallikarjun Kharge and other Opposition MPs arrived at Rajghat after attending a lunch at Moets Restaurant in Delhi’s Connaught Place. Police had erected barricades and diverted traffic as part of security arrangements. Moets Restaurant is located a short distance from Minto bridge.
Citing Railway sources, a number of mainstream media outlets claimed that around 5,000 passengers had missed their trains as several major routes in Central Delhi experienced traffic congestion, with Minto Bridge — a key thoroughfare leading to New Delhi Railway Station — being among the worst affected by the demonstration. However, the reports did not cite any supporting official documentation or statement.
Now, replying to an RTI application by Alt News, the Indian Railways has revealed that it does not have any system or mechanism to maintain station-wise records of passengers who miss their trains.
Who Made the Claim?
India Today journalist Piyush Mishra, citing railway sources, wrote on social media that the routes leading to the railway station were completely blocked due to a lunch meeting hosted by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge at Moets Restaurant in Connaught Place. As a result, more than 5,000 passengers were unable to board their trains.
Railways sources: More than 5,000 passengers were unable to board their trains after access roads to Railway Station were completely blocked due to a luncheon meeting hosted by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge at Moets, CP.
— Piyush Mishra (@Piyush_mi) October 8, 2026
India Today also published a report on this, in which a similar claim was made, citing a railway official.
Subsequently, news websites such as CNN-News18, India TV, and Moneycontrol also made the same claim in their reports, citing railway sources and railway officials. However, these reports provided no information on the methodology or process used to arrive at the figure of 5,000 passengers who missed their trains remains unexplained. These articles neither presented any documentation nor made any reference to an official statement.
Alt News Filed RTI Plea
We sought information from Northern Railway regarding this under the Right to Information Act, 2005. Alt News asked whether the Railways maintained a daily record of passengers who booked tickets for travel from a station but did not board their train (i.e., ‘no-show’ passengers). If so, we requested date-wise data for New Delhi Railway Station (NDLS) for the period between October 1 and October 8, 2026.
Northern Railway responded by stating that no such tool exists within their system. Therefore, the requested information cannot be provided.
The RTI response raises a crucial question: if the Railways has no system to maintain station-wise records of ‘no-show’ passengers, on what basis was the figure of over 5,000 passengers who allegedly missed their trains reported? In the absence of official records, the figure cannot be treated as an established statistic. It could, at best, be an estimate or an individual’s tally, neither of which would constitute verified data.
This, however, does not mean that passengers faced no inconvenience. Alt News is not suggesting that no one missed their trains due to traffic restrictions during the Congress party’s protest on October 8. The distinction is between acknowledging such disruptions and presenting an unverified figure of 5,000 as an established fact.
Besides, the claim was circulated at a time when another major Opposition protest was scheduled for October 10, amid an already charged political atmosphere. The narrative that a Congress procession had caused over 5,000 passengers to miss their trains effectively served the ruling party’s political interests. When media organisations publish such figures on the basis of unsubstantiated claims or statements attributed to unidentified sources, it raises serious questions about the rigour and neutrality of their reporting.

What you see first on a mobile recharge page has become a sticking point between the telecom regulator and India’s two largest operators, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel. Worried that greater visibility for cheaper packs could hurt revenues, the operators are pushing back against the regulator’s directive to display its mandated tariff plans upfront, three people aware of the matter said.
The lower-priced tariff plans mandated by the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai) include the smaller recharge options, the voice-only options, calendar month plans, among others.
In its 1 October directive, the regulator asked telcos to “provide a separate and clearly visible tab or section titled ‘Trai-Mandated Packs’ containing different types of Trai-mandated vouchers, which shall be visible as the first tab on the prepaid recharge section on the websites and mobile applications of the service providers and shall also be prominently displayed on their other exclusive points of sale."
The operators were asked to submit their compliance reports to the regulator within 30 days of the date of the direction.
Trai noted that these low-cost vouchers were neither displayed prominently, nor were they easily accessible and consumers were facing difficulty in locating and subscribing to these plans.
“The operators, however, told the regulator that they are already displaying the plans prominently, and users can easily locate those,” said the first person, an executive at a telecom operator, adding that this was a non-issue.
In response to Mint's queries, senior officials at Jio said the company is fully compliant with Trai regulations. “Customers can view Trai-approved packs on the first page alongside Jio’s own plans,” an official said.
However, the apps and websites of Jio and Airtel still do not show them as the first tab, while Vodafone Idea (Vi) has listed the Trai mandated packs in its first tab, according to information available on the websites and mobile apps of operators.
At meetings with the regulator, the telcos raised concerns that giving these vouchers prime placement could affect their revenues further as they are already facing revenue losses by implementing different voice and SMS-only plans of shorter duration, said a second person in the know.
“When any user visits the website or app, he or she will easily be able to locate the Trai mandated packs on the prepaid recharge window without a hassle. The placement on making it as a first tab or not should be left to operators, given they will decide that based on their commercial interests,” said a third person, an industry executive aware of the matter.
Queries emailed to Bharti Airtel and Trai on Wednesday did not elicit any response until press time.
Inclusive push
In September, in a bid to give more options to price-sensitive consumers, Trai had mandated voice and SMS-only plans for lower validity recharges of 30 days or less. This came after it had noticed operators were offering limited long-validity voice and SMS-only plans.
Low-income consumers, or those using feature phones, require shorter validity packs so that they can recharge as per their needs. The regulator had said consumers who do not need data are often compelled to buy bundled packs with data, limiting their choice and leading to avoidable expenditure.
Following the regulator’s directions, telcos introduced such plans in October-November. Jio offers voice only plans starting ₹147 with a validity of 22 days, while Airtel and Vodafone Idea’s plans start at ₹185 for 28 days. Jio’s 28-day validity plan is priced at ₹177.
Revenue impact
Analysts, however, expect some users of the telcos to shift to the lower-priced voice-only.
“This was designed to improve affordability at the entry level… We estimate downtrading to these can impact Bharti’s mobile revenue by less than 1% at max (assuming all 2G subscribers migrate) and VIL’s (Vodafone Idea) mobile revenue by 2.3%,” said analysts at Axis Capital, in a note dated 2 November. “Impact on VIL is higher, given the higher proportion of 2G subscribers. Impact on blended Arpu (average revenue per user) for both is likely to be less than 1%.”
Arpu is a key metric showing the average monthly revenue per subscriber and is widely used to gauge profitability and monetization. Airtel’s Arpu was ₹271, Jio’s was ₹218.8, while that of Vi was at ₹198 in the September quarter.
“As per the Trai mandate, we have made the changes of ₹185. At this stage, it’s too early to make any assumptions, but our sense in the initial days is minimal disruption. We will continue to watch this space to observe how consumer behaviour changes, and then we’ll look at this,” Abhijit Kishore, chief executive officer of Vodafone Idea, said during the July-September earnings call with analysts on 13 November.
“As we speak today, over the last at least two weeks, we have not seen any significant downgrade, and rather, we have three plans with different validity,” he said.
Kishore said the initial results were not concerning. “We rather see a little bit of an upside with people migrating to a higher plan of ₹199. So, we don’t see that as a major impact at this point in time.”

Though the photo is authentic, there's no broad consensus about when and where it was taken.
A somewhat grainy, black-and-white image (archived) has long circulated online, with some social media users claiming it shows a conversation between the physicists Albert Einstein and Marie Curie.
Einstein, a German Nobel Prize-winning physicist, is best known for his theory of relativity. Curie, a Polish scientist, is best known for her discoveries of the radioactive elements polonium and radium, and is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different science categories.
In fall 2026, one Instagram user who shared the alleged photograph of the two scientific greats wrote that it showed the pair "near a lake" in 1929.
The image also circulated in previous years on Facebook and Reddit (archived, archived).
The image is real, meaning it depicts a real event and wasn't created using artificial intelligence. It appears in the galleries of the trusted picture agency Getty Images, sourced from a physical copy at the Musée Curie in Paris. The Niels Bohr Library & Archives, part of the American Institute of Physics, also holds a copy of the photo.
However, though there is broad consensus that the photo of Einstein and Curie is authentic, there's less consensus about who took it, when and where.
In 2023, the Polish blogger, researcher and journalist Jakub Müller investigated the photograph and concluded that, based on records of Einstein's meetings with Curie, it was likely taken "somewhere between 23rd July and 29th July 1924." According to Natalie Pigeard-Micault, the deputy director of Musée Curie, Curie's daughter Irène took the photo.
Müller's investigation assumed the photo was taken in Geneva, Switzerland, where he said Einstein and Curie met in 1924, 1927 and 1930.
The investigation used historical weather reports to establish that the weather in Geneva in July 1924 was unseasonably cold, perhaps explaining the coat and hat Einstein and Curie wore, which suggested the photo was taken during colder weather.
However, Müller himself also presented evidence that brought into question both the date and location of the photo. According to Müller, the Albert Einstein Archives at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem that Einstein helped found holds a letter from his long-time secretary and assistant Helen Dukas.
Dukas reportedly wrote to Joan Warnow-Blewett from the American Institute of Physics (emphasis ours):
Dear Joan,
today I have to clear up for you a mistake in your catalogue. The picture C74, with Marie Curie, you dated 1925, The Leo Baeck Exhibtion dated it even 1918 in the Engadin (Switzerland). Both dates are utterly wrong. Professor Einstein met Mme Curie first 1911 in Brussels, in 1913 they met with their children for a walking-tour in the Engadin. But the picture C74 has been made quite later. My guess is it was done in November 1929 when Professor Einstein was in Paris for lectures at the Institute Poincare. They saw each other also at the Solvay-Congresses and at Geneva—both were members of ont of the League of Nations Committees. But the latter were always during t sommer-months and they would not be in their coats. Of one thing I am sure: it was neither 1925 or 1918: I have already written to the Baeck Institute. In January of 1926 Professor Einstein was also in Paris for the League of Notions Committee.S. "Einstein on Peace" pp77-78. But my bet is still on 1929—I remember the coat and hat.
Maybe it has not much importance, but I just wanted you to know.
Kind regards,
Helen Dukas
We've reached out to the Albert Einstein Archives at the Hebrew University in Jerusalem to confirm the authenticity of the screenshot of Dukas' letter that Müller shared.
Dukas reportedly sent the letter above in 1979. She died three years later.
At the time of this writing, there is no decisive evidence to prove or disprove either Müller's or Dukas' theories about when and where the photo of Einstein and Curie was taken. In November, the Niels Bohr Library & Archives said the photo was taken in July 1924, while Getty Images said it was taken in 1925.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated a number of other rumors involving Einstein.

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has issued a high-severity vulnerability note, warning about a SQL injection flaw in open-source governance platform DIGIT. “This vulnerability exists in the DIGIT Platform due to improper neutralisation of user supplied input while constructing SQL queries and execution in the affected user and access control service components. An unauthenticated remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending specially crafted input through the affected API endpoint to the targeted system,” noted the agency. The flaw could potentially allow remote cyberattackers to execute unauthorised SQL commands without prior access. Successful exploitation could allow them to manipulate application logic and modify, or delete, sensitive database information. However, the note does not indicate whether any attackers have exploited the vulnerability. The eGov Foundation, which operates the platform, has addressed the issue in DIGIT Core v2.9.3. The foundation has directed the platforms, running the affected deployments, to update immediately to the latest version to resolve the vulnerability, CERT-In added. DIGIT (Digital Infrastructure for Governance, Inclusion & Transformation) is an open-source platform created by eGov Foundation. Currently led by CEO Viraj Tyagi, a cofounder of fintech startup Finnable, the foundation was established in 2003 by Nandan Nilekani and Srikanth Nadhamuni to leverage technology for powering digital public and municipal services The platform provides building blocks and shared data registries for building sector-specific digital public infrastructure (DPI). It enables local governments, civic bodies, ecosystem partners, and NGOs to rapidly deploy large-scale public service applications for use cases like water billing, digital health registries, business licensing systems, vaccination portals, and others. Hence, in case the vulnerability was used to breach applications built on DIGIT’s platform, it could result in leaks of sensitive data and disruption of civic services. Rapid advances in frontier AI models have made it significantly easier for hackers and cyberattackers to exploit weaknesses in software. Recent disruptions involving the likes of Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) have only shone a further spotlight on the risks posed by vulnerabilities in interconnected tech systems.

The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
- Published
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.
"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
The numbers bear this out.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.
The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.
Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.
Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.
And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
There are other pressures.
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.
Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.
"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.
Agriculture is a relatively low-productivity sector, and the government has long sought to protect farmers by setting minimum support prices (MSPs) for certain crops - a price floor at which it promises to buy produce, helping farmers guard against a market crash.
At the same time, food prices are politically sensitive. Sharp increases in the price of staples such as onions and tomatoes can quickly anger consumers, prompting governments to step in with measures such as restricting exports, limiting how much traders can stockpile, or otherwise trying to bring prices down.
The broader story of India's changing food consumption makes the current inflation more interesting.
Households are eating differently from a decade ago. An analysis, external of the 2011-12 and 2023-24 consumption surveys shows that the share of cereals in food spending has fallen sharply, particularly among the poorest households, reflecting the impact of subsidised food programmes.
Meanwhile, consumption of nutrient-rich foods such as dairy, fruit and meat has increased across income groups, with the biggest gains among the poorest, the study revealed.
India's food basket is becoming more diverse. But diversity is meaningful only if ordinary Indians can afford it. Ultimately, food inflation is about what makes it to the plate - and what has to be left out.

Nikhil Kamath-backed beauty and personal care (BPC) startup indē wild slipped back into the red in the financial year ended March 31, 2026 (FY26), posting a net loss of ₹95 Lakh against a net profit of ₹38.5 Lakh in FY25. This is despite the startup’s operating revenue zooming 139% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹59.8 Cr as against ₹25 Cr reported in FY25. indē wild’s widening expenses, which zoomed over 2.5X YoY, weighed heavily on its margins as the startup expanded its operations during the fiscal year. Including other income of ₹2.3 Cr (up 10X YoY), total income during the year stood at ₹62.1 Cr. Founded in 2021 by influencer Diipa Büller-Khosla and her husband, Oleg Büller-Khosla, the BPC brand retails haircare, skincare and lipcare products in the affordable-premium range. It has positioned itself as combining traditional Ayurvedic ingredients and rituals with modern skincare and haircare science. Its products are sold through its own online channels and retail partners, including Nykaa, Tira and Sephora. It has now expanded to international markets in the US and UK through its partnership with Sephora, which has placed the brand’s products across 197 stores in both countries. Earlier this week, the startup raised an undisclosed amount from Zeordha founder Nikhil Kamath’s WTFund. Kamath will also be making his modeling debut through the brand, endorsing its haircare line, Moonlight Growth. Besides Kamath, the startup also counts Unilever Ventures and SoGal Ventures as its investors. It has raised $8 Mn till date. Much of indē wild’s social media virality is driven largely through an influencer-marketing engine online and online community building. It competes in a highly competitive BPC market, with competitors including Kama Ayurveda, Forest Essentials and RAS Luxury Oils, along with more affordable clean beauty brands like Juicy Chemistry, Nat Habit, and Biotique. Expenses Weigh Down Bottom Line The startup slipped back into a net loss in FY26 as its expenses jumped over 156% YoY in FY26 to ₹63 Cr compared to ₹24.6 Cr earlier. Purchase of Stock-In-Trade: As indē wild’s revenue base grew, its inventory expenditure jumped 167% YoY to ₹22 Cr from ₹8.4 Cr in the year-ago period. At the close of FY26, it had inventory worth ₹10.5 Cr on its books. Employee Benefit Expenses: indē wild spent around ₹9 Cr on payroll during the fiscal year under review, a 172.7% increase from ₹3.3 Cr in year-ago period. Marketing & Advertising: Expenses under this head more than tripled YoY to ₹19.7 Cr from ₹6 Cr spent in FY25.

New Delhi, Nov 27: Chief of Defence Staff Gen N S Raja Subramani on Friday said the distinction between war and peace is "blurring" today and there is a "continuous state of contestation", cautioning that warfare in cyber, electronic and cognitive domains is already occurring.
Delivering an address here on the 'Future of warfare and India's preparedness to conduct multi-domain operations', he also said, without elaborating, "We are being subjected to cognitive warfare by our adversaries in an insidious way" to weaken the will and morale of the nation, and emphasised bolstering capabilities in all domains.
The general officer, during an interactive session after delivering his talk at a seminar, also asserted that "we are well-geared, along our northern frontier".
Asked how he saw China successfully launching on Wednesday its Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship carrying three astronauts, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the CDS said Pakistan's space capability is "improving" with China's help, and positional navigation and other domain-related capabilities available with the Chinese will be available to the Pakistanis, so that will have to be "factored into our calculus".
He also spoke on the significance of air power, and said that for bolstering the Navy's prowess, there is a need for more unmanned surface vessels, unmanned underwater vessels and enablers to increase their range.
"We want to be joint in design, multi-domain in orientation, have a tech-enabled capability, be Aatmanirbhar in thought and action, and finally a capable human-centric leadership," the CDS said.
Gen Anil Chauhan (retd), who was the CDS during Operation Sindoor last year, moderated the session hosted by think-tank Vivekananda International Foundation in Delhi.
The CDS, in his address, outlined 10 major trends which, he said, are defining the future of warfare, underlining that the first is the expanding nature of the battlefield.
"Secondly, the distinction between war and peace is increasingly (getting) blurred. We are in a state of continuous contestation.
"Cyber, space, electronic warfare and cognitive warfare are already occurring, and that means they will precede a conflict, they will occur during the conflict, and they will outlast the conflict. So, we cannot say that we are either in a state of peace or war; we are in a continuous state of contestation," he said.
The CDS said that in coordination with the three services, efforts are underway to "modernise our electronic warfare architecture".
Elaborating his point on the idea of "continuous contestation" and the blurring of the distinction between peace and war, he said, "Even today, we are being subjected to cognitive warfare by our adversaries in an insidious manner, to sow (seeds of) division in society, create internal rifts, weaken the will and morale of the nation."
"Therefore, it is important that we understand cognitive warfare and information warfare, and a commander today will have to spend as much time on operations as he has to devote time to information warfare," the CDS added.
It is "not a supporting function", it is a "primary function of the commander". It is one of the important building blocks as far as multi-domain operations are concerned, he said.
He cited multiple conflicts in the last few years, from the Azerbaijan-Armenia conflict to the Ukraine conflict and the US-Israel-Iran conflict.
"Economically, wars in one part of the world can affect everybody... When we look at the Iran-Israel war, we see that closure of Strait of Hormuz in terms of critical minerals, fertilisers, energy is affecting each and everybody in the world, and led to loss of (US President Donald) Trump in the (US) mid-term elections. So, unintended effects," he said.
"The other unintended effect as far as we are concerned is the Makkah alliance," the CDS said.
Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Makkah on August 7. The pact establishes a framework for collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be regarded as an attack against all three.
The CDS also cited Operation Sindoor, terming its second phase an excellent example of joint, integrated, multi-domain operations, and asserted that India not only had control over the escalation matrix and escalation dominance, but it also resulted in a "decisive victory" for India.
Gen Raja Subramani underlined the evolving nature of technology and the warfare, however, cautioning that technological superiority is "only transitory" and this will need constant improvement to stay prepared for future wars.
He emphasised that a whole-of-nation approach is needed to fight and sustain a prolonged war.
The general officer said multiple-domain operations is not about combining all the capabilities, rather it implies integrating different capabilities to "pose multiple dilemma to an adversary".
He said integration of military-space architecture and the ability to communicate effectively are key to carrying out such operations and cyber defence is an integral component of it, he added.
The CDS further said an integrated command and control system is a prerequisite for conducting such operations.
On military preparedness, at a time when multiple conflicts are underway, he said, "We need not look at a prescribed template. We need to have our own template."

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

- The claim that staff at Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas served a Thanksgiving dinner in front of detained parents and children before packing the food away, claiming it was only for employees, is still under investigation.
- The claim came from an NBC report from February that featured an account from a Russian couple held at Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas with their three children.

Around Thanksgiving, a claim (archived) circulated online that staff at Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas served a Thanksgiving dinner in front of detained parents and children before packing the food away, claiming it was only for employees.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement detains non-U.S. citizens at immigration processing centers like Dilley while resolving their immigration cases to "secure their presence for immigration proceedings or removal from the U.S." The Texas Tribune reported in August that Dilley Immigration Processing Center was the only detention center for families in the U.S.
Aaron Parnas, who shares news headlines on social media, posted a video about the claim on TikTok with the caption, "NEWS: CHILDREN IN DETENTION CENTER WERE SHOWN THANKSGIVING MEAL, FORCED TO WATCH AS GUARDS PACKED IT AWAY."
Claims also circulated on Facebook and X (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the claim.
The claim came from an NBC report from February that featured an account from a Russian couple held at Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas with their three children. According to the children's mother, named only as Oksana, families held at the center gathered for what they thought was "a Thanksgiving celebration" in November 2025 to find "turkey, sandwiches, pastries and pies" set out on tables.
However, Oksana said that when a parent asked when the celebration would start, staff told the people gathered that the food was only for staff and packed it away.
At the time of this writing, Snopes had no primary evidence, such as video surveillance from inside the processing center, to prove Oksana's claim to NBC. However, we also had no primary evidence that the incident Oksana described did not take place. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
In an emailed statement to Snopes, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote:
These claims are absolutely FALSE. Detained illegal aliens receive holiday meals in the dining halls with menus tailored to the occasion. Any staff potlucks occur in areas inaccessible to residents.
A spokesperson for CoreCivic, which manages Dilley Immigration Processing Center as part of a contract with ICE, called the claim "patently false." The spokesperson also said that staff offered people detained at Dilley holiday meals and activities, and that any separate staff meal would have happened in a separate area inaccessible to detainees.
We also contacted Elora Mukherjee, the director of the Immigrants' Rights Clinic at Columbia Law School who NBC reported represented Oksana and her partner Nikita in seeking release from Dilley, to ask whether she had heard other accounts from families held at Dilley that corroborated Oksana's account and await a reply.
Mukherjee repeated (time code 48:27) what appeared to be Oksana's account of Thanksgiving 2025 at the center during a forum hosted by the Senate Judiciary Committee's Democrats in March, the month after NBC's report. We await replies to our queries.
Declarations from Dilley paint damaging picture of child detainment
Lawyers who sought to make the U.S. government adhere to the Flores Settlement, which sets minimum standards for the detainment of children, submitted dozens of sworn declarations from detained parents and children at Dilley to a federal judge starting in June 2025, three months after the Tribune reported the Trump administration would reopen the center.
The Flores Settlement said children must be not be held for long periods of time in immigration prisons or detention facilities and should generally be released as quickly as possible. Courts have previously interpreted the legal limit for detention of a child under the Flores Settlement to be 20 days.
Oksana and Nikita's three children had reportedly been detained at Dilley for more than 120 days in February. Using data the government filed as part of its fight to end the Flores Settlement, the Tribune said in an August report that in February, when NBC reported on Oksana and Nikita's family's detention at Dilley, the average length of a child's stay at the center was 47.5 days.
We reviewed 21 declarations submitted on Dec. 8, 2025, shortly after the alleged Thanksgiving dinner at Dilley. However, the declarations were all dated before Thanksgiving 2025, which was on Nov. 27. We reviewed four declarations (N.V.S.M, C.R.G, N.G. and D.C.R.R.) given in November but before Thanksgiving in case the alleged employee-only dinner happened before actual Thanksgiving. None of the declarations we reviewed corroborated Oksana's account.
Lawyers filed more declarations in March 2026. We reviewed 33 declarations given between October 2025 and March. None mentioned Thanksgiving.
The declarations we reviewed attested to the damaging physical and psychological effects of children's detention at Dilley. Speaking to NBC, Oksana and Nikita complained of a lack of activities and education for their children and difficulties accessing basic needs like medicine or fresh food. The Texas Tribune also cited declarations that echoed these concerns.
In February, after NBC published its report, the DHS refuted what Deputy Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis called "false claims about the ICE Dilley facility including that children are denied medical care and don't have educational resources."
It was unclear at the time of this writing whether Oksana, Nikita and their children remained in Dilley or another immigration processing center or whether U.S. authorities had deported or released them.
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated claims related to ICE and immigration enforcement.

Can luxury save Macy's?
Sign up for alerts on breaking news and exclusive reporting from NPR
Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.
"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."
As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade, the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.
The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.
How Macy's got squeezed in the middle
Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.
The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.
And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.
"They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."
When the pandemic hit, store closures had Macy's forecasting an estimated $1.1 billion in losses. Its stock value dropped so low that the company was kicked off the big-league index, the S&P 500.
The way out is up
At one point, Macy's seemed to throw every other thing on discount just to get people buying something.
But it didn't work.
Stores looked disheveled and chaotic. Shoppers regularly noted a lack of workers to help on the floor. Over 2023, sales at Macy's dropped almost 7%.
Soaring inflation all but forced Macy's hand.
As the so-called K-shaped economy split the nation in recent years, folks with less money turned to Walmart or Target, which stepped up their game. Wealthier people continued to be the ones doing most of the spending, but also not at Macy's — leaning toward higher-end shops.
"For their size and scale the choice is almost made for them," says Prendergast, who's spent 20 years in the fashion business, including selling to Macy's at Tommy Hilfiger.
"If you're Macy's you say, 'We're still getting squeezed in the middle, our customer base in the U.S. is getting squeezed in the middle. Where can we go?' And really the only answer is to go up."
The new luxury vision
Luxury is now the big Macy's bet.
The retailer already owns the upscale Bloomingdale's, with its designer brands. Macy's also owns the luxury beauty chain Bluemercury.
In 2024, the head of Bloomingdale's took over the entire Macy's company and announced a turnaround plan, "A Bold New Chapter."
It included closing 150 stores and upgrading more than 300 others. Changes were proposed for the website and the staffing. Stores began to tackle clutter and add nicer items.
"We needed to remove the duplication, the redundancy," says Julie Walsh, senior vice president at Macy's whose team buys women's accessories and beauty products, including shoes, jewelry and makeup.
"When you come onto our floor now, it's a little bit lighter," she says. "So that the product that is on the floor shows up in a meaningful way."
Putting the higher prices to the test
In March, Macy's finally reported a year of growing sales.
The higher-end Bloomingdale's stores continued to drive much of the company's growth, but changes seemed to start paying off at Macy's, too.
Fancier options — like real leather instead of faux, brands like Ralph Lauren and Coach — have been raising the retailer's average selling price. It increased 9% in the latest quarter, executives said in September. They described shoppers' visits as "very steady and very significant."
Barb Anderson-Kerlin, a loyal Macy's shopper checking out the retailer's flagship in New York, says she's noticed a difference at the chain, after years of finding stores that seemed to ramble in all directions.
"The department store was like bedding, towels, pots and pans, perfume," she says. "Because I'd go in and just be overwhelmed. But now it feels like it's easier to see where the brands are."
How far can luxury sales take Macy's?
Still, most shoppers at the flagship store appeared dubious of the image of Macy's as a high-end chain.
"If they want to be luxury," says Chelsea Bates, who is visiting from Tennessee, "I would say serve champagne." She laughs, but notes that other upscale rivals do offer lounges and refreshments, like coffee.
Macy's insists it's not turning away from the middle class — just striving for more. Not picking a whole new lane, but widening the road in a gamble for this bifurcated economy.
"Macy's strength is being able to service our customer across all different categories in all different price points, and we're not changing that," says Walsh.
"What we are doing is making sure that we've got the elevated product," she says. "So it's not to replace it, it's an additive."
One hurdle is just how long Macy's had spent building its middle-price reputation, says Prendergast. Breaking out of the mold is a tough climb.
But, he says, if anyone can do it, maybe it is Macy's — having outlived many rivals over its 168 years.
"They're really the last man standing in that range for a reason," says Prendergast. "Everybody likes to count Macy's down and out, and they continue to prove everybody wrong."

Digital advertising undertaken by Indian beauty and personal care (BPC) brands has come under scrutiny for increased instances of norm violations. Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) latest report, a self-regulatory organisation for advertising, flagged 456 instances of BPC brands flouting norms between the April-September 2026 period. In its half yearly report, the industry body highlighted that the personal care category recorded the highest number of influencer violations, as well as the highest number of uncontested cases. Misleading representations and exaggerated as an overarching theme for ad violations undertaken by these D2C brands. Key concerns that were spotlighted by ASCI were: Unsubstantiated skin and hair transformation claims relating to acne pigmentation, hairfall and dandruff Exaggerated before-and-after visuals and dramatic skin-tone transformation claims. Misleading representations and the reinforcement of negative beauty stereotypes. Laboratory findings contradicted sustainability assertions and product claims. "75% of ads were not contested and promptly modified or withdrawn following ASCI’s intimation. 58% of these involved influencer disclosure violations," ASCI said. For context, ASCI evaluates advertisements against the four pillars of "ASCI Code". These codes evaluate brand communication on factors around dishonesty, offensive or harmful content. The body received 3,951 complaints during the period of which 2,308 were found to violate ASCI code. Beyond personal care, ASCI said that promotion of offshore betting platforms, something that has remained fairly common across social media platforms, has been the most violative among its categories. A high volume of ads for such banned platforms prompted ASCI to report to I4C and the Ministry of Information & Broadcasting (MIB) to enable swift takedown. The body flagged 590 gambling ads to the government in the six month period, 98% of the total 633 ads flagged by the body. Brand Miscommunication In Focus The ASCI report comes at a time when regulatory heat around brand communication has increased sharply across India. Over the past six months, regulators have stepped up their scrutiny of misleading product claims, influencer promotions, comparative advertising and deceptive digital practices. Food and health-related claims have emerged as another area of concern. In June, the CCPA fined beverage brand Storia Foods ₹1 Lakh over the use of misleading ‘100%’ claims. Meanwhile, the FSSAI flagged 15 food brands, including Storia, Two Brothers Organic Farms, PLAN B, The Health Factory and Troovy, over potentially misleading branding and product claims. The scrutiny has also extended to comparative advertising, where brands increasingly use rivals' products to position their own offerings. In August, HUL moved the Delhi HC against D2C home care brand Beco over a campaign which alleged that ingredients in HUL's Vim and Surf Excel products could cause skin irritation and allergic reactions. Subsequently, in September, the Delhi HC restrained Beco from continuing the campaign. The concerns have also extended to the way companies design their digital interfaces to influence purchasing decisions. In June, the CCPA fined edtech major PhysicsWallah ₹5 Lakh for deploying dark patterns, including a pre-selected ₹10 donation option that generated around ₹2.47 Cr from more than 21.36 Lakh users. The regulator also flagged practices that required users to share personal information to access courses advertised as free. Health and wellness advertising has faced similar scrutiny. In October, ASCI's review of nutraceutical advertisements found that all 60 advertisements examined violated its code. The claims included promises of rapid weight loss, anti-ageing benefits and improvements in respiratory health, often without adequate clinical evidence or independent testing to establish the efficacy of the finished products.

Doctors struggle to save babies after parents refuse vitamin K
Every time Torrie LeBlanc failed to persuade a parent to give their baby a vitamin K injection, she thought about the blood-soaked diaper.
It belonged to a newborn delivered last year, in the bustling labor and delivery unit where LeBlanc worked as a physician at the Corewell Health hospital system in Grand Rapids, Mich.
In the early hours the day after the baby girl was born, she suddenly started bleeding "from everywhere," LeBlanc recalled. Her eyes, nose, and rectum all suddenly oozed blood.
The girl's parents cried out for help from their hospital room. Nurses and doctors on the overnight shift rushed her to the neonatal intensive care unit, where they pumped fresh frozen plasma and other blood products into her small body, trying to replace what she was rapidly losing.
Her parents had declined a vitamin K injection for their baby, which is given to most newborns within six hours of birth to prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. With their baby on the verge of bleeding to death roughly 36 hours after birth, the parents agreed to let doctors administer vitamin K.
It worked. The baby survived, largely because she received treatment almost instantly, according to LeBlanc and an attending physician who helped care for the baby. Had the baby been at home when she started bleeding, they believe she would have died.
What LeBlanc witnessed has become much more common in recent years as more parents, influenced by the anti-vaccine movement and broader mistrust of the medical system, refuse to allow doctors to give their babies vitamin K shots at birth.
Nationally, the rate of newborns who do not receive intramuscular vitamin K has more than doubled, rising from 3.1% of newborns in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, according to research published in JAMA in November.
The spike moved LeBlanc, a pediatrician, and her colleagues to launch an initiative to reduce the rising number of vitamin K refusals at this hospital. On average, at least one family here refuses the injection for their newborn every day.
Two years in, the team won a modest victory: Vitamin K refusal rates are now flat at the hospital, even as refusals of other standard newborn medications, including the hepatitis B vaccine, continue to climb.
Still, doctors at the hospital say parents now regularly argue against everything from the once-routine vitamin shot to antibiotics for a critically ill infant.
"I honestly thought it would be easier," LeBlanc said, sitting by a sunlit window near the end of a 10-hour shift. "The more people I talk to, the more I learn about the misinformation that's online and the different reasons that people are refusing."
She paused. "It's a work in progress."
When doctors struggle to talk with parents
LeBlanc began a two-year fellowship at the children's hospital in 2024, certain she could make an impact on vitamin K refusals. After all, it's a vitamin, not a vaccine. How hard could it be to persuade parents to choose a vitamin that could save their baby's life?
Babies are born with very low levels of vitamin K, which is why the injection has been a routine part of newborn care since the 1960s. The shot is safe, with virtually no severe side effects, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. And it effectively prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare condition that can involve bleeding in the brain.
Among babies who receive the shot at birth, fewer than 1 in 100,000 develop the most serious form of bleeding. But babies who don't receive it are 81 times more likely to develop the condition, according to the CDC. Of those who do, 1 in 5 die.
The shot was so effective that many doctors encountered a baby with VKDB perhaps only once in a career.
But doctors in multiple hospitals across the U.S. told KFF Health News that they now regularly see babies develop life-threatening bleeding from vitamin K deficiency. Some of those babies have died or been left with lifelong brain injuries.
Solomon Behar, a pediatric emergency medicine doctor in Los Angeles, recently treated an infant with VKDB who died.
"It just made me sad more than anything else," he said. "This was something that literally was a historical footnote up until the recent modern time, when people have decided that Mother Nature is someone that wants to work with them, rather than is trying to kill us."
Vitamin K refusals have increased dramatically in recent years alongside vaccine hesitancy.
Prominent conservative influencers suggest the vitamin K shot is tied to childhood cancer. Online parenting forums are filled with moms worried that the injection could harm their newborns, and wellness influencers on podcasts and TikTok — including some medical professionals — allege that babies have been injured by the shot or say it's unnecessary or unnatural.
When Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was asked at a congressional hearing in April to assure parents that the vitamin K injection was safe, Kennedy demurred. "I've never said anything about vitamin K," he said.
LeBlanc first saw a case of VKDB during her residency training, when a baby came into the emergency room with a nosebleed. Doctors caught it early, and the baby made a full recovery.
But she also watched as other doctors struggled with how to talk to parents who turned down the shot. "A lot of people just felt uncomfortable talking to families about it, or they didn't know what to say," she said.
Part of that was easy to fix: LeBlanc created a basic fact sheet for parents answering some of the most common questions about the vitamin K injection and explaining the risks of not getting it.
Labor and delivery nurses now use a script to offer routine newborn medications: "The standard of care for all babies born here includes vitamin K, hepatitis B vaccine, and erythromycin eye ointment," it says. "Do we have your permission to give these medications to your baby following delivery?"
The harder part is teaching doctors how to talk to parents about the fears that drive refusals.
"We can't walk into rooms where families don't know us from the doorknob and say, 'You have to do this,'" said Jaspreet Loyal, a pediatrician at Yale New Haven Hospital in Connecticut and a longtime leader in research on vitamin K refusal.
"We have to practice humility, to sit there and listen, and then come back the next day and sort of use that nudge approach."
LeBlanc helped train staffers in motivational interviewing, a technique developed for treating substance use disorders that is gaining popularity for addressing vaccine hesitancy.
It requires doctors to treat parents with a baseline of "unconditional positive regard or acceptance," one study urged. Parents' autonomy is paramount, even if their decisions conflict with medical recommendations. The minute parents feel judged, LeBlanc said, they stop listening.
The most important thing to convey, Loyal said, is "we are on the same team. You're looking out for your child. I'm looking out for your child. We may not fully agree what that looks like, but let's try."
LeBlanc gets only about 50% of parents who initially refuse the shot to change their minds. Other doctors at the hospital said their success rates are closer to 20% to 40%.
A refusal is now included in the patient's electronic medical record, so the family's regular pediatrician can bring it up at the first well-child visit. It also means that if the baby comes into the ER because of bleeding, the staff will immediately be able to see they haven't received the vitamin K shot.
And LeBlanc and Loyal, the Yale expert, argue that the rising rate of refusal means doctors need to be more open to parents who decline the vitamin K injection but want to give their baby liquid drops or crushed supplement tablets instead.
That's controversial: Taking vitamin K orally isn't as effective as the shot and requires multiple doses over several weeks or months, according to researchers. There's also no federally approved oral vitamin K supplement.
"The injection is the gold standard," LeBlanc said. "However, I would rather have them have some protection with the oral than no protection at all."
Finding compromise, with a baby's life on the line
In May, a 2-week-old baby came into Helen DeVos Children's Hospital with symptoms of meningitis, a potentially deadly infection of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
But the baby's parents had declined the vitamin K injection after the baby's birth, which meant the lumbar puncture — in which doctors insert a needle into the baby's lower back to get a sample of spinal fluid — needed to confirm meningitis was risky: What if the baby didn't stop bleeding after the puncture?
Still, as the child's condition worsened, doctors felt it was worth the risk. But then, the parents refused the lumbar puncture as well. LeBlanc recalled the mother telling her that, in her "medical opinion," she did not believe her child had meningitis.
After hours of debate, doctors offered the parents a compromise: They would treat the baby for meningitis, even without a confirmed diagnosis. That meant admitting the baby for two weeks to receive intravenous antibiotics.
Afterward, the mother wrote the medical team a thank-you note, which now hangs on a staff room wall covered with beaming photos of grateful families.
"Almost every single one of you has shown so much grace to us," the mom wrote. "Regardless of differing medical opinions, I'm so grateful for you."
On good days, LeBlanc can see that note as a win, a sign that staff are getting better at working with mistrustful families. On bad days, it feels like a symbol of a losing battle. Both families who watched their baby suffer after not receiving the vitamin K injection — the one whose child nearly died from VKDB, and the one with suspected bacterial meningitis — still declined routine vaccinations when they left the hospital.
At Yale, Loyal has learned not to take any of it personally. "At first, I used to feel like a failure every time: No, I was unable to convince somebody!" she said. Now she takes refusals in stride. "I cannot continue to spend time with someone who I cannot change their mind."
But LeBlanc worries each time she can't persuade a family to get their newborn the vitamin K injection. What if the next time she sees that baby is in the ICU? She would blame herself, she said, for not getting through to the parents.
"I couldn't convince them."
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.
