Several other users also shared the viral clip with similar claims. Below is a gallery of some of these posts:
Fact Check
To determine the authenticity of the viral video and its associated claim, we ran reverse image searches on some of the keyframes. We came across a video posted on Youtube on November 14 by a channel called ‘The Channel’ which shows a set of Chilean stand-up comedian Luis Slimming. At the 0:07 mark, the same attacker who appears in the viral clip, gets up on-stage and attacks Slimming. The rest of the video shows an altercation between the attacker and Slimming, and seemingly other members of his team or audience.
We found similarities in the attacker’s face, movement, clothes and pattern of action in both the viral clip and the original video. Below is a gallery comparing keyframes from the two:
We found an article by The Free Press Journal — Chilean Stand-Up Comedian Luis Slimming Attacked During Live Show; Violent Scuffle Caught On Camera — reporting that stand-up comedian Luis Slimming was attacked by a man during his live comedy show on November 12, at Hotel Antay in Arica city of Chile. This confirmed that the viral video is a digitally altered version of the attack on Slimming, replacing him with a woman.
A closer look at the viral video revealed several inconsistencies in the woman’s response to the attack, indicating that it might be generated using AI. We ran the viral clip through AI-detection tool Hive Moderation, which revealed that it is 64% likely that the video is generated using AI.
To conclude, the viral video of a woman being attacked has been generated using AI by altering the video of stand-up comedian Luis Slimming, who was assaulted while performing on stage on November 12 in Chile. Thus, the claim that the woman was attacked by a Muslim man in the United State for not wearing a burqa is false and misleading.

NVIDIA reportedly halts AI chip shipments to Southeast Asia
Companies like Dell have stopped shipping server hardware to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.
NVIDIA has reportedly put a stop to shipments of AI server hardware to four Southeast Asian countries. According to The Financial Times, a handful of the company's manufacturing partners, including Dell and Supermicro, told clients in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that the chipmaker is not allowing their server orders to be sent to them. The Financial Times reports it's unclear if the halt is temporary. The news comes just days after NVIDIA reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive.
In recent years, Chinese AI labs have turned to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia to gain access to NVIDIA's most powerful chips. They used a gap in US export controls by renting access through cloud compute providers that bought servers with NVIDIA GPUs inside. In recent weeks, the US Commerce Department moved to close that loophole. First by introducing new rules aimed at stopping that exact practice, and second by targeting Megaspeed, the company at the center of the NVIDIA scandal.
On Wednesday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its "Entity List." Companies, including NVIDIA, now need a US license to ship goods covered by US export rules to Megaspeed. Huang had resigned from his position on November 12 after reports surfaced that he had engaged in multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive that some US officials suspect was a Chinese intelligence asset. Megaspeed had leased access to NVIDIA chips to Chinese companies. The Justice Department is also investigating whether Megaspeed broke US export rules.
Under the new US rule, data centers that were already providing large amounts of computing power to companies based in China or other location covered by the rule have 90 days from November 19 to get a license if they want to keep doing so. "There's this new rule but no guidance on execution," one cloud executive told the outlet. "No one knows how to apply for this license while the 90-day clock is ticking. It's causing sheer chaos in the region." Demand from Chinese tech companies led to a data center construction boom in Southeast Asia. NVIDIA booked $104 billion in revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, representing a 72 percent increase from the year before.

Fury cleared to fight Joshua after medical checks
- Published
Tyson Fury has been medically cleared to fight Anthony Joshua in December after the bout was put in jeopardy by claims of a schizophrenia diagnosis.
Fury, 38, spoke of his mental health struggles in a Netflix documentary which was released on Friday, with his wife, Paris, saying he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia.
But Paris has since retracted that statement, saying he "doesn't have this condition" and Netflix have edited the remarks out of their film.
The British Boxing Board of Control (BBBoC) told BBC Sport: "Tyson Fury has been cleared to box on 11 December."
Fury faces Joshua, 37, in a long overdue all-British heavyweight contest at Cardiff's Principality Stadium in the early hours of 12 December.
Originally, the Netflix documentary featured the Furys recalling his admission to hospital in June 2016 with a suspected heart attack.
Doctors said he had suffered an anxiety attack. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia after he left hospital, according to the film.
The NHS describes schizophrenia as a form of psychosis, and symptoms can include hallucinations, delusions and muddled thoughts and speech.
Under regulation 8.1(b) of the British Boxing Board of Control's 2026 rules and regulations, schizophrenia is among the conditions that "may preclude" a boxer from obtaining a first licence, while for an existing licence holder the board "may take such action as in its absolute discretion as it sees fit".
On Thursday, the BBBoC general secretary Robert Smith told BBC Sport that it was "in the process of dealing with the matter" and that it was "confident he [Tyson Fury] will be absolutely fine".
With just two weeks until the British rivals meet for the vacant WBA 'super' heavyweight world title, Fury has been fully cleared to compete.
Fury, who has retired from professional boxing on five occasions, first stepped away from the sport following his world title win over Wladimir Klitschko in November 2015.
In the Netflix documentary, Fury describes a "turning point" in 2017 when he was on a night out for Halloween and had spent two years drinking and taking drugs.
"I went out and I was embarrassed by how I looked," Fury said.
"I was a fat mess and I had a glow-in-the-dark skeleton suit with full face mask on.
"I looked around and could see all the young people and I thought, 'I had the world in my hands and I threw it all away, and now I'm a fat mess addicted to alcohol'."
He says that was the beginning of a comeback which led him to focus more on his family and to return to training.
Fury is a two-time heavyweight world champion and has lost just two of his 39 professional contests.

The United States pushed Venezuela and 
Iraq
 to consider leaving 
OPEC
 earlier this year. Washington even blocked Venezuela from paying its annual membership dues to the oil producers' group, a Reuters report said, citing 10 people familiar with the matter.
The moves were aimed at two of OPEC's five founding members and reflected the Trump administration's efforts to boost oil production and prevent the group's output limits from restricting US energy ambitions.
The US pressure on Venezuela was strong enough to prompt Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to intervene this summer. He persuaded the Trump administration not to pursue the issue further, two people familiar with the discussions told Reuters.
In Iraq, Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi raised the possibility of leaving OPEC at a government meeting this summer after discussions with US officials who encouraged the move. However, Iraq's oil ministry opposed the idea and persuaded him to remain in the group. It suggested that Baghdad could instead seek a higher production quota, the sources said.
The developments come as US oil companies look to expand their investments in both countries. 
Washington was concerned that OPEC's production limits could eventually restrict plans to increase output, according to people familiar with the discussions.
US used financial leverage over Venezuela
After the US removed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, the State Department opened discussions with Venezuelan officials in Washington on whether the country should leave OPEC, five people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The Trump administration wanted US oil majors to revive Venezuela's oil production. Trump had argued that higher output would strengthen energy security in the Western Hemisphere. However, officials feared that OPEC's production policies could stand in the way of those plans.
Washington also prevented Venezuela from paying its annual OPEC membership dues, according to people familiar with the matter. The US controls Venezuela's access to state funds following Maduro's removal.
The State Department did not directly answer questions about blocking the payment. However, it confirmed that Washington has authority over Venezuela's use of state funds held in a US-controlled account.
"The Department receives disbursement requests from the interim Venezuelan government and reviews the requests, including against a list of approved and prohibited uses of the foreign Government Deposit Funds," a State Department official told Reuters.
The official said lower-level US officials may have raised the possibility of Venezuela leaving OPEC earlier this year. However, "it has not been among the issues raised by high-level officials."
Washington argued that the money could be used for more important matters instead of paying OPEC dues, one person familiar with Venezuela's relationship with the group told Reuters.
OPEC membership fees are usually paid in the first quarter of each year. Each member contributes around 2.8 million euros ($3.08 million) towards the organisation's staff salaries, research and travel expenses.
Although the amount is small compared with oil revenues, the payment carries symbolic importance for Venezuela, one of the countries that founded the organisation.
OPEC has the discretion to overlook unpaid dues and does not plan to expel Venezuela over the issue, two OPEC sources told Reuters.
Iraq asked to consider exit amid US oil investments
US officials also encouraged Iraq to leave OPEC during discussions with Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi this summer, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The discussions came as US oil majors Exxon Mobil and Chevron were planning major new investments in Iraq.
Al-Zaidi later raised the possibility of leaving the group at a government meeting. However, Iraq's oil ministry pushed back against the proposal and convinced him to remain in OPEC. It suggested that the country could instead seek a higher production quota.
The issue could resurface, as some members of Iraq's ruling coalition favour leaving OPEC and OPEC+. They view the groups as being dominated by Saudi Arabia and Russia, the sources said.
Unlike Venezuela, there is no indication that Washington tried to block Iraq's OPEC membership dues.
However, the US has considerable financial leverage over Baghdad as well. Iraq's oil revenues continue to pass through an account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, a system established after the 2003 US invasion.
Earlier this year, Washington threatened to restrict Iraq's access to its oil revenues if Baghdad did not reduce Iran's influence in its government.
The US State Department said its discussions with Iraq had focused on improving energy infrastructure and increasing oil production and transportation, rather than OPEC membership.
Trump's long-running opposition to OPEC
The US moves add to the pressure on an organisation that has faced a series of departures in recent years. OPEC has lost four members since 2019, while its share of the global oil market recently hit a low following disruptions caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran, another founding member.
"The risk of OPEC fracture is rising," Dan Alamariu, chief geopolitical strategist at Alpine Macro, told Reuters.
The United Arab Emirates announced its exit from OPEC earlier this year after becoming frustrated with the group's production limits. Angola, Ecuador and Qatar also left in 2024, 2020 and 2019, respectively. There is no indication that the US was involved in those decisions.
Founded in Baghdad in September 1960, OPEC was established by Iraq, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Venezuela. The five oil-producing countries sought greater control over a global market dominated by a handful of Western oil companies.
The organisation now has 11 members and has expanded its influence through OPEC+, an alliance that includes other major producers such as Russia. The group regularly coordinates production levels.
Trump has repeatedly criticised OPEC throughout his business and political career, accusing it of operating as a cartel and monopoly that keeps oil prices artificially high.
The US has also transformed its position in the global oil market over the past decade. It is now the world's largest oil producer, making it a major competitor to OPEC rather than simply a customer.
Venezuela, meanwhile, remains exempt from OPEC+ production quotas as its oil output has fallen sharply after years of sanctions and mismanagement. It produced around 1.2 million barrels per day in September, according to OPEC figures. State oil company PDVSA aims to raise production to 1.5 million barrels per day by the end of next year.
The US government accountability office opened a formal investigation in July into the Trump administration's handling and disbursement of Venezuelan oil revenues following requests from lawmakers for greater transparency.

Mercedes set pace in eventful Qatar second practice
- Published
World champion Kimi Antonelli set the pace ahead of Mercedes team-mate George Russell in a disrupted second practice at the Qatar Grand Prix.
Italian Antonelli was 0.127 seconds quicker than Russell on the medium tyre, as neither driver set a time on the soft compound because of two red flags that punctuated the session.
Lewis Hamilton also came to halt after his Ferrari lost power, with a virtual safety car deployed so the marshals could come to the seven-time world champion's aid.
The McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri plus Red Bull's Max Verstappen completed the top five at the Lusail International Circuit, with the trio setting soft-tyre times that were more than four tenths adrift of the two Mercedes.
The first red flag was to clear gravel off the track after an incident for Ferrari's Charles Leclerc early on, while the other was to recover the Alpine of Pierre Gasly following a high-speed spin.
Frenchman Gasly hit a marker board before beaching himself after taking too much kerb at Turn 14 in the middle of the qualifying simulation runs.
The interruptions led to the second hour being extended by 13 minutes to allow drivers more time on track in the representative conditions.
"It was a productive day," said Antonelli. "We tried a lot of things on the car between FP1 and FP2, but in FP2, it seemed like we did a step back with the car.
"But it was very interesting to see how the car behaved after those changes. It's not easy."
Antonelli, who secured his maiden title in Mexico City earlier this month, was also fastest in the opening session on the mediums. Mercedes did fit the 20-year-old with the soft tyre in the first hour, but he failed to set a lap time on them.
He said he feels it will be close between himself and Russell for the race victory, but added: "You can never write off Max [Verstappen] and the others."
Norris, meanwhile, said Mercedes "were in a different category" to McLaren, highlighting the Silver Arrows "were quicker in every single corner by miles".
The 2025 world champion added: "We seem in a relatively decent position, similar on pace with Red Bull, and similar-ish to Ferrari. So I'd say it's OK."
Four-time title winner Verstappen said it had been a "difficult day" following his issues with heavy steering towards the end of the session.
"The balance of the car is probably too disconnected at the moment to go fast," he added. "It's costing us quite a bit of lap time."
1 of 5
Hamilton also had a moment with Verstappen that was noted by the race control. The Briton was on a flying lap when he got too close to the Dutchman, who was on a long run.
Verstappen said Hamilton had moved under braking, but the stewards decided no further investigation was needed.
The second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar was sixth on the timesheets, with Leclerc leading Hamilton in seventh and eighth, 1.3 seconds away from Antonelli's time.
The two Racing Bulls of British rookie Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson were ninth and 10th.
Leclerc had to head back into the garage after spinning and going through the gravel when Lawson was just ahead of him at Turn Nine.
The Monegasque driver said the car did not feel right, and the Italian team spent a chunk of time repairing the damage to the floor. After the session he said he lost control after going a little bit early on the throttle.
Ferrari arrived in Qatar after another on-track incident between Leclerc and Hamilton, this time in Las Vegas. The pair made contact and Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for the incident, with Hamilton saying on Thursday the team were facing "very, very challenging times".

NBCUniversal will evaluate its process for reviewing ads after it faced backlash this week over an ad from a pro-Palestinian organization that called for an end to US support for Israel.
A person familiar with the matter on Friday said NBCU senior management wasn't aware of the ad until after it ran. The ad drew backlash from prominent Jewish groups and on social media. The person said the ad won't run again, but it wasn't clear if it had been slated to.
Shown during a "Saturday Night Live" Thanksgiving special, the ad begins by depicting a girl who saves up $400 over the course of a year to buy a new bicycle.
It then switches to a different girl who is missing one leg and standing on crutches in front of a pile of rubble, before zooming out to a scene of destroyed buildings.
"Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this," the ad's narrator says. It then invites viewers to visit the campaign site NoMoreForIsrael.com.
The ad, which aired on Wednesday, was placed by the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, a US nonprofit organization that states its mission is to advocate for US policies that advance Palestinian rights and freedom.
NBCU's decision to run the ad drew criticism from Jewish and Israel-focused advocacy groups, which argued that the 30-second spot made misleading and unsubstantiated claims about US aid and the war in Gaza.
The IMEU posted on X later on Friday that it was "disheartened" to learn NBC had decided to discontinue the ad, saying it was "indisputable" and had passed the broadcaster's fact-checking requirements.
'Facts out of context'
In response to the ad, the Israeli-American Council nonprofit published a petition titled "NBC, Where are your standards?"
It calls on the Federal Communications Commission to investigate whether the ad complied with its rules and for NBCU to review its approval process, suspend broadcasting the ad, and publicly apologize if it was approved "without adequate factual substantiation."
"We, the undersigned, express our profound disappointment and outrage at the decision of one of America's leading broadcast networks to provide a national platform for an advertisement that, in our view, takes facts out of context and uses selective information and unsubstantiated accusations to construct a misleading narrative about a complex and painful reality," the petition reads.
The National Jewish Advocacy Center published a five-page letter addressed to Mark Marshall, NBCU's chairman of global advertising and partnerships, asking NBC to explain and document its decision to approve the ad. The group told Business Insider it would hand-deliver the letter to NBCU on Friday.
Citing FCC rules requiring US broadcast stations to maintain public records of ads addressing political issues of national importance, the letter says an incomplete file could result in an FCC complaint. Unsupported factual claims made within the ad "may warrant reconsideration of NBC's approval and a request for corrective action," the letter says.
Jonathan Greenblatt, CEO of the Anti-Defamation League, wrote on X that the ad was "indefensible."
"At a moment of escalating antisemitism, there is no rationale to justify fanning the flames with such a twisted narrative," Greenblatt said.
Ted Deutch, CEO of the American Jewish Committee, wrote on X that NBC should explain how the ad met its standards.
"The suffering of Palestinian civilians is real and heartbreaking," Deutch said. "But using that suffering to demonize Israel while writing Hamas out of the story isn't an honest debate."
The dispute over the ad highlights the broader debate over US military assistance to Israel and over Israel's war in Gaza.

"We are airing this ad because the American people deserve to know where their money is going," Margaret DeReus, the IMEU's executive director, told Semafor.

Overton's day out
England's batters, namely Donald and Phil Salt, stole the headlines in Tuesday's win. Here the bowlers, in particular, Overton came to the fore.

The all-rounder lost his place in England's 50-over side during the series win earlier this month.

In contrast to England, who have won 18 of 21 completed T20s this year and consolidate their place at the top of the rankings, Australia are struggling badly amid their off-field issues.

Restricted NVIDIA chips were installed at a Chinese data center linked to Alice Huang
Bloomberg traced the lineage of one GB300 server rack to Gigabyte Technology.
Well, this is awkward. Bloomberg reports it may have found evidence of a link between a Chinese data center with NVIDIA Blackwell hardware and Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the controversy surrounding Jensen Huang's brief resignation from the company. Looking through documents two different firms submitted to Chinese regulators, the outlet found mention of GB300 NVL72 and GB200 server racks at the Yangtze River Delta Project in Shanghai. One of the companies, Shanghai Shuoyao, listed a GB300 NVL72 rack as collateral to secure an approximately $14 million loan from the Shanghai Innovation Bank.
A single GB300 NVL72 unit houses 72 Blackwell Ultra GPUs and 36 NVIDIA Grace processors, and can weigh about 3,300 pounds. US export rules require a license to ship these Blackwell systems to China. As Bloomberg notes, Jensen Huang once claimed GB300 racks are too big to smuggle. It's unclear how the GB300 and GB200 units made their way to the Shanghai facility, which may eventually house as many as 800,000 servers.
However, Bloomberg was able to partly track the lineage of the GB300 unit. By putting the serial of the rack into a public warranty database, the outlet was able to trace it back to Taiwan's Gigabyte Technology, which PC gamers will know as one of NVIDIA's many add-in board partners. Like other NVIDIA AIBs, Gigabyte buys GPU chips from the company that it then uses to manufacture graphics cards for consumers and servers for enterprise customers.
Gigabyte declined to answer Bloomberg's questions about what company or party originally bought the GB300 rack. A spokesperson told the outlet it "conducts all business in compliance with applicable laws and regulations," adding, "all transactions are subject to our internal compliance requirements and the relevant laws and regulations in effect at the time."
Shanghai Shuoyao, the company that offered a GB300 as collateral, has ties with Megaspeed. Alice Huang took a controlling stake in the Singaporean cloud computing company in 2023 before leaving it in August 2025. Earlier this month, Shanghai Shuoyao said it was one of Megaspeed's service providers, but described its relationship with the company as "limited to ordinary commercial cooperation."
According to Bloomberg, Megaspeed used renderings of the Yangtze River Delta Project in a presentation it shared with investors in 2024. The deck did not list China as the location of the data center. Bloomberg notes it does not have evidence that Megaspeed directly diverted NVIDIA chips to the data center, and the company denies any wrongdoing. The Justice Department is investigating whether Megaspeed broke US export rules. NVIDIA did not immediately respond to Engadget's comment request.
Alice Huang appears to have had a number of other ties to the Yangtze River Delta Project. Most notably, through Kang Wei, the man The New York Times reports was often introduced as her husband and appears to have had ties with China's Ministry of State Security. Bloomberg found him listed as the president of the facility. The publication also found evidence of servers containing NVIDIA's earlier Hopper-generation chips inside the Yangtze River Delta Project. Those GPUs are also illegal to ship to China without permission from the US government.
Jensen Huang is set to testify publicly before Congress on December 3 at 10AM ET.

The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.
India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.
So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.
My own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.
Ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.
‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’
One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.
Trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.
The route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.
The following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she said.
For Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.
Walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.
The trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she said. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.
‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’
The travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.
Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.
But the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” says Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.
Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she says, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.
Travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.
Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.
Discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.
What else we’re reading about
Politics | More than one-third of the international delegates – about 115 people – expected to attend the Congress party’s Bharat summit over the weekend were denied entry to India or had their visas cancelled, according to the Wire. Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry said that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.
Lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.
Culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the big streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
71
Firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The national capital reported its most-polluted Diwali since 2021, data from the Central Pollution Control Board showed.
Vibe check
AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI company. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.
The New Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.

Backloggd urges users to change their passwords after a breach
The website does not store payment, government ID or financial information, so none of that was exposed.
Video game-logging site Backloggd has urged users to change their passwords after announcing a security breach. The website's administrator MrProg wrote in a post dated November 25 that "someone exploited a bug in Backloggd to gain access to the site's admin tools." As a result, the infiltrator was able to access usernames, email addresses, hashed passwords and the IP addresses users signed in from. Payment information was not affected as that's handled through Patreon.
Backloggd admin MrProg said that, while the platform uses "a strong hashing method" to mask login credentials, "weak or common passwords can sometimes be guessed from their hashes." As such, it's best for Backlogged users to change their password for the site and anywhere else they use the same one. (Take this as a reminder to opt for a strong, unique password on every single service you use. A password manager can help handle that, while passkeys and multi-factor authentication add extra layers of security to your accounts.)
MrProg apologized for the security incident. The admin took Backloggd offline as soon as they became aware of the situation to fix the bug and lock out the attacker, who also hid games and restricted some accounts. All users will need to log back in, and MrProg said they're reverting all the changes the attacker made.
"Your game logs, reviews and lists all remain intact," MrProg added. "I'm currently seeking legal guidance to ensure I handle this with absolute care and will share a full notice with more details soon." The site's operator has "already added stricter access to the admin tools and will continue to commit to stronger security features to help protect your account."
Backloggd is a site on which people can log and rate games they play, in a similar fashion to what Letterboxd does for movies. Users can track their game collection, review what they've played, create lists and follow their friends' gaming progress. Backloggd has been around for eight years and it hit 1 million users this month. A native mobile app is coming next year. Those who back the site via Patreon can now check out a beta version of the Android app.

The son of Hamas chief Khalil al-Hayya survived an assassination attempt by the Israeli military on Friday, senior Hamas official Basem Naim has said.

Naim described Izzeldeen al-Hayya, born in 1997, as the Hamas chief's last surviving son, after four others were killed by Israeli forces. The family of one of the late sons also survived Friday's strike. Izzeldeen is the twin brother of Hamam Khalil al-Hayya, who was killed in a 2025 Israeli airstrike targeting Hamas leadership in Qatar. Hayya himself, who was named Hamas' overall leader in July, narrowly escaped assassination in that same Qatar attack.

Rapido’s food delivery platform Ownly is set to introduce distance-based delivery charges for customers in Bengaluru from November 30, marking another revision to its pricing model. Under the revised structure, orders delivered beyond 7 km will attract a delivery fee of ₹70. Ownly informed its restaurant partners that the change could affect order volumes but would not alter their payouts. The development was first reported by Moneycontrol. An Ownly spokesperson confirmed the development to Inc42, saying the charges would help keep the platform affordable while ensuring a sustainable business model. “Ownly’s business model is built on zero commission for restaurant partners, with delivery fees charged transparently to customers. Delivery fees are determined by factors such as distance and city, in line with our commitment to transparent and affordable delivery,” the spokesperson said. This is the second revision to Ownly’s delivery pricing in less than a year. The platform initially offered free delivery, with restaurants bearing the entire delivery cost. It later introduced a ₹25 delivery fee in Bengaluru for orders below ₹99, while orders above that threshold continued to receive free delivery within 7 km. Launched by Rapido in August 2025, Ownly was initially positioned as a zero-commission alternative to Swiggy and Zomato. It was integrated into Rapido’s main app in July and has since expanded to cities including Delhi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Kolkata. The platform will continue to charge zero commissions from restaurants and will not levy separate platform or packaging fees. It also allows restaurant partners to retain control over menu pricing, with online prices aligned with their offline menus. The latest revision signals Ownly’s shift towards monetising delivery operations through customer-paid charges while leveraging Rapido’s existing rider network. However, its ability to sustain this model will depend on whether delivery fees can cover a meaningful share of logistics costs without discouraging customers through higher order costs.

The Screens app will let you turn your iPhone Duo into an itty bitty MacBook
The app’s latest update will turn half the display into a keyboard for tiny typing.
Edovia's Screens is a remote desktop app, which gives you a way to control your computer for the iPhone, iPad, another Mac or even the Vision Pro. Screens 5.10.6, its latest update, adds the ability to turn your iPhone Duo into a tiny MacBook when it's in a partially open, clamshell configuration. When the phone is folded halfway, you can use the app's new Laptop Mode to display your remote desktop on the upper half of the screen and a keyboard with trackpad below.
Its keyboard supports multiple languages, and you can swipe down on keys to see alternative characters like you can on the iPad. The trackpad supports Screens' gestures. Of course, they're not a complete replacement for actual physical keyboards and trackpads, but they could be good enough to use in a pinch, or even regularly if you're used to typing on a screen or don't need to type anything lengthy.
The iPhone Duo's form factor is so unlike previous iPhones that we'd love to see more fun ways developers can use it to create unique experiences for the device's users. Some developers, however, might not find it that easy: Instagram's Adam Mosseri recently said that it will be "pretty challenging" to design Instagram "in a way that feels great" for the device.

'Nobody is going to help us': India's drone and robotics firms face hurdles amid growing military demand
Border tensions and government support are driving India's drone and robotics manufacturers towards defence applications. But experts warn that reliance on imported components and unpredictable military orders could hinder long-term growth.
BENGALURU: Three four-legged robots raced around a specially designed track at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, drawing crowds as they competed to clock the fastest lap.
Param, developed by Bengaluru-based General Autonomy, won the race. But for the company's co-founder Farid Ahsan, the real test lies far from the racetrack - on the military front line.
“What is more hazardous than the job of a soldier on the front lines?” he asked rhetorically.
General Autonomy, which began in industrial automation, is now working with the Indian armed forces to explore military applications for its robotic dogs and humanoids, including surveillance, patrolling and transporting supplies.
It was among several manufacturers showcasing unmanned technologies at the three-day summit from Nov 17 to 19, as India's drone and robotics firms look to tap growing demand from the country’s defence sector.
“The defence market is so big, with orders running into billions of rupees. The projected demand is also extremely high, and it's kind of engulfing the civil market,” Ezhilan Nanmaran, head of product and strategic alliances at Indian drone manufacturer IdeaForge, told CNA.
In August 2026, India's Ministry of Defence signed contracts worth approximately 15.8 billion Indian rupees (US$170 million) with Indian manufacturers Tata Advanced Systems and NIBE for armed drones and related equipment for the Indian Army.
IdeaForge itself secured a 1.37-billion-rupee contract from the ministry in June 2025 to supply the Indian Army with small surveillance drones and accessories, according to its stock-exchange filing.
But industry players told CNA that turning growing demand into a sustainable business will depend on developing reliable technology, reducing reliance on imported components and securing a steady flow of orders.
DEFENCE DEMAND DRIVES INDIA'S DRONE BOOM
The Indian government is pushing to boost domestic defence manufacturing and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers.
“India must work in a mission mode to emerge as a global hub of indigenous drone manufacturing in the next few years,” Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said at an industry conclave in New Delhi on Mar 19.
To support innovation, the government has introduced funding schemes including Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) and Acing Development of Innovative Technologies with iDEX (ADITI), which offers eligible startups grants of up to 250 million rupees each.
The number of new Indian companies founded in the defence-drone sector more than tripled from eight in 2022 to 26 in 2025, with another 33 established in the first 11 months of 2026, according to data from market intelligence firm Tracxn.
Drone manufacturers are increasingly focusing on defence applications over civilian uses such as urban deliveries, where commercial adoption remains limited, analysts said.
Neil Shah, vice-president of research at Counterpoint Research, said India's low-cost motorcycle deliveries, restrictions on long-distance drone flights and lack of landing infrastructure hinder commercial adoption.
“Covering the last mile is very tough in India,” he said. He added that drones were better suited to transporting goods between fixed locations, particularly for time-sensitive deliveries such as medical samples.
By contrast, growing military requirements and government support has created a stronger market for defence manufacturers, according to Shweta Rajpal Kohli, president and CEO of Startup Policy Forum, an Indian startup advocacy group.
“Geopolitics created the urgency. Policy created the suppliers,” she told CNA, referring to changing security priorities and government initiatives that have helped startups develop technologies for the armed forces.
“We would like to get into it (civilian drone applications), but right now we have good traction with police forces and army, so that's where our focus is at,” said Arjun Naga Vinay, assistant sales manager at Bengaluru-based drone firm NeoSky.
The company develops surveillance and mapping drones and is owned by Indian conglomerate RattanIndia Enterprises.
Vinay told CNA that the company had supplied 60 surveillance drones to Karnataka Police and subsequently received a repeat order. It has also trained around 150 policewomen to operate drones.
NeoSky is also helping Indian Army units establish drone-training facilities, providing equipment, simulators and training in drone assembly, maintenance and operation.
Meanwhile, General Autonomy's Farid Ahsan said heightened regional security tensions along India’s border with Pakistan last year prompted the company to shift from industrial automation to defence.
“We understood that the biggest requirement for adopting robotics in India is at the front line,” he said, citing the harsh conditions and risks faced by soldiers.
The company is exploring military applications for its robots with the Indian armed forces, although the machines remain under development and have yet to enter operational service.
HOW DRONES ARE RESHAPING MODERN WARFARE
Drones have become increasingly important in modern warfare, with conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East demonstrating their ability to carry out surveillance, strike targets and challenge traditional military defences.
The Russia-Ukraine war has been a turning point. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, both sides have deployed large numbers of drones to track enemy movements, direct artillery fire and strike troops, tanks and critical military and civilian infrastructure.
Relatively inexpensive drones have also allowed Ukrainian forces to strike Russian targets without relying solely on costly missiles or conventional aircraft. According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, drones had overtaken artillery as the leading cause of front-line casualties by 2025, accounting for up to 80 per cent of losses.
In the Middle East, Israel has used drones for surveillance and strikes in Gaza, while Iran has deployed explosive-laden drones against Israel and other targets in the region.
Iranian-designed Shahed drones - also used extensively by Russia in Ukraine - have demonstrated how large numbers of relatively cheap unmanned aircraft can overwhelm air defences and force opponents to expend costly interceptor missiles.
These conflicts have prompted governments worldwide to step up investment in military drones.
In February, Germany approved an initial 540 million euro order for attack drones, according to a Reuters report. While the US has earmarked US$1 billion to acquire about 340,000 small military drones over two years.
The United Kingdom announced plans in June 2025 to invest more than 4 billion pounds in autonomous military systems, including drones. In June 2026, it also pledged to supply Ukraine with 150,000 drones as part of a broader 752 million pound military aid package, according to its Ministry of Defence.
The surge in spending is creating opportunities for defence manufacturers, although rapidly evolving battlefield threats mean they must continually develop systems capable of resisting electronic interference and other countermeasures.
INDIA'S DRONE MAKERS PREPARE FOR TOUGHER MISSIONS
As India's military needs evolve, drone manufacturers are developing more advanced systems capable of operating in increasingly hostile environments.
IdeaForge's Nanmaran said India's border conflicts with Pakistan and China had highlighted the need for drones capable of withstanding electronic jamming and GPS spoofing - techniques used to disrupt communications and manipulate navigation systems.
“Flying a drone on your own border, looking at your border, is very different from flying in a contested environment,” he said.
Drone companies are also exploring applications beyond surveillance.
IdeaForge is developing a drone called Yeti to transport heavy supplies to remote areas.
Meanwhile, General Autonomy is exploring how four-legged robots and humanoids could patrol military installations, inspect hazardous areas and carry supplies across difficult terrain.
Ahsan said the company was adapting its machines to India's challenging geographical terrain, including mountainous regions, deserts and forests, where equipment developed for other countries might not be suitable.
But he acknowledged that this technology was still at an early stage.
Experience developing drones and robots for India's diverse terrain could also help manufacturers expand into overseas markets with similar conditions.
For instance, IdeaForge has used its drones for high-altitude mapping in the Himalayas and demonstrated their ability to operate in Alaska's freezing conditions to US defence customers, according to its FY2023-24 annual report.
The United States is among IdeaForge's priority overseas markets. The company said in its annual report that it had secured its first US order from a police department in Texas and formed a partnership to explore opportunities in Japan.
'NOBODY IS GOING TO HELP US WHEN THE CHIPS ARE DOWN'
Despite growing military demand, India's drone industry faces challenges including reliance on imported components and difficulties deploying new technologies, said experts.
Hari Kumar R, director of research and development at state-owned Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL), said India had made progress in developing electronic components domestically, but advanced infrared sensors used for night-time military surveillance remained difficult to source.
Speaking at a panel discussion at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, he stressed the need to develop local alternatives and diversify suppliers to prevent disruptions caused by shortages or foreign restrictions.
“Nobody is going to help us when the chips are down. Each country stands up to itself,” he said.
B.K. Das, a senior official at India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), also flagged reliance on imported materials, including rare earth magnets used in drone motors.
“[The challenge is] we do research in isolation,” he told CNA, calling for greater collaboration among India's research institutions, startups and defence companies to develop advanced military systems.
Das said DRDO had established 15 centres at universities and research institutions to help bridge that gap.
Das acknowledged that emerging technologies still needed further development to meet stringent military standards, including the ability to withstand harsh weather, equipment failures and other challenging conditions.
Meanwhile, securing a predictable flow of military orders remains another challenge for Indian startups operating in the space.
Citing Ministry of Defence figures, Kohli said 45 procurement contracts worth about 23.3 billion Indian rupees had been signed under the government's iDEX initiative as of February.
“Revenue is real now, but much of it is still lumpy,” Kohli said, referring to the irregular flow of orders and income for defence startups.
She said emergency military purchases had helped some companies secure business, but sporadic orders made it difficult for startups to plan long-term investments, expand production and retain skilled workers.
“A startup cannot hire engineers or build a factory on orders that arrive in bursts,” she said.
Kohli added that more predictable procurement, stronger domestic supply chains and manufacturing capabilities would be key to building a sustainable defence-tech industry in India.
“The market becomes sustainable when one-time buys turn into multi-year orders,” she said.

Mumbai, November 27, 2026: The two shooters involved in the firing at PC Jain Jewellers in Mahim allegedly travelled by train to Malad and then escaped towards Gujarat via the highway, police sources said. Four teams of the Mumbai Police have been deployed to track down the absconding shooters.
Case Transferred To Crime Branch
According to police sources, the investigation into the firing incident has been transferred from the Mahim police to the Mumbai Crime Branch. Although the modus operandi of the attack resembles that of the Bishnoi gang, police officials have clarified that the gang has no connection with the case. Investigators suspect the involvement of a local gang.
On Wednesday evening, two unidentified men arrived on a motorcycle and opened fire at PC Jain Jewellers, located near Hotel Shobha on L.D. Road in Mahim, before fleeing. No one was injured in the incident. Preliminary investigations indicate that the firing was allegedly carried out over an extortion dispute. The shop owner, Bharat Jain, had reportedly received extortion messages prior to the attack.
CCTV Footage Tracks Shooters’ Escape
The motorcycle used in the crime was later recovered by the police from the Lal Mitti area of Bandra. CCTV footage reportedly revealed that after abandoning the motorcycle and their jackets in the area, the shooters fled towards Bandra railway station, boarded a Borivali-bound local train and got off at Malad. From Malad East, they allegedly escaped towards Gujarat via the highway.
Meanwhile, police investigations revealed that the motorcycle seized in the case had been stolen from Bhiwandi a few days ago. The investigation team is now attempting to obtain CCTV footage from the location where the motorcycle was originally stolen to establish the movements of the accused.

Even as judges have blocked visa restrictions and other limits on foreign scholars and scientists, the Trump administration is winning outside court. New data show a clear drop in the enrollment of international graduate students, a key piece of the U.S. biomedical workforce.
That paradox was on full display last week. On Nov. 16, a federal judge issued a final ruling blocking a proposed four-year cap on how long international students and postdoctoral researchers can remain in the country. The next day, a judge in a separate case issued a preliminary injunction preventing the administration from narrowing eligibility for a work authorization program widely used by foreign students.
To student advocates like Fanta Aw, CEO of the nonprofit NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the rulings represented two wins in two days. “I’ve always believed that our judicial systems are strong and are very much still in play, and I felt relieved,” said Aw, whose organization is a plaintiff in both cases. “Our members, and in particular our students, I felt, were vindicated.”
But data released the same day as the ruling in the visa time limit case paint a less celebratory picture. A survey of more than 800 U.S. institutions conducted by the Institute of International Education found that foreign student enrollment for the current academic year has decreased 9% overall compared with 2025, with a 15% drop among newly enrolled students and graduate students. While IIE won’t have complete data until next year, the preliminary numbers suggest this will be the third consecutive year graduate enrollment has dropped — with the largest year-to-year decrease in at least 20 years, according to historical data from the nonprofit.
That trend extends to biomedicine, where foreign students make up nearly a quarter of life science Ph.D. graduates, according to new survey data from the Association of American Medical Colleges. A poll of 37 AAMC member institutions showed that the number of international students starting biomedical Ph.D. programs has decreased by about 30% since 2024, more than twice the 14% overall decline in matriculation in these programs.
The growing body of data as well as STAT’s interviews with students and immigration experts suggest that, despite the legal losses, the Trump administration’s policies on immigration have had a chilling effect on students considering coming to the U.S., and on those who are already here. Meanwhile, enrollment of foreign students is rising at some Asian universities, and experts warn that these opposing trends could jeopardize the nation’s biomedical preeminence and that it could take years to repair the loss of trust from students who no longer see the U.S. as a welcoming destination.
“People are looking at us from overseas, going, ‘We don’t really recognize this country,’” said Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney based in Boston. Even if Democrats’ new majority in Congress prevents further restrictions, she added, “I think we have a lot of ground to make up.”
When contacted for comment, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson wrote in an email that the agency’s records don’t support the decline reported by IIE, though it didn’t say whether its own data show lower enrollment by foreign students, and that President Trump should be credited for cracking down on rampant visa fraud.
“Institute of International Education’s ‘reporting’ is completely misleading and not backed up by any real evidence,” the DHS spokesperson said. “So far, [the Student and Exchange Visitor Program] has not experienced a 9% drop of foreign student enrollment.”
A recent independent analysis by the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration of the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System, a DHS database that has for more than 20 years monitored foreign students, found that international student enrollment declined by 6.3% between October 2025 and October 2026.
Concerns that the Trump administration would make it difficult for foreign scientists to enter or stay in the U.S. preceded the president’s inauguration. Since then, the administration has enacted travel bans affecting dozens of countries; instituted “extreme vetting” for visa applicants, including the review of social media profiles; and revoked more than 8,000 student visas. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has also stepped up enforcement of alleged visa violations, including the recent detention of a Princeton neuroscience Ph.D. student who had been traveling home after presenting at a scientific meeting.
But many of the administration’s efforts to more tightly regulate international scholars have not come to fruition. That includes the attempt to end “duration of status,” a policy that for nearly half a century allowed students and postdoctoral researchers to stay in the U.S. for the length of their training. DHS’s proposed four-year cap would likely have forced the vast majority of new foreign life science students to apply for extensions to stay in the country given that, on average, it takes five to six years to earn a biomedical doctorate. But a federal judge found that the proposal violated the Administrative Procedure Act, a law that governs how agencies implement new regulations.
The Trump administration has also proposed a $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program meant to give students professional experience; academic institutions would be expected to pay the fee. And DHS is attempting to revive plans to institute a $100,000 fee for H1-B visas, which are often used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as biotech.
Even though these restrictions have not been enacted, they’ve left many foreign students with a clear sense that they aren’t wanted here.
“All these rules, it just made me feel like my immigration was a crime. That’s the biggest recurring feeling that I’ve had these past few years,” said a biomedical Ph.D. student at the University of Washington, who requested anonymity to speak freely. “You know what? I’m just here to study. I’m just learning, and I’m focused on my science. But it has felt very disruptive.”
There are growing signs that fear is impacting student decisions. A poll this summer from the Association of American Universities found that, while domestic student applications for U.S. Ph.D. programs went up by 3% this year, international applications fell 21%.
A more recent survey of 437 universities, including more than 200 in the U.S., found that nearly 60% of U.S. institutions reported lower graduate enrollment between August and October compared with the same period last year. Ninety percent of U.S. respondents cited restrictive government policies as a significant obstacle.
That trend isn’t unique to the U.S. The Global Enrollment Benchmark Survey found that nearly 80% of institutions in the United Kingdom, which has also instituted tougher immigration controls, reported reduced foreign graduate student enrollment. By contrast, nearly 60% of Asian universities that responded, including five Chinese institutions, said graduate enrollment had increased. It’s a shift that Aw says could have major implications for the global economy and the future of innovation.
“There is truly a global competition for talent,” she said. “China has made no secret that one of its most pressing priorities is international education and to bring as many talented students to its shores as they can from around the world. That used to be the United States.”
STAT’s coverage of the federal government’s impact on the biomedical workforce is supported by a grant from the Dana Foundation and the Boston Foundation. Our financial supporters are not involved in any decisions about our journalism.

There were the hours spent prepping for Joe Rogan’s podcast, an afternoon filming videos at Kid Rock’s home in Nashville, and a meeting with the CEO of the company that makes Tylenol, just weeks before President Trump urged pregnant women not to take the drug because he claimed, without evidence, it was linked to autism.
These are some of the appointments documented in health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendar. In a show of “radical transparency,” HHS released the secretary’s partial calendar, which reflects his activities from Feb. 13, 2025, to June 19, 2026.

The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, West Bengal, held a Kolkata food outlet liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practices for charging ₹10 extra for packaging, according to a report by The Indian Express. The bench comprising President Manoj Kumar Rai and member Gopal Chandra Roy directed the food outlet to pay ₹50,000. “OP no. 1 has failed to prove that the complainant requested him to provide packaging and agreed to provide cost for the same. So, deficiency in service on the part of OP no 1 is proved,” the order read. The customer had bought two plates of chicken momos, each priced at ₹109, from the outlet on October 29, 2024. The customer was charged an additional Rs. 10 on the bill, leading to an altercation between the two. The customer demanded that the extra amount be refunded; however, the outlet outright refused. Triggered by the incident, the consumer moved the consumer court, seeking a refund and compensation. The food outlet rejected the allegations, claiming that the customer had requested extra packaging to ensure the food remained safe and hygienic and did not spill while he travelled on a motorcycle. It further maintained that the packaging fee had been disclosed to the customer before the order was placed and that he had agreed to pay it. However, the commission found that the outlet had not submitted any evidence showing that the customer had asked for the momos to be packed separately. Referring to Section 36(5) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, the commission said that the seller is responsible for bearing the expenses involved in making goods ready for delivery, unless there is a different agreement between the parties. “Section 36 (5) of the Sale of Goods’ Act, 1930 provides that unless otherwise agreed, the expenses of and incidental to putting the goods into a deliverable state shall be borne by the seller. Therefore, in view of the aforesaid provision, it is duty of the OP No. 1 as seller, to provide packaging of the goods sold by them for taking it away and the OP No. 1 shall have to bear the cost of such packaging,” the order read, according to The Indian Express report. The commission also pointed out that the food outlet had failed to establish that the customer had been informed about the additional ₹10 packaging fee before placing the order. Concluding that the outlet was guilty of deficiency in service, the commission directed it to return the ₹10 packaging charge to the customer. It also ordered the company to pay ₹100 as compensation and ₹2,000 towards litigation expenses. In addition, the food outlet has been directed to deposit ₹50,000 into the Consumer Legal Aid Account of the Commission. 'Best midfielder in the world' - where does Bellingham rank?
- Published
Is there a better central midfielder on the planet than Jude Bellingham right now?
Not according to Jose Mourinho. The Real Madrid manager might be trying to manage the Englishman's minutes, but he did not hold back in his praise after the 23-year-old came off the bench and scored a superb volley, helping Real overturn a half-time deficit to beat PSV Eindhoven 5-1.
"He has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything," Mourinho said.
"He's an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world."
Bellingham's impressive 45-minute cameo came just nine days after an outstanding, all-action display for England in a 3-2 Nations League win in Spain.
While the former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund player also earned plenty of plaudits for his displays at the 2026 World Cup, where he scored seven times, Mourinho believes Bellingham's unique blend of craft and graft isn't yet fully appreciated.
"He can play as a '10', as an '8', with two pivots, with one," Mourinho said after the win against PSV. "That's why I said, when the Ballon d'Or was discussed, that it was outrageous he wasn't among the top 10."
While wingers like Lamine Yamal or Michael Olise are also likely to be contenders for the 2027 award, is there anyone you would rather have in central midfield than Bellingham?
BBC Sport looks at what makes him so good, and who his closest challengers are.
Jude Bellingham (Real Madrid)
Although only 23, Bellingham is already in his fourth year at Real Madrid and is on course for his most productive campaign since his debut season in 2023-24, when he scored 23 goals and provided 13 assists, including setting up Vinicius Jr in the Champions League final.
He has seven goals and four assists in 18 appearances this season. Only three central midfielders have more goal involvements across Europe's top five leagues, but Bellingham's all-round game is what sets him apart.
He leads his Real team-mates for possession won, duels won and fouls won. And while only Kylian Mbappe has had more shots on target, Bellingham offers far more than just late runs into the box.
He has played more passes into the final third than any other Real player, leads the club for ball carries and is second only to Arda Guler for chances created.
When Bellingham's coaches at Birmingham gave him the number 22 shirt, it reflected their belief that he could play any role, as a number 10, 8 or 4.
He has fulfilled that potential to become the complete midfielder.
Vitinha (Paris St-Germain)
While Bellingham made his senior debut with Birmingham, Vitinha also spent part of his formative years in the Midlands, scoring once in 22 appearances during a loan spell at Wolves - a spectacular long-range strike against Chorley in 2021.
But goalscoring isn't what the Portuguese playmaker is best known for - it is his metronomic passing.
The 26-year-old has played a pivotal role in Paris St-Germain's back-to-back Champions League triumphs, with manager Luis Enrique saying he "embodies the perfect midfielder".
He was named man of the match in the victory over Arsenal last season, having completed 141 of his 150 passes, matching the Champions League final record set by Barcelona's Xavi in 2011.
Vitinha finished third in the Ballon d'Or voting in 2025 but slipped to 14th this year, a ranking Luis Enrique disagreed with.
"It's a real pleasure to have a player with such physical abilities and that mentality," the PSG boss said last month. "He's at an incredible level."
Declan Rice (Arsenal)
Rice finished one place below Vitinha, and four below England team-mate Bellingham, in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings after helping Arsenal win their first Premier League title since 2004.
He briefly played at centre-back as a youngster at West Ham before establishing himself as a top-class defensive midfielder for the Hammers. But since joining the Gunners in 2023 he has taken his game to another level, adding significantly more attacking output.
Rice created 17 big chances in the Premier League last season, as defined by Opta, a total bettered only by Bruno Fernandes and Rayan Cherki.
The 27-year-old has also registered 14 assists in all club competitions since August 2025. While set-pieces have undoubtedly contributed to that tally, he offers much more.
He ranks among the top 4% of central midfielders across Europe's top five leagues for progressive carries, while posting similarly impressive figures for chances created, touches and expected assists.
Rodri (Barcelona)
The 2024 Ballon d'Or winner missed Spain's Nations League defeat by England this month through injury, and his absence was keenly felt as the hosts uncharacteristically struggled for control, at least against 11 men.
It was a far cry from Spain's triumphant Euro 2024 and 2026 World Cup campaigns, both of which ended with him being named player of the tournament.
The 30-year-old completed 756 passes as Spain won their second global title, the highest total ever recorded at a World Cup.
His performances this summer were all the more impressive given that he had taken time to return to his best after tearing his anterior cruciate ligament, an injury that sidelined him for most of the 2024-25 campaign.
The former Manchester City player has slotted in seamlessly since joining Barcelona in August, and averages 106 successful passes per 90 minutes in La Liga - the second-highest figure, behind Vitinha, of any player in the top five European leagues.
- The student playing in La Liga: Introvert Rodri's unique rise to top 
  - Published3 October
Pedri (Barcelona)
Pedri may be six years younger than Rodri, his midfield partner at the Camp Nou, but he boasts extraordinary experience for a 24-year-old, having made more than 250 appearances for Barcelona, not to mention playing at two European Championships and two World Cups.
The Tenerife-born midfielder combines tigerish work-rate with quality in possession.
He has created 26 chances from open play in La Liga this season, the sixth-highest total across Europe's top five leagues, and wins possession an average of 7.6 times per 90 minutes, the 10th-highest figure.
However, such is Spain's wealth of midfield options that he is not even guaranteed a starting place for his country, with Fabian Ruiz preferred for their final three matches at the 2026 World Cup.
Paris St-Germain midfielder Ruiz, who finished 10th in this year's Ballon d'Or rankings, also deserves to be in any debate about the world's best midfielders.
Fermin Lopez (Barcelona)
He might not yet have the profile of Barcelona team-mates Rodri or Pedri, but on current form alone, versatile youngster Lopez is one of Europe's best box-to-box goalscorers.
The 23-year-old already has nine goals and seven assists this season. Counting only goals scored in Europe's top five leagues and the Champions League, no central midfielder has more.
While Lopez can also operate on the wing, the presence of Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon means he has mainly featured as a number eight or a number 10 this term.
The Barcelona academy graduate played only a bit-part role as Spain won Euro 2024 and was unfortunate to miss the World Cup after breaking a bone in his foot in May.
However, a summer off enabled him to hit the ground running this season, and he has not looked back.
