‘The Hunting Wives’ Stars and Creator Break Down Margo and Sophie’s Dangerous Love Affair in Season 2: ‘It’s a F—-ed Up Commitment’ to ‘Move Past’ Murder
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for Season 2 of “The Hunting Wives,” now streaming on Netflix.
Earlier this month, Texas shocked the nation by electing Democrats to the governorship, the U.S. Senate and several more key positions during this year’s midterm elections. But the Lone Star State’s politics have always been seen as dynamic and complicated to those in the know — like fans of “The Hunting Wives,” Netflix’s juicy, campy drama series about a group of wealthy, gun-loving and sexually fluid women from East Texas.
“I love our show, because you see both sides of this coin, and we’re making fun of each side,” says “The Hunting Wives” star Brittany Snow about the series’ depiction of Texas politics. Co-star Malin Åkerman adds, “We’re not going to say that we had anything to do with it, but there’s all these different people saying, ‘The Hunting Wives’ had something to do with Texas going blue!’ It’s a fun little moment for us right now.”
Åkerman plays Margo Banks, the housewives’ confident ringleader whose Republican husband Jed (Dermot Mulroney) is a favorite to become governor. But, in Season 1, her beautiful house of cards is torn apart with the arrival of Sophie (Snow), an East Coast liberal who is shocked by the dirty underbelly of her new Southern home. Margo is full of secrets that she’s intent on keeping from Sophie, and thinks she’s in the clear when the two begin falling in love (and deep, deep lust). But Season 1 ended with Sophie discovering that Margo had gotten pregnant by a teenager, Brad (George Ferrier), before having an abortion and murdering Brad’s girlfriend, Abby Jackson (Madison Wolfe), for uncovering the truth. The only saving grace for Margo is that Sophie can’t do anything with the information, because when her brother, Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), attempts to intimidate Sophie on Margo’s behalf, Sophie hits him with her car and kills him instantly. Now, they’re both in trouble.
Because Sophie hid Kyle’s body and told no one what she did, Season 2 begins with Margo trying to get back into her good graces. Unaware that Kyle is even dead, she keeps calling his number, getting no response until a panicked Sophie uses AI to deepfake Kyle’s voice and keep the illusion up. In person, Sophie tries her best to avoid Margo, but she can’t control herself. So she uses Kyle’s voice to ask Margo whether any of their relationship was genuine. When Margo answers that it was “100% real,” not just a ploy to cover-up the murder, Sophie is finally ready to get back together. She meets Margo at the Banks’ lake house, where they have sex — which is rudely interrupted by Zelda (Dale Dickey), a woman from Margo’s past, who sneaks up and holds a gun point-blank to Margo’s head.
Zelda is the leader of a biker gang in Alba, Margo’s hometown. She suspects Kyle of impregnating and murdering her underage granddaughter, Ellie (Chloe Guidry), and is attacking Margo to get information about Kyle’s whereabouts. Zelda and the gang don’t believe Margo when she says she has no idea where he is until Sophie blurts out that Kyle couldn’t have killed Ellie because she killed him. Zelda pieces together that it was someone in the gang (Cam Gigandet as Gentle John) and shoots him in the head. Soon, the police show up and the gang gets shot to death. Margo and Sophie are escorted home before they can discuss what happened, and Sophie panics, worrying that Margo will tell the police what happened to Kyle. But she doesn’t. After ignoring several calls from Sophie, Margo shows up at Sophie’s apartment and forgives her — they’re even, since Margo is a murderer too.
The two begin secretly dating again, but Jed and his staff keep Margo on a tight leash during his campaign for governor. So Sophie hatches up a plan: If Margo publicly admits that she’s had an abortion, she’ll be able to tank Jed’s campaign and leave him for Sophie while drumming up enough support and attention to maintain her wealthy lifestyle. But right before the couple is set to make a TV appearance, Jed tells Margo that he knows she killed Abby and that Sophie killed Kyle, and that she needs to be a “dutiful wife” if she wants to keep herself and her girlfriend out of prison. Margo does still confess to cheating on Jed and having an abortion on live TV, but instead of advocating for women’s rights, she calls herself a murderer and says that prayer has allowed her to find redemption. The move is received positively by Jed’s rightwing base, and Sophie freaks out. That night, she confronts Margo, who explains to Sophie that she did it to protect her and that they can never speak again. Sophie is enraged, and says that she’ll release her recording of Margo confessing to Abby’s murder unless Margo gives her $10 million. In a brief epilogue set two years later, Sophie is uber-rich but estranged from Margo. She receives a phone call from a mysterious number and only hears panicked breathing on the other end; it’s Margo, who is covered in blood.
Snow and Åkerman, in one interview, and series creator Rebecca Cutter, in a separate conversation, spoke to Variety about the absolute insanity playing out in their East Texan world.
Sophie begins the season in couple’s counseling with Graham (Evan Jonigkeit). What’s going through her head in those scenes? Does she actually want to work on healing her marriage, or is it just about protecting her relationship with her son?
Brittany Snow: When I read the first episode and realized that one of the first scenes is her having a panic attack in her car, and then she later starts hearing sounds on the phone that are not there — I realized she’s sort of losing her mind, and that embeds in her reasoning through the entire show. She’s losing her mind because she’s losing the piece that she’s addicted to, which is Margo. So he’s just trying to fix the negativity and the guilt and shame she feels. So she’s trying to save her marriage. Maybe that’ll fix it. Or maybe she’ll run away from Margot, and maybe that’ll fix it. Or maybe she’s gonna move into this tiny house. Nothing seems to be fixing this hole, so she’s in a very psychologically dark place at the beginning of this show.
Malin, what did it feel like to pick up in such a tenuous place in Margo’s relationship with Jed, where they’re performing happiness for the cameras but barely speaking at home?
Malin Åkerman: I don’t like when Margo’s not on top — but it is fun to play. Margo is in the doghouse. She’s not in the main mansion. She has these bikers from her past who are chasing after her brother. Everything that could go wrong is going wrong. She doesn’t have Sophie available at all. She’s not answering any of her calls, so we find her in a really tough position, and we just want her to get her power back and get back to the unapologetic, outrageous Margo.
How did it feel when you two came back together for the first time, which both characters are obviously craving each other, but they’re still at odds?
Snow: The car scene in the rain was a really difficult scene because there had to be so many things at once happening. The push-pull of a toxic relationship: “Please stay in my car. I love you. I also need you to get out. Also, I killed your brother. Also, I’m gonna have a nervous breakdown.” And it’s all those levels while looking really, really terrible on my part. Like a drowned rat.
Åkerman: I loved that that was the first scene where we see them together, because there was so much going on and there are high stakes. Hopefully people feel the same way, like, “Oh my god! Just stay! Kiss! Get together!”
Snow: It was a good scene. That kinetic energy that we have. The anger that I have. You trying to win me over. It’s a lot!
When Margo is trying to convince Sophie to let her back into her life in the beginning, is she being any more genuine than she was in Season 1? Or is it still about needing Sophie to help her survive and stay out of prison?
Åkerman: I mean, Margo comes first. She’s always gonna have her own back. But I truly think that somewhere deep inside, this is the closest to a feeling of love that Margo has had for anyone. There’s something about Sophie that really draws her in, and she feels the most herself that she’s ever felt. There’s some version of true love, as well as her survival. She can’t turn that off yet because it’s not safe yet to turn it off, and she has to make sure that she’s not going to get called out. So there’s a big duality there.
Where did the idea come from for the biker gang from Margo’s past?
Rebecca Cutter: It was reverse engineering to get Sophie and Margo back together. The biker gang is looking for Kyle, and [since he isn’t available], who can Margo go to when she’s threatened? Sophie’s the only one that knows she killed Abby. Sophie’s the only one that knows the real her. So having that threat come into her life, in the form of Zelda and the gang, sends her directly to Sophie. Then Sophie, having to interact with Margo through the AI deepfake, falls in love with her all over again and feels guilty about what she’s done. It was this perfect storm bringing them back together. The other thing of that makes their reunion possible is that Sophie has grown and changed a lot over the two seasons. She goes from being a very weak character who feels powerless in her life to being this really formidable woman who is an equal to Margo. And realizing that they’re both killers and they both have that same drive and instinct makes them fall in love all the more.
Walk me through what it was like to film all the extreme highs and lows at the end of Episode 3 leading into Episode 4: We start with a sex scene where Sophie and Margo are getting out all of their pent-up frustration from their time apart, when they’re interrupted by Zelda sneaking up with a gun, which eventually leads to Sophie blurting out to them that she killed Kyle followed by a police shootout that kills Zelda and her crew.
Snow: That scene is nuts. That was a nuts shoot. We also didn’t know that the song that was going to be behind it all was going to be, like — [she sings an twangy, upbeat melody] — so we’re acting our asses off, screaming and crying, and then when you see the scene, you’re like, “Wow, it’s kind of funny, actually! Comical!”
Åkerman: You just never know how it’s gonna be edited together. But shooting it was it was a lot, over the course of two or three days. A lot of emotion. Luckily, we shot the two things separately, the intimate scene when Dale Dickey’s character comes in and discovers us, and the living room scene where the shootout happens. It was probably good for us — one mindset to the other. It’s one of my favorite things that Dale Dickey gets to say, with the gun to my head. [While Margo’s head is in between Sophie’s legs, Zelda appears with a gun and says, “Well, lookee lookee what we got here.”]
Snow: The juxtaposition of the show is really encapsulated in that scene. The comedy, the drama, the thriller.
How was it shooting Sophie’s confession that she’s the one who killed Kyle?
Snow: I hate that scene. Because you really see how desperate Sophie is in that moment. I don’t know if any more veins in my neck and forehead could have popped out. She’s desperate, and she doesn’t know if Margo’s going to forgive her, so the fact that she does is pretty crazy.
Åkerman: I loved that scene. You’re brilliant in it. All the veins. I love it all. I love it all.
For most of the rest of episode, we’re left wondering if Margo tells Jed or the police the truth about what Sophie did. What do you think was going through her head in all that off-screen time? How does she decide what to do?
Åkerman: It’s a lot, and but I do think that Sophie is the closest thing to family that she has after her brother. We also know that Kyle is very unhinged and unmanageable, and who knows what he may have done to Sophie if she hadn’t have run him over? She didn’t plan on it. There were a lot of factors that she had to think about. She herself is also a murderer, so she kind of understands.
Snow: We have this in common now.
Åkerman: I do think it was a lot to process. But she almost wins that cat-and-mouse chase, because she goes, “Well, now I’m back on top. I get to pull the strings and call the shots.” There are a lot of different elements to why she makes the decision to come in and say, “All right, this is how it’s gonna go. Now I’ve got you under my thumb again.”
Cutter: Margo is, above all else, a survivor and a schemer. In a very practical sense, she recognizes that Sophie has something on her, with Abby Jackson, and she has something on Sophie, with Kyle. It’s like Russia and the United States. It’s a cold war. But now we’re even, so it’s a great place for them to be.
She has the power again, but the scene also ends in a place that’s romantic and sweet. Usually, high-pressure moments between Margo and Sophie end with a sex scene, but in this one they just hold hands and realize they’re all each other has in the world. Tell me about shooting that.
Snow: Murder brought us together!
Åkerman: Oh my God.
Snow: Sophie’s coming from such a nervous breakdown that any forgiveness feels like such an oasis in her mind, and especially because it comes from Margo. There’s hope in that scene. When you see Kyle’s dead body [get discovered], you realize hope is never going to last long on “Hunting Wives.” But that scene puts us on the same playing field, and alludes to the idea that things are going to be OK in their weird world.
Is that how it feels to you, Malin? Is this the purest their relationship has been?
Åkerman: I don’t know if I’d say the purest. Afterwards, I think it gets purer. But in that moment, Margo holds onto a few other things other than loving intentions. There’s the power dynamic where she’s also deciding that this is OK, and she is now in charge. You’re not gonna call me out for killing Abby Jackson.
Snow: Our physicality in that scene is interesting, because you’re sitting there the whole time just watching me, and I’m pacing around, doing a tap dance. You’re just like, “Dance, monkey.”
Åkerman: But afterwards, I loved that part of filming. We love being in love. That is the closest we get to seeing what a real relationship could be like for these two. We go, “Oh my God, they might make it! They might run off into the sunset together, and everyone else gets killed off.” That’s not what happens. But we get to see a little more vulnerability from Margo, and I thought that was a lovely part of Season 2.
Cutter: It was important to show that the relationship is more than just sex, and that there is this deeper commitment that they’re making to each other to move past this, even though it’s kind of a fucked up commitment. I remember talking in the writers’ room about how Mandy became Margo not by dwelling on the past, but by always being willing to move on, shed her skin and transform. “We’re just gonna take this drink and act like nothing ever happened.” That’s so Margo. That’s what she has to do. She cannot dwell in any past trauma.
During the one episode where things are happy and fun, what is Sophie’s moral compass saying? Margo comes from a tough world and grew up learning to hurt people if it meant protecting herself. But Sophie comes from a more sheltered background. How is she able to reckon with what she’s done? Because she has Margo’s forgiveness, does she feel like a good person again?
Snow: I think she can compartmentalize in a way that’s scary, especially when it comes to her son and her family and what she wants. She sees Margot as a beacon of who she wants to be and who she wants to be with. But she still has to be a good mother, and needs to divorce Graham. So she’s wrestling with the decision to, maybe for the first time in her life, choose herself. And that feels really good to her. She’s going to take a bubble bath in the middle of the day and show up for her girlfriend and do all these things. And then it comes crashing down.
When Sophie hatches up the plan for Margo to publicly announce her abortion so she can leave Jed and be with her, is there ever a moment where Margo genuinely plans to follow through? Or was she lying when she told Sophie she’d do it?
Åkerman: Yeah, I think she had a hopeful moment where she thought maybe this could be their happy ending. There was a glimmer of hope, because that’s the thing that initially attracted her to Sophie. She’s bright and smart, and Margo noticed that about her in that very first scene when we see them together at the NRA party.
She decides to stick with Jed since he’s figured out what happened to Abby Jackson and Kyle, and essentially begins blackmailing her. So why does she still tell the world about her abortion?
Åkerman: I may not have a great answer for you. I think it’s more about the suspense, because we want to believe she’s about to say this, and to give it that really great twist at the end. That was the one scene that I had a lot of trouble wrapping my head around, like, “Why would she admit that?”
Snow: But don’t you think she’s taking her power back? Like, “You can’t cage me, Jed. I’m still gonna say what I want.”
Åkerman: I guess you’re right. Thank you for that!
Snow: I saw it!
Åkerman: I like it!
Cutter: It’s partly to mislead the audience, also because Sophie said something to her on the phone call earlier: “You could be a hero to half the country.” Margo is a very shrewd politician and understands that if she comes forward and gets ahead of it and frames it a certain way, it could actually add to her own power. She plays a card that could have backfired, but we see that it works — and I will be shocked if, someday, a Republican politician doesn’t play this card. Mark my words.
What are your predictions or desires for these characters moving into Season 3?
Snow: Trying to cover up another murder, which always brings them together. I mean, we leave off this season with a cliffhanger, where it’s open to the audience whether Sophie feels like she might hear Margo’s voice or maybe she doesn’t. And Margo’s covered in blood, so we get to see these women in totally different places, physically and mentally, and they’re on a level that makes them feel like equal adversaries in a lot of ways. I just hope for Sophie, in Season 3, to take a chill pill. Maybe some Xanax! To sit in her power and not be so anxious all day. I feel like it’s coming.
Åkerman: I think so too!
Snow: I think she’s going to own herself.
You’ve said that there’s some DNA from the “Real Housewives” reality franchise in “The Hunting Wives.” Are you going to watch Bravo’s new reality show, “Small Town Trouble: Texas,” which seems to have taken some inspiration from your show?
Åkerman: We’re gonna have to watch.
Snow: We’re gonna watch, and we’re gonna like it!
Cutter: I don’t watch that much reality TV, but I think I would have to try it. Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery.

'Lacks basic respect': For jobseekers, being ghosted by recruiters and employers can add to emotional toll
In Singapore, 64 per cent of workers cite long delays as their biggest frustration in the hiring process, according to a 2026 report by job site Indeed.
SINGAPORE: After six rounds of interviews for a compliance role in a bank, Ivy (not her real name) found herself ghosted by the prospective employer.
The 29-year-old assumed she did not get the job when she still had not heard back three weeks after her last interview in June. As at November – five months since her last interaction with the bank – she had yet to be formally updated on the outcome of her application.
Ivy is not alone. More and more jobseekers are finding themselves ghosted by prospective employers.
In Singapore, 64 per cent of workers cite long delays as their biggest frustration in the hiring process, according to job site Indeed's 2026 Southeast Asia Talent report.
Vague job ads, poor communication or delays were major frustrations for 42 to 60 per cent of workers surveyed across Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.
Nearly half of respondents said they would not wait beyond two to four weeks in a hiring process.
To jobseeker Ivy, the silence she received lacked “basic respect”. It left her with self-doubt and confusion as she had thought the hiring team saw her favourably after advancing her through multiple rounds.
“You put in effort to guide me through the process, and I put in effort to prepare for every single one of those interviews,” she said.
“The civil thing to do is to give (me) the outcome instead of just leaving it in complete silence and letting the candidate assume that nothing has happened.”
The experience also left her with a “bad impression” of the company and hiring manager, she said.
CNA has changed the names of some jobseekers in this article who fear retaliation for discussing negative recruitment experiences in their industries.
AN INCREASINGLY COMMON EXPERIENCE
Ivy has since received another offer and started a new job. But for those still in the market for one, a lack of timely updates about hiring decisions is a typical complaint.
A LinkedIn poll conducted by recruitment agency Robert Walters Singapore in 2025 saw 88 per cent of its 300 respondents reporting that they are often ignored or ghosted by prospective employers.
Mr Patrick Tay, assistant secretary-general at the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), has heard feedback about this from workers across different sectors, including professionals, managers and executives (PMEs).
“Workers have mainly shared that they did not hear back after submitting an application or faced delays in receiving an update after their first interview,” the member of parliament told CNA.
Replying to Mr Tay’s parliamentary question on this in August, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) encouraged employers to inform candidates about how interview results will be communicated, and to notify them of the outcome “within a reasonable timeframe”.
An example of such a timeframe is two weeks, according to the Fair Recruitment and Selection Handbook by the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices.
MOM does not track complaints about employers not notifying applicants of hiring outcomes, according to its parliamentary reply.
Official figures show labour turnover and hiring activity in Singapore have slowed.
The latest quarterly average monthly recruitment rate of 1.4 per cent in the second quarter of 2026 was the lowest since the COVID-19 pandemic.
Advance figures released by MOM on Friday (Nov 27) showed long-term unemployment rates edging up for PMETs (professionals, managers, executives and technicians), from 0.6 per cent to 0.7 per cent.
MOM noted that while still within historical range, this number was at the higher end, "suggesting prolonged job search for some workers amid softer hiring in outward-oriented sectors".
Mr Joshua Woo, founder of recruitment agency RecruitFast, said non-replies are not a new challenge in his industry, but may be more noticeable in today’s tough job market.
Recruitment has become increasingly complex amid economic uncertainty, fewer job vacancies, more applicants and longer assessment processes, he said.
“As employers become more cautious, hiring decisions may take longer and, unfortunately, communication with candidates can sometimes fall through the cracks."
Non-binding Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices explicitly state that unsuccessful candidates should be informed of their interview results.
This is also specified in the Tripartite Standard on Recruitment Practices – a set of good employment practices that has been adopted by more than 6,000 entities in Singapore.
Mr Tay said NTUC encourages employers to update candidates at three key points: to acknowledge the application at the point of submission, to inform candidates how and when they can expect to hear back at the interview, and to notify candidates within a reasonable timeframe after the interview.
“For those between jobs, a long silence adds to the stress and uncertainty they already face,” he said.
FRESH GRADUATES AFFECTED
For fresh graduates making the transition from school to their first full-time job, non-replies and delayed replies can add to feelings of insecurity and anxiety.
Computer science and design graduate Nicholas (not his real name), 25, started his job search last May, a year before graduating. He applied for about 500 roles before receiving an offer in November.
While Nicholas said it was still more common for him to learn the outcomes of interviews than not, the long wait for updates added to the emotional toll of his strenuous job hunt.
For example, after interviewing for a traineeship with a foreign bank, two-and-a-half months of silence passed before he was notified that the role had gone to someone else.
Nicholas also found that while hiring organisations may communicate warmly and promptly before and sometimes immediately after interviews, this did not necessarily continue all the way to the final decision.
These experiences left him feeling “little control” over his employment outcomes, despite feeling he had done his best in his preparations, technical assessments and interviews. “I feel very exhausted,” he said.
Mr Wayne Low, 26, obtained honours of highest distinction in English literature and philosophy from the National University of Singapore in May.
He estimated having applied to around 200 positions spanning the public and private sectors. He advanced to the second round of interviews with two prospective employers.
One of them was a local firm where he fielded his second interview with the head of human resources (HR) on Oct 9. After following up, he received a holding reply and had yet to hear back at the time of writing.
“Most job (applications) go like that, they just go quietly into the good night,” he said.
“It feels very impersonal. It makes you feel even more isolated in your job hunt.”
The spotty updates also gave Mr Low misgivings about the firm’s professionalism if he were to work there, since he had applied for a marketing role involving a lot of stakeholder communication.
WHAT HR EXPERTS SAY
Mr Derrick Teo, CEO of recruiting firm Elitez Group, said that employers should aim to give candidates the outcome within one to two weeks, and use holding updates if more time is needed.
"Importantly, candidates who are unsuccessful should also receive closure," said the Institute for Human Resource Professionals-certified HR leader.
"It does not always need to be a lengthy explanation. A brief, respectful email informing them of the outcome is better than leaving them waiting indefinitely."
Mr Woo advised candidates to ask about the expected timeline for a hiring decision after an interview. If no timeline is given, they can follow up politely after three to five working days, and again if necessary.
Recruiters also explained some behind-the-scenes reasons why outcomes may be communicated late.
These include delays in internal approvals, changes to manpower budgets, hiring freezes, overwhelmed HR teams and directives from senior management to reduce headcount, said Mr Woo.
Mr Teo said it is also common for employers to wait for their preferred candidate to accept an offer before finalising the outcomes for other shortlisted applicants.
Further complicating recruitment, Mr Woo has observed an increase in the number of interview rounds, particularly for PMEs.
Entry-level PME roles traditionally required just one round, but some employers have added assessments especially for technical or artificial intelligence-related roles that need more specialised skill sets, he said.
However, none of these considerations justify silence, the recruiters said. And there are good reasons why employers may want to improve their communication.
“Employers are assessing candidates, but candidates are also forming an impression of the organisation through their interactions with HR,” said Mr Teo.
“Clear communication can help build trust and maintain a positive relationship, regardless of the hiring outcome.”
Added Mr Woo: “A candidate who may not be suitable for a particular role today could become a client, colleague or even a hiring manager in the future.
“Maintaining professional relationships and communicating respectfully with candidates should therefore remain a priority.”

Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
- Published
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron calling Brazilian meat "doped".
France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry, which took effect in September.
The Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".
Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.
In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.
Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at the Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.
"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.
Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".
Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".
Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

Director Sooraj Barjatya and actor Ayushmann Khurrana discussed how filmmaking and social attitudes have changed over the years during an interview with Bollywood Hungama for their recently released film Yeh Prem Mol Liya. While Barjatya spoke about the evolution of acting and film presentation, Ayushmann pointed to the changes in the way the film approaches marriage and traditional customs.
EXCLUSIVE: Ayushmann Khurrana says Yeh Prem Mol Liya marks a “quantum leap” for Rajshri Productions; explains how it differs from Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!
Yeh Prem Mol Liya, which released in theatres on November 27, 2026, stars Ayushmann Khurrana as Prem Mishra and Sharvari as Purva Solanki. Directed by Barjatya and produced by Rajshri Productions, the romantic family drama also features Anupam Kher, Supriya Pathak, Seema Pahwa and Saumya Tandon.
Asked how society and filmmaking have changed since he began his career, Barjatya said, “There has been so much change. Technically, we are way ahead. When I see them perform, they make it feel so real.”
He recalled how acting was approached differently when he started making films. “In our time, when I started, acting was acting. The theatres were rough, and our acetate prints would develop lines within four weeks. We used to call them grains. Everything needed to be projected, so performances were often more exaggerated,” he said.
Comparing that approach with contemporary performances, Barjatya added, “Today, acting has become so real. I feel that if you feel it right, you will get it right. That has also progressed.”
However, the filmmaker also expressed a concern about the way films are marketed today. He suggested that there should be less emphasis on marketing around films, although his response in the interview was cut off before he could elaborate on the point.
Ayushmann, meanwhile, described the changes in Rajshri's storytelling through the film's approach to marriage and family traditions. Calling it a significant shift for the production house, he said, “I think Rajshri Productions has taken such a big quantum leap.”
He then referred to a scene from Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!, in which Salman Khan's character asks Mohnish Bahl's character, “Painting pasand aayi? Painting banane wali pasand aayi?” Ayushmann explained that the exchange reflected an arranged marriage setup in which neither the prospective bride nor the groom knew that the marriage was being arranged.
Drawing a contrast with Yeh Prem Mol Liya, he said, “Here, of course, the marriage has happened with mutual consent. After that, he takes his entire family to the girl's house and questions the traditions. He used to follow those traditions, and now he is questioning them. What could be a bigger change than this?”

A new Constitutional Amendment Bill approved by the Union Cabinet on Friday (November 27, 2026) proposes an extension of the existing freeze on the inter-State distribution of Lok Sabha seats for another 25 years, until 2051, addressing the core concern of States that feared a loss of their proportionate strength due to the decline in their share of the national population.
Also read | Lok Sabha seat freeze is no longer linked to population stabilisation
The 132nd Constitutional Amendment Bill marks a significant turn from the 131st Amendment Bill moved by the Centre in April 2026 that sought to redistribute Lok Sabha seats among States according to the 2011 Census population.
The proposed amendment removes the linkage of the existing distribution of Lok Sabha seats to the 1971 Census and links it with provisions related to women’s reservation in Article 334A of the Constitution. The guarantee for a 50% increase in the number of Lok Sabha seats for each State is being written into this, providing that, for the purposes of giving immediate effect to such reservation for women, “the delimitation so undertaken shall provide for an increase of fifty per cent in the number of seats allocated to each State and Union territory in the House of the People.” The total number of seats in the Legislative Assembly of each State and Union territory will also increase similarly, “over and above the number of seats existing immediately before such delimitation”.
The new Bill, accompanied by a fresh Delimitation Bill, proposes to increase the number of Lok Sabha seats in each State by 50%, while the maximum strength of the lower House will rise from the current 550 to 850. If these Bills are passed by Parliament in its special sittings from November 30 to December 3, the path to immediate delimitation will open, which will also bring into force the 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha.
Amendments to Articles 81 and 82, which mandate the size and distribution of Lok Sabha seats among the States, propose to extend a sunset clause for the existing proportion until 2051.
The existing provision in Article 82 that says that “until the relevant figures for the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published, it shall not be necessary to readjust” the distribution of seats is being amended in the Bill and will be changed to read “until the year 2051”.
Article 82 currently has two definitions for population: for the purposes of distribution among States, the 1971 population; and for the purposes of delimitation of individual constituencies within the States, the 2001 Census. The proposed amendment will extend the sunset clause to “until the year 2051”, but the reference to the 1971 Census has been dropped.
The Bill proposes that the distribution among States will be determined “in accordance with Article 334A”, while the boundaries of individual constituencies will be determined by the “latest published census figures available on the date of the commencement of the Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-second Amendment) Act, 2026”.

Clashes mar European games as Macron condemns violence
- Published
Violent clashes marred a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French president Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.
There were also incidents at games between Turkish side Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Be'er-Sheva in Georgia and Sunderland's 1-1 home draw with Poland's Jagiellonia Bialystok.
In Marseille, the build-up to the Europa League match at the Stade Velodrome was affected by incidents in the stands, including the throwing of projectiles and flares between the two sets of supporters.
With 10 minutes to go until kick-off, several Marseille fans ran from a home stand, appearing to pursue a group of Levski Sofia supporters.
They breached the stand designated for away fans, which housed around 500 supporters of the Bulgarian domestic champions.
"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," said the Marseille police prefecture. "Six others were treated on site for various wounds."
Macron spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev about the incidents, with the French president condemning "with the utmost force these acts of violence, which have no place in sport or in public space", and reassured him that "these acts would not go unpunished".
According to news agency Reuters, Radev thanked Macron for his personal involvement following the "attack on Bulgarian citizens" and for the medical assistance provided to the victims.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova said she found video footage of the incidents "shocking" in a statement posted on social media.
"The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world," she added.
"Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety."
Ligue 1 club Marseille said it was "working to understand the precise circumstances of these incidents".
The police source said all the people injured were Bulgarian and there was "no information at this stage regarding any arrests".
Security personnel managed to restore calm, allowing the game to kick-off on time, although there were a few further flare-ups between the fans, notably during the half-time break in a match Marseille won 1-0.
"It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football," said Levski Sofia coach Julio Velazquez
Marseille boss Bruno Genesio added: "We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable."
Meanwhile, the Turkish Football Federation has strongly condemned the "unacceptable" actions of Georgian police towards Besiktas fans who unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during their Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er-Sheva.
Besiktas say they have lodged a complaint with European football's governing body Uefa over "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.
The match had been moved from Istanbul to Batumi, Georgia for safety and security reasons but had to be suspended in the 25th minute after clashes involving Besiktas supporters and local police.
Both the officiating team and the Besiktas players left the field, but play was able to resume 30 minutes later.
Besiktas won the match 2-1.
"We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the Uefa Europa League match," said a statement from the Turkish federation.
Turkish outlet NTV reported that Georgian police had gone into the stands and used pepper spray on the Besiktas fans.
The report added that there were anti-Israeli chants from the Turkish fans and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters to try to calm matters before play restarted.
Hakan Fidan, Turkey's minister of foreign affairs, spoke to his Georgian counterpart Maka Botchorishvili following the incident.
"All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights," a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
At Sunderland, there were crowd disturbances after Jagiellonia Bialystok fans were found in areas of the Stadium of Light with home fans, despite Uefa having imposed an away supporter ban for the Europa League game.
Police and stewards attended some disruption early on during the match.

Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
- Published
As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.
She is thinking about getting around more easily.
The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.
For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.
"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.
But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.
It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.
Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.
The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.
The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.
But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?
The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.
Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.
"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza
"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."
DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.
A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.
The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.
The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.
The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.
At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.
When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.
The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.
Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.
LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.
For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.
"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.
Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.
But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.
"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."
Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.
"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.
The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.
Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.
"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.
But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.
The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.
"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."
For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.
State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.
LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.
"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.
"I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.
Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing.
"Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.
But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?
Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas.
The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.
The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups.
"The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst
"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."
At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.
"We want the partnership to support local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.
Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.
There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.
While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere.
"When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.
Areias shares that concern.
"We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.
Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life.
For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.
But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.
Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.

By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history.
No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi, soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years.
As it turns out, Belonging does not read as incendiary. It errs, rather, towards discretion and legacy-building. It is also, at its best, a heartbreaking story of love and loss.
Gandhi’s voice is measured and generally frill-free. Flourishes do accompany the meet-cute at a Greek restaurant in Cambridge in the mid-1960s that sets off the story. “That January Sunday, which was to change my life,” she writes, “the sky [was] a beautiful azure dotted with puffy white clouds as in a Tiepolo fresco.” The introduction to fellow student Rajiv Gandhi was “a bolt of lightning”.
And, as in a film, there is parental resistance. Sonia’s father, a businessman who worked in construction in a small Italian town, is a second world war veteran, nicknamed Maino the Lion. A 1998 New Yorker profile by Patrick French, briefly a collaborator on Belonging, had him down as “an unrepentant fascist” until his death. Well, was he? We don’t get to find out. Wherever expedient, Gandhi maintains her strategic silence.
Stefano Maino, at any rate, is “padre padrone” – literally, “father master”. When he hears about his middle daughter’s love interest, he brings “his fist down on his writing table” with a shout of “Basta!” And yet, he buys her a ticket to India the moment she turns 21.
On the boy’s side is the person who would come to be described as the world’s most powerful woman, Indira Gandhi, the daughter of India’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. Barely has Sonia landed in Delhi than Indira decides the pair must wed (the news reaches the Mainos via radio; Signor Maino stays away). Indira then manages Sonia’s first pregnancy, directs the name-giving ceremony – you get the picture. Gandhi refers to her, factually, as “my mother-in-law”, but, subverting the stereotype, she becomes a devoted daughter. Walking us through her induction into elite Indian family life, she draws an affectionate portrait of this formidable 20th-century figure.
But family and party allegiance are a distorting lens through which to view history. Charged events, such as Indira’s crushing of a huge railway strike, acquire a benign gloss. The 21 tumultuous months of the 1975 Emergency – which saw members of the opposition arrested, civil liberties curtailed, the press censored, while a despotic nepo-baby (Sanjay, Indira’s younger son) ran amok – are rendered with a brisk calm. Tenderness is reserved for the repercussions on the family in its subsequent period out of power.
Sanjay’s death at 33, just after Indira’s return to power in 1980, leaves the matriarch broken. “In her eyes [Rajiv] was the only one who could come to her rescue.” Gandhi does not interrogate the hereditary approach to democratic politics, but she does recount, affectingly, the fight to protect herself and Rajiv – a commercial pilot with no greater ambitions – and their two children from the inferno.
In the book’s strongest scene, she waits disoriented in a crowded hospital in 1984, “shivering under my dressing gown”, having ferried her mother-in-law’s bullet-ridden body there. Indira was slain by her Sikh bodyguards in revenge for ordering the army into the Golden Temple, Sikhism’s holiest site. As Rajiv embraces her with the words “they want me to be sworn in as prime minister”, Gandhi feels “a rage welling up deep inside me”. “They will kill you too!” she says. “They will kill me anyway,” he replies. The “they” is unspecified, and gives these pages an air of foretold tragedy.
Rajiv’s eventful term plays out under this death cloud. It starts with a pogrom against Sikhs, spearheaded by Congress leaders. Gandhi goes some length to eulogise her husband’s tenure: in reality, it was a troubled and contradictory record. Rajiv was 40, severely underqualified, and grieving. Miscalculations abounded, among them clumsy religious manoeuvring that played into the Hindu-nationalist BJP’s hands, and a military entanglement in Sri Lanka designed to end the civil war with Tamil separatists.
And that death cloud never blows way. The children are withdrawn from school; Gandhi, perpetually anxious, finds her hands trembling in public; Rajiv is once shot at. When he loses the election his successor vindictively withdraws his special security cover. Their son Rahul (the current leader of the opposition) predicts the worst. At a rally in Tamil Nadu in 1991, a Tamil Tiger operative makes to place a garland around Rajiv, then 46, with explosives strapped around her body.
The graphic photograph of the aftermath of that scene is seared into Indian memory. Thanks to the vigilance of her children, Gandhi has never seen it. “I had become the child to be protected, they the parents,” she writes, in a wrenching section. Years later, when she collapses in Japan, a nurse is startled to find her grown children lying on either side of her on the small hospital bed.
Gandhi’s first reaction on hearing the news about Rajiv? “I wanted to die.” Gradually though, she picks up the smithereens of her life. As the remaining Gandhi elder, she picks up the pieces of the splintering Congress party, too.There are few parallels to a life as singular as this. A century ago, Congress had its first foreign-born female president, the British theosophist Annie Besant; farther afield, Janet Jagan, the American-born Jewish wife of Cheddi Jagan herself became president of Guyana – but both women were political activists to begin with. Gandhi, in her words, “had no right – except for the fact that I carried the family name”.
The exhortations to Gandhi to take over the party reveal plenty about Congress culture, and they are eventually successful: the spectator becomes the player. We watch her bone up on her Hindi, lead campaigns, stitch up alliances (including with a party sympathetic to the Tamil Tigers), and combat the BJP, which brands her, among other things, a “Monica Lewinsky” who would establish a “Rome Raj”. In 2004, she leads an alliance of parties to victory.
To her children’s horror, Gandhi is badgered into nearly accepting the post of prime minister. Instead she handpicks a candidate, Manmohan Singh, while keeping charge of the party (eventually leading it for a staggering 22 years) and chairing the ruling coalition as well as an advisory council that keeps a hand on policy levers.
“It had been my choice to become Indian,” she reflects after the long night of the soul that leads her to decline the premiership – a source of fascinated speculation over the years. “I made it out of love for a man, but that love came to encompass his family and his country. And it was this love for India that had demanded the most from me.”
Belonging comes into its own when unpacking those demands, and showing the transition from grief to its successor emotion, resilience.

Republican wants FBI and CIA answers before questioning Nvidia chief
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Penn., on Nvidia CEO's upcoming House committee interview
Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia with President Trump's backing. But the questions surrounding the AI chipmaker and its ties to China are far from settled.
U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staff there is no evidence that Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with the Nvidia chief, was a Chinese spy or intelligence asset, according to a person familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to speak about a closed-door briefing.
There is also no evidence that she initiated the affair to collect intelligence for China's government, the person told NPR's Ryan Lucas on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the matter. She is, however, believed to have passed along information after the affair began.
Trump has said he helped arrange Huang's return as CEO, and Nvidia's board maintains that his reinstatement presents no national security risk. Some Republican lawmakers, however, want to understand how those conclusions were reached.
Speaking to Morning Edition on Wednesday, before NPR obtained the new information, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., said he wants to hear from the FBI and CIA before Huang appears before House lawmakers next week.
For Fitzpatrick, a former FBI special agent who sits on the House Intelligence Committee, the inquiry begins with what federal authorities knew and whether they warned the Nvidia chief of potential espionage threats.
"What briefings did they give? When did they give them?" he asked.
Huang's reinstatement, Fitzpatrick said, should not put those questions to rest.
"The public is rightly concerned, and they deserve answers," he said.
Fitzpatrick also wants to hear from Attorney General Todd Blanche, who on Tuesday described Nvidia as a good corporate citizen, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department faces questions over Nvidia's chip exports to China.
"Anytime you do an investigation, you follow the facts wherever they lead, and you report those facts with unimpeachable integrity," Fitzpatrick said. "You leave no stone unturned."
The debate over Huang's reinstatement extends beyond Washington.
In Silicon Valley, his return has alarmed women and advocates who have spent years pushing for a better workplace culture, renewing questions about the limits of executive accountability.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”

UN warns hunger will deepen in the Middle East
The United Nations warns that hunger is expected to worsen in 16 countries over the next six months, with Sudan and Yemen facing the gravest risks
CAIRO -- Hunger is expected to worsen in 16 countries over the next six months, with war-torn Sudan and Yemen among five nations facing the gravest risk, the United Nations’ food agencies warned Friday. The agencies pointed to conflict, soaring fuel costs linked to war in the Middle East and steep cuts in aid.
The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Program's Hunger Hotspots report covers December through May 2026.
It places Sudan, Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northern Nigeria at the highest level of concern. All five have appeared on the list repeatedly since 2022. The Palestinian territories were moved down one level following the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, though 67% of Gaza’s population still faces crisis-level hunger or worse, and the report warned that the gains were fragile.
In Sudan, a risk of famine is expected to persist through January in 13 areas of North Darfur and South Kordofan, the report said. Nearly 19.5 million people, or 41% of the population, faced crisis-level hunger or worse in the latest nationwide analysis. In two displacement camps in South Darfur’s Eastern Jebel Marra, acute malnutrition rates exceeded the threshold for famine.
Sorghum prices in Sudan more than doubled in a year, driven by the fighting and by higher fuel costs tied to the Middle East conflict. Diesel prices have also more than doubled from a year earlier because of the Middle East conflict, according to the report.
Drought linked to El Niño — a natural warming of Pacific Ocean water that disrupts weather worldwide — has added to the strain, affecting up to 55% of cropland in Sennar state and 70% in Gedaref, two of Sudan’s main farming states.
FAO Deputy Director-General Beth Bechdol told The Associated Press that El Niño-linked drought poses a major threat to Sudan on top of the war, compounding the conflict’s toll on food production.
In Yemen, the report said, hunger is likely to worsen as fighting that resumed in July spreads across multiple fronts.
The country has been at war since 2014, when the Iran-backed Houthi rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year.
The encirclement of the southwestern city of Taiz has created siegelike conditions there, and more than 300,000 people have been displaced since the escalation began, mostly in Taiz, Lahj and Aden provinces. In government-held areas, 1.8 million people face emergency levels of hunger, up from 1.6 million in the previous analysis.
No recent assessment exists for areas held by the Houthis, which have become harder for aid groups to reach as the conflict has intensified. The last nationwide projection, which ran through February, found 18.3 million people, more than half the population, in crisis or worse.
Bechdol said the main obstacles to reaching Yemenis in need were political rather than geographic. She noted that staff from other U.N. agencies had been detained. The Houthis still hold 73 U.N. staffers, including eight from the U.N. human rights office.
Yemen relies heavily on imported food and fuel, and the report warned that attacks on Red Sea shipping threaten that lifeline. Shipping is now disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Black Sea. Gulf fertilizer shipments remain largely halted.
Aid has fallen sharply as major donors have pulled back funding. Food and nutrition assistance to the five countries at the highest level of concern dropped by about 62% between 2022 and 2025, and by 79% in Yemen. Shifts among donor governments in recent years have taken billions of dollars out of humanitarian and development funding, leaving agencies unable to reach as many people as before, Bechdol said.
The predictability of funding matters as much as the amount, Bechdol said, because aid for farmers must arrive during the planting and harvest periods. With El Niño forecasts in hand, she said, agencies should be prepositioning seeds and protecting livestock before disaster strikes, rather than responding to one crisis after another.
“When that window is lost, you don’t get it back,” she said. “We’re funding losses and we’re funding damage.”

Good morning. We’ve got a “Beaver Moon” today. And, of course, there’s Thanksgiving later this week. Here’s a poem for both and neither.
An FDA milestone for limb girdle muscular dystrophy
Yesterday the FDA approved the first drug to treat limb girdle muscular dystrophy, a broad collection of progressive muscle conditions that has long received scant attention from physicians and drug developers. The drug, developed by BridgeBio, is specifically approved for patients with a subtype of the disease that the company estimates affects 2,000 to 3,000 patients in the U.S. and 4,000 to 5,000 in Europe.
“I’m pretty excited about it,” Nicholas Johnson, an LGMD specialist at Virginia Commonwealth University, told STAT’s Jason Mast. “It does appear that they had actually surprisingly robust effects on clinical outcome measures… and it also looks like it’s incredibly safe, so that’s a win-win.” Read more on the approval.
Why Barbara Kingsolver stopped signing books
The Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist Barbara Kingsolver was learning to play hand drums when her fingers started curling in on themselves. She was diagnosed with a genetic condition called Dupuytren contracture, in which the tissue of a person’s palm thickens and tightens, pulling on the fingers.
While the condition is genetic, doctors believe that the gene needs to be turned on in some way — either through age or perhaps a trauma. The drums may have been Kingsolver’s trigger, according to her hand surgeon at the University of Virginia, Bobby Chhabra.
The condition quickly began to impact her work. As a sort of celebrity author, Kingsolver’s book signings are no small feat. “The way I have to do it is sign 60,000 books — that’s an actual figure,” Kingsolver said at a media briefing with UVA on Monday. “It involves hours every day of clenching a pen. And every time I did that, I’d have to go in for another surgery.”
Kingsolver has stopped signing books en masse, but she bristles when people recommend speech-to-text technology for her writing. “This is the way I write, and I need hands,” she said. “As long as I’ve got them, and as long as I can keep them, I’m going to keep writing books.”
4.9 million
In June 2026, that’s how many menopause hormone therapy medications were dispensed to cisgender women in the U.S. between the ages of 40 and 74. It’s a major increase — 141% — from the roughly 2.1 million meds dispensed monthly between July 2023 and February 2024. That’s according to an analysis of national data published last week in JAMA.
The study found that dispensing rose before and after the FDA’s removal of the black box warning in November 2025. Menopause and its precursor, perimenopause, received a flood of attention in those years, reflected in a still-booming business.
AI offers hope in the Last Frontier
Stroke is the fourth-leading cause of death in the U.S., the majority caused by occlusions that block blood flow to the brain. Survival rates are significantly worse for rural patients, and in Alaska, the challenges sound almost insurmountable.
There are five neurointerventionalists in the entire state who can extract clots. Sometimes Alaskans arrive at their village clinics by snow machine or dogsled. Every minute is precious in the aftermath of a stroke, but it can take several hours to arrange a plane, airlift a patient to the airport in Anchorage, and deliver them by ambulance to one of those specialists.
“The distances that we have to cross are enormous. The weather that we have to face is awful. Resource availability is so low,” said Kelly Isaacs, the stroke program manager at Providence Alaska Medical Center in Anchorage.
That’s why, in 2023, a small network of hospitals agreed to use the same AI software to triage stroke patients and get them to the right care faster. STAT’s Katie Palmer reported on how it’s going and what the future of stroke care looks like in Alaska.
The pros and cons of routine PSA screening
A systematic review published yesterday in Annals of Internal Medicine provides important insight into the cost-benefit profile of routine PSA screening. According to the findings from nearly 800,000 men in 13 randomized trials with follow-up for about two decades, routine screening every two to four years between the ages of 55 and 69 led to fewer cases of metastatic disease and prostate cancer deaths. However, increased screening was also linked with an increased risk of false positives (about 150 per 1,000) as well as overdiagnosis (about 20 cases per 1,000).
The review is especially timely. Earlier this month, the American Cancer Society updated its prostate cancer screening guidelines, recommending that men at average risk be tested every two years for prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels in the blood. Routine PSA screening had gone out of favor since 2010 specifically because of the problems identified in the review, though new evidence linking it to reduced disease-specific mortality led to reconsidering the approach. — Annalisa Merelli
‘I worry how easily we can grow used to being alone’
Second-year medical student Brian Zhang is what he calls a “class-goer,” meaning he, and most of his classmates, show up physically to class each day. But in a new First Opinion essay, he notes that preclinical lecture attendance among medical schools has been declining nationally since the pandemic.
“Hard workers are remarkable at hiding stress. Intelligent people are good at forgetting to be kind to themselves,” Zhang writes. “Class gives us a place, an excuse, not only to struggle through challenging coursework in real time together, but be part of one another’s lives.” Read more.

Grocery stores and supermarkets recorded 4.15 billion transactions through the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) in October 2026, accounting for nearly 26% of all merchant payments, according to data from the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).
Overall, UPI merchant transactions rose 5.7% month-on-month to 16.09 billion in October, while their value increased 9.4% to Rs 9.71 lakh crore.
Compared with October 2025, transaction volume grew 23.5%, while transaction value increased 17.6%. These figures cover payments to merchants and exclude person-to-person transfers.
Groceries and restaurants lead in transaction volume
Grocery stores and supermarkets recorded more than twice the transaction volume of fast-food restaurants, the second-largest merchant category by volume.
The three leading categories were:
- Groceries and supermarkets: 4.15 billion transactions, up 5.3% from September and 26.8% from October 2025.
- Fast-food restaurants: 1.60 billion transactions.
- Other eating places and restaurants: 1.35 billion transactions.
Together, these categories accounted for approximately 44% of October’s merchant transactions. NPCI classifies fast-food restaurants and other eating places under separate merchant category codes.
Groceries narrowly surpass debt collection in transaction valueGrocery stores and supermarkets also led among individually identified merchant categories by transaction value, closely followed by debt collection agencies.
- Groceries and supermarkets: Rs 90,225.75 crore, up 7.1% from September, with an average payment of approximately Rs 217.
- Debt collection agencies: Rs 88,360.49 crore, up 15.9%, with an average payment of approximately Rs 3,547.
- Securities brokers and dealers: Rs 82,775.86 crore, up 11.7%.
- Service stations: Rs 46,154.29 crore, up 8.9%.
- Online marketplaces: Rs 12,387.56 crore, up 42.5%.
Among the ten highest-value named categories, debt collection agencies recorded the largest monthly increase in payment value, adding Rs 12,115.96 crore. Online marketplaces registered the highest percentage growth.
Despite groceries leading in both volume and value among named categories, the average payment to debt collection agencies was more than 16 times higher than that to grocery stores.
However, NPCI groups Rs 4.30 lakh crore, or 44.3% of total merchant payment value, under its “Others” classification. Since this combines multiple merchant categories, the rankings apply only to individually identified categories.

Yosano, Kyoto Pref. – For several centuries, daily life on the Tango Peninsula in northern Kyoto Prefecture had a single, inescapable noise as its soundtrack: the clatter of looms weaving silk thread.
Since the early 18th century, the region about two hours north of Japan’s ancient capital has been home to an industry central to the production of silk crepe, the primary material of kimono. In the postwar boom, the sound of the looms was the sound of money itself: Locals called it “gachaman,” a portmanteau of “gachan” (an onomatopoeia for the loom’s sound), and “man” (the Japanese term for ¥10,000), because each mechanical beat was said to earn another stack of cash. At its peak in 1973, the region produced enough fabric to make roughly 9 million kimono a year.
The epicenter of this industry was a bustling street in the town of Yosano so central to the industry it earned the name “Chirimen Kaido” — literally, Silk Crepe Road.
