- The claim that U.S. President Donald Trump offered the job of press secretary to Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White, a white man, by mistake, is still under investigation. People said he was supposed to offer it to Dana White, a Black woman who once worked at the U.S. Department of Defense in a communications role.
- It is true that Trump announced he had offered the job of press secretary of the White House to UFC White. It is also true that there is another Dana White who is a communications professional and worked at the Pentagon in 2017 and 2018.
- As speculation about his supposed confusion intensified, Trump said he had offered the job to the UFC CEO in jest.
- Snopes will update this report if and when additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the White House and are awaiting a response.
In November 2026, a rumor made the rounds that U.S. President Donald Trump offered the job of White House press secretary to Ultimate Fighting Championship CEO Dana White, a white man, by mistake. Instead, people said, he was supposed to offer it to a different Dana White, a Black woman who, as part of a career in communications, once worked at the U.S. Department of Defense.
The claim spread on social media, including on Instagram and Facebook. On X, someone said the Dana White who worked at the Pentagon was included on a short list of people for the press secretary post (archived):
The post included a screenshot of White's profile from the Defense Department website.
Meanwhiles, several Snopes readers reached out, seeking to confirm if the president had mixed up the two Whites.
It is true that Trump said he offered the press secretary job to the UFC's White in a Nov. 7, 2026, post on his social network, Truth Social (archived):
"Dana, please take the job!," Trump wrote.
It is also true that a Black woman with the same name has a career as a communications professional that led her to work at the Pentagon in 2017 and 2018, according to her LinkedIn page.
However, it was not clear whether Trump confused the two Dana Whites, and he later said he intended the offer as a joke. For this reason, we left the claim unrated.
We reached out to the White House for clarification and we will update this report should we receive a response.
Trump's post sparks intense speculation
Shortly after Trump announced the job offer on Truth Social, White House Director of Communications Steven Cheung amplified (archived) Trump's post on X, adding, "Hell yeah! Do it,@DanaWhite! It'll just be like old times!"
Meanwhile, the Dana White who worked at the Pentagon posted on LinkedIn (archived) thanking people for their well wishes on her new job, but specifying that she was not the Dana White Trump had offered the job to.
"It is nice for once that, that Dana White is being confused with this Dana White," she wrote.
The UFC's White reportedly turned down the job, CNN reported on Nov. 7, citing unnamed sources.
As people began to speculate that Trump had confused the two Whites, a reporter asked him on Nov. 8 if he had meant to offer the job to the UFC's White or if he was "kidding around." Trump told her the offer had been a joke. A video from The Independent captured the exchange:
This is not the first time Snopes has covered rumors about Trump mixing up people or things with similar names. For example, we confirmed he confused Iceland and Greenland in a speech, despite the White House's denial. We also examined a rumor he mixed up the terms "transgender" and "transistor."

Trump just can’t quit tariffs
What to know about the president’s latest tariffs announcement.
Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is trying to keep its trade war alive with new tariff announcements.
Who’s getting tariffed? Potentially dozens of countries, including China, the EU’s 27 member states, South Korea, and others. If they take effect, the China tariffs would start at 20 percent and could escalate to as high as 40 percent, while EU tariffs would start at 15 percent and could go up from there.
How? The administration is justifying these tariffs on the basis of an investigation into what it alleges are unfair trade practices by the targeted countries — a step it’s taking only after its previous tariffs regime, which attempted to use emergency powers to impose tariffs, was struck down by the Supreme Court.
Despite Wednesday’s announcement, it’s still not entirely clear when the new tariffs will take effect; according to the US trade adviser, Jamieson Greer, it’s unlikely to be sooner than “a couple months from now.”
What’s the context? Courts have struck down two different attempts by the Trump administration to impose a global tariff regime, including the emergency authority the Supreme Court ruled on in February 2026.
Wednesday’s move is part of its attempt to reconstitute that regime using other authorities, joining a sweeping set of tariffs imposed in July over alleged forced-labor concerns. The US is also engaged in a specific trade fight with Canada: In August, President Donald Trump imposed 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian goods after trade talks fell through.
Why does this matter? Tariffs, as my colleague Eric Levitz has reported, don’t work the way the president seems to think; his project is based on a fundamentally incorrect understanding of economics that’s making things more expensive for American consumers.
Despite that fact, Wednesday’s announcement suggests he’s doubling down, despite persistently high inflation, and undeterred by his crushing midterms defeat earlier this month, when voters motivated by affordability turned out to deliver a historic rebuke.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

A Brazilian beach soccer star has become an unlikely bargaining chip in a dispute over an alleged Russian spy who has been sought by both Moscow and Washington.
The Russian government is seeking a prisoner swap involving Letícia “Lelê” Villar, a Brazilian player jailed since July 2025 for bringing hashish into Russia, for Sergey Cherkasov, an alleged spy serving a five-year sentence in Brazil for using false documents, according to an official who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.
Cherkasov was arrested in Brazil in 2022 after after Dutch authorities denied him entry as he sought to take up an internship at the International Criminal Court using a false Brazilian identity.
In 2023, the US government charged Cherkasov, who had previously used his Brazilian passport to move to the US to pursue graduate studies at Johns Hopkins University, with acting as an agent of a Russian intelligence service and later requested his extradition.
Brazilian police found no evidence that Cherkasov, who used the alias Victor Muller Ferreira, spied on the Brazilian government, companies or institutions.
Brazil rejected a US request to extradite Cherkasov after its Supreme Court had approved his eventual transfer to Russia, subject to the completion of proceedings against him in Brazil. In July, the government separately ordered him expelled once he completes his Brazilian sentence or is released by the judiciary.
Villar, meanwhile, has appealed directly to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva for help securing her release. In a letter to Lula this month, she said “there are no words that can express or convey all the suffering, burden and pain I feel being in this place.”
Brazil’s foreign affairs ministry said it has been following the situation and has been providing consular assistance to her and her family. The Justice Ministry said it doesn’t comment on ongoing cases. The Russian Embassy in Brazil and Villar’s lawyer didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Villar, who has played for Brazil’s national team and won multiple international titles at the club level, isn’t the first prominent athlete whose detention in Russia has become entangled in a prisoner exchange. American basketball star Brittney Griner was released in a one-for-one swap in 2022 for Russian arms dealer Viktor Bout. Griner had been sentenced to nine years in prison after customs officials found vape cartridges containing cannabis oil in her luggage at a Moscow airport.
Lula has cultivated a pragmatic and at times warm relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin, potentially giving Brazil room to navigate the dispute. The two leaders most recently spoke for more than an hour by phone in August.

The Best MagSafe Wallets
Featured in this article
The best MagSafe wallets are compact, slim and svelte, and attach securely to your iPhone (or MagSafe-compatible case). These can be handy if you just want to carry a few cards, like your work badge or your train fare, or if you want to forgo carrying a traditional wallet entirely. MagSafe wallets are great for anyone who wants to travel light and needs only a couple of cards at a time. We’ve tested dozens, and our favorites are below.
Read our MagSafe guides for more useful accessory recommendations, including the Best MagSafe Accessories, Best MagSafe Power Banks, Best MagSafe Wireless Chargers, and Best MagSafe Grips.
Updated July 2026: I’ve added new wallets from Moft, ESR, and Journey. I’ve also checked for accuracy throughout.
What Is MagSafe?
MagSafe is Apple’s magnetic technology built into the iPhone 12, iPhone 13, iPhone 14, iPhone 15, iPhone 16, and iPhone 17 ranges (excluding the iPhone 16e). It comprises of a ring of magnets on the back of the phone, and it was developed to create a faster, more precise wireless charging system. Those magnets on the back also connect to different accessories, such as external batteries, car mounts, and wallets.
If you use a case on your iPhone, you will need to make sure it’s also MagSafe (the case itself will have a ring of magnets inside it). This will ensure a proper connection with MagSafe accessories. If you use a non-MagSafe case, the connection will be very weak, and MagSafe products may just slide off your iPhone. We have lots of case recommendations in our guides:
When buying a wallet, make sure it supports MagSafe or Qi2 connections. It should indicate this prominently in the product description. Qi2 is the wireless charging standard, and all MagSafe iPhones support Qi2. Android phones now also support Qi2 and some have magnets inside, like the Google Pixel 10 series.
MagSafe wallets come with the same ring of magnets that allow them to snap onto the back of the iPhone directly or onto a MagSafe or Qi2 case. This gives the wallet a strong and secure hold on your device. The wallets we’ve included in this guide all have the MagSafe seal of approval.
Which iPhones Support MagSafe?
Apple first introduced MagSafe for its iPhones in 2020. The following models support the technology:
- iPhone 12
- iPhone 12 Mini
- iPhone 12 Pro
- iPhone 12 Pro Max
- iPhone 13
- iPhone 13 Mini
- iPhone 13 Pro
- iPhone 13 Pro Max
- iPhone 14
- iPhone 14 Mini
- iPhone 14 Pro
- iPhone 14 Pro Max
- iPhone 15
- iPhone 15 Plus
- iPhone 15 Pro
- iPhone 15 Pro Max
- iPhone 16
- iPhone 16 Plus
- iPhone 16 Pro
- iPhone 16 Pro Max
- iPhone 17
- iPhone 17e
- iPhone 17 Pro
- iPhone 17 Pro Max
- iPhone Air
Do MagSafe Wallets Work With Android Phones?
To use a MagSafe wallet with an Android phone (or the iPhone 16e), you’ll need to use a MagSafe case. Several case manufacturers have started adding a ring of magnets to Android phone cases in order to port over the same magnetic experience native to iPhones. We have guides to cases designed for top Android phone models featuring magnetic options that should play nicely with third-party MagSafe wallets.
Will a MagSafe Wallet Demagnetize My Credit Card?
No, MagSafe will not demagnetize your credit cards. Credit cards have magnetic stripe encoding that’s strong enough to keep them from being demagnetized, and MagSafe wallets in this guide come with a built-in shield designed to keep your cards safe. However, you may run into issues with hotel key cards and some gift cards. Keep those away as a precaution.
How We Test MagSafe Wallets
I use a MagSafe wallet every day as my primary wallet. I check that it snaps onto the iPhone or MagSafe case firmly—and that it doesn’t slide off when taking my phone out of my pocket, bag, or jacket. I also make sure cards fit well into the sleeve and that they don’t fall out. I only recommend wallets that feel durable, are easy to use, and can hold the standard amount of cards (at least two to three).
Other Good MagSafe Wallets
ESR Geo Wallet Stand: Apple’s Find My app lets you track your devices if they’re lost, and ESR’s Geo wallet has it built right into the wallet itself. This is the wallet I’ve been using for the past few weeks, and outside of its Find My capabilities, I love that it strikes a great balance between size and usability. ESR says it can hold up to three cards, but I’ve been using mine with four—three cards plus my ID—and I can get them all out easily. Although having a wallet with magnetic charging pins is weird—the Find My feature requires a battery that lasts three months—you can turn it off if you don’t care for it (but then, maybe just buy a different wallet). It does kind of suck that you need a proprietary charger to recharge your wallet, though. The magnets adhere well to the back of the phone, and you can pop open the wallet and use it as a kickstand. ESR even includes a strap on the back that works as a phone grip.
OtterBox Symmetry Series Cactus Leather MagSafe Wallet: This wallet is nice and simple, thin, lightweight, has a strong hold on my phone case, and offers a dedicated fabric-covered slot at the bottom to push the cards out (I was able to fit three without much trouble). This OtterBox wallet is made from cactus-based leather, which feels nearly as luxurious as real leather. Just know that cactus leather isn’t as eco-friendly as it’s made out to be—these cases are still infused with layers of plastics.
Spigen MagSafe Classic LS Wallet: This cool-looking wallet incorporates design inspiration from the classic Macintosh computers. The gray might seem a little bit drab, but any Apple enthusiast will likely enjoy the nod to the computers of yesteryear. It’s otherwise pretty standard fare, with space for up to three cards. I like the thumb notch, which makes it easy to slide your cards out.
PopSockets Kick-Out PopWallet: This MagSafe wallet has a built-in PopSockets grip, and a hinge so you can kick it out into kickstand mode. It’s simple and works as intended, and might be up your alley if you want a wallet that can do it all. However, I had some trouble getting it to sit correctly, and once it popped off my phone of its own accord. For these reasons, I recommend it with reservations, and think it’d be better if it were a tad more secure—especially since getting it to hold three cards is a bit of a stretch.
Avoid These Wallets
Ohsnap! Snap Grip Wallet: I had high hopes for this one, mainly because of its build quality. The wallet is aluminum, can hold up to eight cards (depending on whether they have raised lettering or not), has MagSafe support, and comes with a grip that doubles as a kickstand. Unfortunately, the grip is made of plastic, and it broke after a short time (it won’t fold properly back into place). The magnetic hold isn’t as strong as other MagSafe wallets, even with a MagSafe-approved case on my phone. None of that is great, especially at this high price.
Benks 600D MagSafe Wallet with Stand: The Benks 600D MagSafe wallet might be made with Kelvar, but it sure doesn’t feel like it. The inside shell is plastic, and after just a day of use, I spotted a crack in that plastic right next to the hinge. Worse, I tried to apply a bit of pressure to see if the hinge would still hold up, which completely warped the MagSafe ring. Even without clear durability problems, this wallet wouldn’t make the top of the list. It’s reasonably priced at $30 and comes in a handful of attractive colors, but it’s limited to just three cards, and there’s no easy way to get them out.
Apple FineWoven MagSafe Case: Any time this wallet is separated from your iPhone, you’ll get an alert and can track it in Apple’s Find My app. It has a single slot that can fit up to three cards, but to take the cards out, you have to remove it from your iPhone and push the cards up via the slot on the back. Unfortunately, Apple’s MagSafe wallets exclusively use the company’s proprietary FineWoven material (made of recycled materials). It’s a commendable effort to reduce reliance on leather production, but several WIRED reviewers have said the material doesn’t hold up all that well after some time.
Journey Loc8 Universal MagSafe Slim Wallet: My cards would slip out of this wallet if I didn’t have it stuffed full, which makes it an obvious “Do Not Recommend” choice when so many other comparable wallets don’t have this problem.

LA school district blocks Google's AI search features
The company has insisted that AI overviews and search are a package deal.
After Google spent the past month telling schools that its search engine and AI were too "deeply integrated" to be separated, one of the biggest school districts in the country ripped them apart nonetheless. The AP reports that Los Angeles Unified School Distict (LAUSD), which enrolls about half a million students, quietly disabled Google's AI Overviews on school-issued devices.
Although LAUSD didn't make a formal announcement, parents and students noticed the missing AI summaries in search results. That prompted a local advocacy group, Schools Beyond Screens LA, to ask parents to send video evidence. The group then received confirmation from the school district that AI Overviews were indeed disabled, albeit without details on the exact method used. (Third-party tools seem a likely candidate.)
The move came after a Nov. 13 meeting of LAUSD's AI committee, where several Schools Beyond Screens members spoke. A few days later, the AI summaries had vanished from school devices. The district describes the change as temporary and about keeping students' experience "age-appropriate and safe."
Earlier this month, Google walked back one policy on AI in schools that had sparked a backlash: switching on its Gemini chatbot by default for many K-12 students. (Google's AI tools will now be opt-in for students.) But at the same time, the company insisted that the connection between search and AI was a different story. Google VP & General Manager of Education, Chris Phillips, told The New York Times that "search and AI are deeply integrated," and that if a district blocked AI, students "will not have access to Search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available."
If that sounds like Google throwing its weight around to justify its massive AI spending, well, some of the company's own workers might agree. Over 500 of them signed a petition earlier this month, asking their employer to reconsider the strict requirements.
If Google doesn't back down, it could be risking a significant loss of business. New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago are all considering switching search engines if it comes to that.

Christmas came on Thanksgiving for Netflix‘s The Hunting Wives, thanks to a fatuous Donald Trump Jr.
Never slow to put his silver foot in his big mouth, the oldest and most ambitious son of El Presidente got very hot under the digital collar early on Turkey Day over a passionate promo for the soapy and streamy MAGA themed series of two women kissing.
In proclaiming “What is wrong with you??? It’s Thanksgiving” on X on November 26 in reply to Netflix, the no stranger to controversy and speculation Don Jr. looks to have handed the Season 2 launch of the Rebecca Cutter created show the kind of publicity even Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters‘ well-funded team can’t buy.
While the First Louche’s outrage may have struck some as reeking of hypocrisy, or at least lacking all self-awareness, the fact is Don Jr’s tweet has been viewed over 7.5 million times since Thanksgiving morning. Add to that, a flood of media coverage from the highbrow to the gutter press and (we see you Fox News) everything in-between and you have yourself a good old fashion water cooler moment.
Watch on Deadline
Starring Brittany Snow and Malin Åkerman as Sophie and Margo, a East Coastnewcomer to an East Texas town and the town’s leading lady, The Hunting Wives, which is based on the May Cobb novel of the same name. With guns, booze, short leather skirts, cowboy boots, MAGA, murder and lot of sex, the show follows Sophie as loses more and more of her old Boston life and more intimate with the scheming Margo, who’s Dermot Mulroney portrayed oil tycoon husband is running for Lone Star State Governor.
Hunting Wives scribe Brandon Zuck took out a shiv of his own against Don Jr. on Instagram, as well as delivering a backhanded compliment. “Just wait until season 3,” he wrote on his IG Story next to a screen shot of Junior’s tweet. That echoes what Cutter said when Netflix announced Season 3 last month. “Buckle up, because Season 3 will be even more scandalous and twisted,” the showrunner stated.
Further add to Jr’s ill-considered pearl clutching, the fact the actual online clip of Snow and Åkerman’s characters making out has itself claimed 36 million views on the (MAGA? Not MAGA?) Elon Musk-owned platform. All of which means the Streisand effect of Little Don’s post cannot have been helpful in pushing Hunting Wives Season 2’s eight episode debt to number #3 in the Netflix charts in less than 24 hours.
Likely not wanting to throw cold water on a good firestorm, Netflix did not respond to Deadline’s request for comment on Little Don’s tweet and the backlash it’s received. But, why would they? As WME Ari’s brother, former White House Chief of Staff and budding 2028 candidate Rahm Emanuel once said: “You never want a serious crisis to go to waste.”
The seriousness of it all aside, for a streamer that has been short of late of big breakout hits, Don Jr’s foot stamping may have proved the spark to set the already well-watched Hunting Wives on fire — in the best way.
Or as Netflix posted on their official feed later on Thanksgiving: “It’s messy is what it is!”
BTW – The Streisand effect comes from the superstar taking photographer Kenneth Adelman to court for $50 million in 2003 for a pic her took of her Malibu home. Barely noticed before the lawsuit, the photo became widely viewed in the aftermath — thereby destroying the whole point of the Funny Girl star’s effort. Fact: No matter how famous you are, or who your Daddy is, when you tell people not to pay attention to something you don’t like — they always will.

Conspiracy theorists claimed the video served as evidence that “lizard people” walk among us. The man in question, Democratic New York City Assemblyman Jordan Wright, reportedly told the New York Post he’s “obviously” a human.
A video circulating online appears to show a man rolling his eyes in a so-called "reptilian" fashion while standing behind New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a news conference.
The clip, which was posted on X, Facebook and other platforms, reignited a decades-old conspiracy theory claiming shape-shifting reptilians secretly hold positions of power, which Snopes has previously reported on.
Snopes readers wrote in to ask if the video was real or generated using artificial intelligence.
This is a real clip of Democratic New York City Assemblyman Jordan Wright, who reportedly told the New York Post that he is "obviously" human.
Wright's eye roll is visible in multiple credible livestreams of the news conference in question, which Mamdani held on Nov. 20 to announce a plan to shutter Rikers Island, the city's largest jail, by 2032.
For example, Wright's eye roll is visible at the timestamp 1:51 in a YouTube livestream posted by the official New York City mayor's office account, whereas USA Today's livestream shows the eye roll at 1:54.
There's no evidence that the livestreams in question were enhanced using AI, nor would there be any reason to do so.
According to the New York Post, Wright said he has "no idea what was going on in that video."
"Obviously I'm a human being, and my humanity can be seen through my legislation like the $4 million for the WE ACT environmental justice center in Harlem," he reportedly told the Post. "I can't speak to any reptiles or aliens."
We reached out to Wright, who assumed office in the New York State Assembly in January 2025, to verify that he spoke to the Post and await a response.
Background on reptilian conspiracy theories 
As we previously reported, the "reptilian" conspiracy theory was popularized in the modern era by David Icke, a British man who is barred from holding events in countries like the Netherlands and Germany over antisemitic conspiracy theories.
According to the UK anti-fascist advocacy group HOPE not hate, "the 'reptilian theory' is just one element of the hugely convoluted narrative Icke has developed over his long career" that promotes longstanding antisemitic tropes.
In the United States, officials have previously examined whether the conspiracy theory was a possible motive for the Nashville Christmas Day 2020 bomber.
There is, of course, no evidence that a secret race of reptilians controls the world.

J&K Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Friday (November 27, 2026) said not a single foot of blacktopping was carried out on the Amarnath route, while referring to the Sheshnag controversy, and accused the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) of “deliberately pitting Hindus and Muslims against each other”.

“The BJP and those carrying the symbol of pen and inkpot [referring to the PDP] are again trying to foment Hindu-Muslim discord over the Amarnath route. They are alleging macadamisation. I challenge them to prove a single foot of blacktopping done on the route. I am ready to face an inquiry. There is a court [Supreme Court] direction to have a 12-feet stretch,” said Mr. Abdullah.
Mr. Abdullah’s statement came days after local parties, religious leaders, environmentalists and civil society bodies reacted sharply to the presence of an earthmover close functioning to the Sheshnag lake situation at an altitude of 11,780 feet on the way to the Amarnath shrine, which is around 20 km away from the spot.
A report prepared by the J&K Forest Department on the viral video, in which an earthmover was seen close to the lake, said, “The activity seen in the video is part of routine annual maintenance operations being undertaken by the Border Roads Organisation [BRO]. No new road construction or fresh alignment is being undertaken.
It is further clarified that the Yatra track runs along the right-hand side of the lake and is situated at a considerable distance from the lake. “It said the lake remains protected and the maintenance activity in question “was not intended to alter its character or ecological integrity”.
“The matter may, therefore, be viewed in its proper context, keeping in view the directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, the safety requirements of the annual pilgrimage and the longstanding nature of the track maintenance operations,” it added, while underlining that the maintenance and improvement of this track is a longstanding exercise undertaken regularly since 2012 and “not a new activity initiated in 2026”.
However, Opposition Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) president Mehbooba Mufti, who was denied permission to visit the spot with police citing security concerns, has asked the government to allow a team of politicians and experts to visit the Sheshnag lake.
“If the Union Territory [UT] government is relying on satellite images to claim that no construction is taking place at Sheshnag, why not allow us to visit the site and see for ourselves? The JCBs wreaking havoc there are visible for all to see. To dispel all doubts, let the Chief Minister depute a team of political leaders and environmentalists to inspect the site and establish the truth. What is there to hide?” said Ms. Mufti.
Meanwhile, referring to the allegations of irregularities in the Finance Accounts Assistant (FAA) examination conducted by the J&K Service Selection Board JKSSB), Mr. Abdullah said, “Political opponents were exploiting the concerns of unemployed youth and creating unnecessary mistrust about the recruitment process. They took out the question paper from the examination hall, used wireless devices and tried to get answers. But they were caught on the spot. They were arrested. The JKSSB should have been praised for it,” said Mr. Abdullah.
Meanwhile, protests in J&K over the JKSSB recruitments continued with protesters demanding postponement of the upcoming examination for the posts of Sub-Inspector “till reformations are carried out”.
The JKSSB had conducted the Finance Accounts Assistant examination on November 15, 2026, for around 600 posts and around 1,62 lakh candidates appear in it.

Podiatrist Heather McGuire always wanted to serve in a clinic in her hometown of Ventura, Calif. Fifteen years after she opened her practice, she is realizing her dream in the community that raised her, treating suburbanites and agricultural workers with diabetes on Medicare.
But McGuire believes that dream may be ending.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ recent update to how Medicare pays physicians cut the payment rate for certain services provided on the same day by 20% when it’s provided by the same physician or practice. McGuire’s practice already operates on extremely thin margins, and she recently shelved a plan to hire another doctor to improve the practice’s exceedingly long wait times.
It could worsen Medicare recipients’ access to specialist care in Ventura, too. Last week, the podiatrist saw a new patient, a woman in her 80s, who waited two and a half months for an appointment to get her heel pain checked out. When the patient arrived, McGuire found that it wasn’t just heel pain. The woman had also developed an ulcer on her other foot during her long appointment wait. Left unchecked, an ulcer in someone with diabetes can lead to amputations.
“I would be paid 20% less for providing potentially lifesaving or limb-saving treatment care for that wound because she also had another complaint at the same visit,” McGuire said.
Podiatrists, dermatologists, and otolaryngologists are among the biggest losers with this change, according to an analysis by the American Medical Association, an advocacy group for physicians. Opponents of the policy, including the AMA, say it will force patients to return for separate appointments, raise out-of-pocket costs, and increase wait times, especially for patients in rural areas who have less access to specialists.
“If you’re running your own small group practice [accepting Medicare patients], can you still financially do that?” said Miranda Franco, a senior policy adviser at the law firm Holland & Knight. “Or are you going to start thinking about, you know, maybe consolidating into a hospital system or private equity to defray some of that financial loss?”
These billing code changes are an attempt to modernize Medicare and reduce administrative burden, a CMS spokesperson said. It is part of the agency’s broader shift away from specialist care and the fee-for-service model, and one of many reimbursement challenges that specialists are contending with.
Not everyone is against the change in payment rates for services rendered on the same day. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission, a nonpartisan group that advises Congress on Medicare, supports it, saying it will remove redundancies and duplicative payments. The Justice Department has also found multiple instances of providers committing fraud through this billing code.
The cuts to payment rates for same-day services were slated to be 50% when first proposed in 2018, before backlash from physicians and patients softened the blow. Under the final rule, effective Jan. 1, 2027, Medicare will pay for the highest-valued same-day service at 100%, then reduce payment for each additional service rendered on the same day by 20% when physicians perform evaluations and other routine outpatient services. CMS argues the lowered rate is justified because providers use less resources — for patient registration, scheduling, and support, for example — when patients are seen and treated on the same day at the same practice.
Amy Hunsberger, a lawyer with Manatt, a legal advisory and consultancy, said the cuts are partly motivated by the statutory requirement that physician payments cannot increase without Congressional approval, forcing Medicare to cut back on expenses as the agency spends more on health care costs.
“You have a balloon that has so much air in it, and when you reduce payment in one area of services, you’re squeezing the balloon on one side, and it pushes payments out to the rest of the balloon,” said Hunsberger. “This balloon is not updated for inflation and relies on continual, almost annual congressional bailouts to get clinicians to some semblance of reasonable payment.”
Because these policy changes apply to the number of claims relating to health care services rendered on the same day and to any specific specialty, it’s unclear how they will impact Medicare beneficiaries. The American Parkinson Disease Association said patients with Parkinson’s disease are worried that it could impact their ability to get outpatient Botox injections that are critical for relieving pain.
McGuire estimates that the policy change will decrease her profits by 6%. The policy goes into effect on Jan. 1. She doesn’t know how much longer her practice will last.
“There are times where I ask myself if I should just close up shop and call it a day, and go find a job at Trader Joe’s or Starbucks, where I can have a reliable income,” she said. “If it wasn’t for the fact that medicine has always been a calling for me and the joy it brings me to take care of patients, I probably would have done that already. But I’m also getting to the point where I don’t think this is financially viable and a long-term solution.”

Jammu, Nov 27: Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Friday accused political opponents of exploiting the emotions of job aspirants and misleading them over the JKSSB recruitment process, claiming that the recent finance accounts assistant examination was conducted fairly and its question paper was not leaked.
Abdullah emphasised that providing government jobs to youth through a fair and transparent process was the government's responsibility, but regretted that politicians were trying to instigate young people for political gains.
"I must say, with deep regret, that politics has become such a dirty game that politicians are constantly looking for opportunities to exploit situations and play with the emotions of the youth. They try to instigate young people and push them towards the wrong path", he said while addressing the issue in Kathua's Bani area.
He alleged that some political leaders, who earlier held responsible positions, were telling aspirants that they could not compete in the Jammu and Kashmir Services Selection Board (JKSSB) examinations.
Referring to allegations of irregularities in the recent Finance Accounts Assistant examination, Abdullah said he had examined the matter in detail and found that the system had functioned properly.
"When I went into the details of the issue concerning the recent Finance Accounts Assistant examination, which is being used to mislead young people these days, I found that there had been no malpractice in the examination and that the system had functioned properly. The paper was not leaked. There was no theft of the question paper, and no ineligible candidates secured jobs", he said.
However, he acknowledged that some candidates had attempted to cheat by taking the question paper outside the examination hall and seeking answers through wireless communication.
"They were caught on the spot and arrested. They were not allowed to continue with the examination," he said.

In 2001, three films challenged familiar conventions of Hindi-language cinema in very different ways.
Farhan Akhtar‘s “Dil Chahta Hai” offered a new screen language for friendship and young adulthood; Ashutosh Gowariker‘s “Lagaan” turned a village cricket match into an epic about resistance; and Madhur Bhandarkar’s “Chandni Bar” took audiences into the largely unseen world of Mumbai’s dance bars. Twenty-five years later, the filmmakers revisited the films and the risks behind them at “The Legendary 25s,” a session at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa moderated by actor and producer Khushboo Sundar.
One thread connected their stories: all three had encountered the expectations of commercial Hindi cinema before finding the conviction to make something different.
Gowariker and Bhandarkar already had films behind them before “Lagaan” and “Chandni Bar” established their identities as filmmakers. Akhtar, making his directorial debut with “Dil Chahta Hai,” said he had not been interested in making a film that conformed to the prevailing Bollywood potboiler template.
For Gowariker, who is also the IFFI festival director this year, the turning point came after his first two films failed. Having initially tried to make commercial entertainers, he realized that “my next film had to be something I believe in, something that I want to make first, and then hope to God that the audience also likes it. So that’s how the genesis of ‘Lagaan’ happened.”
The idea was an unlikely proposition: a period drama built around a cricket match, with villagers taking on the British. Gowariker wanted to make a film about “a group of heroes.” He researched the British Raj, 19th-century life, cricket and village communities before taking the script back to star Aamir Khan, who had initially rejected the premise. Gowariker asked Khan for just three hours to hear the narration of “Lagaan” before deciding. “He heard it. He laughed, he had tears and he said, ‘I definitely want to do this now,'” Gowariker recalled of the film, which went on to receive an Oscar nomination.
Bhandarkar’s route to “Chandni Bar” was rooted in observation. A visit to a dance bar with a friend gave him the subject for the Tabu-starring film, which he researched by visiting bars across Mumbai for six months. “Even if, in retrospect, ‘Chandni Bar’ had not done well at the box office, I would still be happy because this is the cinema which I wanted to make, and this is the world which I’ve seen,” he said.
His interest in underdogs has continued in films such as “Page 3,” “Corporate” and “Fashion,” which examined the worlds of the media, business and fashion respectively. He has also resisted pressure to turn women-centered stories into male-led films for commercial reasons. From Tabu’s vulnerable character in “Chandni Bar” to Raveena Tandon’s politically ambitious woman in “Satta,” he said he is drawn to complex women rather than idealized portrayals. “My movies are basically a mirror to society,” he said.
With “Dil Chahta Hai,” a buddy movie starring Aamir Khan, Saif Ali Khan and Akshaye Khanna, Akhtar set out to bring a more recognizable version of friendship to the screen. He felt Hindi films’ depictions of male friendship did not reflect how people actually spent time together. “The relationship had become cheesy, filmy,” he said. He cited Mansoor Khan’s “Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak” (1988), which he watched as a schoolboy, as an important influence.
Asked specifically about the older-woman romance in “Dil Chahta Hai,” he said the inspiration for the relationship between the characters played by Akshaye Khanna and Dimple Kapadia came “from many crushes that I had on older women, that’s the honest truth.”
The filmmakers also reflected on how cinema is made and judged. Akhtar described a screenplay as “a living, breathing thing,” evolving through contributions from actors and crew members, sometimes well into the edit. Gowariker, discussing acting, said, “The true performance lies in the pauses where you’re not saying anything.”
On the industry’s fixation with box-office numbers, Akhtar said, “Now the conversation is that I heard you had a great weekend. But I would rather know what you thought of the film.” Gowariker described every new film as “a reset to zero,” adding that the yardsticks had shifted over the years, from silver and golden jubilees to 100-day runs and opening weekends, making comparisons across films of different budgets and genres reductive.
Asked what they would change if they could revisit one another’s films, Akhtar said he would leave “Lagaan” untouched, but if he were the producer, he would ask Gowariker to direct it again. Gowariker said he might add a soulful song to “Chandni Bar,” while Bhandarkar said he would find it difficult to remake either “Lagaan” or “Dil Chahta Hai.”
On AI and visual effects, Bhandarkar said, “AI and VFX can certainly enhance the visual experience and expand the possibilities of filmmaking, but they can never replace the human touch.” Akhtar’s advice to younger filmmakers was to draw on their own unique experiences.

Southeast Asian militaries have a modernization problem: They cannot afford to miss the global shift toward drone warfare, particularly after Ukraine demonstrated the importance of cheap unmanned systems and rapid adaptation. And yet some of the most affordable and readily available technology comes from China — and buying it risks creating a dependency that could bring its own dangers.
That leaves the governments of a $4.5 trillion bloc, collectively the world’s fourth-largest economy, trying to hedge their bets on defense hardware between Washington and Beijing, without getting caught in the slipstream of their superpower rivalry.
Thailand — a formal US treaty ally — offers an interesting case study. America is a long-standing military supplier, with more than $3 billion in active sales that include F-16 fighter jet upgrades, helicopters and armored vehicles. Still, it’s the country with the strongest Chinese defense penetration, including battle tanks, naval systems and UAV technology.
Last year’s Thai-Cambodia border war, the worst ever conflict between two members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, offers a real-time indication of how a military simultaneously modernizing with both US and Chinese weapons might fight. Thailand used combat aircraft imported from Sweden and the US, armed with South Korean guided bombs, alongside a locally developed drone based on Chinese technology, while Cambodia employed Chinese rocket systems. At its height, air strikes and artillery exchanges displaced over 600,000 people in Cambodia and some 400,000 in Thailand, with at least 150 killed.
The use of mixed arsenals is likely to become increasingly common in the region. Indonesia operates Chinese- and Turkish-made drones and is purchasing Indian cruise missiles, while the Philippines uses Israeli-made hardware and Australian-supplied systems. Both are adapting their UAV fleets for surveillance and operations in the South China Sea. Drones are also widely used by all sides in Myanmar’s civil war.
Beijing’s role in Southeast Asian military modernization frequently involves technology transfer and local development, making the Chinese origin of the eventual system much less obvious. China is now one of a small group of countries dominating the international military-drone market, along with the US, Israel, Turkey and Iran — and has been particularly important in making armed UAVs available to countries that struggled to obtain American systems.
China’s importance runs deeper than the weapons it sells, though it’s worth noting that it dominates the commercial drone market, worth more than $5 billion annually. Turkey may be the world’s largest exporter of finished military drones, but those rankings obscure Beijing’s grip on the components and supply chains that increasingly underpin drone warfare. Even Ukraine, which has one of the world’s fastest-growing domestic industries, relies on China for 71% of its imports of key inputs.
Everyone is rushing to buy these new systems, and unlike the West, Beijing is far less picky about who it’s selling to. Most nations opting to buy Beijing’s stack aren’t abandoning Western equipment altogether. But it’s clear that the huge boost in military spending globally is also lifting the sale of Chinese technology, said Gerald Mako, an expert on artificial intelligence and autonomous systems governance and a research affiliate at Cambridge University. The implications extend beyond the capabilities of individual weapons systems to technological dependence and the military balance across the Indo-Pacific, he told me.
Since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term, Washington has shifted its priorities toward the Middle East through its war in Iran, and is now more interested in showy meetings with China and Russia than maintaining a stable presence in Southeast Asia. It’s overstating it to say that US military supremacy in Asia is over, however the gap with China is now narrower than ever.
The Lowy Institute’s 2026 Asia Power Index found that the US-Iran conflict, combined with Washington’s pressure on countries to spend more on their own defense, had contributed to a record decline in US diplomatic influence in Asia.
Nations in this part of the world are used to a US that’s distracted by priorities and conflicts elsewhere. But the collateral damage is glaringly visible this time. Iran’s move to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and disrupt fuel supplies should not be underestimated. The Philippines remains under a national energy emergency eight months after it was declared, while every Southeast Asian government has been forced to introduce emergency measures to cushion the impact of the war .China itself has important weaknesses. Its impressive pace of shipbuilding masks a key question about just how conflict-ready Beijing is. It hasn’t fought a major war since invading Vietnam in 1979 — unlike the US, which starts wars with depressing regularity.
It’s too early to say whether more nations are planning to adopt China’s military systems. The impact of winder adoption would certainly be profound and long-lasting. To counter this, the US, South Korea and other exporters should push to develop more affordable systems. They must be able to integrate easily with Asia’s armed forces while ensuring sensitive data is shared securely. The US could also ease its export regulations and expand sales among nations that have struggled to access its drone technology.
There are always options. But with US focus elsewhere, Southeast Asian nations may be left with only one — China — to help them modernize their militaries.

I understand the convenience and space-savings that e-readers bring. My 2011 Kindle Touch goes with me everywhere I carry my travel backpack, but I’m still a softy for physical books when I’m sitting at home on a lazy Sunday. What started as something of a fanfic send-up of LitRPGs has quickly blossomed into a massive sensation of a series filled with far more depth, heart, and character than the initial premise might indicate. Author Matt Dinniman has an accessible style that will grip any reader with a taste for whimsical adventure. Just be warned that if you leave the books under the tree, you might not see much of the recipient until New Year’s.
Two excellent books that help describe how the Internet’s undersea backbone became a globe-spanning reality were published in 2026. Together, they form a great gift pairing for anyone interested in how humanity first achieved near-instantaneous communication across the world’s oceans—and how the first trans-Atlantic telegraph cable paved the way for a global network of subsea data cables that now faces growing risks from geopolitical conflicts.
James Tabor’s Lightning Beneath the Sea dives into the astounding real-life story of how American entrepreneur Cyrus Field, lacking in expertise but driven by personal fervor, set out to achieve peace on Earth by laying a 2,000-mile telegraph cable made of copper across the Atlantic seafloor in 1866.
To pull off the feat, Field managed to convince some of the greatest innovators and scientific luminaries of his day, such as Samuel F.B. Morse, Lord Kelvin, and Michael Faraday, to join his venture. He also refitted the SS Great Eastern steamship, the largest passenger liner ship built to date, as a cable-laying vessel.
That first ocean-spanning telegraph cable gave rise to more such cables for transmitting messages around the world. Eventually copper gave way to a network of subsea fiber-optic cables that became the Internet’s undersea backbone, and the modern world also became interlinked with submarine power cables and underwater pipelines for carrying oil and gas.
But all that undersea infrastructure is now facing growing danger from the threat of deliberate sabotage, as described in Elisabeth Braw’s book Undersea War. Her book provides a sobering but enlightening look at why subsea cables and pipelines are becoming more tempting targets amid rising geopolitical tensions and conflicts—and how governments and companies are responding to recent cable-cutting incidents around the world.
It’s a little-remembered film for most people, but I absolutely love The Burbs. Sure, it’s more Halloween fare than Christmas, but last year I picked The Thing, so clearly “1980s movies for October” is my December viewing MO.
Starring Tom Hanks, Carrie Fisher, and Corey Feldman, this is a dry, hilarious send-up of suburban life with a horror-adjacent mystery that keeps you guessing. (It’s not scary, though.) I hardly ever hear anyone else talk about this movie, but I love it, and it only recently came out in 4K, so I’m taking this opportunity to shout it out.
If you’re a technically minded Ars reader looking for a nice book to snuggle down with over the holidays, David Woods’ How Apollo Flew to the Moon could be just the thing. (There’s also an audiobook version.) Woods has an accessible style that breaks down complex engineering challenges and their solutions into easily digestible chunks that clarify without oversimplifying. He uses that style to take readers on a detailed trip through the machinery of Project Apollo, from the launch facilities and Mission Control all the way to the specific mechanics of how to navigate to and land on the Moon—and, from there, how to return safely to Earth.
Ever wondered about the insane engineering that let the Saturn V’s first stage burn almost 15 tons of fuel every second as it powered the crew into orbit? Or how to pinpoint a spacecraft’s centimeter-precise distance from Earth on its way to the Moon? Or how Apollo crews tracked their own position with stellar navigation, using sextants and star sightings? Or what a REFSMMAT is, or how television transmissions from the Moon worked, or how they got those crazy lunar buggies onto the Moon’s surface? All these questions and more are given beautifully complete and technically satisfying answers, suitable for both the curious layperson and also the interested engineer. Grab this book and stun your family at Christmas with amazing Apollo trivia—as a bonus, you’ll have the knowledge to make your “We never landed on the Moon!” conspiracy theorist uncle so angry that he stops talking and watches football in grumpy silence! Everyone wins!
As someone who grew up in the classic era of 16-bit SNES RPGs, this 40th anniversary tribute to the series’ history is everything I could have ever wanted in a modern entry. For the past couple of years, I’ve been transforming my tiny office into a sanctuary in the evenings, since I do most of my writing (and gaming) in here then. It started with Govee Hexa panels, then came an RGB TV backlight, then colorful smart bulbs for the built-in light fixtures. Under $300
Trek BellBeats digital bike bell and speaker – $125 One of the great things about cycling is the chance to be alone with my thoughts—just me and my bike. But that can be too much of a good thing on longer zone 2 rides and centuries. Sporting the size and shape of an old-school bicycle bell, the Trek BellBeats is a safer alternative to donning headphones while on the bike. BellBeats pair with your phone via Bluetooth and will play music at a volume loud enough to enjoy your tunes or hear navigation prompts, but they are not so loud that the music drowns out traffic (or the radar on your bike computer). They can be mounted on just about any non-aero handlebars, charge over USB-C, and offer up to six hours of playtime. And as a bonus, they double as a bicycle bell.
I use Bluetooth headphones most of the time, but frustratingly, they don’t work with voice chat on the PlayStation 5, and I needed a good-quality headset for my Friday night multiplayer gaming sessions.
I’ve always liked Fractal Design’s PC cases, so I decided to roll the dice on their affordable-for-the-quality, over-ear headphones. They support Bluetooth, but they also have a USB dongle, so they can be used for voice chat on game consoles, too.
I was surprised by how much I like them, and despite buying them just for the PS5, I’ve ended up using them in other contexts. Part of that is because they’re very comfortable, and the design avoids my glasses frames well.
I also like that, although they are gaming headphones with all the expected bells and whistles for that, they don’t have an over-the-top design.
If you’re in the market for mid-range wireless gaming headphones that look like something you could actually wear in public without embarrassment, these fit the bill so far.

Povec C1 Performance Sunglasses – $250 Photochromic sunglasses are incredibly useful for outdoor workouts. Two of the most popular bike trails near me run through forest preserves, and the lighting changes steadily as the forest canopy closes in or spreads out. My default sunglasses are a cheap, $28 pair from Rockbros. Unlike other photochromic glasses, which change tints via a pokey chemical reaction, the Povec C1 uses a battery to switch between tints in a second. All the rider (or runner) needs to do is swipe the right temple and the lenses will darken or lighten almost instantaneously. The C1 charges via a small USB-C port, and the Povec claims 28 days of battery life with four hours of daily usage. Garmin Varia RCT715 radar camera tail light – $300 Last spring, a friend of mine was the victim of a hit-and-run while on a ride. Although she wasn’t seriously hurt, her brand-new bike was totaled. The driver got an unwelcome surprise a couple of days later when the police knocked on his front door and arrested him. My friend was riding with a Garmin Varia RCT715, a combination taillight and radar with a camera. The 1080p/30 fps camera captured the car’s license plate, making it possible for the police to identify the driver. More than 90 percent of my riding is on roads, and I don’t feel fully comfortable without my Varia. I have it paired with my Garmin Edge 1050 bike computer, but it will work with most other brands via ANT+. The Varia detects approaching vehicles at 140 meters, and I have it set to record video starting when a car is detected and for 30 seconds after it passes. Battery life is up to six hours, depending on whether the taillight is solid or flashing, and video is saved on a 16GB microSD memory card.
My YouTube algorithm has recently fed me videos of testers using an angle grinder to cut through decent bike locks in under a minute. I’ve never seen an angle grinder-assisted theft in person, but I’ve seen enough heaps of bike parts around town to know people’s rides are getting jacked somewhere. As someone known to be neurotic about leaving my bike outside my purview, I’m looking for added security measures to ease my stress. The top officials of the trilateral Makkah Defence Alliance on Friday (November 27, 2026) met in Pakistan's capital and reviewed the evolving regional security situation while condemning "persistent and heinous" attacks by Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthi militia on Saudi Arabia.
Comment | A new security triangle emerges with the Makkah Pact
The Makkah defence agreement, signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in August, establishes a framework for collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack against any one of them would be regarded as an attack against all.
The meeting of the third session of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) — the highest decision-making body of the alliance — was held in Islamabad, which was decorated with the flags of Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
Addressing the media after the meeting, which lasted for more than two hours, Pakistan's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said that the three countries reiterated their commitment to the pact, including collective defence, mutual solidarity and respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, Dawn reported.
“The committee reviewed the evolving regional security situation and reaffirmed the determination of the three countries to continue working collectively towards peace, security, and stability,” he said.
He said the committee also reviewed progress towards implementing the decisions taken at the previous meeting of the Makkah Alliance for Defence.
The two previous meetings of the committee — which comprises the foreign and defence ministers and top military officials of the three countries — were held in Istanbul and Riyadh.
Mr. Dar said the three countries agreed to continue consultations to enhance cooperation and coordination among them in areas of mutual interest, and to support efforts towards de-escalation of regional tensions and encourage peaceful dispute resolution.
The three countries condemned the “persistent and heinous” attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, reaffirming their “collective resolve” to continue efforts in safeguarding Saudi Arabia’s security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity in accordance with the “collective defence provisions” in the pact, Mr. Dar said.
He said that the three countries also pledged to strengthen cooperation in defence industries, joint technological development, training and capacity building “with a view to enhancing the collective capabilities and cohesion of their armed forces in order to address mutual security concerns and contribute to peace and security in the region.”
Earlier, a senior official in the Shehbaz Sharif government told PTI that the Foreign and Defence Ministers as well as senior military leaders from the three countries attended the meeting.
"The agenda focused on the practical implementation of the agreement, including standard operating procedures, coordination mechanisms among political, defence and military institutions, intelligence sharing and air defence cooperation, alongside the Houthi conflict and attacks targeting Saudi Arabia," the official said.
He said a joint statement was expected to be issued later.
The federal government announced a public holiday in Islamabad on Friday (November 27) and imposed special movement restrictions in view of the high-level gathering. A local holiday was also declared in Rawalpindi.
On Thursday (November 26), Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said that the Foreign and Defence Ministers of Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan would attend the meeting.
Terming the meeting as "very important,” Mr. Asif said the “continuous turmoil south of Saudi Arabia will obviously be on the agenda."
"Any threat to Saudi Arabia is a threat to Pakistan and Turkiye according to the pact, which is absolutely clear,” Mr. Asif was quoted as saying by Dawn.
A day earlier, Mr. Dar spoke with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi over the phone and exchanged views on the wider regional situation and efforts to promote peace and security in the region.
Saudi Arabia has faced repeated attacks by Yemen's AnsarAllah movement, commonly known as the Houthis, targeting cities, oil installations and shipping routes amid an escalation in the conflict since July.
On Tuesday (November 24), Houthis targeted a tower in the financial district of Saudi Arabia's capital, damaging the building and injuring 11 people, including two Indians and three Nepalese nationals. On Thursday, Saudi Arabia hit western and southwestern Yemen.
During an emergency meeting of the SPDC in Riyadh on October 5, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye agreed to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.
Earlier this month, the Pakistan Army's spokesman, Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, said that his country is ready to take “all necessary defensive measures” to protect Saudi Arabia amid regional tensions.
In an interview with a Saudi newspaper, the spokesman stressed that Islamabad's commitment to the Kingdom's security, sovereignty and territorial integrity "is absolute and non-negotiable”.
He said that Pakistani troops were already stationed in the Kingdom, where they performed various duties, primarily providing defensive support and participating in exercises and military manoeuvres. He, however, did not disclose specific details.

This is an as-told-to essay based on a conversation with Marie Bailey, a real estate agent who has helped over 300 families move from California to Texas. The story has been edited for length and clarity.
I grew up in Orange County and was living in Los Angeles in 2017 when my family decided to move to Prosper, Texas.
The number one reason was the cost of living, and number two was politics. After the 2016 election, it was just so polarizing. Especially in LA, you couldn't say you voted for Trump.
We sold a 1,500-square-foot house in Seal Beach for the same price as the big 5,000-square-foot house we built in Texas, across the street from a five-acre manmade crystal lagoon. Texas was also much more conservative. There are people who are not conservative, but it's not as polarizing. People are much more chill than they were in LA, which was nice because at the end of the day, your neighbor is your neighbor.
I was not a real estate agent when we moved, but I saw a trend coming in 2018. I decided to be a real estate agent who specializes in helping Californians move to Texas. I was able to share my personal experience. People would come out on scouting trips, and I would have everything mapped out for them and help them decide on areas. I helped over 300 families make the move.
After Texas went blue in the midterms, I'm expecting another trend: I think a lot of people are going to move to Florida.
I am personally moving to Florida and expanding my team there. I was already considering a move, but the midterms solidified my decision. And I'm hearing from a lot of clients and other relocators that they are also thinking about making the move.
The midterms were a shock
I started a Facebook page called "Move to Texas from California" that grew to over 45,000 members. I've already changed the page title to "Moving out of California" because more and more people are interested in moving to other places now, like Florida.
The election was a shock to all of us. I was completely, utterly shocked. The next day, everyone in my group was posting, "Well, we might have to rethink where we're going."
I didn't think Texas was going to go blue, but I did feel a shift happening. Texas making abortion illegal was highly unpopular, even with Republicans, as was making pot a felony. People were disenchanted. I think that's why they lost the election. I don't think it was the Californians that moved here. I think it was those extreme laws that they put in place.
I already have one client who has decided not to build a business in Texas after the election. Another client called me and said, "I need to sell my rental house immediately. I don't see this being good for Texas." And that was a native Texan.
They're concerned taxes are going to go up, as well as about proposals related to immigration and gun laws.
Some people feel like, "Great, we already saw this happen in our state, so we're going to have to rethink things."
I don't think there's going to be a huge Exodus yet, but if these policies go through, then a lot of people might move.
I'm moving my business to Florida
The decision to move for me is not all politics. I have family in Florida and, because I think others will be making the move, it's a business decision as well.
I am actively working on getting my Florida real estate license and plan to run a team there. I'm planning to move by the end of the year. I'm still going to manage a team in Texas. It's a lot of work, and moving is stressful, but I'm doing it: moving at the same time as I get my license and build my team.
I'm planning to move near The Villages because there are so many people retiring there. I'll continue to specialize on relocators — people moving to Florida from anywhere.
Beyond politics, I think a lot of people just want to move to Florida because it's amazing. Orlando is the number one travel destination in the world. One thing I really missed in California was Disneyland, so now I can be closer to Disney World.
Texas is still a wonderful place, and I want the best for it no matter what. I hope that turning blue doesn't dissuade businesses from coming to Texas because that really does a lot for the economy.

Mumbai: The Adani Group is seeking government approval to invest in airlines, looking to expand its presence in India’s aviation sector beyond airports, Group chief financial officer Jugeshinder (‘Robbie’) Singh said on Friday. The move is part of a wider expansion plan that will require substantial funding. Group companies are expected to borrow ₹1.3-1.4 trillion annually over the next two financial years, even as the conglomerate looks to raise more capital from domestic and international markets, Singh said. Speaking on the sidelines of the Trust India Debt Capital Market Summit 2026, Singh said India needed a significant increase in airline capacity to serve its untapped passenger potential. Elaborating on the opportunity, he said more than 60 crore people in India have the potential to fly, and the number of daily flights would need to rise nearly tenfold to 30,000 to meet the demand. With rising incomes and a growing pool of potential flyers, India offers a significant opportunity for growth in air travel and airline capacity. “And that’s why we requested the government to at least allow us to invest, so that we can facilitate the development of airlines. Some fund, some other airline company and things like that, or an entrepreneur who wants to go into that space,” Singh said. The Adani Group has the financial capacity to invest ₹4.5-5 trillion annually and expects its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) to triple over the next five years, Singh said. He outlined an investment and fundraising programme spanning infrastructure, energy, data centres and emerging businesses. The group has committed to investing $120 billion over the next five years, with its annual capital expenditure rising from ₹80,000 crore three years ago to ₹1.1 trillion and ₹1.56 trillion in the subsequent years, Singh told reporters. The group can currently execute investments of close to ₹2 trillion annually, although its theoretical investment capacity is considerably higher, he said. “We have the capacity to invest, we can invest if we want, somewhere around ₹4.5 lakh crore to ₹5 lakh crore a year, from a capital point of view. But to complete that much on the ground, we don’t have the capability,” Singh said, pointing to constraints in execution and the infrastructure ecosystem. To finance its expansion, group companies are expected to borrow ₹1.3-1.4 trillion each in FY27 and FY28. Adani Power will remain a significant issuer in both the domestic public and private debt markets, while other group companies are also looking to tap international bond markets. Singh said the group wanted domestic capital markets to account for 70-75% of its total capital over time, compared with around 56% currently. It also plans to continue raising $3-4 billion annually through equity issuances, primarily to diversify its shareholder base rather than meet immediate funding requirements. Foreign trade agreements could indirectly benefit Adani Ports and the group’s airports business by facilitating greater integration of logistics and economic structures between India and other economies, Singh said. On the group’s financial position, Singh said net borrowings would increase by only around $25 billion over five years, after accounting for debt repayments of $25-30 billion, even as EBITDA triples. He added that the group’s aggregate credit quality had improved from around A-/BBB+ levels in 2018-19 to AA+ currently. Data centres are emerging as another major investment area. Singh said the group had drawn down $900 million against an existing $3 billion financing arrangement, with overall funding agreements expected to reach around $10 billion over the next four years. The group is also exploring opportunities in materials and metals and has expressed interest in entering the airline business. Against this backdrop of expansion, Singh indicated that Adani Airports would be operationally ready for a demerger in calendar year 2027, potentially paving the way for a separate listed entity. “Calendar year 27, we will be ready. Now, what the decision is, that’s for the boards to decide,” he said, clarifying that the proposed route would be a demerger rather than an initial public offering. Adani Airport Holdings was established in 2019 as a subsidiary of Adani Enterprises after the group won concessions to operate six airports. It subsequently acquired a controlling stake in Mumbai International Airport and expanded its portfolio to eight airports with the addition of Navi Mumbai International Airport. Singh said the airport business was approaching readiness for a demerger, having established its ability to fund its own investment programme. Its non-aeronautical revenue share, currently around 60%, was also nearing the targeted range of 60-65%. The airport business has emerged as a significant infrastructure vertical for the group, combining passenger growth with commercial real estate, retail and other non-aeronautical revenue streams. Founded by Gautam Adani in 1988, the Adani Group has grown into a diversified infrastructure conglomerate with 13 listed companies spanning energy, utilities, ports, airports, roads, cement, metals and media. The Election Commission of India (ECI) has fixed a security vulnerability in its website that exposed sensitive personal information and identity documents of registered voters. The flaw was discovered by Reuters during a month-long investigation and reported to the poll body on October 26, 2026. The weakness meant that information such as voters' names, phone numbers, email addresses, date of birth, residential addresses and file paths to uploaded voter identification documents could be accessed via the developer tool of a browser.
The security gap was fixed on Thursday, November 26, after Reuters repeatedly sought a response from the Election Commission. This development comes one month before assembly polls in pivotal states such as Uttar Pradesh, and at a time when the ECI is facing intense questioning on its voter list verification drive. The vulnerability could've been used to harvest voters' personal data in large numbers, security researchers said.
The flaw was connected to the website's call-booking system, which was unveiled in June 2025, according to Reuters. Voters logged in to their accounts and asked for a call from their electorate officer; the browser network tab on the website showed a reference number from their voter registration or information update form.
Using these reference numbers to book calls, Reuters found that the website exposed additional personal details that were not displayed on the main webpage. These comprised personal details, home addresses and file paths to voter-registered ID documents.
The security flaw has been verified by Indian security researchers Karan Saini and Ehraz Ahmed, who studied the report. They said the reference numbers were in a predictable sequence that could enable an attack to guess the numbers and automate the process of gathering sensitive information.
The researchers said cybercriminals could have used publicly available web tools and basic coding knowledge to download identity documents, including passports and national identity cards.
Reuters said that one of its reporters was able to follow the steps to download a copy of his national identity document. It seems the server was trying to check if someone was logged in but failed to verify whether they were allowed to access a certain document, Saini said.
However, Reuters said it could not establish whether anyone had exploited the vulnerability, how long it had existed or how many voters may have been affected.
Reuters first contacted the Election Commission and its three commissioners on October 26, seeking comments on the findings. The institution did not respond to repeated requests.
On Thursday, November 26, an ECI spokesperson told Reuters that the commission's IT division had been asked to examine the issue. Hours later, a review by Reuters and the researchers confirmed that the vulnerability had been addressed. The same approach was no longer available to access sensitive information or document file paths.
Congress spokesman Pawan Khera said the revelations were "deeply alarming" and warned that such exposure could allow for voter information to be targeted for intimidation, profiling and voter suppression.
Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told Reuters that the exposure was accidental. The ECI's website privacy statement also notes that no system is 100% secure.
The incident follows a similar security concern reported in 2019, when researcher Karan Saini found that the commission's online voter search portal was exposing personal information through the browser's network tab.

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.
