The Best Meal Delivery Services and Meal Kits of 2026
Featured in this article
The best meal delivery services and meal kits make your home life easier—and maybe make dinner something to look forward to rather than dread. Our lead tester for this guide, former WIRED Reviews writer Matthew Korfhage, didn’t expect to appreciate meal kits as much as he did, especially since he likes to cook and worked as a food critic on both coasts for more than a decade.
The best meal kits help you climb out of a cooking rut of turning to the same dishes—and the same flavors—over and over. After testing every major meal delivery service over the past two years, we’ve narrowed the field to just a few of the best options for each family and diet. Quite simply, the best meals our testers have eaten from a meal kit come from Marley Spoon, which offers a path to genuinely good home-cooked meals on nights when you might otherwise feel uninspired.
But depending on your priorities, other meal delivery services might be a better option. Home Chef offers the greatest flexibility for busy families while keeping prices affordable. EveryPlate is the best meal kit for people on a tight budget. For a healthful, tailored diet (including an option for true gluten-free meals), we recommend Green Chef. If you’d rather not cook at all, CookUnity is the best prepared-meal delivery service we’ve ever had the pleasure to warm up.
We assessed each meal plan’s recipes, variety, sourcing, ease of preparation, convenience, organization, packaging, ingredient quality, and suitability for different dietary restrictions and needs. We also tested the best new and innovative meal kits for those looking for alternatives to Blue Apron's or HelloFresh’s long-standing meal delivery services. And not for nothing, we sorted out some often maddeningly nontransparent pricing.
Be sure to check out our investigation into whether meal kits are sometimes cheaper than groceries when trying out new recipes, and WIRED's related guides, including Best Plant-Based Meal Kits, Best Food Gifts You Can Buy Online, Best Coffee Subscriptions, and Best Delivery Chocolate Boxes.
Updated November 2026: We’re retesting the kits in this guide, including special holiday offerings from meal kit makers like Marley Spoon. We’ve added some notes reflecting this in relevant sections and checked for accuracy throughout.
More Meal Kits We Liked
These meal kits former WIRED reviewer and lead tester Matthew Korhage tried didn’t make his final cut, but he still recommends them. Here are his thoughts on what he liked and what held them back.
Sunbasket (~$16 per serving): Sunbasket focuses heavily on fresh, organic ingredients and offers a whole lot of variety in its menus. Its recipes are attentive to saucing and to basic good cooking techniques such as deglazing. Like Hungryroot, it also offers breakfasts and snacks to supplement meal options with little extras such as coconut yogurt and sous-vide egg bites. The meal kit also lets you filter out allergen-containing items. WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loved the flexibility and add-ons. During a recent test, I enjoyed an excellent Greek chicken and orzo salad dish—and, wonder of wonders, the advertised prep time was actually the actual prep time (about 30 minutes). The focus on organic ingredients does make Sunbasket one of the more expensive meal kit options, and the annual Thanksgiving meal kit has remained a lovely and welcome extravagance at $200.
Gardencup ($11 to $15 a serving): Gardencup is a little like having the whole menu of Sweetgreen sent to your house or office, except in cylindrical form. Basically, you pick out premade salads, soups, and snacks, and they come in little cups—fresh, lovely, crisp, and ready to eat. I found it to be a great way to keep myself eating healthy when there’s no time to cook at the office (or the home office), which is typically when DoorDash or freezer-meal temptations run wild. It remains among the healthiest prepared food delivery options I know. I even tested Gardencup as a salad option during a cyclospora parasite scare, in part because I missed salad and because Gardencup could attest that it did not use lettuce from any of the suspected sources of the outbreak. The salads remained delicious and delivered a shocking amount of protein in the meat options. But variety of options is not a strong suit. A slackened focus on local sourcing, plus limited transparency on sourcing—Gardencup will disclose only that it sources its greens in the salad belt from Salinas, California, to Yuma, Arizona—has kept Gardencup in my honorable mentions.
Factor ($13 to $17 a serving): Factor is a prepared-meal delivery plan run by HelloFresh, with ready-to-eat meals that look a lot like TV dinners. But there’s a twist: The trays have never been frozen. They were made fresh in a commissary kitchen and shipped with cold packs, so they taste kind of like restaurant leftovers. Consistently, Factor ranks among the best-tasting prepared meal plans I’ve tested, especially when I shrug off the directions and reheat my meals in an air fryer instead of a microwave. Proteins and high-protein meals are a strong suit. Proteins maintain their texture quite well, especially a truffled filet mignon I couldn’t believe I microwaved. Still, some meals, especially carb-avoidant or keto meals, are oddly mushy, while meals centered on proteins and whole starches, like potatoes or rice, alongside veggies like green beans or Brussels sprouts, tended to fare quite well. So did stir-fry-style meals. My gluten-free colleague, Scott Gilbertson, wrote that he had the best luck with Factor’s Mexican fare. I do wish Factor would shed its reliance on the microwave: When I went off-script and used a Ninja Crispi air fryer or convection oven, I had much better results than with the nuker. But non-air-fryer ovens do not seem to offer the same improvement. Like many ready-to-eat meals, it’s a bit more expensive than the kits you cook yourself. Oh, and as a bonus? Factor has a really, truly delicious selection of nutrient-amped juice bottles and elderberry “shots.” I could pretty much subsist on their probiotic cucumber-pineapple green juice.
Fuel Meals ($14 to $15 a serving): Fuel Meals are a no-nonsense, no-fluff, no-added-ingredients, pure-protein-packed nutritive meal plan, with many meals paleo-friendly. Some of Fuel’s meals had as few as five ingredients, essentially the macronutrients plus a modicum of oil and salt. A large percentage of meals are marked gluten-free or dairy-free. Does all this mean less flavor? It can. The meals are also often not beautiful, dominated by a large and no-fuss serving of protein. But Fuel’s meal service offers an admirable focus, especially for those bulking up or watching carbs. Meals are substantive, usually topping 600 calories and 40 grams of protein, with no added sugar, fatty dairy, or carb-heavy filler. As a baby gym rat, I appreciate how clear the macros are, but some meals are high in sodium and often aren’t deficit-friendly.
Wildgrain ($13 to $17 per loaf or box of pastries): This is less a meal delivery service than a way to step up a home meal. Wildgrain is a monthly bread-box delivery: You receive par-baked bread and pastries from small bakeries across the country. This is pretty much the same process that likely happens at local restaurants when your warm bread basket comes out: It’s not quite as high-quality as you’d get directly from an artisan bakery, if you live in places with artisan bakeries. But it’s also as fresh as it gets, and I had a great experience testing the box in October 2025, especially the sourdough breads, which are perfect for large meals with houseguests. You finish baking at home, so you end up with ultra-fresh bread, biscuits, doughnuts, or scones that are still warm and crisp from the oven. A Wildgrain subscription arrives as a monthly box filled with four, six, or 12 items, ranging from a full sourdough loaf or fresh-made pasta to a pack of six doughnuts or four large croissants. Basically, you build your own box each month, choosing from healthy sourdough or pasta and decadent pastries.
Thistle ($12 to $15 per meal): A prior top pick for solo diners with individually prepared dishes that require little to no prep, Thistle is mostly a plant-based meal kit—but you can add sustainable meats to any otherwise vegan meal for $3. It’s also so local and seasonal that the West and East Coasts have different menus, and the whole middle of the country, except Chicago, gets none. (You can check your zip code here to see if you can get delivery.) Former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So used Thistle to get herself to eat more vegetables and thus avoid a life of rickets and/or scurvy. Portions are generous enough to split among meals, and in a nice turn for those who hate disposing of boxes, Thistle's drivers will pick up the cooler bag that held last week’s meal and replace it with a new one full of food. WIRED reviewer Molly Higgins’s favorite meals from Thistle were a whirlwind of textures, including a Mexican-inspired corn and poblano chile salad with adobo pinto beans and a chilled, lemongrass-accented rice noodle bowl that mixed spice, tang, crisp veggies, and deep umami from mushrooms and seaweed. She still dreams about it sometimes. Breakfasts are available at a lower cost, as low as $9.
Tovala (~$9 to $15 a serving): It’s not every day you get to try something that feels super new. Tovala offers perhaps the most ambitious ready-to-heat and prepared-meal delivery solution I’ve seen: the meal kits come with an oven! Unlike the sogginess of many prepared meals, Tovala's recipes come in little foil pans with recipes custom-designed for a small steam oven. The results are often delicious—as was the case during my testing with a sweet chili–glazed salmon with pickled veg and noodles—and the QR code scanning function makes each recipe seamless to cook. Stick with the meal plan for six weeks, and you get a quite affordable and powerful little convection oven, toaster, and steamer. A previous flaw was that Tovala only offered single-serve meals. But as of early 2026, at least four or five meals a week offer two to four servings, making the meal delivery service much more useful to families and couples—and much more economical per serving. But note that it’s also one of the most sodium-filled meal services I’ve tested.
Gobble ($17 a serving): Formerly the top pick for fast-cooked meals, Gobble previously wowed with speed-demon dishes that also offered interesting and worldly flavors. Indeed, the most recent test included Caribbean rondon, an Indonesian peanut curry stir-fry, and steak vierge. But while the flavors have stayed interesting, the focus on fast cooking appears to have waned since my colleague Louryn Strampe tested Gobble. Cook time estimates aren’t printed on the recipe cards, but meals took as long as 30 minutes. For now, Hungryroot has taken the fast-cooking crown. For small households, Gobble is also among the most expensive kits. At most portions, prices approach $17 a serving plus shipping.
Nurture Life ($6 to $7 per serving): Nurture Life is like a restaurant kids’ menu in ready-to-eat meal-kit form. We loved the idea behind this fresh-made, never-frozen delivery meal plan when we tested it a few years back: toddler- and slightly bigger kid-friendly meals, from mac and cheese to spaghetti and meatballs to myriad variations on the chicken nugget. Meal prices have dipped to reasonable levels lately, so it's likely due for a retest—and each plate includes vegetables alongside the greatest hits.
Veestro ($7 to $14 per serving): WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe enjoyed Veestro as a ready-to-eat vegan option, with premade meals delivered fresh and freezable for extra meals on hand in a pinch. The service offers a number of filters for other dietary requirements, and satisfying taste and texture—which is not always a guarantee on ready-to-eat meals. Veestro has updated its menu and offerings since the last time WIRED tested, including several snacky soup offerings. The online menu interface, which lets you sort by ingredients and filter out unwanted ones, is among the best I’ve seen.
Splendid Spoon ($9 to $13 per serving): Splendid Spoon is a nutrition delivery kit that offers plant-based smoothies, soups, bowls, noodles, and shots. Everything here is natural and free of gluten or GMOs, including spaghetti and plant-based “meatballs.” WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe has a big yen for the smoothies in particular ($10 apiece), but wasn’t quite prepared for the intensity of a lemon juice shot that comes as part of a five-pack of dense 3-ounce superfoods.
ModifyHealth ($10 to $13 per serving): The idea behind ModifyHealth is that food can be medicine. Sometimes, I’ll admit, it tasted like it was designed purely for nutrition rather than flavor. ModifyHealth is a prepared meal delivery service tailored to people who need a heart-healthy, low-carb, or low-FODMAP diet to avoid dire digestive or health consequences. GLP-1 weight-loss plans are also available for people with diabetes or others. Gluten-free meals are attested to be made in an entirely gluten-free facility. The meals were simple, benign, and low-sodium but also sometimes a little soggy—a common problem with prepared meals. The plastic top of the packaging was also difficult to disengage from the base of each meal tray—a problem when the plastic is hot after a turn in the microwave. But here’s what I do like: The meals are carefully tailored with consultation from dietitians to help people for whom food can be a source of fear or pain. Many insurance plans cover an additional service: one-on-one dietitian consultation. ModifyHealth also offers a free consultation for those just trying to figure out which diet plan is right for them. For those with IBS in particular, this remains the most focused food plan I’ve seen.
Daily Harvest (prices vary): Daily Harvest is another ready-to-eat meal delivery service specializing in dietary restrictions: plant-based, plus gluten- and dairy-free. Smoothies are a highlight, as are harvest bowls, pastas, and grains. Calories are low. Ingredients are often inventive. The meal’s a lifesaver for the solo vegan eater without time to prep a meal, and WIRED’s Molly Higgins appreciated that the meals mostly relied on the natural flavors of the vegetables themselves, accented with flavors like curry and lemongrass. As with many frozen meals, however, texture wasn't a strong suit. The ready-to-blend smoothies are great, though.
A Meal Kit We Don’t Recommend
Sakara Life ($30+ per serving): Sakara Life offers plant-based weekly menus in fresh, prepared portions, with greens, flavorful sauces, all-organic ingredients, and textural add-ons like seeds or berries. But it’s among the most expensive meal plans we’ve tested, and neither WIRED reviewer who tried it really cottoned to it. Louryn Strampe questioned the science behind detox and cleanse health claims, calling Sakara “egregiously expensive” and full of “bitter veggies and tart fruits.” Molly Higgins, meanwhile, said Sakara Life’s tinctures and metabolism supplements didn’t agree with her system, and that the mostly raw-food plan made her long for “human food.”
Frequently Asked Questions
Are Meal Delivery Services Worth It?
If you're talking raw materials by the pound—meat, zucchini, rice, noodles—meal kits will, of course, cost more than buying food at grocery stores. It's a service, after all, with added value above simple ingredient cost. Unless you've got quite expensive taste, you'll easily be able to make delicious meals at home for less than the $7 to $14 a serving that a meal kit will cost. That said, this doesn't necessarily mean that meal kits are expensive for what they offer. We conducted an experiment, trying to re-create four different meal-kit meals by going to my local grocery store—buying every ingredient provided by the meal kit. Turns out, if you don't have the right sauces and spices at home already, it's very difficult to re-create these tasty meals at grocery stores for less than they cost from a meal kit, in part because you'll most likely have to buy full containers of sauces and spices instead of preportioned ingredients,
So, is HelloFresh worth it compared to a grocery store? Caveats are in order: For staple ingredients and spices you'll use in multiple recipes, the grocery store is, of course, cheaper. Once you buy a container of paprika for an individual recipe, it will also be there for future recipes, whereas meal-kit spices are portioned for the meal. So the real answer is that meal kits can be a quite economical way of trying out a new recipe, or a new style of cooking, without larding up your fridge with condiments you won't use again. For ingredients you'd use less commonly, a meal kit can reduce waste and spoilage, and maybe even compete on price for an individual meal.
If your comparison point is takeout, well, the best meal delivery services on this list will almost certainly be cheaper and more nutritious. We've found that a meal kit in the fridge tends to be a good motivator to cook a nutritious meal—and thus can save both the money and the cholesterol.
To really save on cost, some people like to keep testing out the trial offers and discounts. Much like mattress-in-a-box companies, meal kit companies usually have a running promotion. Usually this takes the form of a trial discount price that'll drop your cost by half or more on the first box, in hopes you'll like the service enough to keep it on at full price.
A meal kit a few times a week ends up balancing out well: It's a motivating factor to eat better, and it means that when you do go to the grocery store, you can do so less mindlessly and more purposefully, given that you've got a few meals' worth of ingredients in the fridge. It's also had the side effect of broadening your culinary toolkit, keeping you from getting stuck in the same ruts.
That said, it's a set grocery expense and not necessarily a small one. Tossing or recycling cold packs and boxes gets tiring. And depending on the time of year, you may prefer shopping in person for what's seasonal and local, when produce is at its peak—an experience you don't get from a meal kit, or from grocery delivery, for that matter. If you're cooking for a bigger household, meal kits can also lose their utility quite quickly. A convenient option for two can become a much larger expense for a family of four or six.
Can I Pause a Meal Kit Service When I Go on Vacation?
Pretty much every meal kit tested has an option to pause subscriptions—and there's no particular limit to how often you can do this. The main thing is to be sure that you've canceled with enough lead time. Some services let you cancel or pause delivery as late as the Friday before a Monday delivery. HelloFresh requires five days' notice. Marley Spoon requires six days, based on one of our testers’ home locations. Some, like Hungryroot, may lock in next week's order as early as the previous Monday, depending on where you live. Read your terms of service, and act accordingly.
For those with more variable schedules, the service we'd probably recommend is Blue Apron, which changed its model last year and no longer locks in delivery each week. You'll have to remember to order a box each week, which can be done where I am with four days' notice.
How to Optimize Meal Kits
Don't order too many meals per week: You know the old John Lennon line: Life is what happens when you're busy, out eating a random burrito, then thinking guiltily about the meal kit at home in your fridge. Aspirations are great, but don't order more meals than you're likely to make, or you'll be sad. Err on the side of caution. Order just enough meals per week that making yourself a recipe from your HelloFresh or Home Chef box is still a delight and a convenience and an overall boon to your life—not an obligation. If you're somewhat improvisational and impulsive, three meals a week is the sweet spot. The prospect of a few easy meals usually saves me from an impulse weeknight DoorDash.
Make room in your fridge: Meal kits take the place of a lot of grocery shopping. But they're also a lot of food, and a lot to keep organized. Clear a tall enough space in the fridge to put the whole meal kit box in, after pulling out the cold packs: This way, you're not left worrying about which groceries belong to the meal kit, and you won't lose any ingredients. You can just pull the whole box out when you want to make a meal. That said, some plans like Home Chef, HelloFresh, and Green Chef are very good at organizing each meal into its own separate bag. An added bonus from these more organized plans is that you'll be able to use less space in your fridge. Over time, this will matter.
Check the recipe cards to make sure you have everything you need to make a recipe: Most meal kits expect that you'll have certain staple ingredients in your home, usually including oil and butter. Recipes also have requirements for cookware. Check this before you start a recipe. Nothing worse than realizing you need a stick of butter on step 5, with carrots already browning in the oven.
Remember, you owe nothing to the recipe: Meal kit services hire recipe developers, and on the best meal kits, these chefs have spent a lot of time optimizing each recipe. But you owe them nothing—nothing! Add spices, change steps, season food when you want to season it. Meal kits can teach you a lot about how to make a good meal and shake you out of tired culinary routines. But it's your meal. Make it how you like. Have fun.
How Do We Test Meal Kits?
Chances are, whatever time of the year, a WIRED reviewer is testing a meal kit. We constantly cycle through various meal kits, testing and retesting each of our top picks at least once a year—and often multiple times, especially when each meal delivery service changes its format or expands to new offerings.
When possible, we order at least four meals a week from each meal delivery service. We prepare meals according to instructions and see how well they go. If we deviate from instructions out of horror or curiosity or a simple sense of culinary propriety, we note this and tell you why.
We check prep times against what's advertised (rarely an exercise in honesty!) and take note of any inconsistencies, vagueness, or frustration in the recipe card instructions. Convenience matters: If a meal kit needlessly recommends a nonstick pan, we like it less—especially if the recipe says to heat that pan before adding food, or later mentions browned fond. Nonstick isn’t cast iron or carbon; there’s no fond. If rice portions are too small, we'll flag that.
The quality and freshness of the produce are important, and the same goes for the meat. Where possible, we look into where the meat was sourced, and check on the reputation, safety, and standards of the meat suppliers. If a meal kit swears it's gluten-free, we verify this—calling certifying organizations where relevant.
We usually try to order as varied a menu as possible. We might check in on gluten-free meals, a seafood item, a vegetarian item, and white and dark meat items. We might also test a Midwestern-style hot dish or Southern meat-and-two alongside meals that draw (or attempt to draw) from global inspirations. Sometimes we test the same meal kit multiple times for different dietary needs, or call in multiple testers to do so. WIRED's vegan tester, Molly Higgins, often tests the same meal kit as lead tester Matthew Korfhate does, but with a different focus.

Owono did not deserve 12-match ban - Pique
- Published
FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique says goalkeeper Jesus Owono did not deserve the 12-match suspension he received following his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel late on in the second-tier match between Andorra and Tenerife on 2 November.
De Miguel died the following day, aged 30, and a disciplinary committee from the Spanish football federation confirmed Owono's ban last week.
In a video posted on social media, Pique said players past and present, plus coaches and other goalkeepers, felt the incident was "an accident".
The former Spain and Barcelona defender added: "I truly believe that imposing the maximum sanction on Jesus for this action puts him in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened."
- Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision 
  - Published3 November
- Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban 
  - Published3 days ago
The 12-match suspension was the maximum punishment Owono, 25, could have received, as the disciplinary committee could only consider the offence on the pitch and not "the tragic outcome of the incident".
Following the decision, Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera said he accepted the regulations do not specifically account for what happened, but acknowledged the ban "might feel light".
Pique also highlighted a recent on-field incident in Spain, when Albacete winger Jose Corpas accidentally kicked Sabadell midfielder Quadri Liameed in the head during a Spanish second division match.
Nigerian Liameed was knocked unconscious but was later discharged from hospital following medical checks, while Spaniard Corpas was shown a straight red card and handed a three-match ban.
"Fortunately Quadri is fine, the consequences in this case were not fatal, and the committee decided to sanction Corpas with three matches," Pique said.
"With all this, my reflection is: what is being sanctioned, the action or the consequences?"
Owono has withdrawn from Equatorial Guinea's squad for Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Zimbabwe this month, and Pique said it was unlikely he would return to action as soon as his suspension is served.
He added: "Jesus is going to need far more than 12 matches before he is available and able to compete.
"No sanction is going to bring [De Miguel] back to us."

Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its social media accounts and radio station.
The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.
"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.
It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.
A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.
Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.
Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?
Significant defeats
Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.
Both have suffered major defeats, lost leaders and faced years of international pressure. IS, which once controlled vast areas of Iraq and Syria, lost its last territorial stronghold in 2019. But jihadism hasn't gone away.
Africa is now the main battleground for jihadism, with al-Qaeda's powerful branches, JNIM in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger) and al-Shabab in Somalia, fighting long-running insurgencies. IS, its bitter rival, has active branches in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Sahel, Mozambique and Somalia.
One major source of inspiration, and envy, whether jihadists admit it or not, is Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa. The former IS and then al-Qaeda commander was once wanted by the US but rose to power in Syria in December 2024 and was welcomed by Western leaders.
Once known by his militant nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, he led the jihadist group Nusra Front - initially linked to IS and then al-Qaeda - and later the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).
He gradually broke ties with both IS and al-Qaeda and distanced himself from their calls for global jihad.
Instead, he focused on Syria, building a local power base in the north-western Idlib province.
What surprised everyone was his growing willingness to work with non-Islamist groups and engage with foreign powers. As HTS advanced on Damascus, its leadership sought to reassure the international community, reaching out even to Russia, a key ally of then-president Bashar al-Assad, to allay fears of an Islamist takeover.
That pragmatism, combined with favourable geopolitical conditions - including a weaker Russia and Iran - helped him take power in Syria.
But the sight of him being welcomed by world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, was even more remarkable.
During Sharaa's visit to the White House in November 2025, Trump sprayed him with his own branded cologne, jokingly asked how many wives he had and praised him as a "very strong leader".
For some jihadists, Sharaa's success has been inspiring. Others, however, see his actions as a betrayal of everything they believe in.
IS has declared jihad against Syria's new Islamist government, branding Sharaa and his officials "apostates", and has carried out attacks against government forces on that basis. Other hardline clerics have taken a similar stance, but have stopped short of openly calling for jihad against Sharaa.
The divide between hardline jihadists and their more pragmatic counterparts has fuelled a bitter online debate since 2025, with rival voices trading accusations of betrayal and even publishing competing books to defend their positions.
For hardliners, going too far can mean abandoning their core beliefs. This might include holding back from imposing their strict version of Islamic law, accepting "man-made" laws or a constitution, taking part in elections, working with non-Islamist groups, or building ties with governments they consider "infidel".
Another source of inspiration for jihadists was the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021, as it showed that an Islamist movement could eventually take control of a country after years of fighting Western-backed forces. It engaged local groups, slowly secured power across the country, used international diplomacy, and bided its time before taking the capital, Kabul, in a lightning offensive.
A means to an end?
Two groups are especially worth watching: al-Qaeda's branches in Mali and Somalia.
In late April, al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, known as JNIM, showed considerable pragmatism by joining forces with nationalist Tuareg separatists - whom it had occasionally fought - to launch a major offensive that threatened Mali's military rulers. It even went as far as to call the Tuaregs "brothers".
But it's not just JNIM's growing military strength that's attracting attention. It's also how the group is presenting itself.
Its propaganda once prominently featured al-Qaeda's leaders, slogans and calls for global jihad. Since late 2024, however, its videos have dropped the familiar al-Qaeda branding.
And instead of talking about global Muslim causes, JNIM has increasingly focused on local problems, portraying itself as a defender of ordinary people against corrupt and abusive rulers.
It has repeatedly accused Mali's military government and its Russian allies of killing civilians and making people's lives worse.
In April, it appealed to "all sincere patriots" to help build a "new Mali", promising security, justice and prosperity alongside Islamic law.
It has even suggested it could have "balanced relations" with Russia, despite the fact they're fighting Russian forces backing Mali's government. Its wording echoed that of HTS to Russia as it advanced on Damascus.
There are parallels with Sharaa's approach in Syria: build local alliances, reassure potential enemies and avoid giving outside powers a reason to intervene.
Africa security specialist Aman Bezreh sees similarities between the two groups, but says JNIM's shift may take time.
"JNIM has indeed shown signs of pragmatism similar to HTS", she says. "However, its rebranding has progressed more slowly because the group is simultaneously focused on expanding into new territories and recruiting from diverse pools."
Taliban v Sharaa
The debate over which path to follow is also taking place within JNIM's leadership, according to Wassim Nasr, a France 24 journalist and jihadism expert.
He says one camp favours the Taliban's approach of taking power through force with minimal concessions. The other, which he says currently has the upper hand, favours an approach closer to that of Syria's HTS - making compromises and building wider alliances to gain power more quickly.
Nasr believes JNIM may borrow from both models, but that a break with al-Qaeda is inevitable as a result of its political evolution.
Like JNIM, al-Shabab in Somalia appears willing to make deals with former enemies.
According to Abdullahi Guji, BBC Monitoring's Somalia specialist, al-Shabab reached a truce in October with a powerful Somali tribe, the Ma'awisley, whose fighters had been at the forefront of the fight against the group.
The tribe has since withdrawn its fighters from the front line, dealing a serious blow to the government's campaign against jihadists, says Guji.
Guji believes the group may soon have a chance to test whether it can seize power and establish itself as an alternative government across wider parts of the country.
African Union forces are withdrawing from Somalia amid funding cuts and the approaching end of their mandate in December. Meanwhile, the Somali government is facing political crises and rebellions, creating vulnerabilities al-Shabab could exploit, he adds.
There's another reason some jihadists may see an opportunity to expand: they believe Western governments have bigger fish to fry.
With the war in Ukraine, US-Iran conflict in the Middle East and growing rivalries with China and Russia, fighting jihadists is no longer the priority it was after 9/11.
The US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban's return to power, followed by Sharaa's rise in Syria, have reinforced that belief.
Colin Clarke, executive director of the Soufan Center, a non-profit research group that focuses on security, says some jihadist groups have learnt that avoiding confrontation with the US can help them escape Western military action and "live to fight another day".
That doesn't mean the West has stopped fighting terrorism. But if jihadists believe it is distracted or less willing to intervene, they may feel emboldened to pursue power.
History lessons
Unlike its fiercely uncompromising rival IS, al-Qaeda has long shown some flexibility in pursuing its goals. But history offers a warning.
After the 2011 Arab uprisings, which largely sidelined al-Qaeda, affiliated jihadist groups in Yemen, Libya and Tunisia began using the name Ansar al-Sharia (Supporters of Sharia) to win local support without carrying the al-Qaeda brand.
In Mali in 2012, al-Qaeda leaders advised jihadists who had seized the north alongside Tuareg separatists not to rush into imposing strict Islamic rules. Instead, they urged them to work with local allies, avoid alienating communities and play down their al-Qaeda links.
The message wasn't to give up their ambitions. It was to show strategic patience until the time was right. That same thinking could be at work today.

So are these groups really changing their ambitions, or just their tactics? Even those advocating compromise aren't necessarily abandoning their dream of establishing a state ruled by their strict interpretation of Islamic law.
Clarke wonders whether this more pragmatic approach could be a "Trojan horse strategy" – a way for jihadist groups to gain power without giving up their longer-term goals.
"The big question is whether being in power actually moderates these groups, or whether they're simply changing their tactics to survive and strengthen their position," he says.
But not everyone is changing tactics.
IS remains firmly committed to its global ambitions and rejects compromise. Al-Qaeda's Yemen branch, AQAP, continues to call for attacks against the US and Israel, and urges "lone wolf" attacks against Western and Jewish targets.
And it's too early to say whether groups like JNIM and al-Shabab will follow the Taliban or Syrian examples, and whether they're willing to make compromises.
Some jihadist groups may become more focused on local politics as they face the challenges of governing. Others may simply be hiding their wider ambitions until they're strong enough to pursue them.
The global jihadist dream may have failed, but jihadism is far from finished.

1Password says it was hacked but users' vaults are safe
The attacker wasn't able to access people's vaults.
1Password has admitted that an attacker was able to infiltrate its system and steal some customer data, but it has assured users in its announcement that their vaults and logins are safe. On November 19, the company started investigating signs that an employee's corporate GitHub account had been compromised. The company found that the attacker used that account to access its source code and inject malicious code to its backend.
The attacker was then able to download customers' data, including people's names and email addresses, the dates their accounts were created and their last sign-in times. They were also able to steal users' public keys, but 1Password said it has no impact to their security. While the bad actor was also able to steal source code from the company itself, it doesn't contain customer data.
"Your vault data, the items in them, and the keys that protect them are safe and were not affected," 1Password wrote. The service doesn't have access to users' actual passwords, recovery keys and other credentials, as well as the secret keys that protect their vaults, so the attacker wasn't able to steal them. Since discovering the breach, 1Password has revoked the stolen token, disabled the affected GitHub account and added new detection tools for similar attacks.
While 1Password said that users' vaults remain safe, the company still advises being vigilant when it comes to phishing attempts. It warned that since users' emails were compromised in the breach, they could be used in attempts to grab people's passwords through fake account recovery and invitation emails.

India, EU have compelling reasons to work more closely, says top EU official Olof Skoog
India and the European Union have strong reasons to deepen cooperation amid concerns over China and Russia, and US trade policies, EU official Olof Skoog says.
India and the European Union (EU), which believe in a rules-based order, freedom of navigation and respect for sovereignty, have compelling reasons to work more closely together against the backdrop of the actions of China and Russia or even the trade policies of the US, EU deputy secretary general for political affairs Olof Skoog said on Friday.
Skoog, who is in New Delhi for political consultations in the run-up to the signing of the India-EU free trade agreement (FTA) next month, welcomed India’s proposals for ending the hostilities but noted in an interview with HT that most such moves had been blocked by Russia. Following are edited excerpts of the interview:
India and the EU are in the final stages of concluding their FTA. How is the process proceeding and how important is it to have a bilateral investment agreement in place too?
The FTA is going well, meaning the 27 countries are looking at it and then there will be a signature on December 16. After that, we have the scrutiny by the European Parliament. Although the ratification comes after that, there could still be preliminary applications as of next year. But the agreement is the agreement, then it’s the implementation. There’s a lot that needs to be worked out. Both India and the EU have the task of enticing, informing and getting the private sector and others to start applying it and understand how to draw the benefits.
On the investment agreement — in order for this new relationship to release potential dividends on both sides, there needs to be predictability, safety and security for investments. There, I think there’s still work to be done. We can create conditions for the private sector to invest more, but for them to drink out of that hole, they need to know their investment is safe for the foreseeable future. That’s where the investment agreement comes in; that’s an integral part of releasing the full potential of the FTA.
How has the India-EU Security and Defence Partnership (SDP) changed cooperation in this sector? How is defence industrial collaboration progressing?
I think we’re already seeing the effects of the SDP in the sense that there’s much more intense consultations, but some of that is to really start working much more intensely and regularly together to understand our security policy environment here, in Europe and everything in between. It’s about starting and deepening that dialogue, and also cooperating more, to pass the same messages to our other partners in the world, those who are less inclined to trust international law and the multilateral system. It’s not very visible but you can already feel that the relationship has moved to a different quality. There’s much less of ‘We cannot discuss this, please don’t touch on that’ — all those sensitivities are gone and we’re in a trusted relationship that means a lot.
But more on tangible results — we are conceptually going from buyer-seller to cooperation on hard security. India and the EU find ourselves in a situation where we’re trying to break some dependencies of the past. That doesn’t mean we are closing in on ourselves — we do it with reliable, predictable partners, but also ones that bring technical added value to what we’re trying to do.
SDP partners have a privileged entry point into that kind of defence cooperation. The EU can provide conditions for that, including loans that we provide to member states, which they can use for big investments and for inviting partners that have SDP agreements, India being one. It opens up new areas of collaboration. Again, it will be up to the defence sector to gauge that added value, both on the Indian side and the European side.
Does India’s long-standing military relationship with Russia act as an impediment?
I don’t know, but certainly, the relationship with Russia is one that is very integral to our dialogue with India. Not just because we are monitoring Russia’s influence around the world, but because the qualitative deterioration of security in Europe isn’t just limited to Russian aggression against Ukraine; [it is] actually a very aggressive posture by Russia vis-a-vis EU countries. Anything that is seen to facilitate that posture of Russia, materially or politically, is very sensitive to Europe. That’s a conversation we’re certainly having but that’s as far as I can see the implications of it.
Do you see the EU working more closely with India on matters such as hybrid threats, disinformation or protection of critical infrastructure?
That’s definitely part of the area where we see a need for further cooperation. Both here and in Europe, we see that is a new threat coming in. For democracies such as India and European countries, the role of foreign interference and manipulation of information is one that will always be used to influence elections through misinformation and other means. The more we compare notes of what we’ve seen in Europe — not just in the EU but also in some neighbouring countries like Moldova and Armenia, where traditionally the Russian influence is quite big. I think there’s a playbook there that is advancing very quickly, very sophisticated — and the more we can compare notes and cooperate on that, it’s very important.
We also see that on maritime security, [and undersea cables], there’s been a lot of incidents in the Baltic Sea, and you can say that’s far away from the Indian Ocean, but in a way, it isn’t because it’s all connected. Given how dependent we are economically on this part of the world, it’s an enlightened self-interest to be very involved in maritime security in the Indian Ocean.
One of India’s main concerns in the Indo-Pacific is China’s assertive actions, such as the maritime disputes in the South China Sea. Do you see the EU and India working more closely together to make the Indo-Pacific more secure and more open in terms of trade?
Whether it’s China, Russia, or in some cases the US hitting us both with tariffs etc, based on this fundamental notion that we’re both better off if international law is respected, there’s predictability, there’s free trade, sovereignty and territorial integrity are respected, UNCLOS [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea] is allowed to function and [there is] freedom of navigation — I think we really see eye to eye on all these issues.
Whether it’s China, Russia, or in some cases the US, there’s a lot that speaks to us, to the added value of deeper cooperation between India and the EU. I very much see that happening.
That will also manifest itself in more concrete cooperation, military exercises, port calls by EU member states. It’s true we don’t have a standing navy or army, but we do have joint operations such as Atalanta and Aspides, and they interact in a very positive way with the Indian Navy in the northern Indian Ocean.
It doesn’t mean we go hand-in-hand as we approach China or the others, but we compare notes and share experiences, and then we have our bilateral efforts with China through dialogue for resolving some issues we have in both trade and security.
Just reflecting on the recent trilateral meeting of some global leaders in China, I don’t think the youth in India or in Europe feels this is the kind of leadership that will provide the best options for our future when it comes to climate change, respect for rules or governance of AI. There is a huge craving for a different kind of leadership, one that respects the rules that provide predictability, that stands up for democracy both internally and in the international sphere. That’s why I’m very stimulated by the fact that India and the EU are coming together, because we are really big players, and there are a lot of smaller countries who are looking for that kind of alternative leadership. If we can provide that, I really think it’s extremely encouraging to see this coming together. And my message is just for India to look at the EU as one of its, if not the most, important partners for the future.
How do you view the efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and what do you make of India’s proposals for ending attacks and creating grain corridors?
First of all, we welcome initiatives by India and others to complement some things we’re trying to do, on releasing grain and opening up the Black Sea to supplies for world food security. But I have to be very open with you and say that, so far, all those initiatives have been blocked by Russia.
Russia is expanding and escalating its attacks against Ukraine and the Ukrainian population because of the stalemate on the frontlines, although most recently, Ukraine has gained terrain. To compensate for that, Russia is taking the war to the cities and the civilian population.
The timetable of Russia, and we see that as they approach new rounds of talks in Abu Dhabi or wherever, is that they are just not engaging on anything that could [lead to a] ceasefire or stop the conflict in order to see what a just and sustainable peace could look like.
Unfortunately, the Russian timetable doesn’t coincide with the American one, which tries to achieve results on the negotiating table soon, nor does it coincide with [Europe’s], India’s or Ukraine’s timetable, which is to try to stop the onslaught and bloodshed now.

India’s Gukesh Dommaraju is making his first defense of the world chess championship against fast-rising Uzbek star Javokhir Sindarov over the next three weeks in the affluent Geneva suburb of Cologny. Both players are 20 years old, making it the youngest matchup in the 140-year history of the sport’s most coveted title. But is that all you need to know? What about the format, how much they’re getting paid and why the world’s No 1-ranked player is watching from the sidelines? Read on for all the answers … When and where is the World Chess Championship? The best-of-14-games contest is set to take place from 24 November to 12 December at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, the picturesque enclave overlooking Lake Geneva. The opening ceremony is scheduled for 22 November, with games played once daily from 24 November except for designated rest days on 27 November and 1, 5 and 9 December. It’s the first time a world title match has been held in Switzerland since 2004, when Vladimir Kramnik retained his title by drawing 7-7 with Peter Leko in Brissago, two years before the sport’s rival championships were reunified. Who is Gukesh Dommaraju? Gukesh Dommaraju, commonly known as Gukesh D, was only 18 when he became the 18th and youngest ever undisputed world chess champion by defeating China’s Ding Liren in 2024. An aggressive player known for creating sharp, tactically complex positions aimed at unsettling opponents, the Chennai native rose to international prominence when he became the second-youngest grandmaster in history at the time, aged 12 years and seven months. Five years later he stunned the chess establishment by winning the eight-man Candidates tournament at 17 to secure a world title shot. He went on to win and shatter the age record held by Garry Kasparov, who was 22 when he dethroned Anatoly Karpov in their 1985 rematch in Moscow. His victory made him a national hero in India, where he was mobbed by supporters on his return and feted by prime minister Narendra Modi. But the 20-year-old has struggled badly for form since then, plummeting to No 26 in the world from a career-high ranking of No 3 after an extended string of underwhelming performances. Gukesh Dommaraju receives a hero’s welcome at Chennai airport after becoming the youngest undisputed world chess champion in December 2024. “Clearly so far I’ve not been able to handle it in the best possible way,” Gukesh admitted in a recent interview. “There have been major setbacks ... Obviously there is something with a lot of expectations, a lot of pressure that I’m dealing with and I’ve not found the right way to maybe handle it.” From Bobby Fischer to Magnus Carlsen: 22 of the most famous world chess championship games Read more Who is Javokhir Sindarov? Javokhir Sindarov is an Uzbek prodigy, roughly six months older than Gukesh. Known for his cool-headed precision and ability to mine advantages from seemingly quiet positions, the Tashkent-born grandmaster earned his crack at the world championship with an imperious performance at this year’s Candidates in Cyprus, finishing unbeaten with six wins and eight draws to turn back a stacked field that included longtime stars Fabiano Caruana, Hikaru Nakamura and Anish Giri. The first player from Uzbekistan to challenge for the title, Sindarov has climbed into the world’s top five after a breakthrough 12-month stretch that included winning the Fide World Cup last November in Goa. He enters the biggest match of his life on a tailwind of confidence, having won a four-player rapid tournament in St Louis three weeks ago over Nakamura, Caruana and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, capped by a brilliancy against the world No 2 that showcased his tactical brio. His ascent has added fuel to a remarkable chess boom in Uzbekistan, where he belongs to a golden generation of grandmasters, along with Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Shamsiddin Vokhidov and Nodirbek Yakubboev, who have transformed the central Asian nation into a global powerhouse with two golds and a bronze at the past three Chess Olympiads. Javokhir Sindarov explains his brilliant victory over Hikaru Nakamura to grandmaster Maurice Ashley after their game in St Louis. “This tournament will be the hardest tournament in my life,” Sindarov said in August of his showdown with Gukesh. “I don’t know if I will get a second chance [at the world championship]. It’s hard to play 14 games against the same person in three weeks.” Tale of the tape Where do they rank internationally? Sindarov, ranked 25th in the world a year ago, has climbed to a career-best No 4 with a Fide classical rating of 2782, while Gukesh has slipped to No 26 with a rating of 2710. That makes Gukesh the lowest-ranked reigning world champion of the Elo era, which dates back to 1971, eclipsing the previous low of No 23 set by Ding in 2024. The 22-place gap between them is the widest of any world championship matchup since the title was reunified in 2006. Who is the current world No 1 in chess? Magnus Carlsen holds the top position in Fide’s world rankings with a classical rating of 2823. The 35-year-old Norwegian has been at No 1 for more than 16 years uninterrupted, though that extraordinary reign is suddenly under threat after a disastrous 10-game winless streak last week in Budapest reduced his once-comfortable lead over his nearest rivals to single figures. He was considered the best player on the planet even before removing all doubt against India’s Viswanathan Anand in their 2013 world title clash. If you can name only one chess player active today, chances are it’s him. The youngest undisputed men’s classical world chess champions Carlsen bolstered his claim as the greatest player of any era in 2021 when he crushed Russia’s Ian Nepomniachtchi in his fourth defense by a margin of four wins and no defeats, the most lopsided result in a world championship match since José Raúl Capablanca’s dismantling of Emanuel Lasker exactly 100 years prior. But he decided against defending it for a fifth time before the 2023 cycle, citing a lack of motivation to endure the months-long slog of preparation that world title matches demand. The abdication marked only the second time in history that a holder voluntarily declined to defend his title after Bobby Fischer controversially forfeited the crown ahead of his scheduled 1975 match with Karpov in Manila. Instead, Ding outlasted Nepomniachtchi in a thrilling, sometimes messy scrap for the vacant title, even if critics including Kasparov branded it an “amputated” event without the world’s best player involved. Ding’s reign lasted only 593 days before Gukesh unseated him in Singapore in 2024, taking the decisive 14th game on a catastrophic blunder to claim a 7½–6½ victory and become the first teenager to win the sport’s biggest prize. Carlsen remains active at the highest level, though he’s increasingly shifted his focus away from classical chess toward alternative formats. In February, he defeated Caruana 2½–1½ in Germany to win the Fide freestyle world championship, his eye-watering 21st world title across classical, rapid, blitz and freestyle disciplines. Also known as Fischer Random or Chess960, the variation randomizes the starting positions of the pieces on the back rank, placing a premium on creativity over rote opening preparation. (He’s also gotten married, become a father and is by all accounts pretty good at fantasy football, too.) How do Gukesh and Sindarov match up? Despite being contemporaries, they have played only three times in classical games. Sindarov holds a 2½-½ advantage with two wins and one draw in their lifetime head-to-head, which dates back to their first encounter as tweens at the Moscow Open in 2018. Their most recent meeting happened in January at the prestigious Tata Steel tournament in Wijk aan Zee, where a tense positional struggle gave way to a wild, time-scrambled endgame before the pair settled for a draw after 78 moves. Allow and continue Gukesh’s form has largely gone off the rails since reaching the summit 23 months ago in Singapore. After making it to No 3 in the world with a peak rating of 2794, the Indian suffered a prolonged run of disappointing results, including a joint-last finish at March’s Prague Chess Festival and last-place showings at Norway Chess and the Chennai Grand Masters. He subsequently withdrew from the classical portion of the Grand Chess Tour and had tumbled to No 32 in the rankings by September, when his live rating briefly dipped below the 2700 barrier for the first time in four years, although his performances improved at that month’s Chess Olympiad. Many of the world’s top players have expressed deep pessimism about Gukesh’s chances in Geneva due to his lengthy slump and Sindarov’s sustained upward tick. So too have the bookmakers, who have installed the Uzbek as a clear frontrunner at roughly 1-3 odds despite Gukesh being the champion. Carlsen has described Sindarov as “a pretty significant favorite”, citing the Indian’s tendency to take excessive risks. “His evaluations are way too optimistic,” the world No 1 said recently. “That makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now his confidence hasn’t been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.” Yet one factor in Gukesh’s favor is his firsthand experience in the cauldron of a world championship match, where the intense psychological and physical rigors of facing the same opponent for weeks on end can be as punishing as the chess itself. Caruana, the world No 3 and former world title challenger who pushed Carlsen to the brink in 2018, has cautioned against writing off the champion despite his struggles. “The kind of ability he had – or has, whatever you want to say – it doesn’t disappear overnight,” Caruana said in September. “So, in my opinion, it can reverse at any moment.” Who are their seconds? Neither Gukesh nor Sindarov has publicly disclosed his full team of seconds, the trusted cadre of advisers who help prepare openings and analyze the opponent. That’s not unusual: players tend to keep the identities of their seconds closely guarded before and during a match to avoid revealing clues about the direction of their preparations. But we do know a little bit. Gukesh will again work with Polish grandmaster Grzegorz Gajewski, who led a formidable backroom team during his 2024 title-winning campaign that included five other GMs and analysts from Poland, India and Germany, with additional support from Anand (acting as more of a mentor than a practical second). According to reporting from ChessBase, Sindarov is expected to be working with Ukrainian coach Roman Vidonyak, while the 22-year-old Abdusattorov, the former world rapid champion and current world No 5, revealed on a podcast that he will be in Geneva to help his compatriot prepare. Another Uzbek grandmaster, Mukhiddin Madaminov, has also been mentioned as a member of Sindarov’s team. Photograph: Europe Echecs What’s the prize money for winning the World Chess Championship? The overall prize fund is $2.5m (£1.9m), unchanged from 2024. Each player will receive $200,000 for each game won, including games won by forfeit. What’s left will be split equally between them. If the winner is decided on tiebreakers, the champion receives $1.3m with the runner-up taking home $1.2m. The same split applies if the match finishes 7½–6½ with 13 decisive games or 8–6 with 14 decisive games. Gukesh’s world ranking Each player received a $200,000 advance on their winnings one month before the first game, deducted from the prize fund. The remaining balance will be remitted to the players within 30 working days after the completion of the match. The stakes are particularly high in a sport where even the biggest stars rarely earn seven figures in annual prize money. According to a new ranking published by World Chess, no player has crossed the $1m mark in tournament winnings in 2026, with India’s Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu leading the way on $666,229. Sindarov ranks third with $589,061, while Gukesh sits 48th with just $41,500. The world championship alone will assure its winner at least $1.25m, enough to vault either player to the top of the annual earnings list. What is the schedule and how does the match work? Gukesh and Sindarov will play up to 14 classical games with each player awarded one point for a win and a half-point for a draw. Whoever reaches seven and a half points first will be declared the champion (and no dead rubbers will be played). The time control for each game is 120 minutes per side for the first 40 moves, then 30 minutes for the remainder of the game, with a 30-second increment per move starting with move 41. That means games can stretch beyond seven hours, testing both players’ concentration and endurance. Players are not permitted to agree to a draw before black’s 40th move, a rule designed to discourage short, uneventful games. A draw claim before then is only allowed in the case of threefold repetition or stalemate, subject to approval by the chief arbiter or deputy arbiter. If the score is level after 14 games, a series of tiebreaks will be played on 12 December, starting with four rapid games at 15 minutes per player plus 10 seconds per move. If still tied, the players will contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed if necessary by two blitz games at three minutes plus two seconds. Further single blitz games will be played until a winner emerges. Three of the past five world championship matches have been deadlocked after the classical portion and required tiebreaks: 2016, 2018 and 2023. The complete official regulations can be found here. The World Chess Championship is typically held every two years, though this schedule has varied over time. A 1993 schism between the International Chess Federation (Fide) and the Professional Chess Association (PCA), a breakaway organization formed by Kasparov and British grandmaster Nigel Short, ushered in an era of competing world championship titles. The title was reunified in 2006 when Kramnik held off Bulgaria’s Veselin Topalov 6-6 (2½-1½) amid a bizarre cheating row over bathroom visits known as Toiletgate. Robert Sapolsky, a biologist and neuroscientist at Stanford University, says an elite chess player can burn up to 6,000 calories a day while playing in a tournament, three times what an average person consumes daily. Karpov infamously lost 22lbs (10kg) during his grueling world title encounter with Kasparov in 1984 before it was called off controversially after five months and 48 games due to concerns over player health. Chess has enjoyed a sustained pop-cultural resurgence since the pandemic, a boom that reached Broadway with last year’s reimagining of … Chess, the cult-classic Cold War musical featuring songs by Abba’s Benny Andersson and Björn Ulvaeus. Starring Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit and Nicholas Christopher, the revival centered on a love triangle involving American and Soviet grandmasters loosely inspired by Fischer and Boris Spassky’s epochal 1972 encounter in Reykjavík (with secondary nods to Karpov and Viktor Korchnoi). Critics were less enthusiastic – the Guardian’s two-star review called it a “messy Broadway revival” that wasted its catchy songs – but the Grammy-nominated cast recording that came out in April goes dumby hard and Michele’s snub for a Tony nod was the worst blunder since Ding’s 55 Rf2?? in Singapore. That Sindarov is even playing for the world title is a historic achievement. His victory came two years after Gukesh became the youngest Candidates winner at 17, then the youngest undisputed world champion at 18. Together, they represent the youngest pairing ever to play for the world title by some distance. Sindarov will celebrate his 21st birthday on 8 December, the scheduled date of Game 12. Sindarov’s emergence is part of an extraordinary period of success for Uzbek chess. He helped the country win its first Chess Olympiad gold medal in Chennai in 2022, when Uzbekistan went unbeaten against a field of 186 teams. They followed it with a bronze in 2024 before another gold on home soil in Samarkand last year, cementing the nation’s place among the sport’s leading powers. And yes, that was him among the Uzbek fans supporting the White Wolves as they made their Fifa World Cup debut last summer in the US. The matchup also reflects the shifting geography at the top of the sport. Gukesh’s victory over Ding made him India’s second world champion after Anand and marked the first time in the competition’s 138-year history that two players from Asia had competed for the crown. Now it will happen for a second world title match in a row. The Fondation Martin Bodmer is a library and museum founded by a Swiss bibliophile who built his collection around what he considered the five pillars of world literature: the Bible, Homer, Dante, Shakespeare and Goethe. (Sounds about white.) Its 160,000 treasures include a Gutenberg Bible, Shakespeare’s First Folio and a copy of Isaac Newton’s Principia Mathematica once owned by his great rival Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Not the worst backdrop for another battle of intellects. Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
BUNIA, Congo — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.
It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.
Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.
CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.
Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.
Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

Electric minivans could be the ultimate in utility, with room for passengers, gear, and huge batteries. While VW’s ID Buzz only gave us 200 miles on a charge in 2023, China’s BYD has just announced a flagship purple peoplemover that can go an estimated 559 miles (900 km) on electricity.
This purple electric Chinese minivan can go up to 559 miles on a charge
The BYD Whale should cost around $45,000, not that you’d be able to buy one here.
It’s called the BYD Whale, and some back-of-the-napkin math suggests it lives up to the name. The van would be bigger than a Honda Odyssey, bigger than a Chrysler Pacifica, and bigger than a Toyota Sienna, at 17.3 feet (5,270mm) long, 6.5 feet (1,996mm) wide, 6 feet (1,815mm) tall, and with a 123-inch (3,130mm) wheelbase.
According to an auto-translated press release, the vehicle should have room for seven passengers and seven suitcases at a time, not that the company has shown off its interior yet. You can see a prominent sensor cluster on its forehead, though, and it’ll come equipped with LiDAR for advanced hands-free driving.
CarNewsChina points out it’s actually not the first with 900 km of CLTC battery range on board — Geely’s all electric Zeekr 009 minivan also claims to offer up to 900 km of range in one configuration. But BYD’s also claiming the can charge its battery from 10 percent to 97 percent in just nine minutes, and it get you from 10 percent to 70 percent in five minutes, according to Electrek.
The Whale will also come in a 248-mile (400 km) plug-in hybrid version as well, and the company’s planning to ship it in China in Q1 of 2027 for around 300,000 yuan. That’s roughly $45,000. As we’ve reported, Chinese cars are becoming quite competitive. Will they make it to the US?

Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson files last-ditch appeal in the High Court
Erin Patterson was convicted last year of killing her three elderly in-laws with a beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms

An Australian woman convicted of murdering her three elderly in-laws with a meal laced with deadly mushrooms has filed an appeal with Australia's top court.
In a case that gripped the world, Erin Patterson was convicted last year of killing her estranged husband’s relatives by feeding them beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms. Patterson has consistently maintained her innocence, saying the deaths were an accident.
The High Court is her last opportunity to appeal after the Court of Appeal in the Supreme Court of Victoria rejected Patterson's attempt to quash her conviction last month.
Her application to the High Court rests on some of the same grounds as her Supreme Court action, according to court documents.
The grounds include arguments that some evidence should have been excluded from the trial and that the jury's accidental accommodation in the same hotel as other people involved in the case undermined the verdict.
"The Court of Appeal erred in its application of principles that justice must not only be done, but be seen to be done," said Patterson's appeal bid, filed by her lawyers on Friday.
Patterson initially received a life sentence with a minimum of 33 years before being eligible for parole.
However, the prosecution appealed, arguing that it was inadequate in light of the seriousness of the crimes.
Victoria's Supreme Court last month upheld the prosecution's appeal and sentenced Patterson to life without parole — only the second time in Australian history such a sentence has been handed down to a woman.
A jury last year found Patterson invited her mother-in-law Gail Patterson, father-in-law Donald Patterson and Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson, to a 2023 lunch at her home in Leongatha, a town of about 6,000 people, some 135 km (84 miles) southeast of Melbourne, and fed them the poisoned lunch.
She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson, Heather’s husband, who survived the meal.
The 11-week trial, held in the nearby country town of Morwell, attracted worldwide attention, and the case has since spawned several podcasts and books.

On Nov. 25, the U.S. Army destroyed 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly explosive compound, in Middletown, Iowa. Officials announced the blasts were successful, and according to the Environmental Protection Agency, its real-time air monitors had not detected any airborne lead more than an hour after the detonation.
In the days leading up to the explosions — which raised widespread alarm due to the public health risks — a rumor spread online that the Army actually planned to detonate more than lead azide, according to a redacted document.
A screenshot of the purported "Emergency Permit" spread across social media, apparently showing that in addition to 68 drums of lead azide, the Army was permitted to treat other, hidden materials as "hazardous waste."
"Is the 68 barrels of lead azide not even the most scary, dangerous, poisonous part?!" One X post read (archived).
The document was real. It was an emergency permit issued by the EPA to the Army, allowing it to treat the lead azide cache as a hazardous material (clearing the way for the military to move forward with the detonation plan) "upon the EPA's finding of an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment."
Because it remains unclear what text was redacted, Snopes has left this claim unrated. We reached out to the Army and the EPA. We will update this story if we receive a response.

Name: Lead Azide
Hazardous Waste Codes: D003 (reactivity), D008 (toxicity characteristic for lead)
CAS Number: 13424-46-9
DOT Shipping Classification: Hazard Class 1.1A, UN0130
Quantity: There are 68 drums of Lead Azide, [REDACTED]

From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
A massive storm that stretched from the Midwest to Manhattan left almost a million people without power by Thanksgiving evening and disrupted holiday travel.
More than 400 flights were cancelled and more than two thousand were delayed around the country on Thursday during one of the busiest travel times of the year. Driving was also made difficult by either heavy rains or snow and ice. Some 81.5 million people were expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA.
Power was partially restored early Friday, but at the peak of the outage more than 980,000 people in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and elsewhere were without electricity. Missouri also suffered blackouts after heavy snowfall.
Several areas were also hit by major flooding, including Old Town Alexandria, Virginia, and Atlantic City, New Jersey, where some low-lying areas had close to 2 to 3 feet of water, according to city authorities.
And there's more flooding forecast. The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Washington DC area on Friday, saying the warning was in effect until 6 pm ET.
"The unprotected area on the Southwest Waterfront at the DC Seafood Market is expected to flood," the weather service said.
"Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone property. If travel is required, do not drive around barricades or through water of unknown depth," the statement added.
On the other side of the country, the West Coast was hit by King Tides with strong waves battering the Bay Area in recent days. King Tides happen regularly, but they have been made worse by climate change and warming oceans, as well as a particularly strong El Niño.
Part of the Pacifica Pier south of San Francisco collapsed on Wednesday, roads saw some flooding and some homes along the coast have been affected.
New York City's Central Park had its wettest Thanksgiving on record with 1.82 inches of rain. The city can expect strong winds on Friday, the weather service said, with gusts of up to 30 miles an hour.
Iconic Macy's parade postponed
Macy's annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in the city has been postponed for the first time in its history and will now take place on Saturday. While it's never been postponed before, it was cancelled altogether for several years during World War II.
Postponing it is causing major logistical problems, as there are around 11,000 participants in the parade, mostly volunteers, many of whom traveled in from out of state. But it's not safe to put up the iconic giant balloons the parade is known for during strong winds.
There have been incidents where those balloons hurt people in past parades, most notably in 1997 when high winds caused a Cat in the Hat balloon to hit a lamp post and then strike a woman in the crowd, leaving her critically injured. Weather grounded all of the balloons for the parade only once, back in 1971.
Saturday's parade will be Macy's 100th. To mark the milestone there will be 100 balloons, Will Coss, the parade's executive producer, told NPR's Morning Edition's host A Martinez.
"Our first parade in 1924 had live animals. But the animals unfortunately scared the children a bit more than our early parade producers anticipated," Coss said, explaining that was when they brought in balloons.
"Each balloon has its own level of complexity so a balloon from 'beginning to end' can take anywhere from 4 to 6 months," said Coss, noting they are all first hand-drawn.
This year there will be eight new giant balloons including Bluey, Hello Kitty and Mickey Mouse from the Sorcerer's Apprentice.
Returning favorites include Spongebob Squarepants, Spider-Man –– and the balloon that made its debut in 1927 as the parade's first inflated character: Felix The Cat.
Black Friday kicks off
Americans are expected to spend more money today than on any other day of the year. But, amid inflation and high gas prices, a survey of almost 8,000 adult consumers found people are cutting back on other spending in order to prioritize expenses during the holiday season.
The National Retail Federation expects some 183 million shoppers to spend over $1 trillion in November/December holiday sales. Many surveyed said the high cost of living would affect how they shopped, with some planning to buy less expensive gifts for fewer people.
The majority of Americans would be shopping online, the Federation said, with 59% planning to use AI this year to help with recommendations, brainstorming gift ideas and scanning retailer sites to find the best prices.
The organization said the top three children's toys this year are LEGO, Hot Wheels and Barbie dolls.
